What is Political Theory?
Every question in Paper I starts here

Before you study Plato, Rawls or Marx, you need to know what "political theory" even is. UPSC asks about this directly, and the ideas here come back in almost every answer you write. Political theory is the systematic thinking about political life . It asks big questions: Who should rule? Why should we obey? What is a just society? What is freedom?
Two kinds of questions

Normative theory asks what should be. Plato's ideal state and Rawls's theory of justice are normative. Empirical theory asks what is . It studies how voters actually behave or how parties actually win. David Easton and Robert Dahl worked this way.
How scholars define it

Andrew Hacker Political theory is a mix of two things: a search for knowledge about politics (science) and a search for the best political order (philosophy). George Sabine Political theory is "disciplined investigation of political problems". He saw it as the history of how thinkers answered the problems of their own times. David Held It is a network of concepts and generalisations about political life, covering ideas about government, state and society.
What political theory does

Explain. It tells us why things happen, such as why revolutions break out. Evaluate. It judges institutions against values, such as asking whether a law is just. Prescribe. It suggests what we should do, such as how to make democracy deeper. Good UPSC answers show all three. Don't only describe a thinker; say what their idea explains and where it falls short.
Theory, thought, philosophy, ideology

Political thought The ideas of a person or a society at a given time, such as Gandhian thought. Political philosophy The most abstract level. It asks about the nature of the good life and of justice. Political ideology A set of ideas meant to drive action, such as liberalism or socialism. It wants to change the world, not just explain it. Political science The study of politics using scientific methods and data.
Is political theory dead?
In the 1950s, many scholars said political theory was dying. Most new work was just history of old ideas, and the scientific study of politics was taking over.
Who said it was dying

David Easton, 1953 In The Political System , he said theory had become mere history of ideas. It was not producing new theory that could guide research. Alfred Cobban, 1953 In his essay "The Decline of Political Theory", he blamed academics for turning away from real political problems. Peter Laslett, 1956 He famously wrote that "for the moment, anyway, political philosophy is dead". He blamed logical positivism, which said value statements were meaningless.
Why it survived

Isaiah Berlin answered back in his 1962 essay "Does Political Theory Still Exist?". He said that as long as people disagree about ends, such as liberty vs equality, political theory will exist. Only in a world where everyone agreed on goals would it die. "Political theory is a branch of moral philosophy." Isaiah Berlin, Two Concepts of Liberty (1958) Leo Strauss and Hannah Arendt also defended the classical tradition. Then in 1971, John Rawls published A Theory of Justice . It is widely seen as the moment normative theory came roaring back.
The end of ideology, history and old methods

Daniel Bell, 1960 In The End of Ideology , Bell argued that the West had settled its big ideological fights. Welfare capitalism had won, so grand political visions were exhausted. Critics said this was itself an ideology. Quentin Skinner and the Cambridge School Skinner's essay "Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas" (1969) said we must read old texts in their own context, as moves in the debates of their time. With J.G.A. Pocock and John Dunn, this gave the history of political thought new rigour. Francis Fukuyama, 1989 His essay "The End of History?" (a book in 1992) claimed liberal democracy was the final form of government. Ethnic wars, 9/11 and China's rise showed the debate was far from over.
Bring it home

Indian debates show theory is alive. Think about reservation (equality vs merit), sedition law (order vs liberty), or the Uniform Civil Code (equality vs group rights). Ambedkar's question in the Constituent Assembly, about political democracy without social democracy, is a normative question. Ending an answer with an Indian example like this lifts your marks.
How UPSC asks this

"Comment: Political theory is dead." (a common style) "Discuss the relevance of normative political theory today." Structure: define theory, show the 1950s decline argument with names and years, show the revival through Berlin and Rawls, then end with how new areas like feminism, multiculturalism and green theory keep it alive.
Traditional Approaches
How politics was studied before the 1950s

An approach is a way of looking. It decides what questions you ask and what evidence you use. Before the Second World War, political science mostly used traditional approaches . These were value-based, used history and law, and focused on the state and its institutions.
Philosophical approach

This is the oldest approach. It starts with values and reasoning, not data. It asks: what is the ideal state, and what is justice? Thinkers: Plato, Aristotle, Hegel, T.H. Green. Strength: it gives us goals and ideals to aim for. Weakness: it can be abstract and hard to test. Critics say it is speculative.
Historical approach

This approach says you can only understand political ideas in their historical setting. Ideas come from real problems of their age. Thinkers: Machiavelli used history as a tool; Sabine and Dunning wrote histories of political thought. Strength: it gives context. Hobbes makes more sense when you know about the English Civil War. Weakness: history can be read selectively, and the past does not always predict the present.
Institutional approach

This approach studies formal structures: constitutions, legislatures, executives and courts. Thinkers: James Bryce ( Modern Democracies ), Herman Finer, Harold Laski. Strength: it is concrete and descriptive. It is good for comparing governments. Weakness: it ignores informal politics like caste, pressure groups and personality. A constitution on paper can differ a lot from politics in practice.
Legal approach

This approach sees the state mainly as a legal body that makes and enforces law. Politics is studied through laws, rights and courts. Thinkers: Jean Bodin and Hobbes (sovereignty as the source of law), A.V. Dicey (rule of law), John Austin (law as the command of the sovereign). Weakness: it is very narrow. Law is only one part of political life.
What they share

They are value-laden : they openly judge what is good. They are state-centric : the state is the main unit of study. They are descriptive and prescriptive , rather than explanatory or predictive. They rely on reasoning, history and legal texts , not surveys or statistics.
Why they were challenged

After 1945, American scholars felt traditional approaches could not explain real political behaviour. They could not explain why democracy collapsed in Weimar Germany or why people voted for fascists. The criticism was that traditional approaches were too formal, too normative and too narrow . This opened the door for the behavioural revolution, which is the next lesson.
Comparative and other traditional methods

Some books add more traditional approaches. Comparative approach Aristotle compared 158 constitutions. Montesquieu, in The Spirit of the Laws (1748), compared laws across countries and linked them to climate, religion and customs. Bryce compared modern democracies. Sociological approach Studies how society shapes politics, as Montesquieu and later Tocqueville did in Democracy in America (1835–40). Psychological approach Graham Wallas, in Human Nature in Politics (1908), argued people act on instinct and emotion more than reason. This prepared the ground for behaviouralism. These bridge the old and the new: they stay value-based, but begin to look at how politics actually works.
Traditional vs behavioural
The next lesson on behaviouralism takes up the right-hand side. Use this contrast as a one-line summary in any answer on the shift in approaches.
Still useful in India

The institutional and legal approaches still matter a lot in India. Debates on the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973), the anti-defection law, or Governor's powers are mainly legal-institutional. But you can only explain coalition politics or caste voting with newer approaches. A strong answer shows both.
How to write this

"Critically examine the traditional approaches to the study of politics." Structure: define approach, describe the four types with one thinker each, give common features, then the behavioural critique. End by saying modern theory has a revival of new institutionalism (March and Olsen, 1984), which shows that institutions still matter.
Behaviouralism & After
The behavioural revolution

In the 1950s and 60s, mainly in the USA, political scientists wanted to make the subject a real science , like physics or economics. Their focus moved from institutions to the behaviour of people: voters, leaders and groups. The roots go back to the Chicago School of the 1920s under Charles Merriam .
Easton's 8 pillars

David Easton listed eight "intellectual foundation stones" of behaviouralism. Remember them; UPSC loves this list. Regularities: behaviour shows patterns. Verification: claims must be testable. Techniques: use proper research tools. Quantification: measure where possible. Values: keep facts and values separate. Systematisation: theory and research must link. Pure science: understanding before application. Integration: work with other social sciences.
Remember the 8

"Real Voters Take Quick Votes, So Politics Improves" The first V is Verification and the second is Values. Regularities, Verification, Techniques, Quantification, Values, Systematisation, Pure science, Integration. Do not just memorise the list. In an answer, group the eight into three ideas: science (regularities, verification, techniques, quantification), theory (systematisation, pure science) and scope (values, integration). This shows you understand the movement, not just its list.
The political system

Easton saw politics as a system . Society sends inputs (demands and support). The system turns them into outputs (decisions and policies). Outputs create feedback , which shapes new inputs. He defined politics as the "authoritative allocation of values" for a society.
Almond and others

Gabriel Almond: structural-functionalism Every political system performs the same functions, like interest articulation and rule-making, but through different structures. Almond and Verba: The Civic Culture (1963) They studied five countries and found three types of political culture: parochial, subject and participant. Karl Deutsch He studied politics as communication, with a "cybernetic" model.
What went wrong

"Science" without relevance. While scholars counted votes, the US faced the Vietnam War, civil rights protests and race riots. Political science had little to say. Status quo bias. By studying "what is", it quietly accepted the existing order. Value-neutrality is a myth. Choosing what to study is itself a value choice. Western bias. Its models fitted the USA but not new countries like India.
Post-behaviouralism, 1969

Strikingly, the critique came from Easton himself. In his 1969 presidential address to the American Political Science Association, called "The New Revolution in Political Science" , he announced post-behaviouralism. Its two watchwords were relevance and action . Research should address urgent social problems, and scholars have a duty to act on their knowledge.
Its main claims

Substance over technique. It is better to be vague about an important issue than precise about a trivial one. Values matter. Scholars should openly discuss values. Engage with crisis. Research must address social crisis. Act. Knowledge brings a responsibility to act. Politicise the profession. Academic bodies should take part in public debates.
Was behaviouralism useless?

No. It gave us survey research, election studies and rigorous methods. In India, the CSDS–Lokniti National Election Studies use these tools to study how Indians vote. Post-behaviouralism did not reject methods. It said methods must serve meaningful questions. Make this point and you will look balanced.
Behaviouralism in India

Indian political science took up behavioural methods from the 1960s. The Centre for the Study of Developing Societies (CSDS) was founded in Delhi in 1963 by Rajni Kothari . Its Lokniti programme runs the National Election Studies, large surveys of how Indians vote. Kothari's Politics in India (1970) used systems ideas to describe the " Congress system ". But Indian scholars also showed the limits of imported models. Western theories predicted that modernisation would weaken caste. Instead, Rudolph and Rudolph in The Modernity of Tradition (1967) showed caste associations adapting to democracy. This is a classic post-behavioural point: methods must be fitted to local reality.
How UPSC asks this

"Post-behaviouralism is a continuation of behaviouralism, not a rejection of it." Comment. "Explain Easton's systems analysis and its limitations." Tip: always mention that the same scholar, Easton, led both movements. Use the systems diagram in your answer; examiners reward neat diagrams. Useful anchors: Easton's The Political System (1953) called for general theory; A Systems Analysis of Political Life (1965) set out the model; the 1969 address launched post-behaviouralism. Add Almond and Verba for political culture, then a short critique and the Indian example of CSDS-Lokniti surveys.
The Liberal & Neoliberal State
Six ways to see the state

The syllabus asks for six theories of the state: liberal, neoliberal, Marxist, pluralist, post-colonial and feminist. Each one answers the same question differently: whose state is it, and what does it do?
The liberal state

For liberals, the individual comes first. The state exists to protect the rights of individuals. It is a necessary evil : needed, but dangerous if it grows too big. Key features are consent , limited government , rule of law , separation of powers and the state as a neutral umpire between competing interests.
John Locke

In Two Treatises of Government (1689), Locke said people have natural rights to life, liberty and property even before the state exists. They form the state through a social contract only to protect those rights better. If the government breaks this trust, people have a right to resist . Government by consent, limited by rights.
Classical to welfare liberalism

Classical liberalism (18th–19th century) Adam Smith, Bentham, early J.S. Mill. A minimal state and a free market, known as laissez-faire. Welfare or positive liberalism (late 19th–20th century) T.H. Green, L.T. Hobhouse, Keynes. Poverty limits freedom too, so the state must provide education, health and jobs. This led to the welfare state after 1945.
Neoliberalism

By the 1970s, welfare states faced inflation, slow growth and debt. Neoliberals argued that the big state was the problem. They want a minimal state , free markets , privatisation , deregulation and lower taxes. In practice this meant Thatcher in the UK, Reagan in the USA, and the Washington Consensus (a term coined by John Williamson in 1989).
Friedrich Hayek

In The Road to Serfdom (1944), Hayek warned that state economic planning leads to tyranny. His key argument is about knowledge . No central planner can know what millions of people know about their own needs. The market's price system spreads that knowledge better than any government can.
Robert Nozick

In Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), Nozick argued for a minimal state , a "night-watchman" state that only protects against force, theft and fraud. Anything more, like taxing the rich to help the poor, violates rights. He famously compared taxation of earnings to forced labour . This book was a direct reply to Rawls.
What critics say

Marxists: the "neutral" liberal state actually protects property owners. Welfare liberals: freedom means little without basic resources. On neoliberalism: it increased inequality, and the 2008 financial crisis showed markets need regulation. Feminists: the public/private split hides injustice inside the family. Two more critiques are worth knowing. Communitarians such as Michael Sandel and Alasdair MacIntyre say liberalism imagines people as isolated individuals, when in fact communities shape who we are. Karl Polanyi , in The Great Transformation (1944), argued that a self-regulating market damages society and always provokes a protective reaction. David Harvey (2005) reads neoliberalism as a project to restore the power of the owning class.
India's journey

India began with a mixed economy and planning under Nehru, close to welfare liberalism. The Directive Principles (Part IV) reflect this. In 1991 , under Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh, India moved towards liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation (LPG). Yet India keeps welfare schemes like MGNREGA (2005) and the National Food Security Act (2013). So India is often described as a hybrid, not a pure neoliberal state.
How to write this

"Neoliberalism is a return to classical liberalism." Critically examine. Structure: show what is similar (market and limited state) and what is new (neoliberalism uses the state actively to create markets, and works globally through the IMF and World Bank). Cite Hayek and Nozick, then India after 1991.
The Marxist State
The state is not neutral

For Marx, the state is not a neutral umpire. It is a tool of the ruling class . In capitalism, that class is the bourgeoisie , the owners of factories and capital. "The executive of the modern state is but a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie." The Communist Manifesto, 1848
Base and superstructure

The economic base is how a society produces things and who owns what. The superstructure is the state, law, religion and culture. In classical Marxism, the base shapes the superstructure. Change the economy and the state changes too.
Where the state comes from

In The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State (1884), Engels argued that the state appears when society splits into classes with opposing interests. The state did not always exist, and it will not always exist. It arose with private property. Engels drew on Lewis Henry Morgan's Ancient Society (1877). Early societies, he said, had no classes and no state, a stage called primitive communism . Once surplus and private property appeared, the owning class needed a body of armed force, courts and officials to hold down the rest. In each age the state served the dominant class: slave-owners in antiquity, the nobility under feudalism, and the bourgeoisie under capitalism.
Withering away

After a revolution, workers set up a dictatorship of the proletariat to crush the old ruling class. Once classes disappear, the state has no purpose left. It does not get abolished; it "withers away" , as Engels put it in Anti-Dühring . Lenin expanded this in The State and Revolution (1917).
Relative autonomy

Marx himself noticed that the state is not always a simple puppet. In The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte , he described a situation where classes were balanced, and the state under Louis Bonaparte gained independence from all of them. This is called Bonapartism . Later Marxists built on it to argue the state has relative autonomy .
Miliband vs Poulantzas

Ralph Miliband: instrumentalist In The State in Capitalist Society (1969), he showed that the elite running the state come from the same class and schools as the capitalists. The state is their instrument. Nicos Poulantzas: structuralist He replied that who sits in office does not matter, and that the state has relative autonomy from individual capitalists. The structure of capitalism forces any state to protect capital, whoever runs it. Their exchange in New Left Review (1969–70) is a UPSC favourite.
Rule by consent

Antonio Gramsci asked why workers in the West did not revolt. His answer was hegemony . The ruling class rules not just by force but by consent . Schools, media and churches make the existing order look natural and common sense. State = political society + civil society, hegemony armoured by coercion. From the Prison Notebooks
Where it struggles

Economic reductionism. It reduces everything to class and neglects caste, gender, race and religion. The withering never happened. The USSR built one of the strongest states in history. The welfare state. Capitalist states gave workers real gains, which is hard to explain as pure class rule. Pluralists argue power is spread across many groups, not held by one class.
Marxism in India

Indian Marxists have tried to explain the Indian state. Pranab Bardhan , in The Political Economy of Development in India (1984), identified three dominant proprietary classes : industrial capitalists, rich farmers and professionals including bureaucrats. No single one rules, so the state balances them. This mixes Marxism with Bonapartist relative autonomy, a good example to use.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the Miliband–Poulantzas debate on the nature of the state." "The state is an instrument of class domination." Comment. Tip: move from Marx to Engels to Lenin, then to Gramsci, Miliband and Poulantzas. Always end with Bardhan or another Indian application. Common slip: mixing up the two debaters. Miliband ( The State in Capitalist Society , 1969) is the instrumentalist : the state serves capital because elites share class background and ties. Poulantzas ( Political Power and Social Classes , 1968) is the structuralist : the state serves capital because of the structure of the system, whoever staffs it.
The Pluralist State
Power is spread out

Pluralists say power in a democracy is spread among many groups : unions, businesses, farmers, religious bodies and NGOs. No single group or class dominates. The state is like an arena or a referee where these groups compete and bargain.
Against the sovereign state

Early 20th-century British thinkers like Harold Laski , F.W. Maitland and J.N. Figgis attacked the idea of an all-powerful sovereign state. They argued that churches, guilds and unions have their own real life and authority. The state is just one association among many. Laski even said that because sovereignty is not absolute, it would be good for political science if the concept were given up.
Robert Dahl

Dahl studied New Haven, Connecticut in Who Governs? (1961) . He asked: who really makes decisions here? He found that different groups won on different issues, such as education, urban renewal and party nominations. No single elite controlled everything. This is polyarchy , rule by many.
Polyarchy

In Polyarchy (1971), Dahl said no real country is a perfect democracy. So he used "polyarchy" for real-world democracies. A polyarchy has two dimensions: public contestation (open competition) and inclusiveness (the right to participate). Its institutions include elected officials, free and fair elections, universal adult franchise, freedom of expression, alternative sources of information and freedom to form associations.
The elite theorists strike back

C. Wright Mills: The Power Elite (1956) A small group from business, the military and politics really runs the USA. Bachrach and Baratz: "Two Faces of Power" (1962) Dahl only saw open decisions. Real power also lies in non-decision making : keeping some issues off the agenda entirely. Steven Lukes: Power: A Radical View (1974) A third face: shaping what people even want.
Neo-pluralism

Later pluralists admitted that groups are not equal. In Politics and Markets (1977), Charles Lindblom argued that business holds a privileged position . Governments depend on business for jobs and growth, so they listen more to business than to anyone else. Dahl himself later accepted that economic inequality distorts democracy.
Groups, cross-cutting ties and polyarchy in practice

Pluralists built their theory on studies of interest groups . Arthur Bentley , in The Process of Government (1908), said politics is nothing but the pressure of groups on one another. David Truman , in The Governmental Process (1951), added the idea of overlapping membership . A person can be a worker, a Catholic and a parent at once, so groups cannot become too extreme. Truman also spoke of potential groups : when an interest is threatened, people organise. This keeps the system balanced. The upshot is a state that acts like a weather vane or broker, responding to whichever group pressures are strongest. Critics say this is too rosy. E.E. Schattschneider famously wrote that the flaw in the pluralist heaven is that the heavenly chorus sings with a strong upper-class accent.
Olson and corporatism

Mancur Olson , in The Logic of Collective Action (1965), challenged the pluralist picture. Large groups with spread-out interests find it hard to organise, because each member hopes others will pay the cost. Small, concentrated groups organise easily and often win. So the group system may favour producers over consumers, and the organised over the unorganised. Corporatism is another rival model. Philippe Schmitter (1974) described systems in which a few state-recognised bodies, such as national employer and labour federations, bargain directly with government. Austria and Sweden are common examples. Here the state shapes groups, rather than groups simply pressing the state.
Pluralism in India

India looks pluralist in many ways: farmer lobbies, caste associations, trade unions and industry bodies like FICCI and CII all press the government. Rudolph and Rudolph , in In Pursuit of Lakshmi (1987), called Indian pluralism "involuted pluralism" . Many groups are fragmented and weak, while the state remains a strong "third actor". The farm laws protests of 2020–21, which led to the repeal of the laws, show group pressure working.
How UPSC asks this

"Neo-pluralism is a self-critique of pluralism." Comment. Structure: early pluralism (Laski), American pluralism (Dahl), the elite critique (Mills, Bachrach and Baratz), then neo-pluralism (Lindblom). End with India's involuted pluralism. Extra points: mention Arthur Bentley and David Truman, who treated politics as group struggle. Include one Indian example, such as farm-law protests, and finish with a verdict: pluralism describes competition well but may overlook unequal power. Add Mancur Olson if the question is about group power.
The Post-colonial State
A state born from empire

Western theories of the state were built on European history. They do not fit well in countries that were colonies, like India, Pakistan or Nigeria. Post-colonial theory asks: what kind of state did colonialism leave behind, and whom does it serve? Many new states were drawn on a colonial map, with borders that cut across older communities. They inherited the colonial army, police and civil service, and often the colonial laws too. Frantz Fanon , in The Wretched of the Earth (1961), warned that a weak national middle class might simply step into the place of the colonial rulers.
Hamza Alavi

In his 1972 essay "The State in Post-Colonial Societies: Pakistan and Bangladesh", Alavi argued that the post-colonial state is "overdeveloped" . Colonial rulers built a powerful military-bureaucratic machine to control the whole colony. After independence, this machine stayed, and it was too strong for the weak local classes to control.
Three classes, one state

Alavi said three propertied classes exist in post-colonial societies: the metropolitan bourgeoisie (foreign capital), the indigenous bourgeoisie and the landed classes . None dominates. So the military-bureaucratic oligarchy mediates between them and gains relative autonomy. This explains why the army so often rules in Pakistan.
Partha Chatterjee

Chatterjee, a key figure in Subaltern Studies , wrote Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986). He argued Indian nationalism borrowed Western ideas of the modern state even while opposing colonialism. In The Politics of the Governed (2004), he separated civil society (a small elite of rights-bearing citizens) from political society (the majority, who deal with the state through welfare schemes and negotiation, not rights).
More ways to read it

Rudolph and Rudolph India's state is both strong and weak : strong in its reach, weak in delivering. Gunnar Myrdal: the "soft state" In Asian Drama (1968), he said South Asian states make good laws but cannot enforce them. Dependency theory Andre Gunder Frank and others argued post-colonial states stay economically dependent on the West.
Limits of the theory

It can over-generalise. India stayed democratic while Pakistan saw coups; one theory struggles to explain both. It can give colonialism too much weight and ignore local agency. Developmental states like South Korea show post-colonial states can succeed economically. Others say the label "post-colonial" hides big differences: direct or indirect rule, settler or non-settler colonies, and different nationalist movements. India's Congress was a mass party with deep roots, while in Pakistan the early Muslim League had a weaker organisation, which left more room for the army and civil service (Ayesha Jalal, The State of Martial Rule , 1990).
Other Indian readings of the state

Pranab Bardhan In The Political Economy of Development in India (1984), he named three dominant proprietary classes : industrial capitalists, rich farmers and professionals including bureaucrats. They compete for state subsidies, which slows growth. Rajni Kothari Described the decline of the Congress system and the rise of a more centralised, personalised state from the 1970s. Atul Kohli In State-Directed Development (2004), he called India a fragmented-multiclass state , less effective than South Korea's cohesive-capitalist state. Sudipta Kaviraj Read Indian state-building as a passive revolution led by bourgeois and bureaucratic elites.
Alavi's model in one picture
Read the arrows as a chain. The state is "overdeveloped" because its machinery is larger than the weak social classes that are supposed to control it.
Is India's state overdeveloped?

India inherited the colonial machine almost whole: the IAS replaced the ICS, and the Indian Penal Code (1860) stayed in force until the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced it in 2024. Yet India differs from Alavi's Pakistan. Regular elections, a strong Congress party in the early decades and firm civilian control kept the army out of politics. Rudolph and Rudolph, in In Pursuit of Lakshmi (1987), called this a weak-strong state . Chatterjee's political society shows the same thing at the ground level: the poor reach the state through negotiation, not through rights.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine Hamza Alavi's concept of the overdeveloped state." "Is the Indian state an overdeveloped state?" Tip: use Alavi for the model, then test it on India. The Indian state was strong (overdeveloped) but civilian control and elections kept the army out, unlike Pakistan. That contrast earns marks.
The Feminist State
Whose state is it?

Feminists say traditional theories ignored one huge fact: the state has mostly been run by men, and it has protected patriarchy , the system of male dominance. Their key slogan was "the personal is political" , popularised by Carol Hanisch's 1970 essay. Even what happens inside the home is shaped by power and law.
Fix the state

Liberal feminists see the state as basically neutral but biased in practice. The answer is reform: equal rights, equal pay, voting rights and anti-discrimination laws. Thinkers include Mary Wollstonecraft ( A Vindication of the Rights of Woman , 1792), J.S. Mill ( The Subjection of Women , 1869) and Betty Friedan ( The Feminine Mystique , 1963).
The state is male

Radical feminists say patriarchy is built into the state itself. Reform is not enough. "The state is male in the feminist sense: the law sees and treats women the way men see and treat women." Catharine MacKinnon, Toward a Feminist Theory of the State (1989) Kate Millett 's Sexual Politics (1970) is another key text.
Carole Pateman

In The Sexual Contract (1988), Pateman argued that the famous social contract of Hobbes and Locke hides an earlier sexual contract . Men agreed among themselves on access to women's bodies and labour. Women were never parties to the contract, only its subjects. So the liberal state was patriarchal from the start.
Class plus gender

Socialist and Marxist feminists link patriarchy to capitalism. Women's unpaid domestic work reproduces the workforce for free, which benefits capital. The state supports both systems together. Thinkers include Juliet Mitchell and Heidi Hartmann , who called the link an "unhappy marriage" of Marxism and feminism.
Debates within

Intersectionality. Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989) showed that race, class and gender overlap. White middle-class feminism ignored many women. Post-colonial feminism. Chandra Talpade Mohanty's "Under Western Eyes" (1984) criticised Western feminists for treating "Third World women" as one helpless group. State as ally? The state has also passed laws protecting women, so it is not only an oppressor.
Postcolonial and Black feminism

Later feminists asked: which women does feminism speak for? Chandra Talpade Mohanty In "Under Western Eyes" (1984/1986), she criticised Western feminists for treating "Third World women" as one passive, oppressed victim group. Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak In "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988), she used the British ban on sati to show how both colonisers and local elites spoke for subaltern women, never letting them speak. bell hooks In Ain't I a Woman (1981), she showed how racism and sexism combine for Black women. These ideas feed into intersectionality : the state treats a poor Dalit woman differently from a rich upper-caste woman, so gender alone cannot explain her position.
Four strands at a glance
Pair each strand with one thinker: Wollstonecraft, MacKinnon, Hartmann, Crenshaw. This gives you a quick frame for any question on feminist views of the state.
India's story

The Indian state has a mixed record. It brought the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992), reserving a third of local body seats for women. The 106th Amendment (2023), known as Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, reserves a third of Lok Sabha and state assembly seats for women, effective after the next census and delimitation. But Dalit feminists like Sharmila Rege show how caste and gender combine, which links to Ambedkar's view that caste is maintained by controlling women.
How to write this

"The state is male." Discuss with reference to feminist theory. Structure: quote MacKinnon, then cover the three strands (liberal, radical, socialist). Add Pateman's sexual contract and intersectionality. End with India's reservation laws as evidence that the state can be both a site of oppression and of change.
Rawls's Theory of Justice
The book that revived political theory

John Rawls (1921–2002) taught at Harvard. His A Theory of Justice (1971) is widely seen as the most important work of political philosophy in the 20th century. It ended the talk of political theory being "dead". Rawls is one of the most-asked thinkers in Paper I. Questions come on the original position , the veil of ignorance , the two principles and the difference principle , and on his critics: Nozick, Sandel and Sen. His later books matter too: Political Liberalism (1993), The Law of Peoples (1999) and Justice as Fairness: A Restatement (2001). He called his theory justice as fairness . The idea is simple: rules are just if they are the ones we would agree to in a fair starting position.
Against utilitarianism

Rawls wrote against utilitarianism , the leading theory of his day. Utilitarians say the right policy is the one that brings the greatest total happiness. Rawls's objection: utilitarianism "does not take seriously the distinction between persons ". It adds up everyone's happiness as if society were one big person. So it could allow sacrificing a minority, even enslaving them, if the majority gained enough. For Rawls, each person has an inviolability that even the welfare of society as a whole cannot override. "Justice is the first virtue of social institutions, as truth is of systems of thought." Rawls, A Theory of Justice, §1 He returns to the social contract tradition of Locke, Rousseau and Kant to build an alternative.
The basic structure

Justice, for Rawls, applies first to the basic structure of society. That means the major institutions: the constitution, the legal system, the economy, property rules and the family. Why? Because these institutions shape our life chances from birth. A child born into a poor family or a low caste starts with less, through no choice of their own. Rawls calls these advantages morally arbitrary . You did not earn your parents' wealth, your talents or even your hard-working character, which depends on upbringing. So a just society cannot just reward whatever the "natural lottery" hands out. It must arrange institutions so that these accidents do not decide everything.
The original position and the veil of ignorance

Imagine people choosing the rules of their society in an original position . It is a thought experiment, not a real historical event. They sit behind a veil of ignorance . They know general facts about society, but not their own place in it. Because no one can tailor rules to suit themselves, the rules they pick will be fair . That is why Rawls calls it justice as fairness.
Primary goods and the maximin rule

What do people want in the original position? Rawls says they want primary goods : things any rational person wants, whatever else they want. Basic rights and liberties. Freedom of movement and choice of occupation. Powers and opportunities of office. Income and wealth. The social bases of self-respect , which Rawls calls perhaps the most important primary good. Since the stakes are huge and they cannot know the odds, Rawls argues they will follow the maximin rule: choose the option whose worst outcome is best . In plain words: you choose the society where, if you turn out to be at the bottom, you are as well off as possible. You would not gamble your whole life on landing at the top.
The two principles of justice

First principle: equal liberty Each person has an equal right to the most extensive scheme of equal basic liberties compatible with a similar scheme for all. These include political liberty, free speech and assembly, liberty of conscience, freedom of the person and the right to hold personal property. Second principle Social and economic inequalities are allowed only if they are: (a) to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged (the difference principle ), and (b) attached to offices and positions open to all under fair equality of opportunity . The wording shifts slightly between the 1971 book and the 2001 Restatement , but these are the core ideas.
Lexical priority

The principles come in a strict order, which Rawls calls lexical (like words in a dictionary). The first principle , equal liberty, comes first. Basic liberties cannot be traded away for economic gains. You cannot sell your vote, or accept censorship, for more income. Within the second principle, fair equality of opportunity comes before the difference principle . Fair equality of opportunity is more than formal non-discrimination. It means people with similar talent and drive should have similar chances, whatever class they are born into. That needs good public schools and limits on inherited advantage. Only then does the difference principle shape how income and wealth are shared.
The difference principle explained

The difference principle does not demand equality . It allows inequality, but only the kind that helps the worst-off . Example: doctors may earn more than others, if that pay draws talented people into medicine and the poor get better healthcare as a result. If the extra pay only helps doctors, it is unjust. Rawls says the difference principle expresses an agreement to treat the distribution of natural talents as a common asset . The gifted may gain from their luck, but only on terms that also improve the situation of those who lost out. He links this to fraternity . In a fraternal society, people do not want to gain more unless those who are worse off gain too. The result is a theory of welfare liberalism , or egalitarian liberalism.
Reflective equilibrium and the later Rawls

How do we test a theory of justice? Rawls uses reflective equilibrium . We move back and forth between our firm judgements (slavery is wrong) and general principles, adjusting each until they fit together. In Political Liberalism (1993), Rawls faced a problem. Modern societies have reasonable pluralism : people hold different religions and philosophies. A theory of justice cannot rest on any one of them. So he recast justice as a political conception, not a full philosophy of life. Citizens with different worldviews can agree on it through an overlapping consensus . Public debate should use public reason : arguments others could accept, not just one's own religious beliefs. In The Law of Peoples (1999), he extended his ideas to international relations but did not apply the difference principle globally.
The big critiques

Robert Nozick , Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974): justice is about how holdings came about, not patterns of distribution. Taxation for redistribution violates self-ownership. Communitarians (Sandel, MacIntyre, Taylor, Walzer): the person behind the veil is an " unencumbered self " with no community or values. Real people are shaped by their communities. Amartya Sen , The Idea of Justice (2009): Rawls seeks a perfectly just society (transcendental institutionalism). We should instead compare real options and remove clear injustices. Primary goods also ignore that people convert resources into freedoms differently. Feminists , such as Susan Moller Okin , Justice, Gender, and the Family (1989): Rawls's heads of households hide injustice within the family. Marxists : Rawls leaves capitalist property relations untouched. G.A. Cohen : if the talented demand incentives, they are not acting from justice themselves.
Rawls and the Indian Constitution

Rawls's ideas fit well with India's constitutional vision. The Preamble promises justice, social, economic and political , before liberty and equality. Fair equality of opportunity mirrors Article 16 . The difference principle echoes the reasoning behind Articles 15(4), 16(4) and the Directive Principles , especially Articles 38 and 39 . In N.M. Thomas (1975), the Supreme Court read reservation as part of equality, not an exception to it. This is a Rawlsian move. The Right to Education Act (2009) reserves 25% of seats in private schools for disadvantaged children. That is fair equality of opportunity in action. Some judges have cited Rawls directly in judgments on equality and reservation.
How UPSC asks this

"Explain Rawls's concept of the original position and the veil of ignorance." "The difference principle is the heart of Rawls's egalitarian liberalism." Discuss. "Critically examine the communitarian critique of Rawls." "Compare Rawls and Sen on justice." Structure: context (against utilitarianism), basic structure, original position with a diagram, primary goods and maximin, two principles and lexical order, difference principle with an example. Then the main critiques: Nozick, the communitarians, Sen and the feminists. End with India: the Preamble, Articles 15–16 and 38–39, and N.M. Thomas. Quote "Justice is the first virtue of social institutions" in your introduction.
The Communitarian Critique
The self is not an island

In the 1980s, a group of thinkers challenged Rawls and liberalism as a whole. They became known as communitarians . The four big names are Michael Sandel , Alasdair MacIntyre , Charles Taylor and Michael Walzer . Interestingly, none of them liked the label much. Their shared claim: liberalism starts from an abstract individual who chooses their own values. But real people are formed by their communities : family, religion, language, nation. A theory of justice must start there. UPSC asks about this debate often, usually as "liberal vs communitarian" or as a critique of Rawls. It also connects to multiculturalism and group rights in India.
Liberal self vs communitarian self

For liberals, the right is prior to the good . The state sets fair rules but stays neutral about what a good life is. Each person chooses for themselves. Communitarians reply that we do not choose our deepest values from nowhere. We discover them in the communities that made us. A neutral state is impossible, and trying to be neutral weakens shared life.
Michael Sandel: the unencumbered self

Sandel, a Harvard professor, wrote Liberalism and the Limits of Justice (1982). He says the people in Rawls's original position are unencumbered selves : selves with no attachments, standing apart from all their aims and loyalties. But real people are encumbered . Some of our ties are not chosen but constitutive : they make us who we are. Being someone's child, or a member of a nation or faith, is not like picking a hobby. Sandel also points to a problem in the difference principle. Rawls treats natural talents as a common asset . But that only makes sense if we already share a strong community. So Rawls quietly assumes the very community his theory leaves out. Later, in Democracy's Discontent (1996) and The Tyranny of Merit (2020), Sandel argued for civic republicanism and against the arrogance of meritocracy.
Alasdair MacIntyre: virtue and tradition

MacIntyre's After Virtue (1981) opens with a striking image. Imagine a world where science has been destroyed, and people use scientific words without understanding them. That, he says, is how we use moral words today. Modern moral debate is interminable : people shout past each other because they have lost the shared framework that gave moral words meaning. His answer is to return to Aristotle and the idea of virtues . Virtues make sense only inside: Practices , like medicine, farming or chess, with their own standards of excellence. The narrative unity of a human life. A living tradition of argument passed between generations. He ends darkly: we await "another, doubtless very different, St Benedict" to build communities that keep virtue alive.
Charles Taylor: atomism and recognition

Taylor is a Canadian philosopher. "Atomism" (1979) Liberals give individuals rights while denying they owe anything to society. But our very ability to be free, to choose and reason, can only develop in a society. So we have a duty to sustain it. Sources of the Self (1989) Identity is formed against a background of what matters, a "horizon" of meaning shared with others. "The Politics of Recognition" (1992) Identity is shaped by recognition, or its absence. Misrecognition can inflict real harm: it can imprison people in a false, demeaning picture of themselves. So minority cultures may deserve public recognition, as with French-speaking Quebec.
Michael Walzer: spheres of justice

Walzer's Spheres of Justice (1983) rejects one single principle of justice for all goods. Different goods have different social meanings , and so different rules of distribution: Healthcare by need. Office by merit. Political power by persuasion and votes. Commodities by the market. Love by free affection. Injustice is when one good dominates others. For example, money buying votes, court rulings or medical care. Walzer calls the goal complex equality : no single good converts into all others. He adds that justice is relative to social meanings. It is found in a community's shared understandings, not deduced from an original position.
How liberals replied

Will Kymlicka , in Liberalism, Community and Culture (1989) and Multicultural Citizenship (1995), argued that liberalism can value culture. Culture gives us a context of choice . So minority rights can be defended on liberal grounds. Rawls himself, in Political Liberalism (1993), said his theory was political, not a claim about human nature. The veil is a device of representation, not a description of real people. Amy Gutmann warned that communitarians want us to live in Salem, but not to believe in witches: they like community but ignore how it can oppress. Many now see a middle ground : liberal rights together with strong civic community.
Dangers in communitarianism

Conservatism: appeals to tradition can defend old hierarchies, such as caste, patriarchy or religious authority. Which community? People belong to many communities that conflict. Who speaks for the community? Oppression within groups: feminists like Susan Moller Okin , in "Is Multiculturalism Bad for Women?" (1997/1999), warned that group rights can trap women under patriarchal leaders. Relativism: if justice is only shared meanings, how do we criticise an unjust society from within? Walzer replies that social critics work from the community's own ideals. A balanced answer shows that both sides have learned from each other.
Political communitarianism

A separate strand, led by Amitai Etzioni , turned communitarian ideas into a political programme in the 1990s. His The Spirit of Community (1993) and the Responsive Communitarian platform argued that rights must be balanced with responsibilities . Families, schools and neighbourhoods should rebuild moral voices. This influenced the " Third Way " of Bill Clinton and Tony Blair, who spoke of "no rights without responsibilities". In Asia, leaders like Singapore's Lee Kuan Yew invoked "Asian values": community, family and order over individual rights. Critics, including Amartya Sen, argued that Asian traditions also contain strong ideas of freedom and tolerance.
Community and rights in India

India's Constitution blends liberal and communitarian ideas. Articles 25–28 give individuals freedom of religion. Articles 29–30 give communities rights to protect their culture and run educational institutions. Personal laws for different religions reflect group recognition. The Uniform Civil Code debate (Article 44) is a liberal vs communitarian question. In Shah Bano (1985), the Court upheld a divorced Muslim woman's right to maintenance. Parliament's 1986 Act was seen as yielding to community leaders. In Shayara Bano (2017), instant triple talaq was struck down. Sabarimala (2018) pitted women's equality against a temple's customary ban on women aged 10 to 50. Rajeev Bhargava calls Indian secularism "principled distance": the state engages with communities rather than staying fully neutral.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine the communitarian critique of liberalism." "Sandel's 'unencumbered self'. Comment." "Explain Walzer's idea of complex equality." "Is communitarianism a threat to individual rights?" Structure: start with the liberal self (Rawls). Then give the four thinkers, one key idea each: Sandel's unencumbered self, MacIntyre's virtue and tradition, Taylor's atomism and recognition, Walzer's spheres. Then the liberal reply (Kymlicka, later Rawls) and the dangers. End with Indian examples: Articles 29–30, personal laws, Shah Bano, and Bhargava's principled distance.
Nozick, Sen and the Capability Approach
Two rival answers to Rawls

Rawls offered one answer to the question "what is a just distribution?" Two powerful replies came from opposite sides. Robert Nozick , Rawls's Harvard colleague, said Rawls gave the state far too much power. Justice is about respecting rights, not engineering outcomes. He stands for libertarianism . Amartya Sen , the Indian economist and Nobel laureate (1998), said Rawls focused on the wrong thing. What matters is not the resources people have, but what they can actually do and be . He built the capability approach , developed further by Martha Nussbaum . UPSC asks about each thinker and about comparisons with Rawls.
Nozick: self-ownership and side constraints

Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) opens boldly: "Individuals have rights, and there are things no person or group may do to them (without violating their rights)." The base is self-ownership . You own your body, your talents and your labour. This draws on Locke, and on Kant's idea that people must be treated as ends, never merely as means. Rights are side constraints . They are not goals to maximise but limits on what anyone may do. You may not violate one person's rights even to prevent more violations elsewhere. So the state's job is narrow: protection against force, theft and fraud, and enforcement of contracts. This is the minimal state .
The entitlement theory

Nozick's theory of justice in holdings has three parts: Justice in acquisition: how unowned things first become owned. He uses a version of Locke's proviso: acquisition is fine if it doesn't worsen others' situation. Justice in transfer: things pass justly by voluntary exchange, gift or inheritance. Rectification: correcting past injustices in acquisition or transfer, such as theft or conquest. If you got your holdings justly, you are entitled to them. Full stop. So justice is historical : it depends on how a distribution came about. Rawls's theory, by contrast, is patterned and end-state : it judges the final distribution by a pattern, such as "benefit the worst-off".
The Wilt Chamberlain example

Nozick's most famous argument uses the basketball star Wilt Chamberlain . Start with any distribution you think is just, say perfect equality. Now a million fans each happily pay 25 cents extra to watch Wilt play. At season's end, Wilt has $250,000, far more than anyone else. Is the new distribution unjust? Everyone chose freely. No one was harmed. Nozick's point: liberty upsets patterns . To keep any pattern, the state would have to keep interfering in free exchanges. He concludes that taxation of earnings from labour is on a par with forced labour . It forces you to work some hours for others' purposes. Nozick also argued that a minimal state could arise from anarchy without violating rights, through private protective agencies. The book's last part offers a framework for utopia : many voluntary communities under one minimal state.
Problems with Nozick

Weak foundations: Thomas Nagel, in "Libertarianism without Foundations" (1975), said Nozick asserts rights without proving them. Rectification: almost all property today traces back to conquest, slavery or fraud. Taken seriously, rectification could justify huge redistribution. Nozick himself admitted this. Self-ownership: G.A. Cohen, in Self-Ownership, Freedom, and Equality (1995), argued that full self-ownership produces unacceptable inequality and unfreedom for the poor. Freedom for whom? Formal freedom to trade means little to someone with nothing to trade. Nozick himself later wrote, in The Examined Life (1989), that his libertarian position now seemed "seriously inadequate".
Amartya Sen: equality of what?

In his 1979 Tanner Lecture, "Equality of What?" , Sen asked a simple question. When we say people should be equal, equal in what ? Utility (happiness)? But people adapt to hardship. A deprived person may learn to want little and report being content. Sen calls this adaptive preference . Primary goods (Rawls)? But people differ in how they convert resources into well-being. A disabled person needs more resources to move around than others. A pregnant woman needs more food. Sen's answer: we should focus on capabilities , the real freedoms people have to achieve things they value.
Functionings and capabilities

Functionings are the things a person actually does or is: being well-fed, healthy, literate, taking part in community life. Capabilities are the set of functionings a person could achieve: their real freedom to choose. Sen's example: a person who fasts and a person who starves both lack food. But the faster has the capability to eat and chooses not to. The starving person has no choice. Justice cares about that difference.
Development as Freedom and The Idea of Justice

Development as Freedom (1999) Development is the expansion of real freedoms, not just GDP growth. Sen names five instrumental freedoms: political freedoms, economic facilities, social opportunities, transparency guarantees and protective security. Famines and democracy In Poverty and Famines (1981), Sen showed famines come from a collapse of people's entitlements , not just a shortage of food. He studied the Bengal famine of 1943. He later argued that no major famine has occurred in a functioning democracy with a free press. The Idea of Justice (2009) Sen rejects Rawls's search for a perfectly just society. He calls it transcendental institutionalism . Instead, he favours comparative justice: compare real options and remove manifest injustices. He uses the Indian ideas of niti (rules, institutions) and nyaya (realised justice in people's lives).
Martha Nussbaum's list

Sen refused to give a fixed list of capabilities. He said each society should decide through public reasoning. Martha Nussbaum disagreed. In Women and Human Development (2000) and Creating Capabilities (2011), she gave a list of ten central human capabilities that every government should guarantee up to a threshold: Life Bodily health Bodily integrity Senses, imagination and thought Emotions Practical reason Affiliation Other species Play Control over one's environment, political and material She drew on Aristotle's idea of flourishing and used fieldwork with poor women in India, including SEWA in Ahmedabad.
Comparing the three

Focus: Rawls looks at primary goods. Nozick looks at entitlements and how holdings arose. Sen looks at capabilities, what people can do and be. State: Rawls supports a welfare state. Nozick wants a minimal state. Sen supports public action in health, education and social security, alongside markets. Method: Rawls uses an ideal contract. Nozick reasons from rights. Sen compares real-world situations. Critics of Sen say the capability approach is hard to measure and too open-ended. Critics of Nussbaum say her list imposes one idea of the good life on all cultures.
Capabilities in Indian policy

The UNDP's Human Development Index (1990), created by Mahbub ul Haq with Sen, measures health, education and income, not just GDP. NITI Aayog's National Multidimensional Poverty Index uses the global MPI method (developed by OPHI and UNDP, inspired by Sen). Its 2023 report said about 13.5 crore Indians left multidimensional poverty between 2015–16 and 2019–21. Rights-based laws like MGNREGA (2005), the Right to Education (2009) and the National Food Security Act (2013) aim at capabilities. Sen and Jean Drèze wrote An Uncertain Glory: India and Its Contradictions (2013), arguing India's growth neglected health and education. On the libertarian side, the 1991 reforms drew on market arguments, though India never adopted a minimal state.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine Nozick's entitlement theory of justice." "Explain Sen's capability approach. How is it different from Rawls?" "Justice as freedom: discuss Sen's critique of transcendental institutionalism." Structure for Nozick: self-ownership, side constraints, the three principles of entitlement, Wilt Chamberlain, minimal state, then Nagel's and Cohen's critiques. Structure for Sen: "Equality of what?", functionings and capabilities (draw the diagram), fasting vs starving, niti and nyaya, Nussbaum's list. End with HDI, MPI and India's rights-based laws.
Social, Political and Economic Equality; Equality vs Freedom
Equal in what?

Equality is a favourite theme: it ties together justice, rights, democracy and every ideology. The word looks simple, but it hides one hard question. Equal in what respect? Votes, money, opportunity, respect, or well-being? Nobody wants identical outcomes in everything. Even Marx did not say people are identical. As Amartya Sen put it, every serious theory demands equality of something . The fight is over which something. This lesson covers the kinds of equality, the debate on equality versus liberty (Berlin, Nozick, Hayek against Tawney, Rawls, Dworkin), and the Indian case. Lesson 0-3-1 covers affirmative action in detail.
Kinds of equality

Formal (legal and political) : equal rights and votes. Mostly achieved in democracies. Social : absence of privilege by birth, caste, race or gender, and equal respect. Economic : reducing gaps in income and wealth. Another way to sort equality: of opportunity (fair competition), of condition (a basic minimum) and of outcome (results). Liberals back the first, social democrats add the second and socialists lean to the third.
Formal and substantive equality; proportional and arithmetical

Formal equality treats all alike in law. Substantive equality asks about real life results. Treating unequals equally can deepen inequality. Anatole France quipped that the law forbids rich and poor alike to sleep under bridges. Aristotle ( Nicomachean Ethics , Book V) separated arithmetical equality (same for all) from proportional equality (like cases alike, in proportion to relevant differences). Indian courts use a similar test: reasonable classification under Article 14 needs an intelligible differentia with a rational link to the aim ( State of West Bengal v Anwar Ali Sarkar , 1952). Harold Laski , A Grammar of Politics (1925), added that liberty needs equality. Without a minimum of economic equality, liberty is empty for the poor.
How far should equality of opportunity go?

Equality of opportunity sounds fair to nearly everyone. But it has levels. Formal : no legal bars. Anyone may apply for any post. Fair or substantive : similar talent and effort should lead to similar prospects, whatever your class or caste. This is Rawls's fair equality of opportunity. It needs good schools, health and nutrition, and sometimes compensatory measures. Luck-egalitarian : differences caused by luck (family, talent) should be offset, but differences caused by choices need not be. The deeper you go, the more the state has to do. A family also passes on advantage through love, books and contacts. Can we, or should we, remove that? Rawls admits this limit, and Brighouse and Swift discuss it in Family Values (2014). In practice, measures include public education, scholarships, nutrition schemes, and reservations.
Rousseau, Marx and Tawney

Rousseau, Discourse on Inequality (1755) Natural inequality (age, health, talent) is small. Moral or political inequality , created by private property and convention, is the serious one. He saw it as the root of social ills. Marx Formal rights hide class inequality. Real equality needs abolition of class. The final principle is "from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs" (1875). R.H. Tawney, Equality (1931) A British socialist. He argued that people differ in talents but should be equal in dignity and in access to the conditions of a decent life. Inequality of circumstance is not natural. He wanted a "strategy of equality" by public education and services.
Rawls, Dworkin, Sen, Walzer

Rawls (1971): inequalities are acceptable only if they benefit the worst-off and attach to jobs open under fair equality of opportunity. Ronald Dworkin , "What is Equality?" (1981) and Sovereign Virtue (2000): equality of resources . People should be responsible for their choices, not their circumstances. This is the base of luck egalitarianism . Amartya Sen , "Equality of What?" (1979 Tanner Lecture): focus on capabilities , the real freedoms people have, not income. Michael Walzer , Spheres of Justice (1983): complex equality . Different goods (money, office, education) belong to different spheres. Inequality becomes tyranny when wealth buys power or honour in other spheres.
Equality versus freedom

Can the two coexist? Positions: Freedom first: Hayek, Nozick, Friedman Equality of outcome needs constant interference with free choices. Nozick's Wilt Chamberlain example (1974): if people freely pay to watch a star, a new unequal distribution arises, and redistribution would violate their liberty. Hayek: equality before law, not material equality. Equality supports freedom: Tawney, Laski, Rawls, Sen A starving person is not free. Equal liberty needs a fair share of resources. Liberty in a divided society is the liberty of the strong. Isaiah Berlin , "Equality" (1956), thought both are real values that can clash. He accepted a trade-off, in his value-pluralist way.
Other challenges to equality

Meritocracy : Michael Young coined the word in a satire, The Rise of the Meritocracy (1958). Sandel's The Tyranny of Merit (2020) argues that the winners wrongly think they deserve everything. Feminist : formal equality ignores care work and the family. Okin attacks the gendered family. Recognition : Nancy Fraser says justice needs both redistribution and recognition of group identities. Difference : Iris Young says equal treatment can erase real group differences. Levelling down : Is equality good if it makes everyone worse off? Derek Parfit's priority view says we should help the worse-off because they are badly off, not because of equality itself.
Measuring inequality

The Gini coefficient runs from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person holds everything). The Lorenz curve plots cumulative income against cumulative population. The more it bends away from the diagonal, the greater the inequality. The Palma ratio compares the top 10% share to the bottom 40%. Thomas Piketty, Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2013 in French, 2014 in English), argues that when returns on capital (r) exceed growth (g), wealth concentrates over time. The UNDP's Inequality-adjusted HDI and Sen's capability lens look beyond income. Note that income inequality, wealth inequality and consumption inequality give different pictures. Always say which one you cite.
Equality in the Indian Constitution

Preamble : "equality of status and of opportunity". Articles 14-18 : equality before law and equal protection (14), no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth (15), equal opportunity in public employment (16), abolition of untouchability (17) and titles (18). Article 15(3) allows special provisions for women and children; 15(4) for socially and educationally backward classes; 16(4) reservation in posts. Directive Principles : Article 38(2) (minimise inequalities in income, and eliminate inequalities in status, facilities and opportunities), Article 39(b) and (c). Courts : E.P. Royappa (1974): arbitrariness violates Article 14. Maneka Gandhi (1978) linked Articles 14, 19 and 21. Inequality data : a World Inequality Lab paper (Bharti, Chancel, Piketty and Somanchi, 2024) estimates that India's top 1% received 22.6% of national income in 2022-23, the highest in its series back to 1922. The paper stresses that Indian data are weak.
How to answer

"Equality and liberty are complementary, not conflicting." Discuss. Examine the different dimensions of equality. Is equality of opportunity enough? Compare the Rawlsian and libertarian views on equality. "Formal equality may perpetuate inequality." Elucidate with Indian examples. Structure: define equality and ask 'equality of what'. Draw the types. Then thinkers in order: Rousseau, Marx, Tawney, Rawls, Dworkin, Sen, Walzer. Put the freedom-versus-equality debate in a two-column table with Nozick and Hayek against Rawls and Laski. Finish with Articles 14-18 and 38-39, plus current inequality data, and conclude that both values need balance.
Affirmative Action
Reservation: the most debated equality policy in India

Affirmative action means taking positive steps to help groups that have been held back by past or present discrimination. It may include quotas, targets, outreach, scholarships and preferences in admission or jobs. The theory question is old: does treating people differently advance equal treatment ? Opponents call it reverse discrimination. Supporters call it the only way to give formal equality real meaning. This is a recurring Paper I theme, in the theory section (equality, justice) and in Paper I Section B (caste, reservation, constitutional provisions). Answers need both theory (Rawls, Dworkin, Nozick, Sandel) and detailed Indian law (Articles, amendments, cases). Learn the case sequence from Champakam Dorairajan to Davinder Singh.
Meaning and forms

The phrase "affirmative action" had appeared earlier in the Wagner Act (1935) on labour relations. US Executive Order 10925 (1961, President Kennedy) was its first use in the context of racial discrimination, and it was developed under President Johnson in Executive Order 11246 (1965). In India it is usually called reservation , and in Britain "positive discrimination". Quotas : fixed seats or posts. Preferences or plus points : extra weight in selection. Outreach and support : coaching, hostels, scholarships, relaxed age limits. Targets and goals : soft aims without fixed numbers. Political reservation : seats in legislatures or local bodies. Beneficiaries may be defined by caste, race, gender, disability or economic status. How you define the group is a major source of dispute.
Arguments for

Compensatory justice : make up for past wrongs such as slavery or untouchability. Distributive justice : today's inequalities in opportunity are unfair. This fits Rawls's fair equality of opportunity , which asks that people of similar talent have similar prospects whatever their class. Representation : public institutions should include all groups. Anne Phillips's "politics of presence" supports this. Diversity and role models : mixed institutions work better and break stereotypes. Social harmony : sharing power reduces resentment. Dworkin , in "Bakke's Case: Are Quotas Unfair?" (1977), argued that race-conscious admission uses race as a means to a wider social good, not because a group is inferior. No one has a right to a place that the policy takes away.
Arguments against

Reverse discrimination : it punishes people who did no wrong. It uses group traits, which clash with individual merit. Merit and efficiency : critics say standards fall. Defenders reply that exam marks measure past advantage, too. Stigma : beneficiaries are doubted as less deserving. Creamy layer : benefits are captured by the better-off members of the group. Entrenching identity : it fixes caste or race as the basis of politics (Nathan Glazer, Affirmative Discrimination , 1975). Libertarian (Nozick): forced preferences violate individual rights. Sandel , Justice (2009), shows that the debate rests on views about desert and the purpose of institutions: is a university rewarding merit or serving a social purpose?
The US experience

In Regents of the University of California v Bakke (1978), the US Supreme Court barred fixed racial quotas but allowed race as one factor to get a diverse class. Grutter v Bollinger (2003) upheld such a plus factor at a law school. In Students for Fair Admissions v Harvard (June 2023), the Court held that race-conscious admissions at Harvard and the University of North Carolina violate the Equal Protection Clause (and, for private universities taking federal funds, Title VI of the Civil Rights Act 1964). It marked a major turn. US policy aims mainly at diversity. Indian reservation rests on representation of historically excluded groups, and is in the Constitution itself.
Reservation in the Constitution: Articles 15 and 16

Article 15(4) : special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs (added by the First Amendment, 1951, after State of Madras v Champakam Dorairajan , 1951). 15(5) : private and public educational institutions (93rd Amendment, 2005). 15(6) : economically weaker sections (103rd Amendment, 2019). Article 16(4) : reservation in public posts for backward classes not adequately represented. 16(4A) : promotions for SC/ST (77th Amendment, 1995). 16(4B) : carry-forward of vacancies (81st). 16(6) : EWS.
Reservation in the Constitution: other provisions

Articles 330 and 332 : seats for SC and ST in the Lok Sabha and Assemblies. 243D and 243T : local bodies. Article 335 : claims of SC/ST in services, consistent with efficiency. Article 340 : commission on backward classes. 46 : promotion of educational and economic interests.
The case law, in order: 1951 to 1992

Champakam Dorairajan (1951): communal quota struck down. Led to the First Amendment. M.R. Balaji (1962): 50% ceiling is a rule of prudence. State of Kerala v N.M. Thomas (1975): Article 16(4) is an illustration of Article 16(1), not an exception. Indra Sawhney (1992): the Mandal case, 6:3. Upheld 27% for OBCs. Excluded the creamy layer, capped total reservations at 50% (except in extraordinary cases), said reservation applies only at initial appointment, not promotion, and required a permanent backward classes body.
The case law, in order: after Indra Sawhney

M. Nagaraj (2006): promotion quotas are valid only with data on backwardness, inadequacy and efficiency. Jarnail Singh (2018): creamy layer concept applied to SC/ST promotions; quantifiable data on backwardness not needed. B.K. Pavitra (2019): upheld a Karnataka law on consequential seniority for SC/ST promotees, with the Court finding that the data requirement was met. Janhit Abhiyan (2022): a five-judge bench, by 3 to 2, upheld the 103rd Amendment and the EWS quota. The majority said the 50 per cent ceiling applies to existing categories, not to this new one.
Mandal to EWS and sub-classification

Mandal Commission (set up 1979 under B.P. Mandal): report in 1980, recommending 27% for OBCs. V.P. Singh's government implemented it in August 1990. 102nd Amendment (2018): constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes (Article 338B). 103rd Amendment (2019): 10% for economically weaker sections outside SC/ST/OBC groups. In Janhit Abhiyan v Union of India (7 November 2022), a 5-judge bench upheld it by 3:2. Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil (2021): Maratha quota struck down for crossing the 50% cap. State of Punjab v Davinder Singh (1 August 2024): a seven-judge bench held 6:1 that States can sub-classify Scheduled Castes to give more benefit to the most disadvantaged. Some judges also urged creamy-layer exclusion for SC/ST. Caste census : in April 2025 the Union government decided to include caste enumeration in the next national Census.
Debates in India today

Key issues for a balanced answer: Sub-categorisation of OBCs : the Rohini Commission (set up 2017) examined unequal sharing of the 27% quota. Creamy layer : income ceiling of Rs 8 lakh was set in 2017. Demands to revise it recur. Private sector and jobs shrinking : public sector jobs are fewer, so reservation reaches fewer people. Dominant groups seek quotas : Jats, Patidars, Kapus and Marathas agitated. It signals competition for scarce state jobs. Ambedkar's view : reservation is a temporary safeguard, tied to representation (Constituent Assembly). Reservation in legislatures was extended repeatedly; the 104th Amendment (2019) ended the Anglo-Indian seats but extended SC/ST seats to 2030. Women : the 106th Amendment (2023) reserves a third of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats, to take effect after delimitation. A fair verdict: reservation has widened representation, but needs better targeting plus schooling and jobs.
How to answer

"Reservation is not a poverty alleviation measure but a tool of social justice." Discuss. Examine the philosophical justification for affirmative action. Is it consistent with equality? Trace the evolution of reservation policy in India through constitutional amendments and judicial rulings. Critically evaluate the creamy layer principle and the sub-classification of Scheduled Castes. Structure: start with the equality paradox. Give the justifications (compensatory, distributive, representation) and the objections (merit, stigma, creamy layer). Add the US contrast in one line. Then the Indian timeline: Articles, First Amendment, Balaji, Thomas, Indra Sawhney, Nagaraj, 77th to 103rd amendments, Davinder Singh. Close with reforms: better targeting, data, and investment in education.
Meaning, Theories and Kinds of Rights
The language of claims against power

Rights are the central vocabulary of modern politics. When a person says "I have a right to...", they claim something that others, including the state, must respect or provide. The syllabus asks three things: what a right is , where rights come from (the theories), and what kinds there are. Each is a regular question. The Indian link is direct: Part III of the Constitution, the Supreme Court's expansion of Article 21, and the balance between rights and duties. Strong answers give the competing theories (natural, legal, historical, social-welfare, Marxist), cite the main thinkers with books, and use Indian cases. The next lesson covers human rights and multicultural rights.
What is a right?

A right is a justified claim or entitlement that a person or group has, which imposes duties on others. Rights are usually protected by law, but may be moral claims that exist without law. Laski, in A Grammar of Politics (1925), described rights as those conditions of social life without which no one can seek their best self. He stressed that rights belong to society and come with duties. Features of rights: They are claims, not favours. They have a holder and a duty-bearer. They are universal within a group. They are limited by the equal rights of others and by public interest. Remember the link with duties. A right of mine is a duty of yours to respect it.
Natural rights theory

The oldest modern theory holds that rights belong to humans by nature, before any government. Rights are discovered by reason, not made by law. John Locke , Second Treatise (1689): the natural rights to life, liberty and property. Government exists to protect them. Thomas Paine , Rights of Man (1791): rights are inherent and defend the people against hereditary rule. The US Declaration of Independence (1776) says all men are endowed with unalienable rights. The French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789) declares rights "natural, inalienable and sacred". Strength : it gives a moral standard against which to judge unjust laws. Weakness : who decides what nature gives? Critics call the idea metaphysical.
Critics of natural rights: Bentham, Burke, Marx

Jeremy Bentham, Anarchical Fallacies (written c. 1795) Natural rights are "nonsense upon stilts". Only laws create rights. Law is backed by sanctions. His test of a good law is utility, the greatest happiness. Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790) He rejected abstract "rights of man". Real rights are the inherited, concrete liberties of a people, developed through history. Karl Marx, On the Jewish Question (1844) The "rights of man" are the rights of an egoistic, separate member of civil society. Political rights give formal freedom, yet leave economic power untouched. True emancipation is human, not just political. These three gave the legal, historical and Marxist theories.
Legal, historical and social-welfare theories

Legal theory (Bentham, Austin): rights are created and enforced by the sovereign state. No law, no right. Strength: clear and enforceable. Weakness: if the state is unjust, there is nothing to criticise it with. Historical theory (Burke, Savigny): rights come from custom and practice over time. Weakness: bad customs, such as untouchability, also have a long history.
