Social-welfare theory (Pound, Chafee, Laski, Ritchie): rights are the conditions that advance the welfare of society and the individual. The state recognises rights because they serve social good. Marxist theory : rights express the interests of the ruling class. Real rights need economic equality and class change. Modern views: Hart 's choice (will) theory says a right gives its holder control over a duty. Raz 's interest theory says rights protect important interests.
Hohfeld, Dworkin and Nozick

Wesley Hohfeld (1913) A US jurist who split "right" into four parts: claim (matched by a duty on others), liberty (privilege), power and immunity . It helps to see what exactly a right gives. Ronald Dworkin, Taking Rights Seriously (1977) Rights are trumps over collective goals. A majority or the state cannot override individual rights just because it would benefit the community. Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) "Individuals have rights, and there are things no person or group may do to them." Rights are side constraints on state action. Both writers give a strong, rights-based liberalism. Rawls places basic liberties first in his lexical order.
Kinds of rights

Karel Vasak proposed the three generations in 1977. They follow the French Revolution (liberty, equality, fraternity). Negative rights need the state to refrain from interfering (e.g., speech). Positive rights need the state to act (e.g., education). Berlin's two liberties echo this. Critics, such as Henry Shue ( Basic Rights , 1980), say all rights need both restraint and provision. Moral versus legal rights ; individual versus group rights . Laski's list: the right to work, to a living wage, to education, to political participation.
Rights, duties and the limits of rights

Are rights absolute? No right is. Free speech does not cover incitement. Property gives way to public purpose. The test is usually proportionality : a limit must serve a legitimate aim and go no further than needed. The link to duties is a theme in many traditions. Gandhi held that rights are earned by doing one's duty (his 1947 note to UNESCO). The Universal Declaration (Article 29) says everyone has duties to the community. Other debates: Inflation of rights : do too many claims weaken the really basic ones? Group rights versus individual rights : see the next lesson. Feminist critique : rights language ignores care and the private sphere, though feminists also use rights to challenge it. Communitarians : rights language stresses conflict, not community.
Rights in the Indian Constitution

Part III (Articles 12-35): equality (14-18), freedoms (19-22), against exploitation (23-24), religion (25-28), cultural and educational rights (29-30), constitutional remedies (32). Ambedkar called Article 32 the "heart and soul" of the Constitution. Evolution : Golaknath (1967), Kesavananda Bharati (1973, basic structure), Maneka Gandhi (1978, Article 21 requires fair, just, reasonable procedure). Article 21 now covers privacy ( Puttaswamy , 2017), livelihood ( Olga Tellis , 1985), a clean environment, health and dignity. Education : Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) and the RTE Act, 2009. Property : ceased to be a fundamental right by the 44th Amendment (1978), and is now a constitutional right under Article 300A. Duties : Article 51A (42nd Amendment, 1976, on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice). Directive Principles give socio-economic rights that courts cannot enforce directly. Minerva Mills (1980) called the balance between Parts III and IV a basic feature.
How to answer

"Rights are the conditions without which no individual can be at his best." Discuss with reference to different theories of rights. Distinguish between negative and positive rights. Critically examine the Marxist critique of liberal rights. How has the Supreme Court expanded the scope of Article 21? Structure: define rights and tie them to duties. Present the five theories in one table: natural, legal, historical, social-welfare, Marxist, each with a thinker, a strength and a weakness. Add the modern theorists (Hart, Dworkin, Nozick). Then kinds and generations. Finish with Part III, the basic structure and Article 21. Mention limits and proportionality.
Human Rights and Multicultural Rights
Rights for humans, rights for groups

This lesson has two parts. The first is human rights : rights claimed by every person simply as a human being, set out in international law. The second is multicultural rights : special rights for cultural, religious or ethnic groups inside a state. They seem to pull in different directions. Human rights are universal and individual. Multicultural rights are group-specific. The big debate is whether group rights can sit with individual liberty. Both feature in Paper I (theory) and, through the Constitution, in Paper I Section B (minority rights, Articles 29-30, personal laws). In Paper II, human rights link to the UN, R2P and humanitarian intervention. Keep these links in mind.
Human rights: idea and history

Human rights are claimed by all people on the basis of humanity: universal , inalienable , indivisible and equal. They grew from natural rights, but after the horrors of the Second World War they became a matter of international law. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948. Eleanor Roosevelt chaired the drafting committee. It is not a treaty but is now widely seen as customary law.
The International Bill of Human Rights

UDHR (1948): 30 articles, covering both civil-political and economic-social rights. ICCPR (International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, 1966, in force 1976). ICESCR (International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, 1966, in force 1976). The Cold War split the two covenants: the West stressed civil-political rights, the Soviet bloc stressed economic-social rights. India has ratified both covenants (1979). Later treaties cover racial discrimination (1965), women (CEDAW, 1979), torture (1984), children (1989) and disability (2006). The Vienna Declaration (1993) said all rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent and interrelated. The UN Human Rights Council (2006) replaced the Commission on Human Rights, and has a Universal Periodic Review of every state.
Universalism versus cultural relativism

Universalists : rights flow from shared human dignity. If rights depend on culture, tyrants can excuse abuses by pointing to tradition. Relativists : the UDHR reflects Western liberal values. Cultures differ on the individual and community. Some states, such as Singapore and Malaysia in the 1990s, pushed "Asian values": order and community before individual freedom. The 1993 Bangkok Declaration reflected this. Amartya Sen , "Human Rights and Asian Values" (1997): Asia is too diverse for one set of values, and tolerance and liberty have deep roots in Asian history (Ashoka, Akbar). Middle paths : Abdullahi An-Naim seeks cross-cultural dialogue. Jack Donnelly speaks of "relative universality". Note too the Third World argument: the right to development and economic justice cannot be ignored.
Critiques of human rights

Marxist : rights ignore economic structures. Feminist : the public-private divide let violence at home go unseen. Rights have been framed in male terms. The campaign "women's rights are human rights" and CEDAW respond. Postcolonial : used selectively by powerful states to justify intervention. Makau Mutua speaks of a "savages-victims-saviours" pattern. Enforcement gap : there is no world government. Treaties rely on state consent and weak monitoring bodies. Sovereignty clash : humanitarian intervention (Kosovo 1999, Libya 2011) and the Responsibility to Protect (UN World Summit, 2005) raise old doubts. Defenders say that the rights regime still gives victims a language and a weapon, even if imperfect.
Multiculturalism and group rights

Multiculturalism accepts that modern societies hold many cultures, and that fair treatment may require recognising differences, not ignoring them. The liberal tradition says: treat everyone as an individual and be "difference-blind". Multiculturalists say that a neutral state is not neutral. A public holiday on Sunday, the language of schools and rules on dress all favour the majority culture. Charles Taylor , "The Politics of Recognition" (1992): misrecognition can harm people. A fair state needs a politics of recognition, not just of equal rights. He pointed to Quebec's language laws. Iris Marion Young , Justice and the Politics of Difference (1990): group-differentiated citizenship and special representation for oppressed groups.
Kymlicka's liberal multiculturalism

Will Kymlicka , Multicultural Citizenship (1995), gives the best-known liberal defence. Culture is the context in which people make choices, so individuals have an interest in their cultural membership. He proposes three kinds of group-differentiated rights. Self-government rights For national minorities such as indigenous peoples or Quebec: autonomy, territory, language. Polyethnic rights For immigrant groups: exemption from rules (e.g., turban for Sikh police in Canada), funding for cultural practices. Special representation rights Reserved seats or places for disadvantaged groups. He separates external protections (a group's shield against the majority, acceptable) from internal restrictions (a group's power over its own members, which liberals must reject).
Critics of multicultural rights

Brian Barry , Culture and Equality (2001): equal rules for all are fairer. Exemptions give an advantage to those with the loudest claim. Susan Okin , "Is Multiculturalism Bad for Women?" (1999): group rights often protect practices that harm women, as the private sphere is where cultures control women. Chandran Kukathas : individuals should be free to leave a group. Groups have no rights beyond individuals' freedom of association. Bhikhu Parekh , Rethinking Multiculturalism (2000): defends a dialogue-based multiculturalism. No culture is perfect, and each should be open to criticism from others, within an "operative public values" framework. Habermas argues that equal rights already protect cultural identity if properly interpreted. Fears of social fragmentation led several European leaders to declare multiculturalism a failure around 2010-11.
Human rights and minority rights in India

Institutions : Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 created the NHRC (October 1993) and State commissions. It was amended in 2006 and 2019. The NHRC can recommend, but its orders are not binding. Courts : Vishaka (1997) used CEDAW to fill a legal gap. The Supreme Court uses international norms where they do not conflict with domestic law. Minority rights : Article 29 (protection of language and culture of any section), Article 30 (minorities' right to set up and run educational institutions), T.M.A. Pai Foundation (2002), Articles 25-28 on religion.
Tribal rights, personal laws and the Indian model

Tribal rights : Fifth and Sixth Schedules, PESA (1996), the Forest Rights Act (2006), and Articles 371 provisions for specific States. Personal laws : Shah Bano (1985), Shayara Bano (2017) and Article 44. Uttarakhand passed a Uniform Civil Code law in 2024, in force since January 2025. India's model is sometimes called "constitutional multiculturalism", mixing group recognition (Articles 29-30, reservations) with a push for individual equality and reform.
How to answer

"Human rights are universal in appeal but culturally contested." Discuss. Examine Kymlicka's theory of multicultural citizenship. Are group rights compatible with individual liberty? Illustrate with the Indian case. Assess the role of the NHRC in protecting human rights in India. Structure: for the first part, give the UDHR and two covenants, universalism versus relativism (with Sen), and critiques. For the second, argue from the limits of difference-blind liberalism: Taylor, Young, Kymlicka and his three rights, then Barry, Okin and Kukathas against. Use India as a worked example: Articles 29-30, Fifth and Sixth Schedules, personal laws and the UCC debate. Sum up with a balanced, dialogue-based position.
Classical Theories of Democracy
Democracy is the most-asked idea in political theory

Democracy sounds simple: rule by the people. But thinkers have fought over it for 2,500 years. Who counts as "the people"? Should they rule directly or through representatives? Is majority rule safe? This lesson covers the classical and early-modern answers: Athens, Plato and Aristotle, Rousseau, Madison, Tocqueville and J.S. Mill. The next lessons cover the modern (elitist, pluralist, participatory, deliberative) theories. For the exam, you need two skills. First, know who said what, in which book. Second, be able to sort theories into types. C.B. Macpherson and David Held give the best sorting schemes, and examiners like them. Questions often ask you to compare direct and representative democracy, or to judge whether Athens was really a democracy.
What "democracy" means

The word comes from Greek: demos (the people) and kratos (rule). Abraham Lincoln's phrase, "government of the people, by the people, for the people" (Gettysburg Address, 1863), is the popular summary. Thinkers separate three things: Who rules : all citizens, or elected representatives. How they rule : by direct vote, by lot, or by election. Why it is good : it protects people from abuse, it develops their character, or it gives results people accept. Heywood adds a useful point. Democracy today is mostly liberal democracy : free elections plus limited government and individual rights. Classical democracy had no such limits. The majority could do almost anything.
Athenian democracy: rule by the citizens

Athens in the 5th century BCE is the model of direct democracy . Citizens did not elect rulers to decide for them. They decided themselves in the Ecclesia , which met on the Pnyx hill about forty times a year. Most offices, including the Council of 500, were filled by lot , not election. Lot treats every citizen as equally fit to rule. Only the generals were elected, since war needed skill. Pericles was re-elected general many times. Pericles' Funeral Oration, reported by Thucydides, praises Athens as a system where power lies with the many, not the few.
The limits of Athenian democracy

Athens was democratic only for a small group. Citizens were adult men born to Athenian parents. Women, slaves and resident foreigners ( metics ) were excluded. Most people living in Athens had no vote. Critics also point out that: Direct democracy only works in a small city-state, where all can meet in one place. Citizens had the free time because slaves and women did the work. The assembly could be swayed by clever speakers ( demagogues ). It condemned Socrates to death in 399 BCE. Yet defenders say Athens offered something modern states lack: real, equal participation. This idea returns in the participatory theories of the 1960s.
Plato and Aristotle: the first critics

Plato, The Republic (c. 375 BCE) Democracy puts power in the hands of the ignorant. Ruling is a skill, like steering a ship, so it needs trained experts. The famous "ship of state" image makes this point. Plato ranks democracy below aristocracy, timocracy and oligarchy, and above only tyranny. He thinks freedom run wild turns into tyranny. Aristotle, Politics (c. 350 BCE) Aristotle sorts governments by the number who rule and by whether they rule for the common good. Rule of the many for the common good is polity . Rule of the many for their own (poor) class interest is democracy , which he calls a deviant form. His best practical answer is a mixed constitution that blends oligarchy and democracy, led by a strong middle class. Note the oddity: for the Greeks, "democracy" was often an insult. It meant mob rule.
Rousseau: the general will

Jean-Jacques Rousseau , The Social Contract (1762), wants true popular sovereignty. Law must express the general will : what citizens want as members of a community aiming at the common good. It is not the same as the will of all , which is just the sum of private wants. His key claims: Sovereignty cannot be represented or handed over. The people must make the laws themselves in assembly. He mocked the English. They think they are free, he said, but they are free only when electing members of parliament. Once elected, they are slaves again. Obeying the general will is real freedom. Those who refuse may be "forced to be free". Rousseau inspired the French Revolution, and also worries critics: he can be read as a route to majority tyranny or even totalitarian democracy (J.L. Talmon).
Madison and Tocqueville: tame the majority

James Madison , Federalist No. 10 (1787), feared factions : groups moved by passion or self-interest, against others' rights. Pure democracy cannot stop them in a majority. His cure is a republic : representatives who "refine" public views, in a large country with many interests so no single faction dominates. Alexis de Tocqueville , Democracy in America (1835 and 1840), admired equality and local self-government in America. But he warned of the tyranny of the majority : public opinion that crushes dissent. He also feared a soft despotism where citizens give up public life for private comfort. His remedies: independent courts, a free press, voluntary associations and local government. Together these give today's liberal-democratic idea of checks on majority power.
Bentham, James Mill and J.S. Mill

In the 19th century, utilitarians argued for democracy. Jeremy Bentham and James Mill ( Essay on Government , 1820) said that rulers pursue their own interest. Only regular elections and the vote can force them to serve the greatest happiness. This is protective democracy . J.S. Mill , Considerations on Representative Government (1861), adds a second reason. Taking part in politics improves people. It teaches them to think about public good. This is developmental democracy . Mill's safeguards He feared that the uneducated majority would pass "class legislation". So he proposed plural votes for the educated, and proportional representation by Thomas Hare's single transferable vote, so minorities get a voice. He also backed votes for women, in The Subjection of Women (1869). Plural voting is rejected today.
Macpherson's four models

C.B. Macpherson , The Life and Times of Liberal Democracy (1977), sorts democratic theory into four models. Protective (Bentham, James Mill): voting protects citizens from rulers. Developmental (J.S. Mill): participation builds moral character. Equilibrium (Schumpeter and pluralists): politics is a market, and parties compete for votes. Participatory : citizens share in decisions in workplaces and communities. Macpherson, a Marxist-liberal, argued that liberal democracy in a market society tends to treat people as consumers of politics. He wanted to bring back the developmental idea. David Held , Models of Democracy (1987), offers a longer list, starting with classical Athens and republicanism. Cite both for a good structure.
Indian roots and the constitutional choice

Democracy has Indian precedents. The sabhas and samitis of the Vedic age, and the gana-sanghas (republics) such as the Licchavis of Vaishali, had assemblies and elected heads. The Buddhist sangha used votes and rules of debate. The historian K.P. Jayaswal studied these in Hindu Polity (1924). Amartya Sen also stresses India's tradition of public reasoning in The Argumentative Indian (2005). The Constitution chose representative democracy with universal adult franchise (Article 326), from the very first election of 1951-52. It adds direct elements as well: gram sabhas (Article 243A) and Article 40 on village panchayats. B.R. Ambedkar warned the Constituent Assembly on 25 November 1949 that political democracy cannot last without social democracy . He said that in politics India would recognise "one man one vote and one vote one value", while social and economic life would still deny "one man one value". This was a warning about a life of contradictions, not a wish.
How to answer

"Is Athenian democracy a model for modern democracy?" Discuss. "Plato's critique of democracy is still relevant." Examine. Distinguish between direct and representative democracy. Which suits a large state? "Tyranny of the majority" - Tocqueville and Mill on the problem. Structure: open with the meaning of demos and kratos, then Athens with its limits. Move to Plato and Aristotle's critique, then Rousseau versus Madison on representation. Add Tocqueville and Mill on safeguards, and use Macpherson to classify. Close with India: Article 326, panchayats and Ambedkar's social democracy. A good one-line verdict: classical democracy gave the ideal of equal participation, while liberal thinkers added limits and representation to make it workable at scale.
Contemporary Theories: Elitist, Pluralist, Schumpeter
When democracy meets reality

Classical theory asked citizens to rule. Twentieth-century scholars looked at real democracies and found something else. Most people did not take part. Parties, bosses and experts took the decisions. So a new group of theorists lowered the target. They defined democracy by what actually happens: competition for power , not rule by all. This is the realist or empirical turn. It fits the behavioural revolution in political science after 1945. This topic is in the syllabus under "contemporary theories". You must know three strands: elite theory , Schumpeter's competitive democracy and pluralism (Dahl). Examiners also expect the critics: Bachrach and Baratz, Pateman, Macpherson, and the radical participatory school.
Three pictures of power

The three schools disagree on how power is spread. Elitists : in every society, a small minority rules. Democracy changes who is in the elite, not the fact of elite rule. Pluralists : power is dispersed among many groups. No one group always wins. Schumpeter : leaders compete for the people's vote, much as firms compete for customers. Schumpeter sits between the two. He accepts elite rule but sees voting competition as the democratic part.
The classical elite theorists

Gaetano Mosca, The Ruling Class (1896) In every society, two classes appear: a ruling minority and a ruled majority. The minority wins because it is organised. The many cannot organise as easily. Vilfredo Pareto, The Mind and Society (1916) Elites rule, but they circulate . Old elites decay and new ones replace them. He described two elite types, lions (who rule by force) and foxes (who rule by cunning). Revolutions merely swap elites. Robert Michels, Political Parties (1911) Even democratic parties and trade unions become oligarchies. Large organisations need leaders, experts and officials. This is the iron law of oligarchy : organisation means oligarchy. All three were wary of democracy and Marxism. They held that equal rule by all is a myth.
C. Wright Mills and the power elite

Elite theory also has a left-wing version. C. Wright Mills , The Power Elite (1956), argued that America was run by a small circle that overlapped across three institutions: big corporations, the military and the executive branch of government. They shared backgrounds and met in the same circles. Unlike Pareto, Mills used elite theory to criticise democracy. The public, he said, had become a passive "mass", while real decisions were made at the top. Note the difference from Marx: for Mills, the elite is based on holding institutional posts, not only on owning capital. Mills came first: Dahl's pluralism (his critique "A Critique of the Ruling Elite Model", 1958, and Who Governs? , 1961) was partly a reply to Mills.
Schumpeter: democracy as a competitive method

Joseph Schumpeter , Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942), rejected the "classical doctrine" that there is a common good the people want. In his view, voters are ill-informed and easily swayed. They have no clear will. "The democratic method is that institutional arrangement for arriving at political decisions in which individuals acquire the power to decide by means of a competitive struggle for the people's vote." Schumpeter, 1942 The role of the people is not to decide issues but to choose and remove leaders . Democracy is a way of picking rulers, a bit like a market. Political parties are firms and votes are the currency. This is the minimalist or procedural view. It is also called the equilibrium model by Macpherson.
Dahl and pluralism

Robert Dahl , in A Preface to Democratic Theory (1956) and Who Governs? (1961), studied New Haven, Connecticut. He found that different groups led on different issues. Power was dispersed , not held by one elite. Leaders needed to bargain with many groups. Earlier, David Truman , The Governmental Process (1951), saw politics as interest-group competition. Dahl then coined polyarchy ( Polyarchy , 1971): rule by the many, the best real-world approximation of democracy. Its institutions, in his later list, are: Elected officials. Free, fair and frequent elections. Freedom of expression. Alternative sources of information. Associational autonomy. Inclusive citizenship. This list is a handy test of whether a country is a democracy.
Is pluralism too rosy?

Bias in the system : E.E. Schattschneider, The Semisovereign People (1960), said the pluralist chorus sings with an upper-class accent. Business and the wealthy organise more easily than the poor. Hidden power : Bachrach and Baratz (1962) showed that elites can keep issues off the agenda, so no visible contest occurs. This is the second face of power (see lesson 0-6-0). Business privilege : Charles Lindblom, Politics and Markets (1977), moved from pluralism. Governments depend on business investment, so business has a privileged position. Dahl too later accepted that corporations distort equality ( Dilemmas of Pluralist Democracy , 1982). Neo-pluralism accepts these points but still defends group competition.
The participatory reply to the realists

The realists seemed to say apathy is healthy. Carole Pateman , Participation and Democratic Theory (1970), pushed back. The realists had misread the old theory. Writers like Rousseau and J.S. Mill valued participation for its effect on citizens. She argued that people learn democracy by practising it, especially in workplaces. Low participation is a problem to fix, not a fact to accept. C.B. Macpherson likewise said that elitist models fit a market society and shrink democracy. Others, such as Peter Bachrach ( The Theory of Democratic Elitism , 1967), argued that elite theory protects the status quo. These critiques lead to the participatory and deliberative models of the next lessons.
Elites, parties and groups in India

Michels in India : critics point to dynastic politics and top-down control in many parties. Intra-party democracy is weak. The Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law, 52nd Amendment, 1985) gives party leaders strong control over legislators. Congress system : Rajni Kothari argued that after independence one dominant party worked as a system of bargaining among factions ("The Congress System in India", 1964). It resembled a pluralist arena inside one party. Interest groups : business bodies (FICCI, CII), unions and farmers' groups lobby. The farmers' agitation of 2020-21 ended with the repeal of the three farm laws in November 2021, which shows how organised groups can force change. Money and elite capture : in February 2024 the Supreme Court struck down the electoral bonds scheme ( ADR v Union of India ) as violating the voter's right to information.
How to answer

"Elite theory of democracy is the denial of democracy." Discuss. Examine Schumpeter's view of democracy as a method. Critically evaluate the pluralist theory of democracy. "Iron law of oligarchy": does it apply to Indian parties? Structure: define the shift from classical to realist theory. Give the three schools with one thinker and one book each. Use Dahl's polyarchy as the pluralist core. Then the critics: Schattschneider, Bachrach and Baratz, Lindblom, Pateman. Finish with Indian cases such as dynastic parties, farm laws repeal and electoral bonds. A table comparing the three schools earns marks.
Representative and Participatory Democracy
Who decides: you or your representative?

No modern state of millions can gather everyone in one square. So most democracies choose representatives . But this raises hard questions. Should an MP follow voters' wishes or use their own judgment? Who gets represented? Does voting once in five years count as self-rule? The opposite answer is participatory democracy : citizens should take part directly and often, in decisions that affect their lives. This lesson sets out both models, the main thinkers and the critiques. It is a standard Paper I topic and links directly to Indian panchayati raj, so answers can be enriched with examples.
Representative democracy in brief

In a representative democracy , citizens elect people to make laws and run government for them. Sovereignty stays with the people, but its use is delegated. Its supporters give four reasons. Scale : it is the only workable form in a large state. Expertise : full-time legislators can study complex issues. Filtering : Madison hoped that representatives would refine passing public passions. Accountability : regular elections let voters remove bad rulers. Its critics say that voters are reduced to a vote every few years. Between elections the gap between rulers and ruled can become wide.
Trustee, delegate, mandate

How should a representative behave? Three classic views: Trustee (Burke) Edmund Burke, in his Speech to the Electors of Bristol (1774), said an MP owes voters their judgment, not blind obedience. Parliament is a deliberative assembly of one nation, not a congress of ambassadors. Delegate The representative carries out the instructions of the constituents. This is close to the Rousseau-style idea that the people's will cannot be replaced. Mandate A party wins office on a manifesto, and voters expect it to be carried out. This is the main working model in party-based systems. Real politicians mix all three. Party discipline in India pushes MPs towards the party line, especially after the Tenth Schedule.
Pitkin's four meanings of representation

Hanna Pitkin , The Concept of Representation (1967), showed that representation has several meanings. Formal : authorisation by election, and accountability afterwards. Descriptive : the legislature mirrors the population, with women, minorities and classes present in proportion. Symbolic : the representative stands for the nation or group, as a flag does. Substantive : acting in the interests of the represented. Later writers like Anne Phillips ( The Politics of Presence , 1995) argue that groups with a history of exclusion need to be present in the assembly. This is the case for quotas. Electoral systems matter too. First-past-the-post tends towards two parties ( Duverger's law , 1951), while proportional systems give a more mirror-like result.
Strains in representative democracy

Distance : elected politicians form a professional class, so voters feel remote from them. Money and lobbies : campaign finance and corporate lobbying tilt policy to the rich. Low turnout and apathy : many do not vote. Populism : leaders claim to speak for "the real people" against elites and institutions. Minority winners : first-past-the-post can give a majority of seats on a minority of votes. Remedies suggested include compulsory voting, proportional representation, campaign finance reform, and more direct instruments such as referendums, recall and citizens' assemblies.
Participatory democracy and its roots

Participatory democracy holds that people should share directly in making decisions that shape their lives: in neighbourhoods, workplaces, schools and the state. Voting alone is not enough. Its roots lie in Rousseau (people make the laws), J.S. Mill (participation educates) and G.D.H. Cole ( Social Theory , 1920), who wanted self-government in workplaces and guilds. It revived with the New Left and student movements in the 1960s. The Port Huron Statement (1962) of Students for a Democratic Society called for participation. The main theoretical works are by Carole Pateman and C.B. Macpherson. Later, Benjamin Barber, Strong Democracy (1984), called representative democracy "thin". He wanted a "strong" democracy of talk, civic action and local assemblies.
Pateman, Macpherson and the ladder of participation

Carole Pateman, Participation and Democratic Theory (1970) Participation develops democratic skills and a sense of responsibility. Workplace democracy is the training school. Participation is also a way to make decisions more accepted. C.B. Macpherson, The Life and Times of Liberal Democracy (1977) He proposed a pyramid of councils: direct democracy at the base (neighbourhood and workplace), with delegates sent up to higher levels, topped by a national assembly. He admitted two hurdles: citizens' apathy under unequal society, and the belief that there is no alternative to the existing system. Sherry Arnstein proposed a "ladder of citizen participation" (1969). Its rungs range from manipulation and tokenism at the bottom to partnership and citizen control at the top. It is a useful test of whether participation is real.
Tools of direct and participatory democracy

These tools bring citizens back between elections. Switzerland uses referendums and initiatives often. The Brazilian city of Porto Alegre began participatory budgeting in 1989, and the idea spread to many cities. The 2016 Brexit referendum shows the risk: a close, complex question can split a country. Critics say participation is time-heavy, favours the educated and well-off, and can be captured by organised minorities.
Can the two models be combined?

Most scholars see the two as partners, not rivals. A common view is that representative institutions give the framework, while participatory practice deepens it at local level. Points in favour of mixing: Participation at local scale is practical, with face-to-face groups. It trains citizens, which improves the quality of representative democracy. Representative bodies can then take decisions across a large area with a better feel of public opinion. Points of caution: participation can be tokenistic, it can duplicate inequality, and some decisions need expertise and speed. Fung and Wright, Deepening Democracy (2003), study such "empowered participatory governance" experiments, including Porto Alegre and Kerala.
Participation in India

Gandhi wanted village republics ( gram swaraj ) built from below. Article 40 (a Directive Principle) asks the State to organise village panchayats. The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992, in force 1993) gave constitutional status to rural and urban local bodies (Part IX and Part IXA). They provide for gram sabhas, regular elections every five years, State Election Commissions, State Finance Commissions and reservation of seats for SC, ST and at least one-third for women. Transparency tools: the Right to Information Act, 2005, and social audits of rural works. Kerala's People's Plan Campaign (1996) devolved a share of the State plan to local bodies. NOTA was introduced after PUCL v Union of India (2013). The 106th Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023) reserves one-third of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats for women, to apply after the next delimitation. Weak spots: elected women's roles are sometimes taken over by male relatives ("sarpanch-pati"), and local bodies lack funds.
How to answer

"Participatory democracy is the answer to the crisis of representative democracy." Discuss. Distinguish between representative and participatory democracy. Examine Pateman and Macpherson on participation. Assess the role of local self-government in deepening democracy in India. Structure: set out the problem of scale and the representative model, with Burke and Pitkin. Name the strains. Present the participatory school with Pateman, Macpherson and Barber, then the tools. Argue that the two are complementary. Use the 73rd and 74th Amendments with their limits as the Indian case, and end with a balanced verdict.
Deliberative Democracy
From counting votes to weighing reasons

In the older models, democracy is about aggregating preferences: add up votes, and the biggest group wins. But what if the preferences are poorly informed, or never tested against other views? Deliberative democracy says legitimate decisions come from public reasoning , in which free and equal citizens give reasons and listen. Voting comes after discussion, not instead of it. The theory rose in the 1980s and 1990s, partly as a response to elitist and market-like models (Schumpeter) and as a way to handle deep disagreement. It is now one of the most active areas of democratic theory, and a frequent exam topic. Know Habermas, Rawls, Cohen, Gutmann and Thompson, Fishkin, and the critics Young and Mouffe.
The core of the theory

Deliberative democrats share four ideas. Reasons, not force : laws must be justifiable by arguments all can accept, not just by power or numbers. Equality : everyone affected can take part, with an equal voice. Openness to change : people can revise their views when they hear better arguments. Public-spirited outcome : talk pushes people to think of common good, not only self-interest. Contrast with the older aggregative model. There, preferences are given and fixed, and the task is to count them fairly. In the deliberative model, preferences are formed and changed through discussion. The term was coined by Joseph Bessette in 1980. Bernard Manin's 1987 article "On Legitimacy and Political Deliberation" helped launch the field.
Habermas: the public sphere and the ideal speech situation

Jurgen Habermas is the central figure. In The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (1962), he traced how 18th-century coffee houses and newspapers created a public sphere where private citizens debated the state. He feared mass media and commerce later weakened it. In The Theory of Communicative Action (1981), he separated communicative action (seeking understanding) from strategic action (seeking success). He described an ideal speech situation : everyone may speak, no one is coerced, and only "the force of the better argument" counts. In Between Facts and Norms (1992), he applied this to law and democracy. Law is legitimate if all affected could agree to it in rational discourse. This is the discourse theory of democracy.
Rawls and public reason; Cohen's ideal

Rawls, Political Liberalism (1993) In a society with reasonable disagreement, citizens should justify basic political decisions with public reason : arguments that others, whatever their faith, could accept. A believer should not say "my scripture says so" and stop there. Joshua Cohen, "Deliberation and Democratic Legitimacy" (1989) An ideal deliberative procedure is one where free and equal participants give reasons and accept outcomes supported by the best reasons. Cohen links legitimacy to this procedure. Both writers come from the liberal tradition. Rawls stresses the content of public reason; Habermas stresses the procedure. Their debate (1995) is in the Journal of Philosophy .
Gutmann and Thompson; Fishkin; Dryzek

Amy Gutmann and Dennis Thompson, Democracy and Disagreement (1996) Citizens should deliberate under the principles of reciprocity (offer reasons others can accept), publicity and accountability . Moral disagreement is permanent, so mutual respect is key. James Fishkin, Democracy and Deliberation (1991) He designed deliberative polling . A random sample of citizens is given balanced information, discusses in small groups with experts, and is polled before and after. Views often shift. The method shows what the public would think if it were well-informed. John Dryzek, Deliberative Democracy and Beyond (2000) Dryzek stresses discursive democracy , including protest, civil society and social movements, not only formal assemblies.
Deliberation in practice

Citizens' assemblies : randomly chosen citizens study an issue and make recommendations. Ireland's Citizens' Assembly (2016-18) discussed abortion and led to the 2018 referendum that repealed the Eighth Amendment. Deliberative polls have been held in many countries. Participatory forums such as Porto Alegre's budget councils. Parliamentary committees that hear experts and the public are a deliberative space, too. Online forums may widen deliberation. Because participants are chosen by lot, these bodies echo Athens. This is sometimes called mini-publics .
Is the ideal fair?

Iris Marion Young , Inclusion and Democracy (2000): the stress on cool, rational argument favours the educated and dominant. She would add greeting, rhetoric and storytelling as valid forms of speech, so that marginalised groups are heard. Chantal Mouffe , The Democratic Paradox (2000): politics is about conflict, not consensus. She proposes agonistic pluralism , where opponents are treated as adversaries, not enemies. A search for rational consensus hides power. Cass Sunstein warned that like-minded groups get more extreme (group polarisation), so online echo chambers can worsen deliberation. Practical doubts : it is slow, small in scale, and who sets the agenda? Defenders say the theory is a standard to judge real politics, not a claim that it already exists.
Deliberation versus aggregation, and decision

Is deliberation a replacement for voting? Most writers say no. Votes are needed to close a debate. The question is the quality of what comes before it. Habermas separates the informal public sphere (opinion formation in media and civil society) from formal decision bodies (parliament). Opinion flows from the first to the second through elections and law. This is his "two-track" model. Test questions for a real system: Are there open spaces for debate (press, universities, civil society)? Are the legislature's debates real, or just party theatre? Do rulers explain decisions with reasons? The theory therefore gives a good yardstick to judge Indian Parliament's functioning.
India's deliberative traditions and gaps

Ancient : Buddhist councils and the sangha's rules of debate. Ashoka's Rock Edict XII urges listening to each other's doctrines and restraint in speech. Amartya Sen , The Argumentative Indian (2005), argues that India has a long tradition of public debate and heterodoxy, which supports democracy. Constituent Assembly (1946-49): about three years of debate, 11 sessions, 2 years 11 months 18 days in all, producing the Constitution after discussion of each clause. Gram sabhas are meant to be forums of local deliberation. Many meet rarely or have low attendance. Parliament : frequent disruption has cut debate time. Standing committees and pre-legislative consultation (2014 policy) help, but many bills pass with little scrutiny. Media and social media : echo chambers and misinformation strain the public sphere.
How to answer

"Deliberative democracy shifts focus from voting to reasoning." Discuss. Explain Habermas's idea of the public sphere and ideal speech situation. Critically examine the feminist and agonistic critiques of deliberative democracy. Is Indian democracy deliberative? Illustrate. Structure: start with aggregation versus deliberation. Give the core features, then Habermas, Rawls's public reason and Cohen, and practical designs (Fishkin, assemblies). Move to critiques by Young and Mouffe. For the Indian angle, use Sen, the Constituent Assembly and the decline in parliamentary debate. Finish by saying deliberation and voting complement each other.
Power and its Three Faces
Power is the core concept of politics

Some scholars call politics the study of power. Who has it? How is it used? Is it always bad? Where is it hidden? These questions run through all the units of Paper I. The syllabus asks about "power, hegemony, ideology and legitimacy". This lesson covers power . The next two cover hegemony and ideology, then authority and legitimacy. The standard way to teach power is through the three faces debate: Dahl, Bachrach and Baratz, and Lukes. Each critic said the earlier view missed something deeper. Add Foucault and Arendt for modern depth. Examiners ask both for the three-faces framework and for its application to Indian politics.
What is power?

Basic definitions: Max Weber , Economy and Society (1922): power is the chance of a person to carry out their will even against the resistance of others. Robert Dahl (1957): A has power over B to the extent that A can get B to do something B would not otherwise do. Hannah Arendt , On Violence (1970): power is the human ability to act in concert, so it needs a group. Violence is different. It is a tool that can destroy power. Two ideas of power: power over (domination, A against B) and power to or with (the capacity to act together, as Arendt and Parsons thought). Related terms: force (physical coercion), influence (persuasion), authority (power seen as rightful) and manipulation .
The three faces at a glance

Each face goes deeper than the last. The first sees only the visible fight. The second sees the hidden fight. The third sees the fight that never starts because people have been shaped to accept things as they are. Lukes presents the third dimension as including the first two, so a full study of power looks at all three.
First face: Dahl and the pluralists

Robert Dahl studied New Haven in Who Governs? (1961). His method: look at concrete decisions on real issues (urban renewal, schools, party nominations) and see whose preferences won. He found that no single elite won everywhere. Assumptions of the first face: Power can be observed in behaviour , in open conflict. Interests are what people say they want ( subjective interests ). If people do not take part, they are apathetic and content. Critics objected that this view could not see the power that works behind the scenes. That led to the second face.
Second face: Bachrach and Baratz

Peter Bachrach and Morton Baratz , "Two Faces of Power" ( American Political Science Review , 1962), argued that power has a second face: agenda control . A can stop an issue from being raised at all, so B's grievances never reach the table. They called this non-decision-making . It rests on a mobilisation of bias , a term from E.E. Schattschneider: institutions and rules that favour some issues over others. Methods include: Threats and sanctions. Rules of procedure and committee control. Delay, and framing issues as "out of bounds". Co-opting leaders. Example: a company that hushes up pollution complaints, or a legislature that never takes up land reform. Lukes's complaint: they still stayed with observable conflict. Bachrach and Baratz also held that without an observable grievance there is no non-decision.
Third face: Lukes

Steven Lukes , Power: A Radical View (1974, 2nd ed. 2005), added a third dimension: power to shape people's perceptions, preferences and beliefs . The most effective power stops conflict from arising by making people want what the powerful want. "Is it not the supreme exercise of power to get another or others to have the desires you want them to have?" Lukes, Power: A Radical View (1974) This ties to Gramsci's hegemony and Marx's ideology. People may not see their real interests , which Lukes defined as what they would choose if they could do so freely and with full information. John Gaventa , Power and Powerlessness (1980), tested this on Appalachian coal miners. Long inequality bred acceptance, which he saw as the third face at work. Critics: how can an outsider judge someone's "real interests"? That risks elitism and paternalism.
Foucault: power as relations, not possession

Michel Foucault (1926-84) changed the debate. In Discipline and Punish (1975) and The History of Sexuality , vol. 1 (1976), he argued: Power is not something held by a ruler. It is everywhere , in relationships, institutions (prisons, schools, hospitals) and daily habits. It is "capillary". Power is productive , not only repressive. It creates knowledge, categories and identities (the "criminal", the "patient"). Power/knowledge : knowledge and power are bound together. Who defines what counts as true holds power. Discipline and surveillance : Bentham's Panopticon is the model. People who might be watched police themselves. Biopower : states manage life itself, through health, census and population policy. Where there is power there is resistance . Foucault does not offer a simple theory, but a way to see power.
Other views: Marx, Mills, soft power

Marxist : power flows from control of the means of production. The state serves the ruling class. Elite theorists (Mills, 1956): power sits in a small circle. Mills added that institutional position gives power. Michael Mann , The Sources of Social Power (1986): four sources, ideological, economic, military and political (IEMP). Joseph Nye : hard power (coercion, payment) versus soft power (attraction through culture, values, policy), coined in Bound to Lead (1990) and developed in Soft Power (2004). Combining both is "smart power". This matters for Paper II. Feminists highlight patriarchal power in family and body.
Power in Indian society and politics

Face 1 : open contests, as in elections, legislative votes and court cases. Face 2 : issues kept off the agenda, e.g., manual scavenging or agricultural labour rights, often ignored in debates. Dominant castes and landlords controlled village councils. M.N. Srinivas's dominant caste (1959) explains local control. Face 3 : the internalised caste order. Ambedkar's "graded inequality" shows how hierarchy gets accepted. Gender norms also work in this way. Foucault : surveillance and data, such as Aadhaar. The Supreme Court in Puttaswamy (2018) upheld Aadhaar with limits. Spyware claims over Pegasus (2021) raised the issue of state surveillance. Gandhi offered a different view: real power rests in non-cooperation, because rulers need people's consent. Kautilya's danda (coercion) is the older state power. Soft power : India's yoga, cinema and diaspora.
How to answer

"Power has three faces." Elaborate. Compare the pluralist and radical views of power. Examine Foucault's contribution to the understanding of power. Distinguish between power, authority and influence. Structure: define power (Weber, Dahl). Present the three faces in order, each with author, work, method and critique. Add Foucault as a break from the 'power over' idea. Use Arendt to contrast power and violence. Illustrate with an Indian case such as caste or agenda control in village councils. End by saying the faces are layers, and each shows what the others miss.
Hegemony and Ideology
Why do people obey without being forced?

A ruler cannot guard every citizen with a soldier. Most rule works because people accept it, or even like it. How does this acceptance get made? Two key concepts answer: ideology and hegemony . Ideology is a system of ideas that makes sense of the world and guides action. Hegemony is leadership by consent: a ruling group wins the approval of others, so its interests look like everyone's. Together they extend the study of power from visible force to culture, schools, media, religion and common sense. This is the third face of power (Lukes), brought out in the last lesson. Both appear regularly in the exam, especially Gramsci, Althusser and the Frankfurt School. A good answer compares the Marxist view with non-Marxist ones.
What is ideology?

The word was coined by the French thinker Destutt de Tracy (1796) as a "science of ideas". Napoleon mocked such thinkers as "ideologues". Since then it has gone through several meanings. Neutral : any belief system about how society should be (liberalism, socialism). Critical (Marx) : ideas that distort reality and hide class domination. False consciousness is the later term (Engels, 1893). Sociological (Mannheim) : all thought is shaped by social position ( Ideology and Utopia , 1929). He distinguished ideology (ideas defending the order) from utopia (ideas challenging it). Heywood says an ideology has three elements: a view of the existing order, a model of the desired future and a way to get there.
Marx: ideology and the ruling class

In The German Ideology (written 1845-46, published 1932), Marx and Engels wrote that the ideas of the ruling class are, in every age, the ruling ideas. The class that controls material production also controls the production of ideas. Ideology therefore serves to: Present class interests as universal ("the national interest"). Make existing arrangements seem natural and eternal (e.g., private property, the market). Hide exploitation : a wage looks like a fair exchange. Marx also wrote of commodity fetishism ( Capital , 1867): social relations appear as relations between things. Religion, he wrote, is the "opium of the people" (1844). Later Lukacs , History and Class Consciousness (1923), developed reification and said the proletariat could reach true class consciousness.
Gramsci: hegemony

Antonio Gramsci wrote the Prison Notebooks (1929-35) in Mussolini's jail. He asked why revolution had succeeded in Russia but failed in the West. His answer: in the West, the ruling class holds power through hegemony , cultural and moral leadership in civil society , not just force. The state is "hegemony protected by the armour of coercion". Ideas become common sense , accepted without question. The working class must build a counter-hegemony through a long war of position (a struggle for culture and institutions), not only a quick war of manoeuvre (direct assault). Organic intellectuals arise from each class and give it self-awareness. A historic bloc joins economic base and ideology. See lesson 0-9-7 for more.
Althusser and the Frankfurt School

Louis Althusser, "Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses" (1970) Distinguished Repressive State Apparatuses (army, police, courts) from Ideological State Apparatuses (schools, churches, media, family). The school is the chief ISA of modern capitalism. Ideology "interpellates" individuals: it hails them and makes them see themselves as subjects with certain roles. Ideology has a material existence in practices. Frankfurt School Horkheimer and Adorno, Dialectic of Enlightenment (1944): the culture industry (films, radio) makes people passive consumers. Herbert Marcuse, One-Dimensional Man (1964): advanced capitalism flattens critical thought through consumerism. His separate essay "Repressive Tolerance" (1965) argued that tolerance in such a society can shield domination. Both go beyond Marx in treating culture as a major site of domination.
Can the powerless resist hegemony?

If ideas can make people accept their lot, is resistance possible? Several writers say yes. James C. Scott , Weapons of the Weak (1985), studied Malaysian peasants. They resist through foot-dragging, gossip, petty theft and sabotage, not open revolt. Scott's Domination and the Arts of Resistance (1990) describes a public transcript (the polite face shown to the powerful) and a hidden transcript (what the subordinate say among themselves). Thus apparent consent can hide disbelief. Gramsci : common sense is contradictory. People hold both ruling ideas and ideas from their own experience. This opens a gap for a counter-hegemony. Foucault : where there is power, there is resistance. Feminist and Dalit movements challenge common sense by renaming experience, e.g., "sexual harassment", "manual scavenging" or "atrocity". Hegemony is never complete. It must be renewed constantly, and it can be lost.
End of ideology? End of history?

Daniel Bell , The End of Ideology (1960): in the post-war West, the big ideological battles had faded, replaced by technical, welfare-state consensus. Francis Fukuyama , "The End of History?" (1989) and The End of History and the Last Man (1992): after the Cold War, liberal democracy has no serious rival. Reply : new ideologies returned. Samuel Huntington's Clash of Civilizations (1996), religious fundamentalism, populism, nationalism and environmentalism show that ideology did not end. Post-Marxists : Laclau and Mouffe, Hegemony and Socialist Strategy (1985), see hegemony as a contest of discourses among many groups, not only classes. Note too that claiming "no ideology" is itself an ideological move, as Marxists say.
Hegemony in international relations

The term is also used in Paper II. Hegemonic stability theory (Charles Kindleberger, The World in Depression , 1973; Robert Gilpin, War and Change in World Politics , 1981): an open world economy needs one leading power to provide public goods. Neo-Gramscian IR (Robert Cox, 1981, "Social Forces, States and World Orders"): hegemony is a world order built on consent as well as power, with international institutions (IMF, World Bank, WTO) spreading dominant ideas. Mearsheimer defines hegemon in offensive realism as the sole great power. Edward Said , Orientalism (1978): Western knowledge of the East served imperial domination, a cultural hegemony using Foucault's power/knowledge.
Hegemony and ideology in India

Caste : Phule, Gulamgiri (1873), and Ambedkar, Annihilation of Caste (1936), saw caste as an ideology of Brahmanical dominance, made to seem sacred and natural. Ambedkar's "graded inequality" explains why the oppressed rarely unite. Colonial : Macaulay's Minute (1835) aimed to create a class of Indians loyal in taste and opinion. Ranajit Guha, Dominance without Hegemony (1997), argued the British Raj ruled by dominance (coercion) because it never won Indian consent. Subaltern Studies (from 1982) drew on Gramsci to study peasant politics. Nationalism : Congress under Gandhi built a broad hegemonic bloc (a "passive revolution", said Partha Chatterjee after Gramsci). Today : debates on cultural nationalism, media power and social media narratives are often framed as contests of hegemony and counter-hegemony. Gramsci is a favourite lens in these essays, but present evidence from both sides.
How to answer

"Hegemony is the key concept in Gramsci's political thought." Discuss. Compare the Marxist and non-Marxist views of ideology. Examine the role of Ideological State Apparatuses in maintaining capitalism. Is the 'end of ideology' thesis valid? Structure: define ideology and give its three senses. Give the Marxist line (German Ideology, false consciousness) and then Gramsci's hegemony with its main terms. Add Althusser, the Frankfurt School and Mannheim. Take the 'end of ideology' debate (Bell, Fukuyama) as the critique. Close with Indian examples such as caste ideology and Guha's dominance without hegemony.
Authority and Legitimacy: Weber and After
Power that people accept as rightful

Take two cases. A robber with a gun gets your wallet. A police officer in uniform asks you to move your car, and you do. Both have power over you, but only the second has authority . You obey the officer because you think the request is rightful . Authority is power that is seen as legitimate. Legitimacy is the rightfulness of rule, the grounds on which people accept that a government has the right to command. Why does it matter? Rule resting on legitimacy is cheaper, more stable and more durable than rule resting on force. Governments that lose legitimacy face protest, collapse or revolution. This lesson is built around Max Weber and what came after: Beetham, Lipset, Easton, Habermas and Arendt. It links directly to the Indian Emergency and judicial legitimacy.
Power, authority, legitimacy, influence

Power : the ability to get others to do something, even against their will. Force : physical coercion. Influence : changing views by persuasion, with no threat. Authority : the right to command, with a matching duty to obey. Authority is institutional (it comes with an office, like a judge) or personal (it comes from character, like a respected elder). Legitimacy : the moral or legal basis on which authority is accepted. Authority is the exercise; legitimacy is the justification. Note the Latin root: legitimus means lawful. A lawful government may still be seen as illegitimate, as in colonial or one-party rule. A government may be legitimate in the people's eyes but not strictly legal, as in some revolutions. Rousseau saw the point early. The strongest is never strong enough unless they turn force into right and obedience into duty.
Weber: the state and its legitimacy

Max Weber (1864-1920) was a German sociologist. In his lecture "Politics as a Vocation" (1919) he defined the state as the human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory. The key word is legitimate . Many groups use force, but only the state's use is seen as rightful. For Weber, rule that depends only on force or self-interest is unstable. Every system of domination tries to cultivate belief in its legitimacy. He studied why people obey, in Economy and Society (published 1922 after his death). He used the ideal type method, that is, pure models that sharpen analysis, though real regimes mix them.
Weber's three types of authority

Traditional : rulers obey custom and are obeyed from habit. Example: monarchy, caste elders. Weakness: change is hard. Charismatic : the leader is believed to have exceptional gifts. It is unstable and faces a routinisation of charisma after the leader dies, turning into tradition or rules. Examples: Gandhi, Napoleon, prophets. Legal-rational : obedience is to impersonal rules and to offices, not persons. Its staff is the bureaucracy : fixed duties, hierarchy, written rules, merit-based appointment. Weber also feared its "iron cage" of rationality.
After Weber: Beetham and Lipset

David Beetham, The Legitimation of Power (1991) Beetham says Weber reduced legitimacy to belief. Legitimacy has three levels: (1) legality , power acquired and exercised by the rules; (2) justifiability , the rules fit shared beliefs about who should rule and why; (3) legitimation , visible acts of consent such as elections, oaths and mass participation. A regime may be seen as lacking if any level fails. S.M. Lipset, Political Man (1960) Legitimacy is the capacity of a system to engender the belief that existing institutions are the most appropriate. Stability depends on both legitimacy and effectiveness . A regime that performs badly for long may lose legitimacy. The key point: Weber sees legitimacy as a matter of what people believe . Beetham treats it as something a scholar can judge, by checking rules, beliefs and consent.
Easton, Habermas, Arendt

David Easton, A Systems Analysis of Political Life (1965) Two kinds of support for a political system. Specific support depends on outputs that satisfy people. Diffuse support is a deeper goodwill towards the system, a reservoir that lasts through bad times. Jurgen Habermas, Legitimation Crisis (1973) Late capitalist states must keep the economy growing and also win mass loyalty. If they cannot meet demands, a legitimation crisis follows. He argued that legitimacy needs a rational discourse among citizens (see deliberative democracy). Hannah Arendt, "What is Authority?" (1954, in Between Past and Future, 1961) Authority needs no force and no argument. It rests on acknowledged hierarchy. Force means authority has failed.
Sources of legitimacy and its crises

Rulers have claimed legitimacy through: Tradition : divine right, descent. Consent : the social contract tradition (Locke, Rousseau) and elections. Law and procedure : constitutions and courts. Performance : growth, welfare, security. This is a major source for China's one-party state. Ideology : nationalism, religion, revolution. Charisma : a popular leader. Signs of a crisis: low turnout, mass protest, civil disobedience, rising use of force, coups, secession and refusal to pay taxes. Responses include reform, elections, constitutional change, or, in bad cases, repression. A distinction: legitimacy of origin (how the government came to power) and legitimacy of exercise (how it governs). A regime can fail on the second after passing the first.
Is Weber enough?

Belief is not everything : people may believe because they were manipulated. Marxists and Gramsci point out that belief can be the product of hegemony. Habermas asks whether the beliefs would survive free reasoning. Ideal types blur : real systems mix types. Modern leaders can be both charismatic and legal-rational. Legitimacy versus justice : a widely accepted regime, such as a colonial or caste order, can still be unjust. Normative theory (Rawls, Raz) asks whether authority is justified , not only believed in. Anarchists (Robert Paul Wolff, In Defense of Anarchism , 1970): no authority can override personal autonomy. Global legitimacy : who authorises the UN Security Council or the IMF? Their authority is contested.
Authority and legitimacy in India

All three types exist side by side: traditional authority (caste panchayats, religious heads), charismatic (Gandhi, J.P. Narayan) and legal-rational (the Constitution, the Election Commission, the civil services). Constitution as source: "We, the people" in the Preamble. Elections since 1951-52 are the main act of legitimation (Beetham's third level). Emergency : on 12 June 1975 the Allahabad High Court ( Raj Narain v Indira Nehru Gandhi ) set aside Indira Gandhi's election. On 25 June 1975 the Emergency began, and lasted 21 months. In March 1977 voters rejected it. It shows a crisis of legitimacy and its repair through the ballot. Judiciary : in the Fourth Judges Case (2015) the Supreme Court struck down the NJAC amendment. Court authority rests on public trust. Contested legitimacy : insurgency areas, and anti-corruption protests such as the 2011 Lokpal agitation. Constitutional morality , urged by Ambedkar, is the idea that institutions must respect the spirit of the Constitution.
How to answer

"Legitimacy is the cement of political order." Discuss with reference to Weber. Explain Weber's typology of authority. Is it relevant to modern India? Distinguish between power, authority and legitimacy. Examine the idea of legitimation crisis. Structure: define the four terms in a short table. Explain Weber's definition of the state and his three types, with an Indian example for each. Then bring in the post-Weber critics (Beetham, Lipset, Easton, Habermas) to deepen it. Add the normative question of justice. For India use the Emergency and the 1977 election, the Constitution and the NJAC ruling. Conclude that legitimacy needs both belief and performance.
Liberalism
The ideology that built the modern world

Liberalism is the dominant ideology of the modern West and the base of most written constitutions, including India's. It puts the individual first and asks what limits should bind the state. It is also the ideology that the others argue with. Marxists attack its idea of the market. Conservatives attack its optimism about reason. Feminists attack its public-private split. Communitarians attack its view of the self. In Paper I, expect questions on classical versus modern liberalism, the neoliberal turn, negative and positive liberty, and liberal critiques. Gauba, Heywood and Bhargava are the standard sources.
Five core ideas

Individualism : the individual is prior to society and has equal moral worth. Liberty : freedom is the supreme political value. Interference needs justification. Reason : people can improve their lives by using reason, so progress is possible. Equality : formal equality before law and equal rights. Liberals disagree on how far to go beyond it. Limited government and consent : power must rest on consent (social contract), be bound by law and be divided (rule of law, constitutionalism, separation of powers). To these add toleration (rooted in the religious wars, Locke's Letter Concerning Toleration , 1689) and, in most forms, a market economy with private property.
From classical to modern to neoliberal

Liberalism is not one doctrine but a family. It changed as industrial capitalism produced poverty and conflict. Classical : free markets, minimal state, "negative" liberty. Modern (also called social or welfare liberalism): the state should enable people to be free, with education, health and social security. Neoliberal : a return to markets and a smaller state, from the 1970s.
Classical liberals: Locke, Smith, Bentham, Mill

John Locke, Two Treatises of Government (1689) Natural rights to life, liberty and property. Government exists by consent to protect them. If it betrays this trust, people may resist. Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations (1776) Market exchange, guided by the "invisible hand", can serve the public good. The state's tasks are defence, justice and certain public works. J.S. Mill, On Liberty (1859) The harm principle : the only reason to interfere with a person's liberty against their will is to prevent harm to others. Free speech matters even when the opinion is false, because it tests truth. Mill also showed how classical liberalism begins to turn social: he backed women's rights and worker cooperatives. Bentham's utilitarianism served as another base for reform and for the rule of law.
Modern liberals: Green, Hobhouse, Keynes

By the late 19th century, industrial poverty made "freedom of contract" look hollow to many. Modern liberals redefined liberty. T.H. Green (1836-82), the British idealist, argued that real freedom is the power to do something worthwhile. The state should remove obstacles such as ignorance and squalor. This is the root of positive liberty in liberal thought. L.T. Hobhouse , Liberalism (1911), defended social reform. J.M. Keynes , The General Theory (1936), said governments should manage demand to prevent mass unemployment. William Beveridge 's 1942 report planned the British welfare state. The American New Deal (1930s) and the post-war welfare state were the practical results. Rawls and Dworkin are the best-known modern liberal philosophers.
Two concepts of liberty

Isaiah Berlin , "Two Concepts of Liberty" (1958), gave the standard terms. Negative liberty Freedom from interference. How much area is left free? Classical liberals and libertarians prefer it. Positive liberty Freedom to be self-directed and fulfil one's potential. It asks about the conditions of choice, like education and income. Berlin feared the positive view could be abused. A ruler might claim to know people's "true self" and force them to be free. Soviet and fascist states did just that, he thought. He defended negative liberty as safer and admitted that values like liberty and equality can conflict ( value pluralism ).
Neoliberalism: Hayek, Friedman, Nozick

The 1970s brought stagflation and doubts about Keynes. Thinkers revived market liberalism. F.A. Hayek , The Road to Serfdom (1944) and The Constitution of Liberty (1960): central planning ends in tyranny. Prices carry knowledge no planner can have. "Social justice" is a mirage. Milton Friedman , Capitalism and Freedom (1962): economic freedom is a condition of political freedom. He backed monetarism and school vouchers. Robert Nozick , Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974): the minimal state only. In politics, this became Thatcherism (UK, from 1979) and Reaganism (USA, from 1981), and later the "Washington Consensus": privatisation, deregulation, trade opening and fiscal discipline.
Critiques of liberalism

Marxist : liberal rights, such as property and contract, hide class power. Formal equality sits on top of economic inequality (Marx, On the Jewish Question , 1844). Conservative : abstract individualism ignores tradition and community (Burke, Oakeshott). Communitarian : the liberal self is "unencumbered" (Sandel, MacIntyre). Feminist : the public-private divide leaves the family outside justice (Okin; Pateman, The Sexual Contract , 1988). Multicultural and postcolonial : liberalism claims universality but carried empire. Mill defended British rule in India for "backward" peoples. Environmental : endless growth conflicts with ecological limits. Defenders reply that liberalism can absorb these challenges, as modern liberalism did with welfare and rights.
Liberalism in India

Early liberals : Raja Ram Mohan Roy, then the Moderates in Congress (Naoroji, Gokhale, Ranade), who sought constitutional reform. The National Liberal Federation was set up in 1919. Constitution : Preamble (liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship), fundamental rights in Part III, judicial review and independent courts. Yet it mixes liberal rights with socialist directives in Part IV. Economy : Nehru's mixed economy until 1991, when the July 1991 reforms (Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh) brought liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation. Courts : Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down Section 66A of the IT Act on free speech. K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) made privacy a fundamental right. Navtej Singh Johar (2018) decriminalised consensual same-sex relations.
Is liberalism in retreat?

Since the 2008 financial crisis, liberalism has faced doubts. Populist movements have grown, inequality has risen in many states, and some leaders speak of "illiberal democracy" (a phrase popularised by Fareed Zakaria, 1997, and used by Viktor Orban in 2014). Defenders, such as Fukuyama in Liberalism and Its Discontents (2022), argue that liberalism needs to be renewed, not abandoned. Critics like Patrick Deneen, Why Liberalism Failed (2018), say its individualism wore away community. For the exam, a balanced answer notes that liberalism has changed repeatedly and that its core, the protection of individual rights under law, remains attractive and contested.
How to answer

"Liberalism is a political ideology in transition." Discuss. Distinguish between classical and modern liberalism. Examine the neoliberal critique of the welfare state. Explain the concepts of negative and positive liberty. Which is more important? Structure: define liberalism by its core ideas. Trace the three phases with thinkers and books. Use Berlin to deal with liberty. Present the critiques from the left, the right, communitarians and feminists. Add India: the Preamble and Part III, 1991, and the privacy and speech cases. End with a verdict on whether liberalism is adaptable.
Socialism and Marxism
The ideology of the many who work

Socialism arose as a protest against the misery and inequality of early industrial capitalism. It dreams of a society based on cooperation and shared ownership, not private profit. Within it, Marxism is the most powerful and most-asked branch. Marx's theory shaped revolutions in Russia (1917), China (1949), Cuba and elsewhere, and still shapes academic debate. The syllabus asks you to understand the family of socialisms: utopian, Marxist, Leninist, revisionist and democratic socialism. You also need to explain why the USSR collapsed (1991) and what remains of socialism today. The India link is strong: Nehruvian socialism, the Preamble and the Directive Principles.
Core socialist ideas

Community : humans are social beings, and their nature is shaped by relationships. Cooperation over competition. Equality , especially of outcome and condition. Socialists want to reduce class divisions. Need : goods should be shared according to need, not only merit or market value. Common ownership : the main means of production (land, factories, banks) should be owned in common, by the state, cooperatives or the community. They split over means (revolution or reform) and ends (full communism or a regulated market with a strong welfare state). Heywood groups them as fundamentalist (abolish capitalism) and revisionist (reform it).
Utopian and early socialists

The word "socialism" appeared in the 1820s-30s. Early thinkers imagined model communities. Robert Owen (1771-1858), mill owner, built the New Lanark model and the New Harmony community in the USA. He urged cooperative villages. Charles Fourier (1772-1837), French thinker who planned communities called phalansteries. Henri de Saint-Simon (1760-1825), who wanted society run by scientists and industrialists. Marx and Engels called them utopian : they appealed to reason and goodwill but had no theory of class struggle or of how change would occur. Their own approach, they said, was scientific socialism .
Marx and Engels: the method

Karl Marx (1818-83) and Friedrich Engels (1820-95) wrote The Communist Manifesto (1848). Marx's later masterwork is Capital , Volume 1 (1867). Historical materialism : the way a society produces its material needs (the base ) shapes its laws, politics and ideas (the superstructure ). History moves through stages, each driven by conflict between classes: ancient slavery, feudalism, capitalism, then socialism and communism. The Manifesto begins: the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles. Details are in the Western thought lesson on Marx (0-9-6).
Marx on capitalism and the end goal

Surplus value : workers produce more value than they are paid for, and capitalists keep the difference. This is exploitation. Alienation : under capitalism, workers are cut off from their product, their work, other people and their human nature ( Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts , 1844). Crises : competition, falling profit rates and overproduction create recurring crises. The working class ( proletariat ) grows and becomes conscious. Revolution : the proletariat takes power. A transitional dictatorship of the proletariat follows ( Critique of the Gotha Programme , 1875). Communism : a classless, stateless society that works on the principle "from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs".
Lenin and the Russian turn

V.I. Lenin (1870-1924) adapted Marxism to a backward, peasant country. What Is To Be Done? (1902): workers alone reach only trade-union consciousness. A disciplined vanguard party of professional revolutionaries must lead. The party's rule of open debate but binding decisions was later formalised as democratic centralism (1905-06). Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (1916): capitalism survives by exporting capital to colonies. War among powers is a result. The State and Revolution (1917): the bourgeois state must be smashed, not taken over. The Bolshevik seizure of power came in October 1917. Stalin then built "socialism in one country", with forced collectivisation and heavy state control. Trotsky argued for permanent world revolution. Mao relied on the peasantry (China, 1949).
Reformist socialism and social democracy

Eduard Bernstein, Evolutionary Socialism (1899) The revisionist. Capitalism was not collapsing, the middle class was not disappearing, and workers had the vote. So socialism should be won by gradual reform and democracy. Kautsky and Luxemburg opposed him. The Fabians (founded 1884) Sidney and Beatrice Webb, G.B. Shaw. Gradual, educative change through Parliament. The Labour Party grew from this tradition. Social democracy after 1945 Anthony Crosland, The Future of Socialism (1956): the goal is equality, achieved through growth and welfare, not nationalising everything. In the 1990s, Anthony Giddens's The Third Way (1998) shaped Blair's New Labour, accepting markets.
Critiques and the crisis of socialism

Economic : Hayek and von Mises argued central planning cannot handle information ("calculation problem"). Shortages and low innovation hit the USSR and East Europe. Political : one-party rule, repression and the gulag. Liberals say socialism ignores individual freedom. Theoretical : Marx underrated nationalism, religion and the staying power of capitalism.
