Class is no longer the only identity (feminists, race, ecology). Collapse : the Berlin Wall fell in 1989 and the USSR dissolved in December 1991. Fukuyama's "end of history" thesis followed. Responses: market socialism (John Roemer), China's "socialism with Chinese characteristics" (market reforms from 1978), and a revival of social democracy and ecological socialism.
Socialism in India: from the CSP to the Constitution

Before 1947 : Congress Socialist Party (1934) with Jayaprakash Narayan, Acharya Narendra Dev, Ram Manohar Lohia. The Communist Party of India was founded in 1925 (Kanpur). M.N. Roy was among the early Marxists. Bhagat Singh also read socialism. Nehru : Congress's Avadi session (1955) resolved on a "socialistic pattern of society". The Planning Commission (1950), public-sector industry and mixed economy followed. Constitution : Directive Principles, Articles 38 and 39 (equitable distribution, no concentration of wealth). The 42nd Amendment (1976) added "socialist" to the Preamble. On 25 November 2024 the Supreme Court dismissed petitions seeking its removal ( Balram Singh v Union of India ), saying Parliament's amending power extends to the Preamble.
Socialism in India: Gandhi, Ambedkar and the Left

Gandhi and Ambedkar : Gandhi's trusteeship; Ambedkar's state socialism ( States and Minorities , 1947). Left politics : Kerala elected one of the world's first communist governments through the ballot in 1957, under E.M.S. Namboodiripad. The Naxalbari uprising began in 1967. Congress Socialist Party (1934) brought Acharya Narendra Dev, Jayaprakash Narayan and Ram Manohar Lohia together inside Congress. The Avadi session (1955) adopted a "socialistic pattern of society" as the goal. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added the word "socialist" to the Preamble.
How to answer

"Marxism is dead, but Marx lives." Comment. Distinguish between scientific and utopian socialism. Examine Lenin's contribution to Marxism. Discuss the evolution of social democracy. How does it differ from Marxism? Structure: define socialism and its strands. Move from utopian to scientific. Explain the Marxist method and critique of capitalism briefly, then Lenin and the revisionist split. Cover the 1991 crisis and survival strategies. Add India: Nehru, Articles 38-39, the Preamble and Kerala. A comparison table of Marx, Lenin and Bernstein helps.
Fascism, Gandhism and Feminism
Three very different ideologies in one lesson

The syllabus lists three ideologies together: Fascism , Gandhism and Feminism . They share little. Fascism worships the nation-state and the leader. Gandhism trusts moral force and small communities. Feminism asks how gender shapes power. Each is a regular source of questions, and the three together suit comparative questions. Learn one clear definition, key thinkers with books and years, and one critique for each. Gandhi's ideas are covered in depth in lesson 0-8-3, so here we treat him as an ideology. For fascism, the aim is to define it precisely and to distinguish it from authoritarianism and communism.
Fascism: the core features

Fascism arose in Europe between the world wars, in Italy under Benito Mussolini (in power from the March on Rome, 1922) and in Germany under Hitler (Chancellor, 1933). The word comes from the Latin fasces , a bundle of rods with an axe, a Roman symbol of authority. Ultra-nationalism : the nation, often a race, is supreme. Anti-individualism : the individual is nothing apart from the nation. Leader principle : the Duce or Fuhrer embodies the nation. Struggle and militarism : war is noble and purifying. Anti-liberalism, anti-communism, anti-rationalism : it prefers will, myth and action to reason. Corporatism : classes are merged into state-run bodies, so no class struggle. Mussolini's slogan: everything within the state, nothing outside it, nothing against it.
Fascist thought and the totalitarian state

Mussolini and Gentile, The Doctrine of Fascism (1932) The philosopher Giovanni Gentile wrote the first part; Mussolini signed it. It rejects liberalism, socialism and pacifism and glorifies the state. Hitler, Mein Kampf (1925-26) Nazism added racial theory : the "Aryan" race against Jews, Slavs and others. The Holocaust murdered about six million Jews. Hannah Arendt, The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951) Total rule uses terror and ideology to dominate every part of life. She links it to anti-Semitism, imperialism and the isolated masses. Umberto Eco, "Ur-Fascism" (1995) Lists fourteen typical features, such as the cult of tradition, fear of difference and a permanent enemy.
Why fascism rose, and what it is not

Causes : shock of World War I, the Great Depression, fear of communism, humiliation after Versailles (Germany) and weak democracy. Marxist view (Dimitrov, 1935): fascism is the open dictatorship of finance capital. Others stress the middle classes , mass politics and propaganda. Robert Paxton , The Anatomy of Fascism (2004): study what fascists do, in stages from movement to rule, not just what they say. It differs from communism (which claims class equality) and from ordinary authoritarianism , because fascism mobilises the masses in a party movement. Defeat in 1945 ended the regimes, but "neo-fascist" and far-right movements persist, and the label is much debated.
Gandhism: a way of life as a politics

Gandhism is a moral and political philosophy of M.K. Gandhi (1869-1948), not a formal system. Its core is the unity of means and ends : good ends need pure means. In Hind Swaraj (1909), Gandhi attacked modern industrial civilisation. He saw it as materialist, violent and unjust, and he pointed to the railways, lawyers and machinery as signs of this. Swaraj meant more than self-rule. It was self-rule over oneself, and a society built from self-governing villages. He drew on the Bhagavad Gita , Jain and Buddhist ahimsa, Tolstoy, Ruskin's Unto This Last (which he turned into Sarvodaya ) and Thoreau.
Key Gandhian concepts

Gandhi's methods of satyagraha include non-cooperation, civil disobedience, fasting and boycott. Examples: Champaran (1917), the Salt March (1930) and Quit India (1942). The constructive programme (khadi, village industry, removing untouchability, communal unity, education) is the social side. On the state, he was a philosophical anarchist: the ideal is an "enlightened anarchy" with minimal state power and decentralised units, like "oceanic circles" of villages.
Gandhism: critics and relevance

Impractical : critics say a modern state needs industry, defence and large institutions. Ambedkar saw the village as a "sink of localism" and a "den of ignorance", where caste rules (his speech in the Constituent Assembly, 1948). He also disputed Gandhi on varna. Marxists : trusteeship asks capitalists to give up power voluntarily. It hides class conflict. Feminists say his ideas on women's roles were limited, though women joined his movements in large numbers. Relevance : Gandhian ideas shaped Martin Luther King Jr., Nelson Mandela and civil resistance movements. They inform debates on environment (limits to consumption, Schumacher's Small Is Beautiful , 1973), peace and local self-government.
Feminism: meaning and waves

Feminism is the movement and theory that studies women's subordination and seeks to end it. Key terms: sex (biological) versus gender (social roles), and patriarchy (rule by men, in family and state). Its slogan, "the personal is political", says that private life, like housework and violence at home, is a matter of power. The "wave" scheme is a rough guide, and critics note that it leaves out many movements outside the West.
Schools of feminism

Liberal Equal rights and opportunity within the existing system: vote, education, work. Wollstonecraft, Mill, Friedan, and Okin's later work on the family. Marxist and socialist Women's oppression comes from capitalism and private property. Engels, The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State (1884). Socialist feminists add patriarchy to class (unpaid domestic labour). Radical Patriarchy is the root. It must be uprooted in family, sexuality and culture. Millett, Sexual Politics (1970); Firestone, The Dialectic of Sex (1970). Black, postcolonial and postmodern See next card.
Key feminist thinkers

Mary Wollstonecraft , A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792): women appear weak because they are denied education. J.S. Mill , The Subjection of Women (1869): legal subjection of women is a wrong. Simone de Beauvoir , The Second Sex (1949): "One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman." Woman is treated as the "Other". Betty Friedan , The Feminine Mystique (1963): the "problem that has no name" among American housewives. Kimberlé Crenshaw (1989): coined intersectionality . Black women face overlapping race and gender discrimination. Judith Butler , Gender Trouble (1990): gender is performed, not natural. Chandra Mohanty : warns against treating "Third World woman" as one victim category ("Under Western Eyes", boundary 2 , 1984).
Fascism, Gandhism and feminism in India

Feminism : reformers like Savitribai Phule and Jyotirao Phule (girls' school, Pune, 1848), Pandita Ramabai, Tarabai Shinde ( Stri Purush Tulana , 1882) and Begum Rokeya ( Sultana's Dream , 1905). Laws: sati abolition (1829), Widow Remarriage Act (1856), Hindu Code Bills (1955-56). Constitution: Article 15(3), Article 14, and Article 39(a) and (d). Vishaka (1997) led to the POSH Act (2013). The 106th Amendment (2023) reserves a third of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats for women. Courts : Shayara Bano (2017) struck down instant triple talaq; Joseph Shine (2018) struck down adultery law; Indian Young Lawyers Association (2018) opened Sabarimala to women. Gandhism : Sarvodaya and Bhoodan (Vinoba Bhave, 1951), Panchayati Raj and Article 40, khadi, and Chipko. Fascism : Gandhi wrote to Hitler in 1939 and 1940. The Constitution's rights, secular state and independent judiciary are safeguards against totalitarian rule.
How to answer

"Fascism is the negation of liberal democracy." Discuss. Examine Gandhi's critique of modern civilisation and its relevance today. Explain the various strands of feminism. Is Gandhi's concept of trusteeship a feasible alternative to socialism? Structure: for fascism, define it, give six features, then thinkers (Mussolini, Arendt) and causes. For Gandhi, start from Hind Swaraj and give means-ends, satyagraha, sarvodaya and trusteeship, then critics (Ambedkar, Marxists) and relevance. For feminism, give the waves, the schools and one Indian example for each. Close with a comparison table, if the question asks for it.
Conservatism
The ideology that distrusts blueprints

Conservatism is often dismissed as 'resisting change'. That is too simple. It is a way of thinking about society : be careful with inherited institutions, because they hold wisdom no single mind can design. UPSC asks about it in Paper I as one of the main ideologies, and it links to Burke, Oakeshott and the New Right. Knowing its internal split makes your answer stand out.
Five conservative themes

Most conservative writers share a few instincts. Tradition : customs carry accumulated experience. Human imperfection : people are limited and flawed, so grand schemes fail. Organic society : society grows like a living body, it is not a machine. Hierarchy and authority : natural differences of role are normal. Property : it gives security and a stake in order.
Burke: reform to preserve

The founder-figure is Edmund Burke , in Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790). He attacked the revolution for tearing up the social contract between the dead, the living and the unborn. His principle: a state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation . So he accepted slow, careful reform. He did not oppose change as such.
Oakeshott: rationalism in politics

Michael Oakeshott , Rationalism in Politics (1962), gave a modern version. The rationalist thinks politics is problem-solving by abstract reason and plans. Oakeshott said real political knowledge is practical , learned by doing, like cooking skill and not a recipe book. Politics is 'sailing a boundless sea', where tradition is the only harbour. He preferred a state that keeps order and lets people pursue their own ends.
Paternalistic and libertarian strands
The One Nation tradition (Benjamin Disraeli) accepts social reform to avoid class war. The New Right mixes neoliberal economics with neoconservative social values: law and order, family, nation.
Pessimism about human nature

Conservatives take a darker view of people than liberals or socialists. Hobbes and Burke's followers see humans as insecure and prone to conflict. So order, authority and a strong state matter more than abstract rights. This explains the stress on law and punishment , and doubt about egalitarian engineering. Compare Rousseau or Marx, who think society corrupts a basically good human being.
Critiques

Critics raise four points. It defends privilege by calling it tradition. Whose tradition? Women, slaves and the poor were excluded from 'inherited wisdom'. It has no fixed content : it simply defends whatever exists, even bad institutions. The New Right is self-contradictory : markets dissolve the very traditions it values. Radical thinkers call it a mask for class power (Marx).
Conservatism and other ideologies

Be ready for comparison questions. Liberalism : individual first. Conservatism: society and institutions first. Socialism : equality by design. Conservatism: inequality is natural and useful. Fascism : also anti-liberal, but it is revolutionary and mass-mobilising, while conservatism is cautious and elite-led. Note the 'conservative liberal' overlap in economics, as with Hayek.
Conservatism in India

India has no party formally called conservative, but conservative ideas appear in many places. Gandhi's trust in village tradition, the Swatantra Party (1959) defending property and markets against Nehruvian planning, and cultural nationalism that cherishes civilisational heritage all show some of the themes. The Constituent Assembly too showed Burkean caution: it kept British institutions and reformed them slowly. Also useful: Ambedkar warned that 'tradition' in caste society often protects hierarchy.
How UPSC asks this

"Conservatism is not opposed to change but to a certain kind of change. Discuss." "Distinguish paternalistic conservatism from the New Right." "Examine Oakeshott's critique of rationalism in politics." Structure: define conservatism, give the five themes, Burke and Oakeshott, the two strands, critique, then Indian example like the Swatantra Party.
Anarchism
A politics without a state

Anarchism says that the state is both unnecessary and harmful , and that people can live well through voluntary cooperation. The word comes from the Greek anarkhos , 'without a ruler'. It is often misread as chaos or bomb-throwing. In theory it is a serious critique of authority. Paper I asks about it in the ideologies unit, usually with Proudhon, Bakunin and Kropotkin.
The anarchist argument
All anarchists reject the state. They differ on property and on methods .
Proudhon: mutualism

Pierre-Joseph Proudhon , What is Property? (1840), gave the famous answer 'property is theft'. He meant property that lets owners exploit others' labour. He wanted small producers, mutual banks and fair exchange, and a federation of communes. He was the first to call himself an anarchist. Marx attacked him in The Poverty of Philosophy (1847).
Bakunin: collectivist, revolutionary

Mikhail Bakunin (1814-76) fought Marx inside the First International. His charge: Marx's 'dictatorship of the proletariat' would only make a new ruling class of party bureaucrats. He wanted immediate abolition of the state and collective ownership of production. He believed in spontaneous revolt by peasants and workers. Many see his warning as correct about Soviet Russia.
Kropotkin: mutual aid

Peter Kropotkin , Mutual Aid (1902), answered the social Darwinists. Nature, he argued, shows cooperation as much as competition, so human society can run on mutual aid without coercion. He favoured anarcho-communism : free communes, 'from each according to ability, to each according to need'.
Varieties of anarchism
Left anarchists want a stateless, egalitarian society. Anarcho-capitalists want the state replaced by the market. Nozick's minimal state is not anarchism, but he starts from the anarchist question.
Critiques

Critics raise several objections. Without a state, who stops the strong preying on the weak? Hobbes's problem. Is it utopian ? Human nature may not be so cooperative. Big problems like pollution and trade need coordination. Small stateless experiments (Spain 1936-39) were crushed by stronger armies. Defenders reply that states themselves are the greatest source of war and violence.
Anarchism and Marxism

Both seek a classless, stateless society. The split is over the path . Marxists use the state (dictatorship of the proletariat) and let it 'wither away'. Anarchists say that a state, once built, never withers. Link this to Lenin's State and Revolution (1917) and to later critiques of bureaucratic socialism.
Gandhi and philosophical anarchism

Gandhi called his ideal Ram Rajya and 'enlightened anarchy': a society of self-governing villages in 'oceanic circles', where state power is minimal. He said that the best government is the one that governs least. Differences: Gandhi insisted on non-violence and moral discipline, and he accepted the state as a necessary evil for now. Vinoba Bhave's Sarvodaya and J.P. Narayan's partyless democracy carry the same strand.
How UPSC asks this

"Compare anarchism and Marxism on the state." "Examine Gandhi's ideas as a form of philosophical anarchism." "Critically evaluate Kropotkin's idea of mutual aid." Structure: define, state critique, three thinkers, varieties, link with Marxism, criticism, Gandhi. Bakunin (1814-76) and Kropotkin (1842-1921) are the two anarchist thinkers to name first. Kropotkin's Mutual Aid (1902) argued that cooperation drives social life as much as competition does.
Multiculturalism
One state, many cultures

Almost every state is culturally plural. Multiculturalism asks how a liberal state should treat minority languages, religions and ways of life. Should it be 'blind' to difference, or recognise it? This is a Paper I favourite because it links liberalism, rights, the communitarian critique and Indian secularism.
Recognition, not just tolerance

Classic liberalism offers equal individual rights and neutrality. Multiculturalists say neutrality is a myth : public holidays, language and school curricula usually reflect the majority culture. So minorities need recognition and sometimes special measures. The aim is equal respect and a fair chance to keep one's culture, not separatism.
Kymlicka: group-differentiated rights

Will Kymlicka , Multicultural Citizenship (1995), argues from liberal premises. Culture is the 'context of choice' that gives individuals meaning, so protecting it protects autonomy. He lists three kinds of group rights: self-government rights (national minorities), polyethnic rights (immigrants: exemptions, funding), special representation rights . He separates external protections (acceptable) from internal restrictions on members (not acceptable).
Taylor: the politics of recognition

Charles Taylor , Multiculturalism and the Politics of Recognition (1992). Identity is formed through recognition by others. Misrecognition can harm like oppression. Taylor, a communitarian, distinguishes the politics of universalism (same rights for all) from the politics of difference . His example is Quebec's French-language policy.
Parekh and Young

Bhikhu Parekh , Rethinking Multiculturalism (2000), proposes intercultural dialogue : no culture is perfect, so each should be open to criticism by others. He denies that liberalism is the only standard. Iris Marion Young pushes for group representation for oppressed groups, in Justice and the Politics of Difference (1990).
Liberal vs multicultural views
Kymlicka tries to bridge the two, while Barry and Okin attack multiculturalism from within liberalism.
Critiques

Brian Barry , Culture and Equality (2001): group exemptions break equal citizenship. Susan Okin , 'Is Multiculturalism Bad for Women?' (1999): protecting a culture may protect patriarchy. It can freeze cultures and ignore internal diversity. Conservatives say it weakens national unity. The leaders of Germany, Britain and France declared multiculturalism a failure in 2010-11.
Policy models

States handle diversity differently. Assimilation : minorities adopt the dominant culture (France's laicite). Integration : common civic rules, room for difference. Multiculturalism : official support for cultural diversity (Canada, since 1971). Canada's Multiculturalism Act (1988) is the standard example. Will Kymlicka's Multicultural Citizenship (1995) defends group rights for national minorities and immigrant groups, but he treats the two differently. France's 1905 law separating church and state is the root of its strict laicite.
India as a multicultural state

India has long practised group-differentiated rights: Articles 25-30 (religious freedom, cultural and educational rights of minorities, Art. 29-30), Schedules Five and Six , linguistic states, reservations and personal laws. Rajeev Bhargava calls this contextual secularism , with principled distance and not strict separation. The Shah Bano case (1985) and the Uniform Civil Code debate (Art. 44) show the Okin-style tension between group rights and gender equality.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine the case for group-differentiated rights in a liberal democracy." "Is multiculturalism compatible with gender justice?" "Evaluate Kymlicka's views on minority rights." "How does the Indian Constitution reflect a multicultural approach?" Structure: liberal neutrality, then Kymlicka and Taylor, Parekh, critiques from Barry and Okin, then India (Arts. 25-30, UCC debate).
Green Political Theory
Politics for a finite planet

Green political theory is the newest major ideology. It starts from one fact: economic growth on a finite planet has limits . It then asks how politics, economy and ethics must change. It is rising in UPSC because it links Paper I theory with Paper II issues like climate justice and sustainable development.
Shallow versus deep ecology

Arne Naess coined the terms in 1973. Shallow ecology (environmentalism): protect nature because it serves humans. Use technology and regulation. Deep ecology (ecologism): nature has intrinsic value , humans are part of the web of life, so we need a basic change of worldview. This is the anthropocentric versus ecocentric divide.
Core green principles
Heywood's summary: ecologism puts nature, not humans, at the centre.
Limits to Growth and Schumacher

The Club of Rome's Limits to Growth (1972) warned that resource use cannot rise forever. E.F. Schumacher , Small is Beautiful (1973), argued for human-scale, 'Buddhist' economics. The Brundtland Report (1987) defined sustainable development as meeting present needs without compromising future generations. Greens say this still accepts growth, so it is a compromise.
Ecofeminism and social ecology

Ecofeminists (Vandana Shiva, Maria Mies) link the domination of nature with the domination of women, both treated as resources. Murray Bookchin 's social ecology says ecological crisis comes from social hierarchy, so the fix is decentralised, directly democratic communities. Compare eco-socialism : capitalism is the root of the crisis.
Green politics in practice

Green parties arose in the 1970s-80s, e.g. Die Gruenen in West Germany (1980). Movements: Chipko, Greenpeace, Fridays for Future. Policies: carbon limits, renewable energy, degrowth, rights of nature (Ecuador's 2008 constitution). Green theory also supports environmental justice : the poor suffer pollution most while the rich cause most of it.
Justice across time and species

Greens extend justice in two directions. Intergenerational justice : we hold the planet in trust for the unborn, a Burkean echo. Interspecies justice : animals and ecosystems have claims too, argued by Peter Singer (animal liberation, 1975) and Tom Regan (animal rights). Legal moves include rights of nature: Ecuador (2008), and the 2017 Uttarakhand High Court order treating the Ganga and Yamuna as legal persons, later stayed by the Supreme Court.
Critiques

It is utopian : how to end growth in poor countries? Eco-authoritarian risk: strong state to enforce limits. Developing countries say the North grew by polluting and now restricts them. Technology optimists believe innovation can decouple growth from damage. Guha and Martinez-Alier's Varieties of Environmentalism (1997) argue that Northern deep ecology ignores the environmentalism of the poor in the South, such as forest and water struggles.
India's green thought

Gandhi's line 'the earth provides enough for everyone's need but not for everyone's greed' is the standard quote. Chipko (1973, Uttarakhand), Narmada Bachao Andolan , and Ramachandra Guha's Environmentalism: A Global History and the idea of 'environmentalism of the poor' (Guha and Martinez-Alier) are central. India's stance in climate talks: common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR). The Mission LiFE call (2022) stresses lifestyle change.
How UPSC asks this

"Distinguish shallow and deep ecology." "Examine green political theory as a challenge to modern ideologies." "Is sustainable development a contradiction in terms?" Structure: state the ecological premise, deep vs shallow, principles, thinkers, critiques, link to Gandhi, Chipko and CBDR. Sample line for the answer: Arne Naess coined 'deep ecology' in 1973, asking whether human-centred values themselves need to change, while shallow ecology seeks reform within industrial society.
Postmodernism
Suspicion of grand stories

Postmodernism is a mood and a method more than one school. Its core claim: the big stories of modernity, such as progress, reason, science and revolution, are not neutral truths but products of power and history. It matters for Paper I because it challenges liberalism and Marxism alike, and links to Foucault, Lyotard and Derrida.
Incredulity towards metanarratives

Jean-Francois Lyotard , The Postmodern Condition (1979), defined postmodernism as 'incredulity towards metanarratives'. A metanarrative is a grand story that claims to explain all history: Enlightenment progress, Marxism's classless society, liberal freedom. Lyotard says these have lost credibility. In their place are local, plural narratives and 'language games'.
Knowledge and power

Michel Foucault argued that knowledge is never innocent: power/knowledge work together. What counts as 'normal', 'sane' or 'criminal' is defined by institutions such as the clinic, prison and school. Power is everywhere, productive and not only repressive. Resistance is therefore local and constant, not one grand revolution.
Derrida and deconstruction

Jacques Derrida ( Of Grammatology , 1967) argued that texts do not have one fixed meaning. Meaning rests on binary oppositions (male/female, reason/emotion) where one side is privileged. Deconstruction exposes and unsettles these hierarchies. Politically, it makes us question categories like 'nation' and 'citizen'. The word 'deconstruction' is Derrida's own, and Of Grammatology (1967) also takes apart Rousseau's Essay on the Origin of Languages. A political example is the category of 'citizen', which depends on who is excluded from it.
What postmodernists reject
Rorty adds pragmatism : drop the quest for foundations, keep conversation.
Impact on political thought

Postmodern ideas shaped feminism (Judith Butler: gender is performed), postcolonial studies (Said, Orientalism , 1978), identity politics, and radical democracy (Laclau and Mouffe, 1985), which values permanent conflict over false consensus. They also reshaped IR (the discourse analysis of security) and critiques of development. In IR, Richard Ashley's 'The Poverty of Neorealism' (1984) attacked realist theory for treating the state as a fixed, unexamined fact. This is why postmodern work is used in critical security studies.
Critiques

Habermas : it is a 'performative contradiction'. To argue that reason is power, it still uses reason. It abandons the unfinished project of modernity. Marxists: it shifts attention from class and economics to culture. Relativism: if there is no truth, how to condemn injustice? Dense, obscure language.
Postmodernism vs post-structuralism

The terms overlap. Post-structuralism is the philosophical method (Foucault, Derrida), which attacks fixed structures of meaning. Postmodernism is the wider cultural and political condition and attitude. In exam answers, use both sensibly and name the thinker. Foucault's Discipline and Punish (1975) and Lyotard's The Postmodern Condition (1979) are the two texts most often cited for this comparison. Derrida's 1966 lecture 'Structure, Sign and Play in the Discourse of the Human Sciences' is an early statement of this critique of fixed centres of meaning.
Subaltern studies and beyond

The Subaltern Studies group (Ranajit Guha, from 1982) and Partha Chatterjee's Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986) read Indian history from below and question Eurocentric narratives. Ashis Nandy's The Intimate Enemy (1983) shows how colonialism harms the mind. Critics, such as Sumit Sarkar, said the group moved from Marxism to postmodern culturalism.
How UPSC asks this

"What is meant by 'incredulity towards metanarratives'?" "Evaluate Foucault's idea of power/knowledge." "Assess the postmodern critique of modernity and the Habermasian reply." Structure: define the term, Lyotard, Foucault, Derrida, impact, then critiques, then Subaltern Studies. Habermas attacked several postmodern thinkers in The Philosophical Discourse of Modernity (1985), arguing that their attack on reason can feed conservatism. Use this as the main critique in the Habermasian reply.
Dharmashastra and Buddhist Traditions
India's oldest political ideas

The syllabus opens Indian political thought with two ancient traditions: the Dharmashastra and the Buddhist tradition. They answer old questions in different ways. Where does the king's power come from? What is his duty? Is social order fixed by birth or made by people? This lesson gives you the key texts and ideas, with names that examiners look for. The next lesson covers the third great tradition: Kautilya's Arthashastra .
What is dharma?

Dharma comes from the root dhr , to hold or sustain. It means the order that holds society and the cosmos together. In politics, it means duty. Every person has a duty that fits their varna (social class) and ashrama (stage of life). This is called varnashrama dharma . The king's own duty, rajadharma , is to protect this order. The king does not make dharma. He upholds it. So dharma stands above the king, like a higher law.
The Dharmashastras

Dharmasutras The older prose texts, such as those of Gautama, Apastamba and Baudhayana. Manusmriti The best-known text, usually dated around the 2nd century BCE to 2nd century CE. Patrick Olivelle places it in the 2nd to 3rd century CE. It sets out duties of the four varnas and of the king. Yajnavalkya Smriti Later and more legal. Its commentary Mitakshara (12th century) shaped Hindu inheritance law under the British.
Rajadharma: duties of the king

Protection (raksha): the king's first duty is to protect his subjects and the varna order. Danda: the rod of punishment. Manu says danda is the king; without it the strong would roast the weak like fish on a spit. Taxes: often set at a sixth of the produce, as payment for protection. Council: the king should consult ministers and learned Brahmins. If the king fails in protection, some texts say he shares in his subjects' sins.
The Mahabharata's Shanti Parva

In the Shanti Parva, the dying Bhishma teaches Yudhishthira about rajadharma. He tells how people first lived well under dharma, then fell into disorder and matsya nyaya , the law of the fish. They went to Brahma, who gave them a king. One account says people first made an agreement among themselves, failed, then asked for a king and agreed to pay taxes. Some scholars, such as U.N. Ghoshal and K.P. Jayaswal , have compared this to a social contract . Others think the comparison goes too far, since the king's authority is still divine.
The Buddhist alternative

The Aggañña Sutta of the Digha Nikaya gives a different story of the origin of kingship. At first, beings lived in harmony. As greed grew, people began to hoard rice and steal. So they gathered and chose one among them to keep order, offering him a share of rice in return. He was called Mahasammata , "the great elect", or the one agreed upon by all. This is often read as an early social contract theory and as a challenge to divine kingship.
Buddhism against varna

The same sutta mocks Brahmin claims to be born from Brahma's mouth. It says Brahmins are born from women like everyone else. Varna, it says, came from people's occupations , not divine birth. A person's worth comes from their conduct, not their birth. The Buddhist sangha was run by discussion, voting and rules of procedure. Some scholars link it with the gana-sanghas , the republican states of ancient India such as the Licchavis of Vaishali.
Dhamma and the righteous king

The Buddhist ideal king is the chakravartin , a universal monarch who rules by dhamma, not by force. The best example is Ashoka (c. 268–232 BCE). After the Kalinga war, his edicts shift from conquest by arms to dhamma-vijaya , conquest by righteousness. His edicts teach tolerance of all sects, kindness to animals and care for subjects. Rock Edict XII asks people to honour other faiths. Rock Edict XIII records his remorse over Kalinga.
Comparing the two traditions

The Dharmashastras give a hierarchical order fixed by birth. Ambedkar burned the Manusmriti in public at Mahad on 25 December 1927 as a symbol of caste oppression. The Buddhist tradition is more egalitarian and closer to consent, but its kings still had great power. Neither tradition gave ordinary people formal rights against the king. Western scholars once claimed ancient India had no political theory. K.P. Jayaswal 's Hindu Polity (1924) challenged this.
Ancient republics: the gana-sanghas

Not all ancient Indian states were monarchies. Buddhist and Jain texts describe gana-sanghas : states ruled by a council of heads of clans. Examples include the Vajji (Vrijji) confederacy , led by the Licchavis of Vaishali, and the Shakyas of Kapilavastu, the Buddha's own clan. Decisions were made in an assembly hall (santhagara) after debate. They may have voted with wooden tokens called shalakas , as the Buddhist sangha did. In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta, the Buddha lists seven conditions for the Vajjis' welfare. The first two are to meet often in full assembly, and to meet, act and disperse in harmony. Scholars like Romila Thapar warn against calling them democracies in the modern sense. Power lay with an elite of kshatriya clans, not all people. Still, they show that government by discussion has deep roots in India.
Two traditions compared
Use this contrast to open or close an answer. Note the shared point: both traditions expect the ruler to protect his subjects.
Living legacies

India's Constitution draws on these traditions. The Dharma Chakra on the national flag and the Lion Capital of Sarnath, the national emblem, come from Ashoka. Ambedkar chose Buddhism in 1956 because of its stress on equality, liberty and fraternity. Debates on Hindu personal law , such as the Hindu Code Bills of the 1950s, show how Dharmashastra ideas were reformed by modern law.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the concept of rajadharma in ancient Indian political thought." "Compare the Brahmanical and Buddhist theories of the origin of the state." Structure: define dharma, then rajadharma and danda from Manu and the Shanti Parva. Contrast with the Aggañña Sutta's Mahasammata. Use Ashoka as the Buddhist ideal in action. End with the modern legacy: emblem, flag and Ambedkar.
Kautilya's Arthashastra
India's great book of statecraft

The Arthashastra is a detailed manual on how to run a state: its economy, army, spies, laws and foreign policy. Tradition credits it to Kautilya , also called Chanakya or Vishnugupta, the minister of Chandragupta Maurya (c. 4th century BCE). The text was lost for centuries. R. Shamasastry found a manuscript and published it in 1909, with an English translation in 1915. Scholars such as Thomas Trautmann and Patrick Olivelle think the text we have was compiled and revised over time, reaching its final form around the early centuries CE.
Artha: the science of wealth and power

Artha means material well-being. Kautilya says artha is the most important of the three goals of life (dharma, artha and kama), because the other two depend on it. The state's job is to gain and protect territory and to bring yogakshema , the welfare and security of its people. "In the happiness of his subjects lies the happiness of the king." Arthashastra 1.19 So Kautilya's realism serves welfare, not just the ruler's ego.
Saptanga: the seven limbs

A state has seven limbs, in order of importance: swami (king), amatya (ministers), janapada (territory and people), durga (fortified city), kosha (treasury), danda (army) and mitra (ally). It is an organic view: if one limb fails, the whole body suffers.
Mandala: the circle of states

The diagram shows one line of the circle. The mandala theory places the would-be conqueror ( vijigishu ) at the centre of a circle of states. The immediate neighbour is a natural enemy , and the state beyond is a natural friend . Two more states matter: the madhyama (middle king) and the udasina (a neutral king stronger than both).
Shadgunya: six policies

Kautilya lists six measures of foreign policy: Sandhi: peace or treaty. Vigraha: hostility or war. Asana: staying quiet, watching. Yana: marching, preparing to attack. Samshraya: seeking shelter with a stronger power. Dvaidhibhava: the double policy: peace with one, war with another. The choice depends on whether you are weaker, equal or stronger. He also lists four means: sama (persuasion), dana (gifts), bheda (division) and danda (force).
Administration and spies

A large salaried bureaucracy with superintendents (adhyakshas) for mines, trade, forests and more. A strong treasury : "all undertakings depend on the treasury." A detailed network of spies (gudhapurushas) to test ministers and watch the public. Testing ministers (upadha) through temptations of dharma, wealth, desire and fear. The king's day is divided into sixteen parts, each with set duties. Max Weber said that compared with this book, Machiavelli's Prince is harmless.
Law and justice

Kautilya names four sources of law: dharma (sacred law), vyavahara (evidence and transactions), charitra (custom) and rajashasana (the king's edict). Strikingly, he says that when they conflict, the king's edict, if based on justice, prevails. This raises the state's authority above tradition. Punishment should be neither too harsh nor too mild. Too harsh, and people fear the king. Too mild, and people despise him. Just punishment brings dharma, artha and kama.
Kautilya and Machiavelli

Both are realists . Both put the state's survival first and accept deceit and force. Kautilya is far more comprehensive : economy, law, welfare and war. Machiavelli wrote a short book of advice. Kautilya ties the king to dharma and welfare. Machiavelli separates politics from Christian ethics. Kautilya wanted stability and expansion ; Machiavelli wanted Italian unity in a crisis. Some scholars call Kautilya India's first theorist of a welfare state .
Economy and welfare in the Arthashastra

The Arthashastra imagines an active, almost interventionist state. The state runs mines, forests, weaving, liquor and salt, and sets up state farms (sita land). Superintendents fix weights and measures , control prices and check traders' profits. The king must support orphans, the old, the sick and helpless women. Labour contracts and wages are regulated. Masters who mistreat workers are fined. Settling new land (janapada nivesha) and building irrigation are royal duties. This is why some scholars call Kautilya's state a kind of early welfare state . Others warn that its aim was revenue and power, with welfare as a means to keep people productive and loyal.
Kautilya in modern India

India's diplomatic enclave in New Delhi is called Chanakyapuri . Strategic thinkers use the mandala idea to read India's neighbourhood: hostile neighbours (Pakistan, at times China) and the value of friends beyond them, such as Afghanistan, Iran, the Central Asian states and the Indo-Pacific partners. Shivshankar Menon , a former National Security Adviser, and analysts at the Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses (IDSA) have written on Kautilya's relevance to Indian strategy.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss Kautilya's saptanga theory of the state." "Examine the relevance of Kautilya's mandala theory to India's foreign policy." "Compare Kautilya and Machiavelli." Structure: text and dating, artha and yogakshema, saptanga (draw it), mandala (draw it), shadgunya, administration. End with modern relevance through Chanakyapuri and the neighbourhood policy.
Vivekananda
Spiritual nationalism and social service

Swami Vivekananda (1863-1902), Narendranath Datta before renunciation, was Ramakrishna Paramahamsa's disciple. He gave modern Hinduism a confident, service-centred voice and shaped the moral basis of Indian nationalism. UPSC asks about his Vedanta, nationalism, education and views on caste and religion. His 1893 speech at the Parliament of the World's Religions in Chicago made him famous abroad. He founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897 to combine monastic life with relief and education.
The five key ideas
Practical Vedanta and Daridra Narayana

Advaita says the one Brahman is in all. Vivekananda gave this a social turn: since God is in every person, serving the poor ( daridra narayana ) is worship. He criticised priests who preach renunciation while the people starve: 'I do not believe in a religion that cannot wipe the widow's tears.' The Ramakrishna Mission (1897) was built on this: relief, schools, hospitals.
Chicago and universal religion

At the Parliament of the World's Religions , Chicago, 11 September 1893, he opened with 'Sisters and brothers of America' and spoke on tolerance and acceptance of all faiths, comparing religions to different rivers flowing to one sea. He rejected the claim of any one faith to be the only truth. His book Raja Yoga (1896) and talks on Karma, Jnana and Bhakti yoga followed.
Nationalism and strength

His nationalism is cultural and spiritual : India's mission is to give spiritual wisdom to the world, while learning science and organisation from the West. He urged youth: 'Arise, awake and stop not till the goal is reached' (adapted from the Katha Upanishad). He praised physical strength: 'You will be nearer to heaven through football than through the Gita.' Aurobindo, Subhas Bose and many revolutionaries drew inspiration from him.
Caste, women and the masses

He attacked untouchability ('don't-touchism') and priestly privilege, and called the neglect of the masses a national sin. He believed caste as it existed was a product of history that should be dissolved by uplifting the lowly rather than pulling down the upper. He predicted the rise of the Shudras and urged women's education: 'It is impossible to think of the welfare of the world unless the condition of women is improved.'
Critiques

Dalit and anti-caste thinkers say he did not reject varna, only its abuses. Neo-Hindu revivalism: used by Hindu nationalists, though he praised Islam's brotherhood. Rationalists find his appeal to spirituality unscientific. Supporters: a Vedantic humanist who put the poor first. He also backed the Ramakrishna Mission's famine relief work, which shows that his service ideal was practical as well as spiritual. Critics say his Vedanta was a selective reading of the scriptures.
Education

His definition: education is 'the manifestation of the perfection already in man' . He wanted man-making education: character, strength of mind, independent thinking, combining Western science and Vedantic spirit. The idea shaped Gandhi's basic education and National Education movements (1905). Sister Nivedita (Margaret Noble), his Irish disciple, opened a girls' school in Calcutta in 1898 with his backing. It is a strong example of his education ideal in practice.
Relevance today

His birth date, 12 January, is observed as National Youth Day (since 1985). Ideas of service, volunteering and youth leadership feature in government schemes and ethics papers (GS Paper 4). The Ramakrishna Mission continues his work. His phrase 'daridra narayana', God in the poor, is the moral base of the Mission's relief work after floods and cyclones. His call to 'arise, awake' comes from the Katha Upanishad and is often used in youth speeches.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine Vivekananda's concept of practical Vedanta." "Discuss Vivekananda's ideas on nationalism and social reform." "How relevant is Vivekananda's concept of education today?" Structure: life, Vedanta and service, universal religion, nationalism, caste and women, education, critique. Name his lectures 'Practical Vedanta' and 'Lectures from Colombo to Almora' as sources. His death at Belur in 1902, at the age of 39, is a useful closing detail.
Rabindranath Tagore
The poet who doubted nationalism

Rabindranath Tagore (1861-1941) was a poet, educator and thinker, and in 1913 the first non-European Nobel laureate in literature (for Gitanjali ). In politics he was an internationalist and a critic of aggressive nationalism , a stand that makes him vital to Paper I. He translated Gitanjali himself from Bengali into English, and the 1912 London edition, with an introduction by W.B. Yeats, brought him Western fame.
Tagore's main ideas
Nationalism (1917)

In lectures given in Japan and the US in 1916-17 and published as Nationalism (1917), Tagore described the nation as an organised political and commercial power , a machine that crushes human values and breeds aggression and race hatred. He condemned the West's imperial nationalism and warned India not to imitate it. He said India's real problem is social, not political: caste and communal divides.
Debates with Gandhi

Tagore called Gandhi 'Mahatma' and admired him, but they debated. On non-cooperation (1920-21) he feared a negative, narrow spirit and burning of foreign cloth as wasteful. On the charkha , in The Cult of the Charkha (1925), he said that spinning cannot be the way to swaraj, and called for free thought. Gandhi answered in 'The Poet and the Charkha'. The 1934 Bihar earthquake exchange: Gandhi called it divine punishment for untouchability, Tagore rejected the idea.
Swadeshi Samaj and rural reconstruction

In Swadeshi Samaj (1904) Tagore urged that Indians build self-reliant society independent of the state, through village cooperation, schools and local work. He founded the rural institute at Sriniketan (1922) near Santiniketan to test this with cooperatives and village crafts and health work. Tagore founded Visva-Bharati University at Santiniketan in 1921 as a meeting place of world cultures. It is an institutional example of his belief that education should connect the village and the world.
Education: Santiniketan and Visva-Bharati

Tagore disliked rote schooling as 'a cage'. In 1901 he opened a school at Santiniketan with classes under trees, and in 1921 Visva-Bharati, 'where the world makes a home in a single nest'. He stressed creativity, the arts, nature and the meeting of cultures. Visva-Bharati became a central university in 1951.
Critiques

Some nationalists felt he was detached from the freedom struggle. His own Ghare Baire (1916) shows nationalism's moral risks, but he supported Swadeshi in 1905. Critics say his stress on society ignored the need to win power from the British. In 1919 he gave up his knighthood to protest Jallianwala Bagh, proof of his political courage.
Tagore and others

Compare: Gandhi (village, moral action), Nehru (liked Tagore's internationalism and modernity), Vivekananda (spiritual nationalism). Tagore sits closer to a cosmopolitan liberal humanism. His song Jana Gana Mana became India's national anthem, Amar Shonar Bangla Bangladesh's. His 1917 book Nationalism, based on lectures given in Japan and the United States, warned that nationalism had become a political and economic organisation that could threaten other peoples.
Relevance today

His warnings echo in current debates on aggressive nationalism, citizenship and cultural identity. The poem 'Where the mind is without fear' ( Gitanjali ) is a favourite essay quotation. Santiniketan was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023. His 1930 Hibbert Lectures, published as The Religion of Man (1931), argued for a humanism beyond any single creed. That speaks to present debates on religion and public life.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine Tagore's critique of nationalism." "Compare the views of Tagore and Gandhi on swaraj and education." "Discuss Tagore's idea of universal humanism." Structure: Nationalism 1917, Gandhi debates, Swadeshi Samaj, education, critique, relevance. A strong answer can cite his 1917 Nationalism lectures, his 1921 letter to Gandhi on non-cooperation, and his 1919 renunciation of knighthood after Jallianwala Bagh. His last major statement, the 1941 address 'Crisis in Civilisation', is worth citing on the limits of Western progress.
Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and Sri Aurobindo
Two answers to colonial modernity

In the 19th century, Indians faced a hard question: how should we respond to British power and Western ideas? Sir Syed Ahmed Khan said Muslims must embrace modern education and cooperate with the British to rise again. Sri Aurobindo said India must reject foreign rule outright and draw strength from its own spiritual tradition. The syllabus pairs them, so expect questions on each and on how they differ.
Sir Syed Ahmed Khan (1817–1898)

Sir Syed came from a Mughal noble family in Delhi and worked as a judicial officer for the East India Company. During the revolt of 1857 he stayed loyal to the British and saved British lives at Bijnor. After 1857, the British blamed Muslims for the revolt. Muslims were falling behind in education and government jobs. Sir Syed set out to rebuild trust with the British and to modernise Muslim society. His essay Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind (The Causes of the Indian Revolt, 1859) blamed British policy, especially the lack of Indians in the legislature.
Education and reason

He founded the Scientific Society (1864) to translate Western works into Urdu. He started the journal Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq (1870) to spread social reform. He founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh in 1875. It became Aligarh Muslim University in 1920. He argued that Islam and science do not conflict. The Quran, the word of God, cannot contradict nature, the work of God. This rational approach was called naturalism ; his opponents mocked him as a "nechari".
Two nations?

Early on, Sir Syed called Hindus and Muslims "two eyes of the beautiful bride that is India". Later, he opposed the Indian National Congress (founded 1885). In speeches at Lucknow and Meerut in 1887–88, he argued that in elections the Hindu majority would dominate, and that Muslims should keep away from Congress agitation. Many historians see this as an early form of the two-nation idea. Others say he spoke of separate communities with distinct interests, not separate nation-states. Pakistan's founders later claimed him as a forerunner.
Sri Aurobindo (1872–1950)

Aurobindo Ghose was educated in England, at St Paul's School and King's College, Cambridge. He returned to India in 1893 and served the Maharaja of Baroda. He became a leader of the Extremists in Congress, during the protests against the Partition of Bengal (1905). He wrote for the paper Bande Mataram . He was tried in the Alipore Bomb Case (1908–09) and acquitted. After a spiritual experience in jail, he left politics in 1910 and moved to Pondicherry . The Sri Aurobindo Ashram there was formally founded in 1926, with the Mother.
New Lamps for Old and boycott

In his articles "New Lamps for Old" (1893–94), Aurobindo attacked the Moderates' petitions and loyalty to Britain as politics of begging. His essays on passive resistance (1907) set out a plan: boycott of British goods, schools, courts and administration, and building national alternatives in their place. He also said that if the British met passive resistance with violence, the people had a right to defend themselves. His goal was complete independence , purna swaraj, long before Congress adopted it in 1929.
Spiritual nationalism

For Aurobindo, the nation was not just land and people. It was a living mother , a form of divine power, or shakti . Nationalism is a religion that has come from God. Paraphrase of his Bombay speech, 1908 Later, in The Ideal of Human Unity and The Human Cycle , he looked beyond the nation toward a spiritual unity of humanity, through free nations working together.
Comparing the two

Aim: Sir Syed wanted Muslim uplift within British rule. Aurobindo wanted complete freedom from it. Method: Sir Syed chose education and loyalty. Aurobindo chose boycott and mass resistance. Source: Sir Syed used Western reason. Aurobindo used Indian spirituality. Critique: Sir Syed's later views fed communal separation. Aurobindo's Hindu imagery could exclude Muslims, though he himself opposed communal politics.
The Aligarh movement

Sir Syed's work grew into the Aligarh movement , a broad effort to modernise Muslim society. The Muhammadan Educational Conference (1886) spread modern schools across India. He wrote a commentary on the Quran using reason, and urged Muslims to read it afresh rather than rely only on traditional scholars. He supported the English language as the key to jobs and knowledge. He criticised polygamy, but defended purdah and moved slowly on women's education. Aligarh trained a new Muslim middle class. Many of its graduates later led the Muslim League (1906). Others, like the Ali brothers, joined the Khilafat and national movements. His critics among the ulema of Deoband (founded 1866) rejected his Western leanings.
Sir Syed and Aurobindo
The two stand at opposite ends of the early response to colonial rule: cooperation and reform against rejection and resistance.
Legacies today

Aligarh Muslim University remains a major institution. In 2024, a seven-judge bench of the Supreme Court overruled the 1967 Azeez Basha judgment, which had denied AMU minority status. The Court left the final decision on AMU's status to a regular bench. Aurobindo's birthday, 15 August , is also India's Independence Day. He gave a message to the nation that day in 1947. Auroville near Pondicherry, founded in 1968, carries his vision of human unity.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss Sir Syed Ahmed Khan's views on education and politics." "Examine Sri Aurobindo's idea of spiritual nationalism." "Was Sir Syed a communalist or a modernist?" Structure: context of 1857 and Bengal partition, then each thinker's life, method and key ideas. Give a balanced reading of Sir Syed's "two nations" remarks. Compare them in a short table or list.
M.K. Gandhi
India's most-asked thinker

Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948) is among the top thinkers in Paper I questions, alongside Marx, Rawls and Ambedkar. He was a lawyer trained in London who found his politics in South Africa (1893–1914), fighting racial laws. He led India's mass movements from 1919 to 1947. His key text is Hind Swaraj (1909), written on board a ship from London to South Africa. Gandhi said he never changed its basic message.
Truth and non-violence

Gandhi's whole thought rests on two ideas. Satya (truth) At first he said "God is Truth". Later he reversed it: "Truth is God". This let atheists share the search too. Ahimsa (non-violence) Not just not killing, but no ill will toward anyone. It is the means to truth. For Gandhi, means and ends are linked like seed and tree. Impure means cannot give a pure end.
Satyagraha

Satyagraha means "holding on to truth", or soul-force. Gandhi first used it in South Africa in 1906, against a law forcing Indians to register. It is not "passive resistance", which he called the weapon of the weak. Satyagraha is active, and is for the brave. The satyagrahi does not hate the opponent. They accept suffering on themselves to convert the opponent's heart, not coerce them. Methods include non-cooperation, civil disobedience, fasting and hartal.
Hind Swaraj: a critique of modern civilisation

In Hind Swaraj , Gandhi said India was enslaved not by the British but by modern civilisation itself. Railways spread plague and famine. Lawyers and doctors profit from conflict and illness. Machinery makes people slaves of wants. Swaraj does not mean "English rule without the Englishman". It means self-rule : rule over oneself. Anthony Parel , editor of the standard edition (1997), treats it as the key to all of Gandhi's later thought.
The Gandhian state

Gandhi is often called a "philosophical anarchist". The state, he said, represents violence in a concentrated form. His ideal was Ram Rajya : rule of moral law, where people govern themselves. He imagined " oceanic circles " of self-reliant villages. It would not be a pyramid with power at the top. Power would spread outward from the individual to the village and beyond. The outer circles would serve the inner ones, not rule them. He accepted that a minimal state would be needed in practice, with as few functions as possible.
Trusteeship and economy

Trusteeship: the rich should hold wealth as trustees for society, keeping only what they need. Gandhi hoped to change hearts, not seize property. Swadeshi: use local goods and serve your neighbours first. The charkha (spinning wheel) was its symbol. Bread labour: everyone should do some physical work. He took this from Tolstoy and Ruskin. Sarvodaya: welfare of all. The word comes from his 1908 Gujarati paraphrase of Ruskin's Unto This Last .
Gandhi on caste and religion

Gandhi fought untouchability , calling untouchables Harijans (people of God), and founded the Harijan Sevak Sangh (1932). Dalit leaders found the name patronising. Early on, he defended varna as a division of labour, while rejecting the idea of high and low. This set him against Ambedkar. On religion, he believed in sarva dharma samabhava , equal respect for all religions. He was killed in 1948 by Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist.
Saint, strategist or reactionary?

Ambedkar , in What Congress and Gandhi Have Done to the Untouchables (1945), attacked Gandhi's defence of varna and the Poona Pact. Marxists like R. Palme Dutt said he protected Indian capitalists through trusteeship. Nehru found Hind Swaraj's rejection of industry unworkable. Bhikhu Parekh praises his moral politics but questions his views on sexuality and celibacy. Partha Chatterjee called Gandhian thought a "moment of manoeuvre" that mobilised peasants while keeping elite control.
Gandhi's movements in practice

Gandhi tested his ideas in real campaigns: Champaran (1917): indigo farmers in Bihar against forced cultivation. His first satyagraha in India. Kheda and Ahmedabad (1918): peasants' revenue relief and a mill workers' strike. Non-Cooperation (1920–22): boycott of courts, schools and foreign cloth. He called it off after the violence at Chauri Chaura in February 1922. Civil Disobedience (1930–34): began with the Dandi March against the salt law. Quit India (1942): "Do or die." Note the pattern. Gandhi chose symbolic issues, like salt, that every Indian could join. He also kept tight control, and withdrew when violence broke out. Critics saw this as caution; he saw it as fidelity to ahimsa.
Gandhi's movements
Learn this order. Each step widened the base of the movement, from a local grievance to a national demand.
Gandhi in the Constitution and beyond

Gandhian ideas sit mainly in the Directive Principles : Article 40 (village panchayats), Article 43 (cottage industries), Article 47 (prohibition) and Article 48 (protecting cows). The 73rd Amendment (1992) gave panchayats constitutional status, partly fulfilling his vision. Worldwide, Martin Luther King Jr., Nelson Mandela and Aung San Suu Kyi drew on satyagraha. Since 2007, the UN marks 2 October as the International Day of Non-Violence.
How UPSC asks this

"Gandhi's satyagraha is a moral and political weapon." Discuss. "Discuss Gandhi's critique of modern civilisation in Hind Swaraj." "Is Gandhi a philosophical anarchist?" Structure: truth and ahimsa, means and ends, satyagraha, Hind Swaraj, the oceanic-circle state, trusteeship. Then the Ambedkar and Marxist critiques. End with Gandhi in the DPSPs and global movements.
B.R. Ambedkar
Thinker of social democracy

Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar (1891–1956) was born into the Mahar caste, treated as untouchable. He earned doctorates from Columbia University and the London School of Economics , and became a barrister. He chaired the Constituent Assembly's Drafting Committee and was independent India's first Law Minister. He is one of the most-asked thinkers in Paper I. Key works: Annihilation of Caste (1936), Who Were the Shudras? (1946), The Untouchables (1948) and The Buddha and His Dhamma (1957).
Caste as graded inequality

In his 1916 Columbia paper, "Castes in India", Ambedkar said caste is kept alive by endogamy : marrying only within the group. Later, in Annihilation of Caste , he said caste is not a division of labour but a division of labourers . It ranks people by birth and blocks free choice of work. He called it graded inequality : each caste looks down on those below, so the oppressed never unite against the system. This is why caste lasts.
Annihilation of Caste (1936)

This was a speech written for the Jat-Pat Todak Mandal of Lahore. The organisers cancelled it when they saw the text, so Ambedkar published it himself. Caste cannot be reformed; it must be annihilated . Caste rests on the authority of the shastras . So the shastras themselves must lose their authority. The real remedy is inter-caste marriage . A political revolution must be preceded by a social revolution . Gandhi replied in Harijan , defending varna. Ambedkar answered him in turn.
Liberty, equality, fraternity

Ambedkar said he took these ideals not from the French Revolution but from his master, the Buddha . He insisted they form a trinity . Liberty without equality produces the rule of the few. Equality without liberty kills initiative. Without fraternity , neither can become natural. For Ambedkar, democracy is not just a form of government. It is "a mode of associated living", a phrase he took from his Columbia teacher John Dewey .
Political versus social democracy

In his last speech to the Constituent Assembly on 25 November 1949 , Ambedkar warned: "On the 26th of January 1950, we are going to enter into a life of contradictions. In politics we will have equality and in social and economic life we will have inequality." B.R. Ambedkar, Constituent Assembly, 25 November 1949 He urged constitutional methods, warned against hero-worship (bhakti) in politics, and said political democracy cannot last without social democracy.
Representation and the Poona Pact

At the Round Table Conferences, Ambedkar demanded separate electorates for the Depressed Classes. The British Communal Award of 1932 granted them. Gandhi began a fast unto death in Yerwada jail, saying separate electorates would divide Hindus. To save his life, Ambedkar signed the Poona Pact (September 1932): joint electorates with reserved seats instead. Ambedkar later said the pact left Dalit representatives dependent on caste-Hindu votes. This history shaped reservation in the Constitution.
State socialism and conversion

In States and Minorities (1947), he proposed state socialism : key industries and agriculture owned by the state, written into the Constitution itself. He founded the Independent Labour Party (1936) and later planned the Republican Party of India. On 13 October 1935 at Yeola he said that though he was born a Hindu, he would not die a Hindu. On 14 October 1956 at Nagpur, he converted to Buddhism with lakhs of followers. His Navayana Buddhism stressed social equality over ritual.
Debates on Ambedkar

Gandhi vs Ambedkar: reform of Hinduism versus exit from it. Gandhi saw caste as a distortion of varna; Ambedkar saw varna as the root. Marxists said class, not caste, is primary. Ambedkar replied that caste is a real structure of power in India. Some argue his trust in state and law was too great. Christophe Jaffrelot and Gail Omvedt show how his ideas grew into a wide Dalit movement, from the Dalit Panthers (1972) to the BSP.
Ambedkar's struggles and federal ideas

Mahad Satyagraha (1927): Dalits drew water from the Chavdar tank, which a public resolution had opened to all. Kalaram Temple entry movement at Nashik (1930–35). Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924), with the motto "educate, agitate, organise". Papers: Mooknayak (1920) and Bahishkrit Bharat (1927). He resigned as Law Minister in 1951, partly over the stalling of the Hindu Code Bill . On the Constitution, he said India is a " Union of States ": the federation is not the result of an agreement, so no state can secede. He also warned that a constitution is only as good as those who work it. A good one, badly run, will fail.
Ambedkar's struggle
The line runs from social protest to constitutional design to a religious turn, which gives you a natural structure for a long answer.
Ambedkar in the Constitution

Article 17 abolishes untouchability. Articles 15(4) and 16(4) enable reservation; Articles 330 and 332 reserve seats for SCs and STs. He called Article 32 , the right to constitutional remedies, the "heart and soul" of the Constitution. The SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 carries his legacy forward. Since 2015, 26 November is observed as Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas).
How UPSC asks this

"Ambedkar's idea of social democracy." Discuss. "Compare Gandhi's and Ambedkar's views on caste." "Why did Ambedkar choose Buddhism?" Structure: life and context, caste as graded inequality, Annihilation of Caste, the liberty-equality-fraternity trinity, the 1949 warning, Poona Pact. Then the Gandhi debate, and his place in the Constitution.
M.N. Roy
From communist to radical humanist

Manabendra Nath Roy (1887–1954), born Narendra Nath Bhattacharya, started as a Bengal revolutionary. He travelled the world looking for arms for India's freedom. In Mexico in 1919 he helped turn the Socialist Workers' Party into the Communist Party of Mexico , one of the first communist parties outside Russia. He then worked closely with Lenin in the Communist International. Later he broke with Marxism and built his own philosophy, radical humanism . His journey from Marx to humanism is what UPSC asks about.
Debating Lenin

At the Second Congress of the Comintern (1920), Roy debated Lenin on the colonies. Lenin Communists should support the national bourgeoisie, such as Congress, against imperialism. Roy The colonial bourgeoisie would compromise with imperialism. Communists should build mass movements of workers and peasants instead. Both sets of theses were adopted in amended form. In 1920 at Tashkent, Roy helped set up the émigré Communist Party of India .
Break with communism

Roy was expelled from the Comintern in 1929, after disagreeing with Stalin's line. He came back to India secretly in 1930. He was arrested in July 1931 on old charges from the Cawnpore (Kanpur) Conspiracy case, sentenced to six years, and released in November 1936. He joined Congress for a time, then broke with it. During the Second World War he backed the Allies against fascism, which isolated him from the national movement. He founded the Radical Democratic Party in 1940.
Where Marx went wrong

Economic determinism ignores the role of ideas and of human will. Making class the only unit erases the individual . The dictatorship of the proletariat became the dictatorship of a party, then of one man. Marx underrated the middle class , which was growing, not disappearing. Ends cannot justify means. A free society cannot be built with unfree methods. He set out these views in Beyond Communism (1947) and Reason, Romanticism and Revolution (1952–55).
Radical humanism

His 22 theses , the "Principles of Radical Democracy", were adopted at Dehradun in December 1946. In December 1948 he dissolved his party and launched the Radical Humanist Movement . Its starting point, in a phrase borrowed from the Greek thinker Protagoras, is that man is the measure of all things . The individual, not class, nation or party, is the centre of value. Human beings are by nature rational and seek freedom . Freedom is the progressive removal of all barriers to the full growth of each person's potential. Roy called his view new humanism , to separate it from older humanist traditions.
Organised democracy

Roy distrusted political parties . He said they concentrate power and turn citizens into voters only. He proposed organised democracy : a network of local people's committees . These would educate citizens, nominate candidates and keep representatives accountable, with rights of recall. Power would flow from the bottom up. The state would be decentralised, and citizens politically awake. This is sometimes called partyless democracy , an idea shared with Jayaprakash Narayan.
Cultural renaissance first

Roy argued that political freedom needs a prior cultural and philosophical revolution , as the European Renaissance came before democracy. Indians, he said, needed to drop fatalism and blind faith and embrace science and reason. So a band of radical humanists should spread rational thinking through education, not seize power. This made his movement small and intellectual.
Limits of Roy's thought

His trust in human rationality seems too optimistic. Partyless democracy was never shown to work at scale. His support for the British war effort made him unpopular and cut him off from the masses. His movement stayed among a small elite of thinkers. Yet his early, sharp critique of Stalinism and his defence of individual freedom against all forms of totalitarianism look far-sighted today.
Roy on Gandhi and nationalism

Roy was a sharp critic of Gandhi . He said Gandhism was a revivalist, backward-looking ideology. It used religion to mobilise peasants while protecting landlords and the Indian bourgeoisie. He was also critical of nationalism itself. Nationalism, he said, puts the nation above the individual and can easily slide into fascism. This was why he backed the Allies against fascism in the war. In India in Transition (1922), one of the first Marxist analyses of Indian society, he argued that Indian capitalists would ally with the British, so freedom would need workers and peasants. These views explain his isolation, but also his distinct place in the syllabus as the radical humanist perspective on Indian nationalism.
Roy's journey
The path from revolutionary to humanist explains why his later work stresses freedom and reason over class struggle.
Roy's place in India

Roy is a bridge between Indian Marxism and Indian liberalism . His idea of decentralised, participatory democracy echoes in Jayaprakash Narayan 's partyless democracy and his 1974 call for Total Revolution . He also drafted a Constitution of Free India (1944), proposing a federal state with people's committees. In the freedom movement, he stands for the Radical Humanist perspective, which the syllabus lists in the nationalism unit too.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss M.N. Roy's critique of Marxism." "Explain the main features of Roy's radical humanism." Structure: life in three phases (revolutionary, communist, humanist), the 1920 Lenin debate, his critique of Marx, the 22 theses, organised democracy. End with critique and link to JP Narayan. Useful anchors: Roy helped found the Communist Party of India at Tashkent in 1920. His books include India in Transition (1922), New Humanism: A Manifesto (1947) and Reason, Romanticism and Revolution (1952). Do not confuse his radical humanism with the older Western humanism of the Renaissance.
Jawaharlal Nehru
The architect of modern India's mind

Nehru (1889-1964), the first Prime Minister (1947-64), shaped India's institutions and its political culture. Yet he is not a classical 'thinker' in the manner of Gandhi or Ambedkar, so UPSC asks about his ideas in action : democracy, secularism, socialism, planning, scientific temper and non-alignment.
Nehru's main ideas
The Discovery of India

Written in Ahmednagar Fort jail (1942-45) and published in 1946, The Discovery of India sees India as a palimpsest : layer upon layer of cultures, none wiped out. Unity in diversity is the central theme. He rejects both communal history and blind Westernisation. His earlier works, Glimpses of World History (1934) and An Autobiography (1936), show a wide, humanist and Marxist-influenced outlook.
Democratic socialism and planning

Nehru was drawn to Marxist analysis of class and imperialism but rejected violence and dictatorship. His middle path: democratic socialism , a mixed economy with a strong public sector. Landmarks: National Planning Committee (1938), Planning Commission (1950), Industrial Policy Resolution (1956), 'socialistic pattern of society' (Avadi session, 1955), Second Plan (Mahalanobis model, heavy industry). Dams were 'the temples of modern India'.
Secularism and scientific temper

For Nehru the state must be neutral between religions yet treat all fairly: equal respect , not hostility to religion. He opposed majority communalism more than minority communalism, as it could pose as nationalism. He urged a scientific temper : questioning, evidence and reason. The phrase appears in Discovery of India , and now in Art. 51A(h) as a Fundamental Duty (42nd Amendment, 1976).
Foreign policy ideas

He saw peace and development as linked. Principles: non-alignment, anti-colonialism and anti-racism, Panchsheel (1954 agreement with China), Bandung (1955), the NAM founding (Belgrade 1961). He tried to give a newly independent India an independent voice between the two blocs. The 1962 war with China is held up as the failure of his idealism.
Critiques

Right : favoured the Westernised elite, appeased minorities. Lohia and the left : dynastic, Congress-centred and elitist, and neglected caste. Swatantra : planning produced a licence-permit raj. Agriculture and primary education got less priority. The Hindu rate of growth (about 3.5 per cent). Defenders: built institutions, held democracy and secular state together under hard conditions.
Nehru and Gandhi

They were close but different. Gandhi: village, decentralisation, moral politics, non-violence as creed. Nehru: modern industry, state-led growth, secular rationalism, non-violence as policy. Gandhi named Nehru his heir in 1942. Both rejected communalism and wanted an inclusive nation. Gandhi's Hind Swaraj (1909) criticised modern industrial civilisation, while Nehru's Autobiography (1936) saw industry as needed to end poverty. Nehru's 'Tryst with Destiny' speech of 14 August 1947 is the best known statement of the nation he helped build.
His legacy today

Institutions with his stamp: IITs, ISRO precursors (INCOSPAR 1962), AIIMS, CSIR, parliamentary democracy and the first Lok Sabha elections (1951-52). Contemporary debate on secularism, state versus market and foreign policy often goes back to Nehru, for or against. The Planning Commission was set up in March 1950, and the Second Five Year Plan of 1956 gave heavy industry a large share of investment under the Mahalanobis model.
How UPSC asks this

"Nehru's idea of secularism was a mixture of western and Indian traditions. Discuss." "Examine Nehru's contribution to the idea of planned development." "Critically assess Nehru's vision of India as seen in The Discovery of India." Structure: idea, text, five pillars, critique, Gandhi contrast, legacy. A useful critique: the 1954 Panchsheel agreement with China was praised abroad, but critics link Nehru's 'forward policy' to the 1962 India-China war.
Ram Manohar Lohia
The maverick socialist

Ram Manohar Lohia (1910-67) was a socialist leader who tried to make socialism Indian . He stressed caste, language and rural India, and is the intellectual root of much OBC politics in the Hindi belt. He appears in Paper I's Indian thought and in questions on non-Congressism and backward-caste politics.
A socialism for India

Lohia felt that Marx's class analysis, built on Europe, is incomplete for India, where caste and class overlap. His slogan: caste is 'closed class' and class is 'open caste'. Without breaking caste, there can be no equality. He also rejected both the Western capitalist and the Soviet models as 'twin evils' using huge machines and centralised power.
Seven revolutions (Sapta Kranti)

He called for simultaneous struggles against seven injustices. Inequality of man and woman Inequality of colour Caste (inequality by birth) Foreign domination, and for national and world freedom Economic inequality Violation of private life by the state Armaments, in favour of satyagraha Lohia was one of the founders of the Congress Socialist Party in 1934, and the seven revolutions set out the full socialist agenda he wanted in the 1950s.
Chaukhamba Raj and decentralisation

Lohia proposed a four-pillar state (Chaukhamba Raj): village, district, province and Centre, each with real power. Power should be shared down to the village. He favoured small-unit technology (like the charkha in modern form), not giant machines, in a Gandhian way. He attacked the 'permanent government' of the elite.
Backward castes and women

The Samyukta Socialist Party slogan is credited to him: 'Sansopa ne bandhi gaanth, pichhde pawen sau mein saath', meaning backward castes, women and the poor should get 60 per cent of opportunities. He backed reservation in jobs and politics beyond SC/ST. He also campaigned for Indian languages with the slogan Angrezi Hatao (remove English as the language of power).
Wheel of History and Guilt of Partition

Wheel of History (1955) argues that history moves between periods of caste-based hierarchy and class-based change. Marx, Gandhi and Socialism (1963) mixes the three. In Guilt of Divided India (1960) he blames Congress leaders' weariness and the British for Partition. His 'Chaukhamba Raj' idea of four pillars of power (village, district, province and nation) showed his decentralising socialism on paper.
Non-Congressism
Lohia's non-Congressism (from 1963) urged opposition parties to unite against Congress dominance. It worked in 1967, though most of the SVD governments were short lived.
Critiques

Aggressive anti-English stand hurt the south and modern education. The Samyukta Socialist Party was fragmented, with little organisation. Later 'Lohiaites' (Mulayam Singh Yadav, Lalu Prasad, Nitish Kumar) are accused of dynastic and caste politics, far from his vision. Supporters: he put caste, gender and decentralisation on the agenda before others.
Lohia's legacy

Mandal reservations (1990), Panchayati Raj and the OBC political rise in the Hindi belt draw on his thought. On gender he raised violence and equality, and on caste he influenced 1967 coalition politics. Samyukta Vidhayak Dal governments in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar in 1967 ran on an anti-Congress platform, which was his non-Congressism in action.
