UPSC asks about the general will , his view of freedom and his place among the social contract thinkers. The Discourse on Inequality (1755) and The Social Contract (1762) are the two texts most often set in UPSC answers. Rousseau also wrote Emile in 1762.
Natural man and the fall

In Discourse on the Origin of Inequality (1755) Rousseau says the natural man is free, peaceful, and moved by self-love ( amour de soi ) and pity. The rise of private property and vanity ( amour-propre ) produced inequality, conflict and a false contract favouring the rich. Unlike Hobbes, he thinks society, not nature, corrupts humans. Famous opening of The Social Contract (1762): 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.'
The social contract
The contract is made among equals, not with a ruler. The ruler (government) is only an agent of the sovereign people.
The general will

The general will is what the people want as citizens, looking to the common good . It differs from the will of all , which is the sum of private interests. It is always right, says Rousseau, though not always enlightened, so a wise 'Legislator' may be needed. Citizens who refuse to follow it can be 'forced to be free', meaning forced to obey the law they gave themselves.
Sovereignty and democracy

Sovereignty is inalienable (cannot be given away), indivisible and absolute . It cannot be represented: 'The English people thinks it is free; it is mistaken; it is free only during the election of members of Parliament.' He preferred direct democracy in small states, as in Geneva or Corsica, with a civil religion to bind citizens.
Freedom and equality

Rousseau's freedom is moral self-rule : obeying a law I made. He insisted that no citizen should be rich enough to buy another, or poor enough to be forced to sell himself. His Emile (1762) proposes a natural education, and his view of women there is traditional, criticised by Wollstonecraft.
Critiques

Isaiah Berlin : 'forced to be free' is positive liberty and a route to tyranny. J.L. Talmon , Origins of Totalitarian Democracy (1952), links the general will to Jacobin terror. Who defines the general will? Easily claimed by a party or leader. Direct democracy is hard in large states. Defenders: Rousseau cares about law and rights, and about equal citizens.
Rousseau vs Hobbes and Locke

Hobbes : fear of death, absolute sovereign. Locke : protect property, limited government, consent and revolution. Rousseau : community and common good, sovereign people. He moves from the individual's rights to the collective's moral freedom. Kant, Hegel and Marx all learn from him. Rousseau wrote in 1762, more than a century after Hobbes's Leviathan (1651), and his answer to Hobbes's fear was moral freedom through the general will.
Rousseau in India

The idea of popular sovereignty is in the Preamble: 'We, the People of India'. Gandhi's village democracy and JP's participatory model have a Rousseauian flavour. Debates on referendum, recall and the Supreme Court's reading of the 'will of the people' invoke him. Mind the contrast with the Constituent Assembly's choice of representative democracy.
How UPSC asks this

"Explain Rousseau's concept of the general will." "'Man is born free and everywhere he is in chains.' Discuss." "Compare Rousseau's social contract with those of Hobbes and Locke." Structure: state of nature, contract, general will, sovereignty, freedom, critiques, comparison, Indian link. The line 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains' opens Book I, chapter 1 of The Social Contract (1762), so quote it with that source.
Strategies of the Freedom Struggle
One goal, many strategies

India's freedom struggle was not one movement with one method. Over 62 years, from the Congress's founding in 1885 to independence in 1947, leaders tried petitions, boycotts, mass satyagraha, council politics, armed revolution and an army in exile. Part of the story is also about how they argued over methods. This is the main exam angle. UPSC asks you to compare strategies , not to list events. Three questions to carry: Who led and who joined? What was the method? What did it achieve and fail to achieve? The topic opens Paper I Section B. Good answers link events to the ideology behind them, which connects to the later lessons on peasants, workers and perspectives (liberal, socialist, Marxist, radical humanist, Dalit).
The map of strategies

Moderates used petition and prayer; Extremists boycott and swadeshi; Gandhi mass satyagraha. Others entered councils, took up arms, or (the INA) raised an army abroad. The strategies overlapped. A Gandhian movement could run alongside council entry, and revolutionaries worked in parallel. Bipan Chandra's India's Struggle for Independence (1988) describes the Gandhian pattern as Struggle-Truce-Struggle (S-T-S), with a constitutional wing working between phases to keep the movement fresh.
The Moderates, 1885-1905

The Indian National Congress was founded in December 1885 in Bombay, with A.O. Hume as organiser and W.C. Bonnerjee as first president. The Moderates (Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta, Surendranath Banerjea, Ranade) trusted British fairness. Their method was often called prayer, petition and protest . They demanded: More Indians in councils and services (simultaneous ICS exams in India). Reduction of military spending and land revenue. An end to the "drain of wealth" (Naoroji, Poverty and Un-British Rule in India , 1901; also R.C. Dutt). Gains : the Indian Councils Act 1892 and economic criticism that undermined the claim of benevolent rule. Limits : a narrow elite base, and little mass contact. Radicals called it "political mendicancy".
The Extremists and Swadeshi, 1905-1919

Lord Curzon announced the Partition of Bengal in July 1905; it took effect on 16 October 1905. Bengal's response launched the Swadeshi and Boycott Movement . Lal-Bal-Pal (Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal) with Aurobindo pushed for swaraj , which Tilak called a birthright. The four planks: swadeshi, boycott of foreign goods, national education (National Council of Education, 1906) and passive resistance. Tilak used festivals (Ganapati, Shivaji) to mobilise people. The Congress split at Surat in 1907. Repression followed: Tilak was jailed for six years in 1908. The Muslim League was formed in 1906, and Morley-Minto reforms (1909) introduced separate electorates. Bengal partition was annulled in 1911. The Home Rule Leagues (Tilak and Annie Besant, 1916) and the Lucknow Pact (Dec 1916) revived unity.
Gandhi's method: satyagraha

Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915. His method, satyagraha (insistence on truth), was based on non-violence, willingness to suffer and an appeal to the opponent's conscience. His first Indian experiments were local: Champaran (1917): indigo cultivators against the tinkathia system. Ahmedabad (1918): mill workers' wage dispute, with a fast. Kheda (1918): peasants and revenue remission after crop failure. In 1919, against the Rowlatt Act , he called the first all-India hartal. The Jallianwala Bagh massacre (13 April 1919, Amritsar) turned moderate hopes into anger, and the Khilafat issue gave a chance to join Hindus and Muslims. New features: mass base (peasants, women, workers), non-violence, a Hindi-speaking style and the Congress as a mass organisation.
Mass movements: 1920-34

Non-Cooperation (adopted 1920): boycott of courts, schools, councils and foreign cloth, with khadi and national institutions. It was suspended by Gandhi after violence at Chauri Chaura (5 February 1922). Civil Disobedience : after the Lahore session (December 1929) declared Purna Swaraj , 26 January 1930 became Independence Day. The Dandi march (12 March-6 April 1930) broke the salt law. Gandhi-Irwin Pact: 5 March 1931. Gandhi attended the Second Round Table Conference in 1931. The movement was resumed and withdrawn by 1934. The Communal Award (August 1932) and the Poona Pact (24 September 1932) between Gandhi and Ambedkar settled depressed-class representation.
Constitutional struggle: councils and elections

When mass movements paused, the constitutional path kept political life active. Swaraj Party (January 1923): C.R. Das and Motilal Nehru, who wanted to enter councils and "wreck from within". They used walkouts and defeated government bills. Opposed by the "No-Changers" (Rajagopalachari, Rajendra Prasad). Simon Commission (1927): all-white, boycotted by most. Lajpat Rai died after a police lathi-charge in 1928. The Nehru Report (1928) was the Indian reply, a draft constitution. Government of India Act 1935 : provincial autonomy. In the 1937 elections , the Congress won a majority in 5 of 11 provinces and formed ministries in several more. The ministries resigned in 1939 over India's entry into World War II. Congress leaders Nehru, Bose and the socialists disliked office-taking, but it brought administrative experience and mass contact.
Revolutionaries and the INA

Early revolutionaries : the Chapekar brothers (Pune, 1897), the Anushilan Samiti in Bengal, and Ghadar Party in North America (1913). Abroad: Shyamji Krishnavarma, Madame Cama, V.D. Savarkar. HRA and HSRA : the Hindustan Republican Association (1924, Ram Prasad Bismil, Sachindranath Sanyal) and the Kakori train action (1925). Later, the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association (1928) with Chandrashekhar Azad, Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru. Bhagat Singh, an atheist socialist, threw a bomb in the Central Assembly (April 1929) and was hanged in March 1931. Surya Sen led the Chittagong armoury raid (April 1930). Subhas Chandra Bose left Congress in 1939 (Forward Bloc), reached Germany and then Southeast Asia. He took charge of the Indian National Army in 1943 and set up the Azad Hind government in Singapore. The INA trials (Red Fort, November 1945) stirred public feeling and shook the loyalty of Indian soldiers.
Quit India and the endgame

August Offer (1940) and individual satyagraha (1940-41). The Cripps Mission (March 1942) offered post-war dominion status with an option for provinces to stay out, and was rejected. Quit India : 8 August 1942 (Bombay Gowalia Tank). "Do or Die." Leaders were arrested on 9 August, and the movement became a leaderless mass uprising, with parallel governments in Ballia, Tamluk and Satara. Aruna Asaf Ali, Jayaprakash Narayan and Usha Mehta (Congress radio) became symbols. 1945-47 : Wavell's Simla Conference (1945), INA trials, the Royal Indian Navy mutiny (February 1946), the Cabinet Mission (1946), Direct Action Day (16 August 1946), Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947) and the Indian Independence Act (18 July 1947). Independence came on 15 August 1947 along with Partition.
Why did India become free? Historians disagree

Nationalist view (Bipan Chandra and others, India's Struggle for Independence , 1988): a broad anti-colonial movement under Gandhi's leadership forced the end of British rule. Cambridge School (Anil Seal, John Gallagher, Gordon Johnson): Indian politics was a competition among local elites for state patronage, and nationalism was a cover. Marxist (R.P. Dutt, India Today , 1940; A.R. Desai): the movement was led by the bourgeoisie, who compromised with imperialism to protect class interests. Subaltern Studies (Ranajit Guha, from 1982): elite nationalism ignored peasants and tribals, who had their own autonomous politics. Other factors : World War II weakened Britain, the INA and naval mutiny shook the Raj's loyalty, and the Labour government was ready to leave. A strong answer weighs several causes, not one.
What the strategies left behind

Constitution : the Karachi resolution (1931) promised fundamental rights and economic programme. The Nehru Report of 1928 shaped Part III and ideas on minorities. The 1935 Act supplied much of the Constitution's structure. Political style : hartals, padyatras, fasts and civil disobedience are still used. The Anna Hazare movement (2011) and the farmers' protests of 2020-21 echoed Gandhian methods, with debates on whether they matched them. Memory politics : Azadi Ka Amrit Mahotsav (launched in March 2021, concluded in 2023) and debates about forgotten heroes, tribal leaders like Birsa Munda and women freedom fighters. Open questions : is Gandhian non-violence a universal method or a product of its time? Debates about Bose, Bhagat Singh and the role of armed struggle also continue.
How to answer

"The Gandhian strategy of struggle-truce-struggle was an effective approach to the freedom struggle." Discuss. Compare the Moderate and Extremist methods. Assess the role of constitutional struggle in the national movement. How did revolutionary and INA activities complement mass movements? Structure: frame the strategies in a table, then give each phase in date order with its leaders, method, gains and limits. For S-T-S, link the mass phases (1920-22, 1930-34, 1942) to the constitutional gaps. Use the historiography debate for analysis. Close by saying that strategies were complementary and that the war and the INA shifted the final timing.
Peasant, Worker and Revolutionary Movements
The freedom struggle from below

The mainstream story centres on Congress leaders. But peasants, tribals, workers and young revolutionaries made their own movements, with their own demands. Sometimes they joined the national movement. Sometimes they ran ahead of it, or against it. The syllabus puts three streams together: peasant , worker and revolutionary movements. Examiners ask how these fed the national movement and how they tested its leadership, which was largely middle class and wary of class conflict. Learn this lesson in three parts: peasants (and tribals), workers, and revolutionaries. For each, know the key events, leaders, methods, outcomes and a one-line judgment. Link to Subaltern Studies and Marxist readings.
Peasant revolts before 1900

Early peasant action was local, spontaneous and aimed at specific exploiters: planters, moneylenders and zamindars. Most did not question British rule itself. Indigo revolt (Bengal, 1859-60): peasants refused to grow indigo under forced contracts. Dinabandhu Mitra's play Nil Darpan (1860) exposed the planters. The Indigo Commission followed. Pabna agrarian leagues (1873-76, Bengal): resistance to rent increases. Led by Ishan Chandra Roy. Deccan riots (1875): peasants attacked moneylenders in Pune and Ahmednagar. The Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act came in 1879. Tribal revolts : Santhal hul (1855-56, Sidhu and Kanhu), and the Munda ulgulan led by Birsa Munda (1899-1900), against outsiders and land alienation. These show that agrarian grievances in colonial India came from revenue systems, debt and commercialisation.
Peasants and the national movement, 1917-1940s

Awadh Kisan Sabha (1920, Baba Ramchandra, with Nehru's help): against evictions and extra dues. Eka movement (1921-22) followed. Moplah revolt (Malabar, 1921): tenants against landlords, mixed with Khilafat feeling; it turned communal in places. Bardoli (1928): Vallabhbhai Patel led a no-tax campaign against a rise in land revenue, and won; he gained the title "Sardar". Kisan Sabhas : Swami Sahajanand Saraswati founded the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha (1929). The All India Kisan Sabha was set up in Lucknow in April 1936, with N.G. Ranga and others. It demanded abolition of zamindari. Its tensions with Congress deepened in the late 1930s.
Late peasant armed struggles

Tebhaga (Bengal, 1946-47): sharecroppers demanded two-thirds of the crop, not half. Led by the Kisan Sabha and communists. Telangana (1946-51): against the Nizam's landlords ( jagirdars and deshmukhs ). The Communist Party led an armed struggle. It continued after Hyderabad's accession (Operation Polo, September 1948) and was withdrawn in 1951. Punnapra-Vayalar (Kerala, 1946) and the Warli revolt (Maharashtra, 1945-47). Outcome : Peasant pressure shaped the Congress agrarian programme (Karachi 1931, the Faizpur session of December 1936) and led to zamindari abolition after independence. The First Amendment (1951) and the Ninth Schedule protected land reform laws. Limits : middle-class Congress leaders feared class war and landlord support. Gandhi preferred reconciliation of classes, not conflict. Marxists say this blunted radical land reform.
The working class and trade unions

Early phase : philanthropic efforts by individuals such as N.M. Lokhande (Bombay Mill Hands Association, 1890). Strikes followed the Swadeshi movement (1905-08) and Tilak's trial (1908) in Bombay. After 1918 : strikes grew with post-war inflation. B.P. Wadia founded the Madras Labour Union (1918). Gandhi guided the Textile Labour Association in Ahmedabad (1920). AITUC was founded in Bombay in October 1920, with Lala Lajpat Rai as the first president. Legal change : Trade Unions Act, 1926 (registration, legal status); Trade Disputes Act, 1929 (limits on strikes); Royal Commission on Labour, 1929-31. Communist influence : the Communist Party of India (1925), the Workers and Peasants Parties and the Girni Kamgar Union led the Bombay textile strike (1928). The Meerut Conspiracy Case (1929-33) tried 31 labour leaders. After independence: INTUC (May 1947), HMS (1948), and UTUC (1949).
Did the Congress and workers/peasants pull together?

Link : the Congress needed their numbers, and mass campaigns drew on rural resentment. The Karachi resolution (1931) promised fundamental rights and relief for workers and peasants. Distance : the Congress stood for national unity across classes. Business groups such as Tata and Birla helped fund it. Fear of class conflict kept it from backing radical land redistribution or industrial strikes without limits. Communists and socialists : the Congress Socialist Party (1934) pushed the Congress left. Communists cooperated, split and rejoined at different times. In 1942 they opposed Quit India after the USSR entered the war, which cost them credibility. Subaltern view (Guha, Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency , 1983): peasants had their own political consciousness. They used the nationalist leaders' names for their own ends.
Revolutionary movements, phase one

The revolutionaries believed that British rule could end only by force. Their idea of the nation was often religious or heroic. Maharashtra : Chapekar brothers killed Rand in Pune in 1897. Bengal : Anushilan Samiti (1902) and Jugantar (Barindra Ghose). The Alipore Bomb Case (1908): Khudiram Bose was hanged; Aurobindo was acquitted in 1909. Rash Behari Bose took part in the Delhi bomb attack on Viceroy Hardinge (1912). Abroad : India House in London (Shyamji Krishnavarma; Savarkar), Madame Cama in Paris and the Ghadar Party (1913, San Francisco; Lala Har Dayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna). The Komagata Maru incident (1914) and the failed Ghadar uprising of 1915 followed. Main weakness: small, secret groups with no mass base, easily suppressed.
Revolutionary movements, phase two

After Chauri Chaura and the end of non-cooperation, young people turned to a new idea: a revolution with a social aim. HRA (1924, Kanpur): Ram Prasad Bismil, Sachindranath Sanyal, Jogesh Chatterjee. The Kakori train robbery (9 August 1925). Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan, Roshan Singh and Rajendra Lahiri were hanged. HSRA (September 1928, Delhi): socialist goals added. Members: Chandrashekhar Azad, Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru, Bhagwati Charan Vohra. They killed Saunders in Lahore (December 1928) to avenge Lajpat Rai. In April 1929 Bhagat Singh and B.K. Dutt threw bombs in the Central Assembly to "make the deaf hear". Jatin Das died on hunger strike in September 1929. Chittagong armoury raid (18 April 1930): Surya Sen, with Ganesh Ghosh, Ananta Singh, and later Pritilata Waddedar. Bhagat Singh was hanged on 23 March 1931 with Sukhdev and Rajguru. He wrote Why I Am an Atheist (1930).
Violence versus non-violence

Gandhi's view : his 1930 article "The Cult of the Bomb" argued that violence was unsuitable for a mass struggle and would invite repression. Revolutionaries replied with Bhagwati Charan Vohra's "The Philosophy of the Bomb" (1930). Role : the revolutionaries gave courage and inspired youth. Bhagat Singh's trial turned him into a national hero, as Nehru recorded. Ideas : they moved from religious symbols to socialism and secularism, calling for "Inquilab Zindabad". Their goal was not just to end British rule but social revolution. Limits : few members, no mass organisation, harsh crackdowns. A balanced judgment: they did not defeat the Raj but they affected the national mood, and complemented rather than contradicted the mass movements.
Echoes today

Agrarian : the farmers' agitation of 2020-21 against the three farm laws led to their repeal in November 2021. Kisan unions and a demand for legal MSP continue. The Land Acquisition Act, 2013, and the Forest Rights Act, 2006, are responses to old tribal and peasant grievances. Labour : Parliament passed the four labour codes in 2019-20 (wages, industrial relations, social security, occupational safety). The Union government brought them into force on 21 November 2025, replacing 29 older laws. Unions have protested. Rules continue to be notified. Left-wing extremism traces back to Naxalbari (1967), whose roots lie in the Telangana and Tebhaga traditions. Memory : Bhagat Singh, Birsa Munda and others are celebrated in state commemorations, with fresh debate on their ideas.
How to answer

"The peasant movements in colonial India were localised and reflected agrarian grievances more than anti-colonial sentiment." Discuss. Assess the role of the working class in the national movement. Examine the ideological transformation of the revolutionary movement from 1900 to 1931. Why did the Congress leadership keep its distance from radical peasant and labour movements? Structure: answer each stream in the same way: the cause, key events with years, leaders, relation to Congress, outcome, then an evaluation. Use the Subaltern and Marxist perspectives for analysis. Make a table of three streams (peasant, worker, revolutionary) with method and legacy. Add one present-day link such as the farm laws or labour codes.
Perspectives: Liberal, Socialist, Marxist, Radical Humanist, Dalit
Five readings of the same struggle

Every group in the national movement asked: Freedom from whom, for whom, and to do what? The British were the obvious enemy, but liberals, socialists, Marxists, radical humanists and Dalit leaders also named other enemies: poverty, capital, caste, superstition. This lesson covers five perspectives. For each, learn the leaders, their key text or organisation, what they thought nationalism was for, and where they differed from Gandhi and the Congress. Examiners like comparative questions, such as "Compare Gandhi and Ambedkar on the caste question" or "Evaluate the Marxist critique of the Indian National Congress". A matrix of perspective by theme will help you answer quickly.
A quick comparison grid

The differences can be reduced to three questions: What is the main contradiction (colonial rule, class, caste, or the loss of individual freedom)? Who is the agent of change (the educated elite, workers and peasants, the rational individual, the oppressed castes)? What is the method (constitutional reform, mass action, revolution, education and law)?
The liberal perspective

The early Congress was liberal. Dadabhai Naoroji , Mahadev Govind Ranade , G.K. Gokhale , Pherozeshah Mehta and Surendranath Banerjea believed in British ideals of law, representation and free speech, and asked Britain to live up to them. Economic nationalism : Naoroji's drain theory, R.C. Dutt's Economic History of India (1902-04). Social reform : Ranade and Gokhale (Servants of India Society, 1905) stressed that political freedom needs social reform. Method : gradual, constitutional, with an emphasis on rights and councils. Later liberals : after 1918 many left the Congress, forming the National Liberal Federation (1919). Tej Bahadur Sapru and M.R. Jayakar were prominent. Critique : too elitist, dependent on British goodwill, and slow. Yet the liberals' constitutionalism, rule of law and individual rights fed straight into the Constitution of 1950.
The socialist perspective

Socialist ideas grew among Congress members in the 1920s and 1930s, driven by the Russian Revolution, the Depression and Nehru's influence (his 1927 visit to the USSR; presidency of Lucknow 1936). The Congress Socialist Party (CSP) was founded in 1934 inside the Congress, with Acharya Narendra Dev, Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia, Achyut Patwardhan, Asoka Mehta and others. Its aims: Make the Congress a mass organisation of workers and peasants. Link freedom with the removal of economic exploitation: abolition of zamindari, nationalisation of key industries. Use Marxian analysis but reject its dictatorship. They kept faith in democracy and in Gandhi's mass action, but not his trusteeship. Jayaprakash Narayan's Why Socialism? (1936) was a key text. The socialists played a big part in the Quit India underground (1942).
Lohia and JP: Indian socialism's own path

Ram Manohar Lohia (1910-67) In Wheel of History (1955) he argued that caste and class are linked in India and that ownership alone does not explain power. He wanted a socialism of the "four pillars" ( chaukhamba state): village, district, province and centre. He stressed small-unit technology , seven revolutions (against inequality of caste, class, sex, colour, colonialism, arms and for civil liberty), and special opportunities ( vishesh avsar ) for backward castes, women and minorities. Hence the slogan of 60 per cent reserved for the backward. Jayaprakash Narayan (1902-79) After Marxism he turned to Gandhian ideas: Sarvodaya in the early 1950s (he pledged his life, jeevandan , to Vinoba's movement in 1954), and partyless democracy in A Plea for Reconstruction of Indian Polity (1959). In 1974-75 he called for Total Revolution (Sampoorna Kranti).
The Marxist perspective

Origins : M.N. Roy helped form a Communist group at Tashkent (1920). The CPI was formally founded in India in Kanpur in 1925. Leaders: S.A. Dange, Muzaffar Ahmad, S.V. Ghate, P.C. Joshi. The party was banned in the 1930s and faced the Kanpur and Meerut cases. Analysis : Marxist writers saw British rule as colonial exploitation and the Indian capitalists as a class with divided interests. R.P. Dutt's India Today (1940) argued the bourgeoisie compromised with imperialism. A.R. Desai's Social Background of Indian Nationalism (1948) read nationalism through class. D.D. Kosambi studied history from below. Critique of Congress : a bourgeois party, using the masses for its own aims and stopping movements before they went too far (Gandhi-Irwin Pact, Chauri Chaura). Strategy : unite workers and peasants, but the CPI's line shifted: the "Peoples' War" line of 1942 (supporting the war effort after the USSR was attacked) isolated it from Quit India.
Assessing the Marxist view

Strengths : it highlighted exploitation, class and the role of workers and peasants. Marxists pushed the freedom movement to take up land reform and labour rights. Poverty and economic issues became part of the nationalist programme. Weaknesses : it underplayed caste, religion and culture. It applied European class categories mechanically. Gramsci-influenced later Marxists admit that Congress built a hegemonic bloc with real mass support, not mere manipulation. The Comintern problem : the line from Moscow (e.g., 1928 "sectarian" turn, Calcutta Thesis 1948) often fitted India poorly. Dalit critique : Ambedkar called Marxism blind to caste (see his "Buddha or Karl Marx", 1956). He saw capitalism and Brahminism as twin enemies of the labouring poor. The fair verdict: Marxism enriched the debate and economic analysis, but fit India only partly.
The radical humanist perspective: M.N. Roy

Manabendra Nath Roy (1887-1954) began as a Bengal revolutionary, became a founder of the Mexican and the Indian communist parties, and a Comintern leader. He clashed with Lenin at the Second Comintern Congress (1920), over whether colonial nationalists could be allies. Expelled from the Comintern in 1929, he returned to India in 1930, was jailed (1931-36), joined Congress, then left. He formed the Radical Democratic Party (1940). His change in thought: from Marxism to Radical Humanism or New Humanism (1946-47; the 22 Theses). Core ideas: Man is the measure of all things, and is rational and moral. Freedom of the individual is the goal of social progress, not class or party. Rejection of party politics: replace it with people's committees ( Politics, Power and Parties , 1960) and a cooperative economy. Basis: science, reason, and ethics, not religion. Detailed in lesson 0-8-5.
The Dalit perspective: Phule to Ambedkar

Jotirao Phule (1827-90): Gulamgiri (1873) described caste as Brahmin enslavement of the shudras and atishudras. Founded the Satyashodhak Samaj (1873). With Savitribai Phule he began girls' schooling in 1848. South India : Sri Narayana Guru ("one caste, one religion, one god"; his 1888 consecration of a Shiva idol at Aruvippuram challenged Brahmin monopoly), Ayyankali, Periyar E.V. Ramasamy's Self-Respect Movement (1925) and Iyothee Thass. B.R. Ambedkar (1891-1956): Mooknayak (1920), Mahad satyagraha (1927, for water, with a burning of the Manusmriti), Kalaram temple entry at Nashik (1930), Poona Pact (1932), Independent Labour Party (1936), Annihilation of Caste (1936), and the Scheduled Castes Federation (1942). He gave his views in What Congress and Gandhi Have Done to the Untouchables (1945). Core claim: political freedom without social freedom is hollow. The depressed classes needed their own political safeguards. Ambedkar embraced Buddhism on 14 October 1956 at Nagpur.
Gandhi and Ambedkar on caste and nationalism

Diagnosis : Gandhi first defended the varna order but sought to remove untouchability (he called Dalits Harijans ). Ambedkar called for annihilation of caste itself. Remedy : Gandhi trusted a change of heart among caste Hindus and the Harijan Sevak Sangh (1932). Ambedkar demanded legal safeguards, separate electorates and political power. Poona Pact (1932): after Gandhi's fast, Ambedkar gave up separate electorates in return for reserved seats (148 in provincial legislatures, up from 71). Village : Gandhi romanticised it; Ambedkar saw it as a centre of oppression. Link back to the others: socialists such as Lohia took caste more seriously after independence. Marxists, for their part, were criticised for not seeing it earlier.
These perspectives in today's politics

Liberal : constitutionalism, free press and the rule of law, defended in cases like Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and Puttaswamy (2017). Socialist : the Janata and Janata Dal family, Lohia's social justice politics and Mandal (1990), and welfare rights. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added "socialist" to the Preamble. Marxist : the Left parties (CPI, CPI(M)) and trade unions, with Kerala as their historic stronghold. Maoist groups claim the Naxalbari legacy. Radical Humanist : ideas on decentralisation and civil liberties groups. Dalit : Ambedkar's Constitution is central. Dalit political assertion includes the Bahujan Samaj Party (1984) and the 2018 debate on the SC/ST Atrocities Act. Reservation continues (see lesson 0-3-1). The caste enumeration decision in the next Census (announced April 2025) revived these debates.
How to answer

"Dalit perspectives on nationalism differ sharply from the mainstream." Discuss. Examine the Marxist critique of the Indian national movement. Evaluate M.N. Roy's contribution as a radical humanist. Compare Gandhi's and Ambedkar's approaches to the caste question. Structure: open with the framing questions (enemy, agent, method). For each perspective give leaders, key text, central claim and critique, in a table if possible. Always link to Gandhi and the Congress for comparison. Keep one balanced paragraph: how each perspective widened the aims of the movement, and how the Constitution drew on all of them.
Legacies of British Rule
The Constitution did not start from zero

The Constituent Assembly met in 1946. But the state it inherited had been built over 190 years of company and Crown rule. The courts, civil services, police, army, laws, railways and the Westminster-style parliament all had colonial roots. The Constitution kept some, reworked others and rejected a few. This is a standard Paper I Section B theme. Questions ask: What did the 1935 Act contribute? Which colonial legacies helped India, and which hurt it? How far did India break with its colonial past? Learn it in three parts: (1) the chain of Acts from 1773 to 1947; (2) the administrative, legal and political legacies; (3) the nationalist inheritance, which was equally important: the Nehru Report, the Karachi resolution and the habit of constitutional debate.
From Company to Crown: the main Acts

Note the pattern: control moved from the Company to Parliament (1773-1858), then power to Indians grew in small steps (1861-1935), always with safeguards for the Crown. The Indian Independence Act (18 July 1947) ended it.
Steps toward representative government

Charter Act 1833 : India's laws made by one authority, the Governor-General in Council. Introduced a Law Member (Macaulay was the first). Indian Councils Act 1861 : portfolio system, nominated Indians in legislative councils (a first step to cabinet government). 1892 : indirect election element and the right to discuss the budget. Morley-Minto 1909 : elected members in councils and separate electorates for Muslims , which began a communal political path. Montagu-Chelmsford 1919 : dyarchy in provinces (reserved and transferred subjects), a bicameral Centre, direct elections, a Public Service Commission, and a very limited, property-based franchise (only a few per cent of the population). Simon Commission (1927-30) and the Round Table Conferences (1930-32) preceded the next step.
The Government of India Act, 1935: structure

The 1935 Act was the longest Act passed by the British Parliament up to then (321 sections, 10 Schedules). It is the most important legacy for the Constitution, and many of its provisions were carried over, sometimes word for word. Provincial autonomy : dyarchy ended in provinces; ministers responsible to legislatures. The Governor kept special powers. Federation with princely states (never started, as states did not join). Three lists: Federal, Provincial and Concurrent. Federal Court (1937), the forerunner of the Supreme Court. Federal and Provincial Public Service Commissions . The Reserve Bank of India (1935, by a separate Act).
The Government of India Act, 1935: emergency and franchise

Emergency provisions (Section 93: Governor's rule when provincial government failed) which became Article 356. Franchise extended to roughly 10-12 per cent of the population. Separate electorates kept for Muslims and others. Depressed classes got reserved seats in joint electorates under the Poona Pact (1932), which the 1935 Act followed.
Administrative and legal legacies

Civil services : the ICS "steel frame" became the IAS. Article 312 provides for All-India Services. Sardar Patel defended them in the Assembly. Law : Macaulay's Indian Penal Code (1860), the Evidence Act (1872), the Contract Act (1872), the Civil and Criminal Procedure Codes. In 2023, Parliament replaced the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, in force from 1 July 2024. Judiciary : a unified court hierarchy, common law, precedent, rule of law and independent judges. District administration : the Collector, revenue system and police structure (Police Act 1861). Army and police : professional, apolitical in intention. The army stayed under civilian control. English as an administrative language, and English-medium higher education.
Legacies that cause problems

Preventive detention : from Bengal Regulation III of 1818 and the Defence of India Rules to Article 22 and later laws. Sedition (Section 124A IPC, 1870): the Supreme Court put it in abeyance in May 2022 ( S.G. Vombatkere v Union of India ). The new BNS (2023) has a different offence, Section 152, on acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; critics say the concern remains. Emergency and Centre-biased federalism : Section 93 and Article 356, misused many times until S.R. Bommai (1994). Colonial-era laws : Official Secrets Act 1923; AFSPA (1958) modelled on a 1942 ordinance; the Land Acquisition Act 1894 (replaced in 2013); forest laws that took away tribal rights. Bureaucratic culture : secretive, hierarchical, distant from citizens. Divide and rule : separate electorates and census categories hardened identities. The Constituent Assembly decided on joint electorates in 1947, and in May 1949 it dropped reservation of seats for religious minorities.
The nationalist inheritance

The framers drew as much from the freedom struggle as from British law. Nehru Report (1928) : a draft constitution with fundamental rights, joint electorates and responsible government. The Constituent Assembly demand was raised from 1934 (M.N. Roy's idea in 1934, then Congress, 1935). Karachi Resolution (1931) : fundamental rights and a basic economic programme (adult franchise, abolition of untouchability, secular state, labour rights). Sapru Committee (1945) : a non-party committee with detailed constitutional proposals. Experience of provincial self-government (1937-39) and of civil liberties campaigns. Cabinet Mission Plan (May 1946) : set the terms for the Assembly; provincial legislators elected members, with seats allotted by community. Granville Austin, The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation (1966), called the Constitution a document drafted by those who had practised self-government and civil liberties, which gave it a firm base.
Continuity or break?

Continuity view : a large part of the Constitution comes from the 1935 Act. Ambedkar, answering charges of copying, said the Constitution drew on other countries but adapted them for India's needs, and defended the borrowing in the Assembly. Break view : radical changes. Universal adult franchise from the start (Article 326) in a poor, mostly illiterate country. Fundamental rights and judicial review. The abolition of untouchability (Article 17). The Directive Principles, an unprecedented social-justice aim. Critics : Gandhians and socialists said it ignored village India. K. Hanumanthaiya (17 November 1949): "We wanted the music of Veena or Sitar, but here we have the music of an English band." Others called it a "carbon copy" of the 1935 Act. Marxists said it protected property. Post-colonial lens : postcolonial writers ask if the state apparatus, built for control, can serve democracy.
Colonial legacies today

Criminal law overhaul (2024): the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act replaced. Debates continue about whether the new codes break far enough from colonial attitudes. Police reform : Prakash Singh v Union of India (2006) directed reforms because the Police Act 1861 still governs the ethos. Implementation is partial. Civil service : lateral entry, Mission Karmayogi (2020) and demands to reform generalist administration. Federalism : Governors and Article 356 remain in the news, over Governors' assent to bills. In State of Tamil Nadu v Governor of Tamil Nadu (8 April 2025) the Supreme Court set timelines and treated long-pending bills as deemed assented. Then, on the 16th Presidential Reference (20 November 2025), a five-judge bench held that courts cannot impose timelines and that deemed assent is alien to the Constitution, though prolonged, unexplained inaction can face limited judicial review. Place names and symbols : renaming of Rajpath to Kartavya Path (2022); the Navy ensign changed in 2022; Parliament's new building (2023). Economic : the colonial tax and land revenue legacy shapes the debate on agrarian distress.
How to answer

"The Government of India Act, 1935 was the blueprint for the Constitution of India." Discuss. Examine the colonial legacies in India's administrative and legal system. How did the freedom movement shape the Constitution? Has India decolonised its institutions? Evaluate. Structure: start with the timeline of Acts in a diagram. Pick the 1935 Act and list what India took from it (federal scheme, lists, Governor, emergency, PSC, Federal Court, RBI). Then separate the helpful legacies (rule of law, civil service, parliamentary experience) from the harmful ones (preventive detention, sedition, Article 356). Add the nationalist inheritance (Nehru Report, Karachi). End with the post-2023 criminal law changes as a modern link.
Social and Political Perspectives in the Constituent Assembly
A constitution made by argument

The Constituent Assembly sat for 2 years, 11 months and 18 days (December 1946 to November 1949). It held 11 sessions and about 165 sittings. Its debates, published in 12 volumes, are the best record of what the framers meant. For UPSC, the focus is not just on process but on ideas . Who sat in the Assembly? Whose voices were heard, whose absent? Where did members disagree: on the strength of the Centre, language, minority rights, property, socialism, the village, and the place of religion? This lesson maps those disagreements. It uses Granville Austin's classic work as the base: the Constitution as a "seamless web" of three strands, national unity , democracy and a social revolution . Link this lesson with the Preamble, Directive Principles and federalism later.
How the Assembly was formed

Set up under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946). Members were indirectly elected by provincial legislatures (themselves chosen on a limited franchise). The plan allotted 389 seats: 296 for British India and 93 for princely states. The Congress won a large majority in the 1946 elections (208 of 296 British Indian seats), with the Muslim League 73. After Partition, membership fell to about 299. Dr Rajendra Prasad was President. B.N. Rau was Constitutional Adviser. The Drafting Committee had seven members, with Ambedkar as chair. The Constitution had 395 Articles and 8 Schedules when adopted.
Who sat in the Assembly

Leaders and lawyers : Nehru, Patel, Rajendra Prasad, Maulana Azad, K.M. Munshi, Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, N. Gopalaswami Ayyangar, B.N. Rau (adviser), T.T. Krishnamachari. Ambedkar : elected from Bengal, then from Bombay after Partition, with Congress help. Tribal voices : Jaipal Singh Munda argued for tribal rights and was heard in the Fifth and Sixth Schedule debates. Women : 15 members, among them Hansa Mehta, Durgabai Deshmukh, Sarojini Naidu, Vijayalakshmi Pandit, Renuka Ray, Sucheta Kripalani, Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, Begum Aizaz Rasul, Ammu Swaminathan, Dakshayani Velayudhan. Other voices : Muslim League members (to 1947), Anglo-Indians (Frank Anthony), Sikhs (Hukam Singh), a few communists (Somnath Lahiri) and socialists (K.T. Shah), and princely state representatives. Critics: not chosen by universal franchise; Congress dominated; few Dalit, tribal and women members. Austin replies that Congress itself contained many views, so debate was real.
The Objectives Resolution and the guiding vision

On 13 December 1946, Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution. It was adopted on 22 January 1947 and is the source of the Preamble. India to be an independent sovereign republic . A Union of territories with autonomous units and residuary powers. All power derived from the people. Justice, equality and freedom for all, and safeguards for minorities, backward and tribal areas, and depressed classes. Nehru said it was a declaration, a pledge and a dedication. It sought the middle path between Western liberal democracy and Soviet-style socialism. Austin's three strands: national unity and integrity, democratic government, and a social revolution to end hunger, inequality and caste. The framers saw all three as one "seamless web".
Centre and states: a strong Union

Partition, riots and the integration of over 500 princely states pushed the framers to a strong Centre. Article 1: India, that is Bharat, is a Union of States . Ambedkar explained that the Union is indestructible, and that states cannot secede, unlike in a compact between states. The Constitution has a federal structure with unitary features: Seventh Schedule lists, Governors, Article 356, All-India Services and single citizenship. K.C. Wheare called it "quasi-federal". Dissent : members from the South and from smaller states feared domination. Some wanted a looser union. Special cases : Article 370 for Jammu and Kashmir (draft Art. 306A, accepted in October 1949; abrogated in August 2019) and Articles 371 onwards for other states.
Language: Hindi, English and the regions

Language was the most heated argument of 1949. Hindi supporters (Purushottam Das Tandon, Seth Govind Das, R.V. Dhulekar) wanted Hindi as the national language. Members from non-Hindi regions, such as T.T. Krishnamachari, warned of "Hindi imperialism". The outcome was the Munshi-Ayyangar formula (September 1949): Hindi in the Devanagari script as the official language of the Union (Article 343), not "national language". English to continue for 15 years (till 1965), with Parliament able to extend. Regional languages in the Eighth Schedule (14 at first, 22 now). Article 351 directs the Union to promote Hindi. The compromise led to the Official Languages Act 1963 and the anti-Hindi agitations in Tamil Nadu (1965).
Minorities, separate electorates and rights

Separate electorates were a legacy of 1909. After Partition, most Muslim and Sikh members agreed to drop them. Sardar Patel , chair of the Advisory Committee on Minorities, argued for a united nation. The Assembly accepted joint electorates with reserved seats for SC and ST (Articles 330, 332). Reservation for religious minorities was dropped in May 1949. Rights of minorities were kept through Articles 25-30. Secularism : no state religion, equal respect for all faiths. The word "secular" was added to the Preamble in 1976, and K.T. Shah's attempts to insert "secular" and "socialist" were rejected in 1948. Religion and reform : debates on cow protection (ended as Directive Principle, Article 48) and on a Uniform Civil Code (Article 44, again a Directive Principle; Muslim members objected).
Rights, property and the social revolution

Fundamental Rights versus Directive Principles : B.N. Rau and the Sapru Committee split rights into justiciable and non-justiciable. Social-economic aims went into Part IV. Ambedkar called the Directive Principles an "instrument of instructions" for governments. Property : the hardest compromise. Nehru and the socialists wanted zamindari abolition and compensation fixed by Parliament. Patel and conservatives wanted full compensation. The result was Article 31, soon amended (First Amendment 1951, Ninth Schedule). Socialism : K.T. Shah and the Left wanted a socialist state. The majority preferred a mixed economy. The Directive Principles (Articles 38, 39) carry the egalitarian aim. Untouchability : abolished by Article 17 with little dissent. Preventive detention (Article 22) was fiercely debated. Critics, such as Hriday Nath Kunzru, objected.
Gandhians, socialists and other critics

Gandhian : Shriman Narayan's Gandhian Constitution for Free India (1946) and members like K. Santhanam and K. Hanumanthaiya wanted a base of village panchayats. The result: Article 40 as a Directive Principle, and constitutional status only in 1992. Socialist and Marxist : K.T. Shah, Somnath Lahiri. The Constitution protected property and had an elite-led process. Federal/regional : smaller states and regions wanted more powers. Hindu traditionalists : some sought a basis in ancient institutions and Hindu values, such as cow protection. Others, like the Hindu Mahasabha later, criticised the Constitution. Dalit : Dalit members joined the debate on safeguards; Dakshayani Velayudhan insisted on real equality. The Assembly rarely voted; Austin notes the habit of reaching consensus through accommodation.
Ambedkar's closing speech, 25 November 1949

On the last day of debate, Ambedkar gave three warnings. Grammar of anarchy : now that constitutional methods exist, give up unconstitutional methods such as civil disobedience, non-cooperation and satyagraha. Hero worship : do not lay your liberties at the feet of any great man. Bhakti may be a path to salvation in religion, but in politics it leads to dictatorship. Social democracy : political democracy cannot last unless it rests on social democracy, which recognises liberty, equality and fraternity as principles of life. He also pointed to the contradiction in the republic being born: equality in politics, but inequality in social and economic life. In his words, we must remove it soon or those who suffer inequality will blow up the structure of political democracy. He added that without fraternity, equality and liberty would be no deeper than coats of paint.
The Assembly's legacy today

Constitution Day : 26 November has been observed since 2015. The 75th anniversary in 2024-25 brought special Parliament debates, in December 2024. Reading the debates : courts cite the Constituent Assembly Debates to interpret provisions. Recent debates about the "basic structure", the Preamble (see Balram Singh , 2024) and federal balance often go back to them. Unfinished agenda : Article 44 (UCC), language policy, women's representation (106th Amendment, 2023) and the status of Governors. Legitimacy question : Today's critics ask whether an indirectly elected Assembly could speak for all, while defenders point to its pluralism and to long continuity. Global view : the Assembly is cited as a model of a deliberative process in a deeply divided society (see lesson 0-5-3).
How to answer

"The Indian Constitution is a 'seamless web' of national unity, democracy and social revolution." Discuss. Discuss the social and political perspectives in the Constituent Assembly. Examine the debates on language, federalism and minority rights in the Constituent Assembly. What are the main criticisms of the Constituent Assembly? Are they valid? Structure: set the context in short: composition and timeline. Present Austin's three strands. Then take 4 to 5 debates (Centre-states, language, minorities, property and DPSP, village), each with who argued what and the compromise reached. Add Ambedkar's closing speech for depth. Evaluate with critics' points and the later record of the Constitution.
Civil Liberties and Human Rights Movements
Who defends rights against the State?

Constitutions promise rights, but the State itself can violate them through custodial torture, preventive detention, encounter killings or special security laws. Civil liberties and human rights movements are groups of citizens, lawyers and journalists who document such violations and fight them in courts and in public. In India these movements were born out of the Emergency (1975-77) , when over a lakh people were detained and the Supreme Court denied habeas corpus in ADM Jabalpur (1976). Exam questions ask about their origin, achievements, the tension between security and liberty, and laws such as AFSPA, UAPA and the sedition provision.
Origins and main organisations

APDR (Association for Protection of Democratic Rights, West Bengal, 1972), formed in the wake of the Naxalite crackdown. PUCL (People's Union for Civil Liberties): founded as the People's Union for Civil Liberties and Democratic Rights under J.P. Narayan's inspiration in 1976; reorganised as PUCL in 1980. Rajni Kothari was among its leaders. PUDR (People's Union for Democratic Rights, Delhi): its 1984 report Who Are the Guilty? (with PUCL) documented the anti-Sikh violence. Others: Naga People's Movement for Human Rights, Manipur's families' associations, Human Rights Law Network, and Amnesty International India (which halted operations in 2020 after its accounts were frozen).
Civil liberties vs democratic rights

Indian groups debated their focus: Civil liberties approach (PUCL): defend liberal freedoms of all, against any State excess, without a class line. Democratic rights approach (PUDR, APDR): rights are tied to the struggles of workers, peasants, tribals and Dalits; violations come from the structure of power, not just bad officials. A.R. Desai (ed.), Violation of Democratic Rights in India (1986) A Marxist sociologist's documentation of how the State's development model produced repression of the poor. Upendra Baxi Called for "social action litigation" and a human rights view grounded in suffering, in The Future of Human Rights (2002).
Courts and rights movements

ADM Jabalpur (1976): no habeas corpus during the Emergency; H.R. Khanna's dissent. Overruled in Puttaswamy (2017). PIL era : Hussainara Khatoon (1979) on undertrials; Sunil Batra (1978) on prisoners' rights; Nilabati Behera (1993) on compensation for custodial death. D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997): arrest guidelines (identification, memo, informing relatives, medical checks). PUCL v. Union of India (1997): phone tapping limits; PUCL (2014) guidelines on encounter killings. Extra-Judicial Execution Victim Families Association v. Union (2016): even in areas under AFSPA, excessive force is open to inquiry; Manipur encounter cases investigated. Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down section 66A of the IT Act. S.G. Vombatkere (May 2022): sedition (s.124A IPC) kept in abeyance. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (2023) dropped "sedition" but section 152 punishes acts endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity.
Laws under challenge

AFSPA (1958): gives armed forces powers to shoot, arrest and search in "disturbed areas", with immunity from prosecution without central sanction. The Jeevan Reddy Committee (2005) recommended repeal. Irom Sharmila fasted against it from 2000 to 2016. AFSPA areas in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur were reduced from 2022. UAPA (1967): amended in 2004, 2008, 2012 and 2019 (allowing individuals to be designated as terrorists). Bail is very hard (section 43D(5)); NIA v. Zahoor Watali (2019) made it stricter. Preventive detention: Article 22 allows it; laws such as the National Security Act (1980) and state Public Safety Acts. Internet shutdowns: Anuradha Bhasin (2020) required proportionality and publication of orders.
Security vs liberty

The State's case: India faces insurgencies, terrorism and Maoist violence; special laws are needed and rights groups sometimes ignore violence by armed groups. The movements' case: Low conviction rates under UAPA suggest misuse as process-as-punishment. Custodial deaths and encounters continue; India has signed (1997) but not ratified the UN Convention against Torture. Impunity under AFSPA erodes trust in border regions. Critique of the movements: dependence on courts; urban, middle-class leadership; limited reach. Partha Chatterjee's distinction between civil society and political society suggests the poor often negotiate rights through politics rather than legal activism. A balanced answer accepts both security and rights, and demands accountability: independent inquiry, quick trials, and review of special laws.
NHRC and the 1993 Act

The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 created the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), set up in October 1993, and allowed State Human Rights Commissions. It followed the UN's Paris Principles on national institutions. The NHRC can inquire into violations by public servants, visit jails, and review laws and safeguards. Its findings are recommendations . It cannot enforce them, which is its main weakness. It generally cannot look into events more than a year old. For complaints against the armed forces, it can only seek a report from the Centre. The 2019 amendment allowed any former Supreme Court judge, not only a former Chief Justice, to head it, and shortened the term of the chair and members to three years.
Cases to cite

Bhima Koregaon case (arrests from 2018): activists held under UAPA; Father Stan Swamy died in custody on 5 July 2021 while awaiting bail, at 84. Manipur (2023-26): violence, internet shutdowns and the Supreme Court's committee of former judges. Ladakh (September 2025): protests and the detention of Sonam Wangchuk under the National Security Act (September 2025; revoked March 2026). Kashmir after 2019: detentions and internet restrictions; Anuradha Bhasin (2020). NHRC: GANHRI deferred its accreditation review in 2023-24. New criminal laws (in force 1 July 2024) extended police custody options, which rights groups criticised.
Human rights theory in brief

Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948); the two covenants of 1966 (ICCPR and ICESCR), which India ratified in 1979. Three "generations": civil-political, socio-economic, and group rights (development, environment), a framework from Karel Vasak. Cultural relativism and the "Asian values" debate of the 1990s. In India, the Supreme Court has used international law to fill gaps ( Vishaka , 1997).
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the role of civil liberties movements in Indian democracy." "Security laws versus civil liberties: examine with reference to AFSPA and UAPA." "Human rights movements in India have been largely urban and court-centred." Comment. Structure: Emergency origin; organisations and their approaches; landmark cases; contested laws; critique on both sides; recent cases; conclude with accountability-based balance.
Women's and Environmental Movements
Two movements that changed what politics means

The women's movement and the environmental movement widened Indian politics beyond class and caste. They asked who does unpaid work, who controls forests and rivers, and whose "development" counts. Both produced laws, judgments and new ideas such as ecofeminism and the "environmentalism of the poor". UPSC asks about their phases, key cases and debates.
Phases of the women's movement

Reform era: social reformers on sati, widow remarriage and education; women in the freedom struggle. Towards Equality (1974): report of the Committee on the Status of Women in India, with Vina Mazumdar as member-secretary, showed women's position had worsened in many respects. It sparked women's studies. Autonomous women's groups from the late 1970s: campaigns on dowry deaths, rape, sati and domestic violence. Mathura case ( Tukaram v. State of Maharashtra , 1979): an open letter by four law professors led to the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 1983.
Landmark campaigns and laws

Roop Kanwar sati (Deorala, 1987) led to the Commission of Sati (Prevention) Act, 1987. Shah Bano (1985) and the 1986 Act raised the question of personal law and women's rights. Bhanwari Devi (1992), a sathin gang-raped for stopping a child marriage, led to Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) guidelines and the POSH Act, 2013 . Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 . Nirbhaya (December 2012) led to the Justice J.S. Verma Committee and the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act, 2013. Shayara Bano (2017) on triple talaq; Joseph Shine (2018) on adultery; Sabarimala (2018). Women's reservation: one-third in local bodies (1992); the 106th Amendment (2023), came into force on 16 April 2026; its quota awaits delimitation.
Feminist thinkers in India

Radha Kumar, The History of Doing (1993) An illustrated history of women's movements and campaigns in India from 1800 to 1990. Uma Chakravarti, Gendering Caste (2003) Caste and gender are linked: control over women's sexuality maintains caste purity ("Brahmanical patriarchy"). Gopal Guru, "Dalit Women Talk Differently" (1995) Dalit women face both caste and patriarchy; mainstream feminism and Dalit politics both overlooked them. Nivedita Menon, Seeing Like a Feminist (2012) Shows how patriarchy shapes everyday life, from family to law.
Environmental movements

Bishnoi sacrifice (Khejarli, 1730): Amrita Devi and others died protecting trees; an early symbol. Chipko (from 1973, Chamoli in Uttarakhand): villagers hugged trees to stop commercial felling. Gaura Devi led the women of Reni in 1974. Leaders included Chandi Prasad Bhatt and Sunderlal Bahuguna. It led to a 15-year ban on green felling in the Himalayan forests of Uttar Pradesh (1980). Appiko (Karnataka, 1983): Chipko's southern counterpart. Silent Valley (Kerala, 1970s-80s): campaign by KSSP and others stopped a hydroelectric dam; declared a national park in 1984. Narmada Bachao Andolan (from 1985, Medha Patkar, Baba Amte) against displacement by Sardar Sarovar. In NBA v. Union of India (2000), the Supreme Court allowed construction to continue. The World Bank withdrew in 1993. Plachimada (Kerala, 2002): villagers against a Coca-Cola plant over groundwater. Niyamgiri (Odisha, 2013): Gram Sabhas rejected bauxite mining.
Thinkers on environmental politics

Ramachandra Guha, The Unquiet Woods (1989) Chipko as a peasant movement rooted in resistance to state forestry, not just ecology. Madhav Gadgil and Ramachandra Guha, This Fissured Land (1992) An ecological history of India showing how colonial and post-colonial forest policy hurt local communities. Guha and Joan Martinez-Alier, Varieties of Environmentalism (1997) The environmentalism of the poor : in the South, struggles are about survival and livelihood, unlike Northern concerns with wilderness. Vandana Shiva, Staying Alive (1988) Ecofeminism : women and nature are both exploited by "maldevelopment". Bina Agarwal, "The Gender and Environment Debate" (1992) Feminist environmentalism : women's link to nature comes from their material role and work, not from essence.
Achievements and limits

Achievements: laws (POSH, domestic violence, Forest Rights Act 2006, Environment Protection Act 1986), institutions (NCW, National Green Tribunal 2010) and public awareness. Limits: Women's movement criticised as urban, upper-caste and middle class; Dalit and Muslim women raise separate voices. Laws often poorly implemented (conviction rates, ICCs under POSH). Environmental movements struggle against the growth agenda; dams and mines largely go ahead. Charges of being "anti-development" and restrictions on NGOs under FCRA.
Women in politics and the law

Article 15(3) lets the State make special provisions for women and children. The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) reserved at least one-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities for women. Many states later raised this to half. Studies of panchayats show real gains in local attention to water and sanitation. They also show a problem: in some places a male relative acts for the elected woman, a practice known as the sarpanch-pati problem. The 106th Amendment (2023) extends the one-third rule to the Lok Sabha and state assemblies, to take effect after the next census and delimitation. Debate continues on a quota within the quota for SC, ST and OBC women.
Recent cases and issues

M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024): a right against the adverse effects of climate change. Joshimath land subsidence (2023) and Himalayan projects. Hasdeo Aranya and Great Nicobar projects. Wrestlers' protest (2023) against the then federation chief over sexual harassment allegations. R.G. Kar case (Kolkata, August 2024) and protests on doctors' and women's safety. Women's reservation : the 106th Amendment in force from 16 April 2026, but the 131st Amendment Bill to speed delimitation was defeated on 17 April 2026.
How UPSC asks this

"Trace the evolution of the women's movement in India." "Environmental movements in India are movements of the poor." Discuss. "Compare ecofeminism and feminist environmentalism." Structure: phases and campaigns of the women's movement with laws; feminist thinkers including Dalit feminism; environmental movements (Chipko, NBA, Silent Valley); thinkers (Guha, Shiva, Agarwal); achievements and limits; recent cases.
The Emergency, 1975-77
India's darkest democratic hour

For 21 months, from 25 June 1975 to 21 March 1977, India lived under a national Emergency. Civil liberties were suspended, the press was censored and the opposition jailed. The episode shapes how we think about executive power, judicial independence and constitutional safeguards . The Emergency was proclaimed on 25 June 1975 under Article 352, after the Allahabad High Court verdict of 12 June 1975 against Indira Gandhi.
Road to the Emergency

The ground was 'internal disturbance'. Justice Jagmohanlal Sinha ruled in State of UP v Raj Narain that Indira Gandhi's Rae Bareli win was invalid for electoral malpractice. The Supreme Court gave a conditional stay on 24 June.
What happened

Fundamental rights suspended (Art. 359); MISA used for detention; about 1 lakh arrested. Press censorship; newspapers like the Indian Express protested. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added 'socialist, secular, integrity', Fundamental Duties, curbed judicial review, and extended Lok Sabha's term to six years. Sanjay Gandhi's five-point programme: forced sterilisation and slum clearances (Turkman Gate). Twenty-point programme of Indira Gandhi.
ADM Jabalpur v Shivkant Shukla (1976)

The Supreme Court, 4:1, held that during the Emergency a detained person could not move a High Court for habeas corpus, since the right to life and liberty (Art. 21) was suspended. Justice H.R. Khanna dissented, saying life and liberty cannot be taken away without the authority of law, and he was superseded as CJI. In Puttaswamy (2017) the Court declared ADM Jabalpur wrongly decided.
The 1977 election and Shah Commission

Indira Gandhi called elections in March 1977. The Janata Party (JP's push) won about 295 seats, Congress about 154; Indira and Sanjay lost their seats. Morarji Desai became the first non-Congress PM. The Shah Commission (1977-78) inquired into excesses, finding abuse of power, and the Janata government passed the corrective amendments.
44th Amendment (1978)

Safeguards added: 'internal disturbance' replaced by 'armed rebellion' ; the Cabinet's written advice to the President is needed; the Emergency must be approved by special majority within one month and renewed every six months; Arts. 20 and 21 cannot be suspended ; Lok Sabha can vote to revoke it by simple majority; the right to property was removed from Part III (to Art. 300A); Lok Sabha term reduced to five years again.
Why and what now?

Defence : law and order was collapsing, the Emergency was constitutional, and it brought discipline. Critique : personal motive, centralisation, 'committed judiciary' and bureaucracy. Scholars: Granville Austin's Working a Democratic Constitution (1999) calls it a test and a lesson. Related debate on 'authoritarian democracy' and the party's internal decay. In 2024 the Government declared 25 June as Samvidhan Hatya Diwas .
Lessons

Constitutional safeguards need active citizens, press and courts. Judicial independence is fragile (supersession of judges in 1973 and 1977). Basic structure survived: Indira Nehru Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975) and Minerva Mills (1980) limited the 39th and 42nd Amendments. Opposition unity after JP changed the party system.
Legacy today

The 1977 mandate became the model for 'anti-incumbency' voting; the lesson reappears in debates about preventive detention (NSA, UAPA), internet shutdowns, and press freedom. Questions often ask you to compare the Emergency with Art. 356 or with 2020s concerns about democratic backsliding. The 44th Amendment (1978) replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' as the ground for Article 352, and it restored key safeguards.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the causes and consequences of the Emergency of 1975-77." "How did the 44th Amendment secure the Constitution against misuse of emergency powers?" "Was ADM Jabalpur rightly decided? Examine the dissent of Justice Khanna." Structure: causes, events, 42nd Amendment, ADM Jabalpur, 1977 polls, 44th Amendment, lessons.
Civil Services Reform
The steel frame under strain

India's civil services run policy delivery from block to Centre. Reform of recruitment, training and accountability is a perennial question across Paper I, GS II and GS IV. Know the committees and the recent moves : lateral entry and Mission Karmayogi. Sardar Patel defended the All India Services in the Constituent Assembly as essential to national unity, and the civil services remain a central Paper I and GS IV topic.
Constitutional base

Art. 308-314 : services of the Union and States; Art. 311 protects against dismissal without inquiry. Art. 312 : All-India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS) by Rajya Sabha resolution. Art. 315-323 : UPSC and State PSCs. Sardar Patel is called the patron saint of the All-India Services. The 'steel frame' phrase is from Lloyd George (1922).
Who recommended what
Second ARC

Chaired first by Veerappa Moily. It stressed ethics in governance , performance management, fixed tenures, curbing political interference, lateral entry , and e-governance. It proposed a Civil Services Authority and a restructured Section 311. Many recommendations are still pending. The Second ARC was set up in 2005 and reported in stages over several years, with 15 reports in all. The Second ARC also recommended a Public Service Law to set common standards across all services.
Accountability and neutrality

Problems: frequent transfers, political pressure, lack of specialisation, corruption, weak performance appraisal. T.S.R. Subramanian v Union of India (2013) directed fixed tenure and Civil Services Boards for transfers. Prakash Singh (2006) did similar for the police. Tools: Lokpal and Lokayukta Act (2013), RTI (2005), Citizens' Charter (1997), 360-degree appraisal.
Lateral entry

The Government sought specialists at joint secretary and director level from outside the service. The first call was in June 2018 (10 posts), and appointments began in 2019 (the 2017 NITI Aayog proposal). In August 2024, a 45-post advertisement was withdrawn after concerns that reservation was missing. Supporters: expertise, fresh ideas. Critics: reservation, politicisation, and undermining the career bureaucracy.
Mission Karmayogi

Launched in September 2020 as the National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building . Its platform, iGOT Karmayogi , offers online learning; competency frameworks aim to move from 'rule-based' to 'role-based' training. A Capacity Building Commission oversees it. It is the main recent reform to know.
Generalist versus specialist

Fulton Report (UK, 1968) criticised generalists. India's IAS model is generalist, a 'jack of all trades'. Weber's ideal bureaucracy: rule-bound, neutral and merit-based. Others: development administration (Riggs) stresses attitude change. Challenges: politicians versus 'committed bureaucracy', and cadre allocation, plus the 'permanent versus political executive' tension.
The way forward

Priorities: merit-based and transparent selection, specialised mid-career tracks, tenure security, performance-linked promotion, digital delivery, and ethical training. Also reforms of State PSCs (paper leaks) and the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024 . Lateral entry started in 2018, when the central government invited applications for joint secretary posts from outside the civil service. Mission Karmayogi (2020) aims to build officers' competencies through online training on the iGOT Karmayogi platform.
How UPSC asks this

"Evaluate the need for civil service reforms in India." "Lateral entry is a boon or a bane? Discuss." "How does Mission Karmayogi change civil service capacity building?" Structure: constitutional base, committees, accountability, lateral entry, Mission Karmayogi, debate, way forward. Strong answers cite the Second ARC's 2005 first report and the 2018 lateral entry advertisement as concrete evidence for both sides of the debate.
Preamble, Fundamental Rights and Duties
The Constitution's heart: promise, rights, duties

"Salient features of the Constitution" is among the most repeated topics in Paper I Section B. Within it, the Preamble , Fundamental Rights (Part III) and Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) are asked in many forms: Is the Preamble part of the Constitution? Has Article 21 become the most important right? Should duties be enforceable? The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950 . It was adopted on 26 November 1949 after nearly three years of debate. It has 395 Articles and 8 Schedules at the start; it has now over 450 Articles and 12 Schedules. Granville Austin, in The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation (1966), said its aims were threefold: national unity, democracy, and social revolution . Rights and duties show how it tried to join them.
The Preamble: source, aims and status

The Preamble comes from Nehru's Objectives Resolution (13 December 1946, adopted 22 January 1947). It begins "We, the People of India", showing that authority comes from the people. Nature of the state Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic. The words socialist and secular , and integrity , were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) . Objectives Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty (thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), Equality (status and opportunity) and Fraternity (dignity of the individual, unity and integrity of the nation). Status: In Berubari Union (1960) the Court said the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution. In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) it held that it is part, and amendable, but its basic features cannot be destroyed. LIC of India (1995) confirmed it is an integral part. The Preamble is not enforceable in court; it is an aid to interpretation.
Fundamental Rights at a glance

Part III covers Articles 12 to 35. Article 13 makes laws that violate rights void, which is the base of judicial review. The right to property was removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment (1978) and is now a legal right under Article 300A . Ambedkar called Article 32 the "heart and soul" of the Constitution. It lets anyone go straight to the Supreme Court. Some rights hold against everyone (Articles 14, 21). Others, such as Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30, are for citizens only.
Equality, reasonable classification and arbitrariness

Article 14 : equality before the law and equal protection of the laws. It allows reasonable classification : the group must be based on an intelligible difference with a link to the law's aim. Reservations are an example. In E.P. Royappa (1974), the Court said that equality is opposed to arbitrariness . Anything arbitrary violates Article 14. This turned equality into a tool for reviewing the fairness of state action. Article 15 bars discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, but allows special provisions for women, children, SC/ST and backward classes. 15(6) adds the economically weaker sections (103rd Amendment, 2019). Article 16 is equality in public jobs. Article 17 abolishes untouchability and Article 18 abolishes titles.
Article 21: from narrow to wide

Article 21 says no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty "except according to procedure established by law". A.K. Gopalan (1950): any procedure made by a valid law is enough. A narrow reading. Maneka Gandhi (1978): the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable . Articles 14, 19 and 21 form a "golden triangle". This brought due process into Indian law. Since then, Article 21 has covered the right to livelihood ( Olga Tellis , 1985), clean environment, health, speedy trial, and dignity. Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) made education a right for ages 6-14; the RTE Act followed in 2009. K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (24 August 2017, nine judges) held that privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21. This led to rulings that decriminalised homosexuality ( Navtej Johar , 2018) and struck down adultery as an offence ( Joseph Shine , 2018).
Freedoms under Article 19 and their limits

Article 19(1) gives citizens six freedoms: speech and expression; assembly; association; movement; residence; and profession or business. Article 19(2) to (6) allow reasonable restrictions , such as for sovereignty, security, public order, decency and contempt of court. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Court struck down section 66A of the IT Act for vagueness and its chilling effect on speech. Press freedom is read into Article 19(1)(a) ( Romesh Thappar , 1950, and later cases). The right to strike or to bandh is not absolute. Articles 20 and 22 protect people in criminal law: no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination, and rules on arrest and preventive detention. Preventive detention remains controversial. Remedies under Article 32: writs of habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. High Courts have wider writ power under Article 226.
Fundamental Duties: Article 51A

The original Constitution had no duties. The 42nd Amendment (1976) added Part IVA and Article 51A, on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice, with ten duties. The 86th Amendment (2002) added an eleventh: a parent or guardian must give education to a child between 6 and 14. Respect the Constitution, the flag and the national anthem. Cherish the ideals of the freedom struggle. Uphold sovereignty, unity and integrity. Defend the country when called. Promote harmony and renounce practices that demean women. Preserve composite culture; protect the natural environment and have compassion for living creatures. Develop scientific temper and humanism; safeguard public property; strive for excellence. Duties are not justiciable and carry no penalty by themselves. The Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999) suggested ways to give them effect. Courts use them to interpret laws and test whether restrictions on rights are reasonable.
Rights, duties and balance

Too many limits? Critics say restrictions on liberty, such as preventive detention and sedition (now replaced by section 152 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, in force from 1 July 2024), dilute rights. Duties debate: Supporters say a rights-only constitution makes citizens passive. Opponents say duties were added during the Emergency to strengthen the state, and enforcing them risks authoritarianism. Many scholars see them as moral guidelines. Positive vs negative rights: Part III is mostly "freedom from" the State. The Directive Principles ask for "freedom to" through welfare. Courts have joined them (see next lesson). Enforcement gap: Article 32 is powerful but slow, and the poor have limited access. Private power: rights bind the State, but private actors such as companies and platforms also affect rights. Courts have begun to extend some rights to private bodies.
Rights in recent years

Climate: in M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India (21 March 2024), the Supreme Court recognised a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change as part of Articles 14 and 21. Digital access: in 2025, the Court read access to digital services as part of Article 21 in a case on KYC for acid-attack survivors and persons with visual disabilities. Speech: Shreya Singhal's principles guide cases on online speech. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (2023) replaced the IPC. Personal liberty: bail rulings emphasise "bail, not jail", including in cases under the UAPA and PMLA. Data: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 followed Puttaswamy. Equality: 2024's Davinder Singh and the EWS case show the court balancing Articles 14, 15 and 16.
How UPSC asks this

"Is the Preamble a part of the Constitution? Explain its role." "Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are complementary." Discuss. "Examine the evolution of Article 21 through judicial interpretation." "Should Fundamental Duties be made enforceable?" Structure: Objectives Resolution to the Preamble; Berubari to Kesavananda on status; list of rights with Article 13; Article 14 and arbitrariness; Gopalan to Maneka to Puttaswamy; Article 19 limits; duties with the 42nd and 86th Amendments; critique; recent cases (climate, digital access).
