Directive Principles
A promise that courts cannot enforce, yet cannot ignore

The Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in Part IV (Articles 36-51) set the goals of a welfare state: a fair share of resources, decent work, education, health, and peace. They are non-justiciable : no one can go to court to compel the State to follow them (Article 37). Yet Article 37 also says they are "fundamental in the governance of the country" and that the State must apply them when making laws. This tension is what examiners test. Typical questions: Are the DPSP useful or only "pious wishes"? What is the relation between Part III and Part IV? How have courts used the DPSP? Which amendments gave the DPSP priority? The idea comes from the Irish Constitution (1937) , and, in spirit, from the welfare ideals of the freedom movement, including the Karachi Resolution (1931) on fundamental rights and economic policy.
Three groups of Directive Principles
Part IV was drafted with the advice of B.N. Rau. Later amendments added Articles 39A, 43A, 48A (42nd, 1976), 43B (97th, 2011) and changed 45 (86th, 2002).
Granville Austin and Ambedkar on the DPSP

Granville Austin, Cornerstone of a Nation (1966) Part III and Part IV together are "the conscience of the Constitution". They form a seamless web : rights give political freedom; directives aim at social and economic justice. Austin saw them as the heart of the "social revolution". B.R. Ambedkar, Constituent Assembly, November 1948 The directives are "instruments of instructions" to those who govern. A government that ignores them may face voters at the next election. He wanted economic democracy , not only political democracy. Ambedkar warned that political equality without social and economic equality would be a contradiction (speech of 25 November 1949). K.T. Shah's critique Shah is widely credited with calling them a cheque on a bank payable at the bank's convenience. The sharper point: a right without a remedy is weak. Shriman Narayan Agarwal, Gandhian Constitution for Free India (1946) The source for the Gandhian directives such as village panchayats and cottage industry.
Part III versus Part IV: the long legal contest

Champakam Dorairajan (1951): Directive Principles must "run subordinate" to rights. Parliament answered with the First Amendment (1951). Golaknath (1967): Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights. 25th Amendment (1971) : added Article 31C , protecting laws made to implement Article 39(b) and (c) from challenge under Articles 14, 19 and 31. Kesavananda Bharati (1973): upheld Article 31C in part, but struck down the bar on judicial review. 42nd Amendment (1976) : extended Article 31C to all Directive Principles. Minerva Mills (1980): struck down this extension. The Court said the Constitution rests on a balance between Parts III and IV, and giving absolute priority to either would destroy it. Since 1980 courts read them together. The Directive Principles are used to give meaning to rights and to test whether restrictions on rights are reasonable.
How the Court has used the Directive Principles

Education: Mohini Jain (1992) and Unni Krishnan (1993) read a right to education into Article 21 through Article 41 and 45. The 86th Amendment (2002) then inserted Article 21A. Equal pay: Randhir Singh (1982) used Article 39(d). Bonded labour: Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984). Livelihood: Olga Tellis (1985), from Article 39(a) and 41. Legal aid: Article 39A shaped Hussainara Khatoon (1979), on prisoners awaiting trial. Environment: Article 48A in the M.C. Mehta cases. Cow slaughter: State of Gujarat v. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi (2005) upheld bans, relying on Article 48. Resources: in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (5 November 2024), a nine-judge bench held, by majority, that not every private resource is a "material resource of the community" under Article 39(b), limiting the sweeping view of earlier cases.
Directive Principles turned into law

Many programmes put the directives into action: Article 40: the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) gave local bodies a constitutional base. Article 39 and 41: the zamindari abolition, land ceilings, MGNREGA (2005), and the National Food Security Act (2013), which covers about two-thirds of the population. Article 43: minimum wages laws and the four labour codes (in force from 21 November 2025). Article 45 and 21A: the Right to Education Act (2009) and early childhood care under the National Education Policy 2020. Article 47: public health missions, and alcohol prohibition in some states (Gujarat, Bihar and Nagaland). Article 44: the Uniform Civil Code remains incomplete. Goa has its old Portuguese-era code. Uttarakhand passed a UCC law in 2025. The 22nd Law Commission invited views on a UCC in June-July 2023. Article 50: the judiciary was separated from the executive in most states by the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
Directive Principles and political theory

Link Part IV to ideas you studied in Paper I Section A. Positive liberty and social rights. Rights in Part III are mostly negative : the State must not interfere. The directives ask the State to act: to feed, educate and employ. This follows T.H. Green and the later welfare-liberal tradition. Rawls. Article 38(2) (reduce inequalities in income, status and opportunities) and Article 39(b)-(c) (resources not concentrated) echo the difference principle and the concern with the basic structure. Marx and socialism. The "socialistic" group seeks a more equal economy without abolishing private property. Critics on the left call this too mild. Gandhi. Village self-rule (Article 40), cottage industry (43) and prohibition (47) reflect Hind Swaraj and trusteeship ideas. Three key differences from Part III: Fundamental Rights: enforceable by courts; limit the State; mostly civil and political; individuals hold them. Directive Principles: not enforceable; guide the State; mostly social and economic; the community benefits.
Useful compass or empty promise?

Case for them: They shape policy and legislation and give courts a basis to read social justice into rights. They help voters judge governments on performance. Many have become rights through later laws (education, food, work). Case against: They are unenforceable, so governments pick and choose. For example, the UCC and prohibition have been pursued unevenly. They are a mixed bag of ideas: some contradictory (a free market and a socialistic order) or outdated (prohibition). Some are used to justify majoritarian policy (Article 48 cattle laws). Fiscal limits and "freebies" debates: the Court has been asked to define welfare versus populist giveaways. Balanced view: DPSP are the moral and political compass of the State, not a court-enforced list. Their strength is in democratic pressure and in judicial interpretation.
Directives in today's debates

UCC: Uttarakhand's 2025 law is the first by a state since Independence (Goa's civil code is a Portuguese-era law); a national UCC has not been enacted. 39(b): the November 2024 ruling matters for land, redistribution and tax debates. Article 41, 47: food security, cash transfers and women-targeted schemes. Article 48A and 51A(g): climate rulings such as M.K. Ranjitsinh (2024). Article 40: the state of panchayats' powers and finances. Article 51: India's foreign policy values, such as peace and respect for international law, are cited in strategic autonomy debates.
How UPSC asks this

"Directive Principles are the conscience of the Constitution. Do they have any legal force?" "Trace the relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles in the case law." "Explain the classification of the Directive Principles with examples." "Should the Uniform Civil Code be enforced under Article 44?" Structure: define Part IV and Article 37; three groups with Articles; Austin and Ambedkar; the legal contest (Champakam to Minerva Mills); key judgments and laws that gave them life; critique; recent issues (39(b) 2024, UCC); balanced conclusion.
Parliamentary System and Amendments
One system, one procedure for change

This lesson joins two topics that UPSC often asks together: the parliamentary system and the amending power . Both show how the Constitution balances stability with change. The framers chose the parliamentary system after a debate. Some wanted a presidential system, with a fixed term and a separate executive. They picked the British model because India already knew it from the Government of India Acts, and because they wanted a government that is answerable every day to the legislature. On amendments, Nehru and Ambedkar wanted the Constitution to be neither too rigid nor too flexible. The result is an amending process in Article 368 with three levels of difficulty. Typical questions: Is India's parliamentary system a copy of Westminster? Has the Prime Minister become too powerful? What are the limits on amendment? Which amendments changed India most?
Why parliamentary: Ambedkar's reasoning

In the Constituent Assembly (4 November 1948) Ambedkar compared the two forms. The American executive is more stable , since it cannot be removed by the legislature. The parliamentary executive is more responsible , since it can be dismissed by a vote. The draft Constitution chose responsibility , because India's needs required daily accountability more than fixed terms. Walter Bagehot, The English Constitution (1867) Distinguished the "dignified" part (the Crown) from the "efficient" part (the Cabinet). In India, the President is dignified, and the Cabinet efficient. A.V. Dicey, Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885) Parliamentary sovereignty is the central principle in Britain. In India, Parliament is not sovereign : the Constitution is supreme, and courts can review laws. Juan Linz, "The Perils of Presidentialism" (1990) Argued parliamentary systems survive better, as presidents face fixed terms and deadlock. Often cited in defence of India's choice.
The parliamentary executive in the Indian Constitution

Article 74: there shall be a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President. The 42nd Amendment (1976) made the advice binding. The 44th (1978) allows the President to send it back once for reconsideration. Article 75(3): the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. Article 75(1A): ministers capped at 15% of the Lok Sabha (91st Amendment). The PM can be from either House, e.g. Manmohan Singh from the Rajya Sabha. In Shamsher Singh (1974) the Court held that the President and Governors act on the advice of ministers, except in situations where the Constitution gives discretion.
Indian, not British: the differences

Written Constitution and judicial review, against Britain's flexible, unwritten arrangement. Republic : an elected head of State for a five-year term, not a hereditary monarch. Federal structure : Union and states, and a Rajya Sabha. Fundamental Rights that bind Parliament. No strict separation of powers, but the Court has said that essentials of each organ cannot be taken over ( Ram Jawaya Kapur , 1955; Kesavananda , 1973). Parliamentary supremacy is limited by the Constitution; the Indian Parliament is a creature of the Constitution. The prime-ministerial debate: Richard Crossman said the British Cabinet had turned into "prime-ministerial government". Many scholars apply this to India, especially in periods of a strong leader and a single-party majority. Others stress that coalition years (1989-2014) diluted this tendency. The test is how much Cabinet and Parliament really decide.
Amending the Constitution: Article 368

Parliament's power to amend comes from Article 368 . An amendment bill can start only in Parliament (not in a state legislature), needs the President's assent (compulsory since the 24th Amendment, 1971) and has three routes: Simple majority , outside Article 368: creating or altering states (Articles 2-4), Parliament's quorum, citizenship, the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, Rajya Sabha seats in the Fourth Schedule, and so on. Special majority : a majority of the total membership of each House and two-thirds of members present and voting. Most amendments, including Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles. Special majority plus ratification by half of the state legislatures : election of the President, the Union and state executive powers, the Supreme Court and High Courts, the distribution of legislative powers, the Seventh Schedule, representation of states in Parliament and Article 368 itself. The 101st Amendment (GST) was ratified in this way. There is no provision for a referendum or a constitutional convention, and no joint sitting for amendments.
The limits: from Shankari Prasad to Kesavananda

Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965): Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights. Golaknath (1967): Parliament cannot, since an amendment is a "law" under Article 13. 24th Amendment (1971): Article 13 does not apply to amendments under Article 368. Kesavananda Bharati (24 April 1973, 7:6): Parliament can amend any provision but cannot destroy the basic structure . 42nd Amendment (1976) tried to bar all judicial review of amendments. Minerva Mills (1980) struck those clauses: limited power is itself a basic feature. The next lesson develops basic structure. Remember the doctrine here as the key limit on Article 368: amendment is not revolution .
Amendments that changed India

1st (1951): Article 15(4), Ninth Schedule, reasonable restrictions on speech. 7th (1956): reorganised states and abolished Part A, B, C classes. 24th, 25th (1971): parliamentary power over rights; Article 31C. 42nd (1976): the "mini-Constitution": Preamble words, Fundamental Duties, wider DPSP priority. 44th (1978): reversed the Emergency changes; removed property as a Fundamental Right. 52nd (1985), 91st (2003): defection law. 61st (1989): voting age from 21 to 18. 73rd and 74th (1992): local government. 101st (2016): GST. 103rd (2019): EWS quota. 104th (2019): ended nominated Anglo-Indian seats and extended SC/ST seat reservation to 2030. 106th (2023): one-third seats for women. 99th (2014): NJAC; struck down in the Fourth Judges Case (16 October 2015).
Is the Constitution too easy or too hard to amend?

Too easy? Over 100 amendments in about 75 years, against 27 in the US. With a strong majority the executive can amend quickly, and bills have passed with little debate. Many amendments were made by ruling parties to overcome court rulings (such as the 39th and 42nd). Not too easy: most amendments are technical; the basic structure doctrine and the need for two-thirds in each House and half the states for federal features prevent abuse. Several bills have failed or been struck down: the NJAC (2015), and the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, which fell in the Lok Sabha on 17 April 2026 for want of a two-thirds majority. Flexibility is a strength. K.C. Wheare's view was that a constitution needs a path for change but also safeguards. Ambedkar, in the Constituent Assembly, defended the procedure as less rigid than the US one: most parts need only a special parliamentary majority.
Parliament and amendments in the news

One Nation, One Election: the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024 (with a companion bill) is before a Joint Parliamentary Committee, whose tenure has been extended more than once. It needs a special majority; ratification by states is debated. 130th Amendment Bill, 2025: introduced on 20 August 2025, it would remove a Prime Minister, Chief Minister or minister who is in custody for 30 consecutive days on a serious charge. It was sent to a JPC, which deferred its report in July 2026. 131st Amendment Bill, 2026: defeated on 17 April 2026 (298 for, 230 against), after the 106th Amendment was put into force on 16 April 2026. Functioning of Parliament: PRS data show Parliament now sits for roughly 55 to 70 days a year, against over 120 in the 1950s, and that fewer bills go to committees. Disruptions and the long gap without a Deputy Speaker in the 17th Lok Sabha.
How UPSC asks this

"Critically examine the working of the parliamentary system in India. Has it become prime-ministerial?" "Discuss the procedure for amending the Constitution. Does Article 368 give Parliament unlimited power?" "Assess the impact of the 42nd Amendment." "Would a presidential system suit India better?" Structure: Ambedkar's responsibility argument; features and Articles; differences from Britain; prime-ministerial tendency; Article 368 routes; the cases from Shankari Prasad to Minerva Mills; key amendments; critique; current examples (129th, 130th, 131st, 106th). Conclude that India's model is a constrained parliamentary system with a flexible-yet-protected constitution .
Judicial Review and Basic Structure
Who guards the Constitution?

Judicial review is the power of courts to test laws and executive acts against the Constitution and strike down those that violate it. The basic structure doctrine goes further: even a constitutional amendment cannot destroy the Constitution's core features. Together they decide who has the last word: Parliament or the Supreme Court. This is among the most important themes in Paper I, linked to nearly every other topic, from rights to federalism. The idea has US roots in Marbury v. Madison (1803). In India, the Constitution gives textual support through Article 13 (laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void), Article 32 and 226 (writs), Articles 131-136 (jurisdiction) and Articles 124 onwards (the judiciary). Examiners ask: What is the basic structure? How did the doctrine evolve? Is it undemocratic? How has the Court used it? Prepare a case timeline and a few current examples.
How the doctrine evolved

The idea of implied limits came from German jurist Dietrich Conrad , whose 1965 lecture at Banaras Hindu University was cited by Justice Mudholkar in his Sajjan Singh dissent. Nani Palkhivala argued the case for the petitioners in Kesavananda .
Kesavananda Bharati (24 April 1973)

Swami Kesavananda challenged Kerala's land reform laws, which were placed in the Ninth Schedule. A 13-judge bench, the largest in the Court's history, heard it for 68 days. The 7:6 verdict held: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, under Article 368. But it cannot change the basic structure or framework of the Constitution. Different judges listed different features: Sikri (supremacy, republican and democratic form, secular character, separation of powers, federalism); Shelat and Grover added the mandate to build a welfare state and the unity and integrity of the nation; Hegde and Mukherjea added the sovereignty of India and the essential features of individual freedoms; Khanna's concurrence was decisive. Article 31C was upheld in part: laws for Article 39(b)-(c) are protected but still open to review. A day later, on 26 April 1973, A.N. Ray became Chief Justice, superseding three senior judges (Shelat, Hegde, Grover). It was widely seen as a response to the verdict.
After Kesavananda: the Emergency and recovery

Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975): the Court struck down the 39th Amendment's clause removing the PM's election from judicial scrutiny, citing free and fair elections and rule of law as basic features. ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla (1976): during the Emergency, a 4:1 majority said no habeas corpus remedy was available. Justice H.R. Khanna's lone dissent became famous. The ruling was overruled by Puttaswamy (2017). 42nd Amendment (1976): tried to put amendments beyond review. Minerva Mills (1980): struck down the clauses; limited amending power and the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are basic. Waman Rao (1980): Ninth Schedule laws before 24 April 1973 are protected. I.R. Coelho (2007): laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after that date can be reviewed on rights and basic structure.
The accepted list of basic features

The Court has never given an exhaustive list. Features recognised in cases include: Supremacy of the Constitution, and the rule of law. Sovereign, democratic, republican structure; parliamentary democracy. Secularism ( Bommai , 1994) and federalism. Separation of powers, independence of the judiciary and judicial review ( L. Chandra Kumar , 1997). Free and fair elections ( Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain , 1975). Fundamental Rights' essence and the balance with Part IV ( Minerva Mills ). Unity and integrity of the nation; equality and the "golden triangle" of Articles 14, 19 and 21. Welfare state, social justice and the principle of reasonableness. Note: the doctrine tests constitutional amendments . Ordinary laws are tested against specific provisions, as the Court clarified in State of A.P. v. McDowell (1996). Other countries have followed the idea, including Bangladesh ( Anwar Hossain Chowdhury , 1989).
Judicial review in action and the judges' appointments

Writs under Article 32/226: habeas corpus, mandamus, certiorari, prohibition, quo warranto. PIL: relaxed locus standi since the late 1970s. Hussainara Khatoon (1979) on undertrial prisoners and Vishaka (1997) on sexual harassment, where the Court made guidelines in the absence of a law. Appointments: S.P. Gupta (First Judges Case, 1981) gave the executive primacy; the Second Judges Case (1993) established the collegium and the CJI's primacy; the Third (1998, Presidential reference) set it as the CJI and four senior-most judges. 99th Amendment and NJAC: struck down in the Fourth Judges Case on 16 October 2015 (4:1, Justice Chelameswar dissenting) as breaching independence of the judiciary, a basic feature. Article 142 allows orders for "complete justice". It has been used for broad directions, and critics say it can be overstretched.
What the courts review besides statutes

Administrative action: tests of legality, reasonableness (the Wednesbury test), proportionality and fair procedure (natural justice). Maneka Gandhi made fairness part of Article 14 and 21. Ordinances: in D.C. Wadhwa (1987), repeated re-promulgation of ordinances was held a fraud on the Constitution. Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) confirmed that the satisfaction of the President or Governor is reviewable. Emergency and President's Rule: reviewable after Bommai (1994); the 38th and 44th Amendments' effect on Article 352 and 356. Mercy and pardon: reviewable on limited grounds ( Epuru Sudhakar , 2006). Tribunals: in L. Chandra Kumar (1997) the Court held that High Court and Supreme Court review over tribunals cannot be excluded. The Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 was challenged on independence grounds. Parliamentary proceedings: courts avoid interfering in internal matters (Article 122), but Speakers' decisions on defection are reviewable ( Kihoto Hollohan , 1992). Rule of thumb: courts judge legality , not wisdom . Yet that line moves as new rights are recognised.
Guardian or usurper?

The case for: the doctrine protects minorities from a transient majority and stopped the Emergency-era attempts to place the executive beyond law. H.R. Khanna 's dissent in ADM Jabalpur and his role in Kesavananda are held up as moral anchors. The case against: Alexander Bickel called this the counter-majoritarian difficulty in The Least Dangerous Branch (1962): unelected judges overturning elected representatives. The basic structure is judge-defined and vague, so the Court becomes the final author of the Constitution. Collegium opacity: judges appoint judges, with little transparency. Judicial overreach: the Court has set policy on pollution, vehicles and cricket administration. S.P. Sathe ( Judicial Activism in India , 2002) distinguished legitimate activism from overreach; Upendra Baxi and Rajeev Dhavan wrote critically on the Court's role. Balanced conclusion: the doctrine is an essential check, but the Court must use restraint and open its own appointment process.
The Court and the political branches, 2023-2026

Article 370 (11 December 2023): the Court upheld the revocation of J&K's special status, adopting a deferential approach. Electoral bonds (15 February 2024): struck down on voters' right to information. Tamil Nadu v. Governor (8 April 2025): used Article 142 to set time limits and "deemed assent"; critics, including the then Vice-President, questioned the use of Article 142. In November 2025, a five-judge bench answering the Presidential reference said courts cannot fix such deadlines. Waqf Act (15 September 2025): partial stay, with the Court saying it will be slow to stay statutes. SIR of electoral rolls: upheld in May 2026 as within the Election Commission's powers. Delimitation and ONOE: arguments about whether changes affect the federal structure or electoral equality, which could return to the basic-structure debate if they pass. Chief Justice Surya Kant (from 24 November 2025) leads the Court until February 2027.
How UPSC asks this

"Explain the doctrine of basic structure. How has it protected the Constitution?" "Judicial review versus parliamentary sovereignty: which should prevail in India?" "Judicial activism has become judicial overreach." Examine. "Evaluate the collegium system and the NJAC verdict." Structure: define judicial review and Article 13; evolution (Shankari Prasad to Kesavananda); features; post-1973 cases (Raj Narain, Minerva Mills, Coelho); appointments (three judges cases, NJAC); critique (Bickel, Sathe); current examples (electoral bonds, Governors' case, Waqf); close with a case for restraint plus transparency.
The Union Executive
Who really rules at the top?

The Union Executive consists of the President , the Vice-President , the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers . The core question in exams is: Is the President only a rubber stamp, and is the Prime Minister too powerful? Article 53 vests the executive power in the President. But Article 74 says it is exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. Ambedkar explained in the Constituent Assembly (4 November 1948) that the President is head of the State, not of the Executive. He compared the President's place to a "ceremonial device on a seal". In practice the picture is more subtle. The President has some reserve powers, especially in a hung House. And the Prime Minister's real power depends on majority, party and personality. This lesson covers election, powers and role of the President and Vice-President, then the Prime Minister, the Cabinet and the permanent civil service.
How the President is elected and removed

Qualifications: citizen, at least 35 years, eligible for the Lok Sabha, holding no office of profit (Article 58). Election (Articles 54-55): an electoral college of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and of state legislative assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry). Nominated members and Legislative Council members do not vote. Method: single transferable vote by secret ballot. The vote values are weighted so that states and the Union count equally (the 1971 population is still used, frozen by the 84th Amendment until the first census after 2026). Term: five years (Article 56); can be re-elected. Impeachment (Article 61): for "violation of the Constitution". Either House can start with notice signed by a quarter of its members; two-thirds of the total membership of each House must vote in favour. No President has been impeached. Droupadi Murmu was elected in July 2022 as the 15th President, the first from a tribal community.
Powers of the President

Executive: appoints the PM, ministers, Governors, judges, Attorney General, CAG, election commissioners. Legislative: summons and prorogues Parliament, dissolves the Lok Sabha, addresses it, nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha, and can issue ordinances when Parliament is not in session (Article 123). Assent: on a bill the President may assent, withhold assent, or return it once (not a money bill). A return of the bill, if passed again, must be signed. There is no time limit, which allows a "pocket veto" (Zail Singh and the Postal Bill, 1986). Pardon: Article 72, in cases of court-martial, death sentences and Union law offences, on ministerial advice. Emergency powers: Articles 352, 356, 360. Advisory jurisdiction: the President may ask the Supreme Court for its opinion under Article 143.
Discretion in practice

Most of these powers are used on ministerial advice. The 42nd Amendment (1976) made that advice binding; the 44th Amendment (1978) allows the President to ask the Council to reconsider once. Areas where the President has more room: Choosing a Prime Minister when no party has a majority. The President usually invites the leader of the largest party or alliance and asks for proof of majority. Presidents Shankar Dayal Sharma (1996) and K.R. Narayanan (1998, 1999) handled such moments. Returning an Article 356 recommendation: in 1997 and 1998, President K.R. Narayanan sent back the Union Cabinet's advice to impose President's Rule in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. Pocket veto on a bill. Returning bills for reconsideration, as Presidents have done with the Office of Profit Bill (2006, A.P.J. Abdul Kalam). Cases: Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955) said the real executive power lies with ministers; Shamsher Singh (1974) said that the President acts on advice in all matters except where the Constitution provides otherwise.
The Vice-President

Election (Article 66): by an electoral college of all members of both Houses (elected and nominated), using the single transferable vote. State legislatures do not vote. At least 35 years old. Roles: ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha , and he casts a vote only in a tie. He acts as President when that office is vacant, for up to six months until a new election. Removal (Article 67(b)): by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha passed by a majority of its members and agreed by the Lok Sabha. The 15th Vice-President is C.P. Radhakrishnan , elected on 9 September 2025 (452 votes to Justice B. Sudershan Reddy's 300), after Jagdeep Dhankhar resigned on 21 July 2025. Comparison: the US Vice-President is on the ticket with the President. India's Vice-President is elected separately and is not an executive deputy.
The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers

Appointment (Article 75): the President appoints the PM, usually the leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha, and then other ministers on the PM's advice. A minister who is not an MP must become one within six months. Three ranks: Cabinet ministers, Ministers of State (some with independent charge) and Deputy Ministers. The Cabinet is the inner group that takes decisions. The PM works with Cabinet committees, which do much of the work. Collective responsibility (Article 75(3)) to the Lok Sabha: all ministers sink or swim together. Individual responsibility to the President. Size: capped at 15% of the Lok Sabha by the 91st Amendment (2003). Article 78: the PM must tell the President about Cabinet decisions. Lord Morley called the PM inter stellas luna minores , the moon among lesser stars. Harold Laski called him the "pivot". In India, Nehru was dominant, Shastri collegial, Indira Gandhi centralised, Narasimha Rao and Vajpayee had to manage allies. After 2014 the PMO became central again.
The PMO, Cabinet Secretariat and the permanent executive

Cabinet Secretariat: under the Cabinet Secretary, it serves the Cabinet and its committees and coordinates departments. Prime Minister's Office (PMO): built up under Nehru as the PM's secretariat and renamed in 1977; headed by the Principal Secretary. Critics speak of a PMO-centric style that reduces the Cabinet. Civil services: the All India Services and central services under Articles 308-314. Article 311 protects civil servants from arbitrary dismissal. The UPSC (Article 315) recruits. The "steel frame" phrase came from British Prime Minister Lloyd George, and was valued by Sardar Patel as a unifying force. Neutrality vs commitment: a debate since the 1970s on whether officers should be committed to the government's goals. Max Weber's ideal type of a rational-legal bureaucracy and Fred Riggs's idea of the "prismatic" society are often used: the Indian bureaucracy has a modern form but is mixed with patronage and caste networks.
India's President compared with the US President

India Indirectly elected by an electoral college; nominal executive; acts on advice; ministers sit in Parliament and are accountable to it; the President cannot veto an amendment bill; impeachment requires violation of the Constitution; emergency powers on Cabinet's written advice (44th Amendment). United States Elected through the Electoral College; real executive; Cabinet secretaries are outside Congress; the veto can be overridden by two-thirds; fixed four-year term with a two-term limit; impeachment for "high crimes and misdemeanors". Why it matters for debate: some call for a presidential system in India for stability and strong leadership. Reasons against: India's diversity needs a shared executive, and a directly elected single leader may concentrate power. Juan Linz's work ( The Perils of Presidentialism , 1990) argues that fixed terms can produce deadlock and zero-sum fights. India's experience shows that a parliamentary system can also produce a dominant executive, so the real safeguards are institutions, rather than only the form of government.
Today's executive

President Droupadi Murmu (since 25 July 2022) used Article 143 in May 2025 to ask the Supreme Court whether courts can set deadlines for Governors and the President on state bills. The Court's opinion in November 2025 said they cannot fix such timelines. Prime Minister Narendra Modi began a third term on 9 June 2024, leading an NDA coalition of about 70 ministers, after the BJP won 240 seats. Vice-President Radhakrishnan chairs the Rajya Sabha. Ministers in custody: the 130th Amendment Bill, 2025 would remove a PM, Chief Minister or minister held for 30 consecutive days on serious charges. A JPC has delayed its report. Ordinances: debate on how often they are used; many farm or tax measures first appeared as ordinances. Civil services: lateral entry advertisements in 2024 were cancelled after political objections about reservation.
How UPSC asks this

"The President of India is a constitutional head with real reserve powers." Discuss. "Examine the growing centralisation of power in the Prime Minister's Office." "Explain collective responsibility. Has it weakened in coalition governments?" "Discuss the discretionary powers of the President in a hung Parliament." Structure: Articles 53, 74 and Ambedkar's description; election and impeachment; list of powers with Articles; the 42nd and 44th Amendments on advice; discretion in a hung House and Narayanan's actions; the VP; PM and Cabinet, collective responsibility; PMO; civil services; recent cases (Article 143 reference, 130th Amendment Bill); balanced conclusion.
Parliament
The people's forum, under pressure

Parliament is the centre of the parliamentary system. It makes laws, controls money and holds the executive to account. Yet scholars and presiding officers have warned for years that its working is declining: fewer sittings, frequent disruptions, less committee scrutiny. UPSC asks about structure and powers , the role of the Rajya Sabha , the committee system , the Speaker and the decline of Parliament. You need articles, numbers, examples and a view. Walter Bagehot, in The English Constitution (1867), listed five functions of the House of Commons: the elective function (choosing the government), the expressive (voicing the people's mind), the teaching , the informing and the legislative . Many add scrutiny of the executive as the most important today.
Structure: President, Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha

Lok Sabha (Articles 81-83) Maximum 550 members (530 from states, 20 from Union Territories). Present strength is 543; the 104th Amendment (2019) ended the two nominated Anglo-Indian seats. Five-year term, which can be extended one year at a time during a national Emergency. Minimum age 25. Led by the Speaker (Article 93). Rajya Sabha (Articles 80, 83) Maximum 250: 238 from states and Union Territories, and 12 nominated for expertise in literature, science, art or social service. Present strength is 245. A permanent House: one-third retire every two years; six-year term. Minimum age 30. Chaired by the Vice-President. Rajya Sabha members are elected indirectly by state assemblies using the single transferable vote. Seats are allotted by population, not equally as in the US Senate. The domicile requirement was removed in 2003, and open ballot was introduced for the Rajya Sabha elections. The Lok Sabha has the last word on money bills, the control over the Council of Ministers, and in joint sittings (the Lok Sabha has more members).
How a bill becomes a law

Ordinary bill: either House, equal powers. The Rajya Sabha may delay but not block a money bill. Money bill (Article 110): only in the Lok Sabha, on the President's recommendation. The Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes within 14 days; the Lok Sabha may reject them. The Speaker certifies a bill as a money bill. Constitutional amendment: both Houses by special majority; no joint sitting. Joint sitting has been used three times: Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), Banking Service Commission Repeal Bill (1978), Prevention of Terrorism Bill (2002).
Controlling the purse: the budget

Article 112: the annual financial statement. Presented on 1 February since 2017, when the Railway Budget was merged with the Union Budget. The government cannot spend from the Consolidated Fund (Article 266) without Parliament's authorisation through an Appropriation Act . A Contingency Fund (Article 267) is for unforeseen needs. Stages: general discussion; demands for grants ( cut motions are used to signal protest); the Appropriation Bill; the Finance Bill. A guillotine ends debate on remaining demands. Control after spending: the CAG audits; the Public Accounts Committee examines the reports. Controversy: the Aadhaar Act, 2016 was passed as a money bill, which kept the Rajya Sabha out. In K.S. Puttaswamy (Aadhaar) (2018), a 4:1 majority upheld this. In Rojer Mathew (2019), the Court referred the wider question of misuse of the money bill route to a larger bench. The issue is still pending.
Controlling the executive

Question Hour (starred, unstarred, short notice), Zero Hour (an Indian invention, since 1962), and calling-attention notices. Motions: adjournment motion, no-confidence motion (under Rule 198, needs 50 members to support), censure, cut motions and motion of thanks to the President's address. Debates: short-duration discussions, half-hour discussions. Committees: the main arm of scrutiny. Main committees Public Accounts Committee (since 1921; the Chair is traditionally from the Opposition), Estimates Committee (1950), Committee on Public Undertakings (1964), and Department-Related Standing Committees (set up in 1993, now 24). Joint Parliamentary Committees are ad hoc: examples are the Bofors (1987), the stock market scam (1992), the 2G (2011) and the 2025 Waqf bill committee.
The Speaker and the Chairman

The Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha (Article 93) and presides, decides on points of order, certifies money bills, decides on defections under the Tenth Schedule and disqualification, and has a casting vote only in a tie. G.V. Mavalankar , the first Speaker (1952-56), set conventions of impartiality. Neelam Sanjiva Reddy resigned from his party on becoming Speaker (1967). The Speaker does not vacate the seat on dissolution but remains till the new House meets. Deputy Speaker: traditionally from the Opposition; the post stayed vacant throughout the 17th Lok Sabha (2019-24). Speaker Om Birla was re-elected in the 18th Lok Sabha on 26 June 2024. The Leader of the Opposition, Rahul Gandhi, was recognised after a gap of ten years. Criticism: Speakers belong to parties, so their decisions on defection and suspension often seem partisan. The Supreme Court ( Kihoto Hollohan , 1992; Keisham Meghachandra Singh , 2020) has asked for timely and reviewable decisions.
Role of the Rajya Sabha

Strengths: it represents states and, in theory, offers a second look at bills; it protects continuity (it cannot be dissolved); it brings in experts through nominated members; it has special federal powers: Article 249 (Parliament can legislate on State List subjects if two-thirds of the Rajya Sabha agrees in the national interest), Article 312 (creating All India Services). Weaknesses: Seats go by population, so it is not an equal federal chamber like the US Senate. It has been used by parties to place leaders who cannot win elections. The residence rule was removed in 2003. It has less power than the Lok Sabha on money and in confidence votes. The Sarkaria Commission and the NCRWC (2002) saw it as useful but wanted it more representative of states. Still, it has delayed or amended important bills, such as the Lokpal Bill (2011-13).
Is Parliament declining?

Sittings: the first Lok Sabha sat for about 135 days a year (an average above 120 in the 1950s). Recent Houses sit for roughly 55-70 days a year (PRS Legislative Research). Disruptions: repeated walkouts and adjournments waste time. In December 2023, 146 MPs were suspended in the winter session. Bills passed in disrupted sessions get less debate. Committee scrutiny: the share of bills sent to committees fell from 71% in the 15th Lok Sabha to about 16% in the 17th (PRS). Ordinances and money bills are used to bypass the Rajya Sabha. Anti-defection law reduces MPs' independence, since party whips rule. Reforms suggested: a minimum number of sitting days (the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution suggested 120 for the Lok Sabha and 100 for the Rajya Sabha), automatic referral of bills to committees, a Parliamentary Budget Office, Opposition-chaired committees and a less partisan Speaker.
The 18th Lok Sabha so far

After the 2024 election, the BJP-led NDA has 293 members, and the INDIA bloc 234, giving a stronger Opposition than the 17th Lok Sabha. Waqf (Amendment) Bill, 2024-25: sent to a Joint Parliamentary Committee of 31 members before passage in April 2025. Three new criminal laws (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita and others) took effect on 1 July 2024. Constitutional bills: the 129th Amendment (simultaneous elections) and 130th (removal of ministers in custody) are with JPCs. The 131st Amendment Bill failed on 17 April 2026 for want of a two-thirds majority. New Parliament building (inaugurated 28 May 2023) and the women's reservation law (106th Amendment, in force from 16 April 2026; the quota waits for delimitation) are changes in form and composition. Debates on the SIR of electoral rolls and on foreign policy episodes tested whether the Opposition can force discussion.
How UPSC asks this

"Parliament's role as a legislature has diminished. Discuss the reasons and remedies." "Examine the role of parliamentary committees in strengthening accountability." "Does the Rajya Sabha serve any useful purpose?" "The Speaker's role has become controversial. Examine." Structure: Bagehot's functions; composition and powers; law-making and money bills; budget control; committees; Speaker and Rajya Sabha; indicators of decline (sittings, committees, disruptions); reforms (NCRWC 120 days, committees); recent cases (Waqf JPC, 2023 suspensions); end with a hopeful view.
The Supreme Court and the States
The apex court as federal umpire, and the state's own organs

This lesson joins two things: the Supreme Court , which sits at the top of a single integrated judiciary and settles disputes between the Union and states, and the state governments : the Governor, Chief Minister, legislature and High Court. Why together? Because federalism is tested in both places. The Supreme Court decides who has what power. The Governor and the Chief Minister show how the Union and states actually work together. Likely questions: powers and jurisdiction of the Supreme Court; judicial independence and the collegium; the role and misuse of the Governor; the working of High Courts and subordinate courts; recent Supreme Court judgments on federal questions. Keep links: Article 131 and 143 (jurisdiction), Article 124 (judges), Articles 153-167 (Governor), Articles 168-212 (legislature), 214-231 (High Courts).
One integrated judiciary

Unlike the US, India has no separate state court system. This is one of the unitary features of the Constitution. Appeals go up from the district court to the High Court to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court (Articles 124-147) sits in Delhi. The strength was raised to the Chief Justice and 33 other judges in 2019. A judge retires at 65 and a High Court judge at 62. Judges of the Supreme Court are removed only by Parliament on proof of "misbehaviour or incapacity" (Article 124(4)): an address by each House with a majority of total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting. The Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 provides the process. No judge has been removed so far.
Jurisdiction of the Supreme Court

Original (Article 131): disputes between the Union and states, or between states. Examples: suits by Kerala (2024) over borrowing limits and by West Bengal over central agencies. Writ (Article 32): enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Appellate (Articles 132-134): constitutional, civil and criminal appeals from High Courts; special leave (Article 136) . Advisory (Article 143): opinions on questions of law or fact referred by the President. Not binding in the way a judgment is. Used for the Ram Janmabhoomi reference (1993), the 2G reference (2012), and the 2025 reference on Governors' timelines. Review (Article 137) and curative petitions ( Rupa Ashok Hurra , 2002). Article 141: its law binds all courts. Article 142: orders for "complete justice". Article 129: court of record with power to punish contempt.
Independence, appointment and accountability

Independence is supported by security of tenure, fixed salaries charged to the Consolidated Fund, bar on practice after retirement in the same courts, and a ban on discussing a judge's conduct in Parliament (except in removal). The appointment story: the First Judges Case (1981) gave the executive primacy; the Second (1993) and Third (1998) set up the collegium (CJI and four senior-most judges). The NJAC under the 99th Amendment was struck down on 16 October 2015. Critiques of the collegium: opaque, no written criteria, little diversity (few women, few judges from marginalised groups), lack of a secretariat, "judges appointing judges". Critiques of the executive role: risk of pressure. Pendency: across Indian courts, more than five crore cases were pending in 2025 (National Judicial Data Grid), and many High Court posts are vacant. Fast-track and commercial courts, e-courts and mediation (Mediation Act, 2023) aim to reduce delay.
The Governor and the State Executive

Governor (Articles 153-162): appointed by the President, five-year term at the President's pleasure. Must be at least 35. He appoints the Chief Minister (Article 164), usually the leader of the majority, and summons and prorogues the legislature. Chief Minister and Council (Articles 163-164): collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly. The Governor acts on their advice except where the Constitution gives discretion. Governor's discretion: choosing a CM in a hung House, reserving bills for the President (Article 200), sending reports for President's Rule (Article 356), and in the Sixth Schedule areas. Ordinances (Article 213) when the legislature is not in session. The Sarkaria Commission advised that Governors be eminent persons from outside the state, not recently active in politics, and consulted with the Chief Minister. The Punchhi Commission (2010) suggested a fixed five-year term, removal only by a resolution of the state legislature.
State legislature and High Courts

Legislative Assembly: 60 to 500 members (smaller in a few small states), directly elected, five-year term. A Legislative Council (Article 169) exists in only six states: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Bihar and Uttar Pradesh. Parliament can create or abolish a Council if the Assembly passes a special majority resolution. The Council has limited powers; the Assembly has the final say on ordinary bills. High Courts (Article 214): 25 now. Judges are appointed on the collegium's advice. Powers: writs under Article 226 (wider than Article 32 since they can issue them for any legal right) and superintendence over subordinate courts (Article 227). Subordinate courts are overseen by the High Court (Articles 233-237). The District Judge is appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court. The Law Commission and the Supreme Court have supported a proposed All India Judicial Service (Article 312), which has not materialised.
Courts on federal questions: landmark cases

S.R. Bommai (1994): reviewable President's Rule; federalism as basic structure. Nabam Rebia (2016): Governor cannot call or advance a Session of the Assembly on his own; Speaker's powers. Subhash Desai (11 May 2023): Governor's floor test in Maharashtra in 2022 had no valid basis; the Speaker's appointment of a whip was illegal; the previous government was not restored because Uddhav Thackeray resigned without facing the test. Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018, 2023): the elected government controls services except for police, public order and land; Parliament later passed the GNCTD Amendment Act, 2023. Mineral Area Development Authority v. SAIL (25 July 2024): a nine-judge bench held by 8:1 that states can tax mineral rights; royalty is not a tax. A boost to states' fiscal power. State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to the Governor of Punjab (10 November 2023): Governors cannot sit on bills indefinitely. State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor (8 April 2025) and the Presidential reference opinion (November 2025).
Strengthening or stretching the Court's role

The Court as guardian of federalism: its judgments on Delhi, minerals, and the Governors' conduct are cited as protection for states against central overreach. The counter-view: The Court has itself favoured the Centre in many cases, including Article 370 in 2023, where federal arguments about J&K's statehood were set aside. Directions such as "deemed assent" may stretch Article 142 and conflict with the separation of powers, as the 2025 reference debate showed. Delay: a constitution bench decision can take years. Governors' appointments continue to be political. Reports of tension in Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, Punjab and Delhi's Lieutenant Governor persist. Scholars: Upendra Baxi on the Court's "social action litigation"; S.P. Sathe on activism; Granville Austin's Working a Democratic Constitution (1999) on the Court's shifting role.
What to cite from 2024-2026

CJI B.R. Gavai (May-Nov 2025) led the Presidential reference bench; CJI Surya Kant took over on 24 November 2025 and retires on 9 February 2027. Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025: interim order on 15 September 2025 partially stayed. SIR of electoral rolls: upheld in May 2026. Governors: disputes in several opposition-ruled states over bills and university chancellorships. Kerala v. Union (2024): original suit on net borrowing limits. Statehood: J&K Chief Minister Omar Abdullah (from October 2024) heads a government that works with a Lieutenant Governor with wide powers; statehood is pending. Delhi: the Delhi Assembly election of February 2025 brought a BJP government, so the long conflict between an AAP government and the Centre ended.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. Has the apex court expanded its role?" "Evaluate the collegium system and the case for judicial appointments reform." "The office of the Governor has become a source of Centre-state friction. Discuss." "Judicial delays threaten access to justice. Suggest measures." Structure: integrated judiciary; Supreme Court jurisdictions with Articles; independence, collegium, NJAC; pendency and reforms; Governor's role and Sarkaria-Punchhi advice; legislature and High Courts; landmark federal cases; critique; recent examples; end with trust and transparency as the solution.
The Governor and Article 356
Where federalism is tested

The Governor and President's Rule are the most contested Centre-State flashpoints. Every few years a new case (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Punjab, Delhi, Manipur) puts them in the news. UPSC asks both on the constitutional position and on abuse and reform . Article 356 was used about 100 times before 1994, and S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) made the Governor's report and the floor test open to judicial review.
The Governor's office

Art. 153-154 : a Governor for each state, executive power vested in him. Art. 155-156 : appointed by the President, holds office at the President's pleasure, normal term five years. Art. 163 : acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, except where the Constitution requires discretion. Art. 164 : appoints the Chief Minister. Art. 200-201 : assent to bills; reserve for the President. Art. 213 : ordinance power.
Discretion and the dual role

The Governor is both constitutional head of the state and agent of the Centre . True discretion exists in: choosing a CM when no party has a clear majority, reporting breakdown to the President (Art. 356), reserving bills for the President, and in some tribal areas (Sixth Schedule, Assam). In Shamsher Singh (1974), the Supreme Court held that apart from these, he is bound by ministerial advice. The Sarkaria Commission (1988) wanted Governors chosen after consulting the CM.
Article 356: President's Rule

Art. 355 is the Union's duty to protect states. Beyond one year, extension needs a national Emergency or an EC certificate (44th Amendment, 1978). Parliament takes over state legislative power (Art. 357).
S.R. Bommai (1994)

The leading case, a nine-judge bench. It held that: the proclamation is subject to judicial review for malafide or irrelevant grounds; the Centre must show material; Parliament's approval is needed or the proclamation lapses; the assembly should be suspended, not dissolved , until approved; secularism is part of the basic structure , so a state violating it can face 356; a floor test is the way to test a majority, not the Governor's opinion.
Misuse over time

The first use was in Punjab in 1951, and in 1959 the Kerala E.M.S. Namboodiripad ministry was dismissed. The surge came in 1977 (Janata dismissed nine Congress states) and 1980 (reverse). Over 100 uses have been recorded. Later notable cases: Bihar assembly dissolution ( Rameshwar Prasad , 2006), Arunachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand in 2016 ( Nabam Rebia and the Uttarakhand High Court), and Manipur , where PR was imposed on 13 February 2025 and revoked on 4 February 2026 when a new ministry took office.
Governors and state bills: Tamil Nadu (2025)

In April 2025 a two-judge Bench in State of Tamil Nadu v Governor set timelines for Governors on bills and used Article 142 to treat ten bills as deemed assented . The President then made a reference under Art. 143. On 20 November 2025 the Court's advisory opinion held that there is no deemed assent and courts cannot fix timelines. It said the Governor has three options under Art. 200 (assent, reserve, return) and cannot sit on bills indefinitely, and that delay can be reviewed in a limited way. Verify the latest in current affairs.
Reform proposals

Sarkaria (1988): Art. 356 as last resort; Governor should be eminent, non-political, outside the state. Punchhi (2010): five-year fixed tenure; impeachment-like removal by legislature; 'localised emergency' under Art. 355 instead of 356. Venkatachaliah (2002): CM consulted; selection by committee including the VP and the Speaker. Inter-State Council (Art. 263) as forum.
Federal politics today

Conflicts between Governors and opposition-ruled states (Tamil Nadu, Kerala, West Bengal, Punjab, Telangana) over bills, university chancellorship and appointments continue. The Punchhi and Sarkaria ideas are quoted both by states and the Court. Note: the Delhi Lt Governor is separate, governed by Art. 239AA and the 2023 Supreme Court ruling on services.
How UPSC asks this

"The role of the Governor is a source of Centre-State friction. Discuss." "Examine the judicial safeguards against the misuse of Article 356." "Do the Presidential Reference (2025) and Bommai together settle the Governor's powers?" Structure: constitutional text, discretion, 356 procedure, Bommai, misuse, Sarkaria/Punchhi, Tamil Nadu 2025.
Judicial Activism and PIL
When courts act for the people

India's Supreme Court is among the most powerful in the world. Public Interest Litigation (PIL) and judicial activism opened justice to the poor but also raised the charge of judicial overreach . This is a standard Paper I theme and appears in essays. The idea began with Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer in the late 1970s. Hussainara Khatoon (1979), on undertrial prisoners, is an early landmark case.
Meaning and roots

Judicial activism is a proactive role in protecting rights and filling gaps; restraint is deference to the legislature. The term is credited to Arthur Schlesinger (1947). In India, after the Emergency, the Court sought to repair its image ( ADM Jabalpur , 1976). Judges P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer relaxed locus standi and let letters count as petitions ( epistolary jurisdiction ). Basis: Art. 32 (Supreme Court) and Art. 226 (High Courts).
Landmark PILs
Hussainara Khatoon was the first big PIL, on speedy trial under Art. 21.
Expanding Article 21

In Maneka Gandhi (1978) the Court said that 'procedure established by law' must be fair, just and reasonable. From that, it read into Art. 21 the rights to livelihood ( Olga Tellis , 1985), clean environment , education ( Unni Krishnan , 1993), privacy ( Puttaswamy , 2017), dignity , health and food. Other PIL directions: D.K. Basu (1997) arrest guidelines; Vineet Narain (1997) on CBI independence; Prakash Singh (2006) police reform; NALSA (2014) recognised transgender persons.
Judicial appointments

The Court even took charge of its own appointments. Second Judges Case (1993) and the Third Judges Case advisory (1998) created the collegium . In 2015 it struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC as violating the basic structure (independence of the judiciary). Critics find the collegium opaque and self-perpetuating.
How a PIL works

Any bona fide person or group can approach the Supreme Court or a High Court for the benefit of those who cannot, such as the poor, prisoners or bonded workers. The Court may treat a letter as a writ petition, appoint commissions to find facts, name an amicus curiae to assist, and issue continuing mandamus to monitor compliance. The usual rules of standing, pleadings and court fees are relaxed. In 2010 ( Balwant Singh Chaufal ) the Court laid down guidelines to screen out private or frivolous petitions.
Overreach and the checks

Separation of powers : courts making policy, such as the Delhi CNG order and the 2012 2G licence cancellation. Misuse of PIL : 'publicity interest litigation', frivolous cases. The Court has imposed costs and set 2010 guidelines. No accountability or expertise on technical matters. Defenders: executive failure forces courts to act, as in Vishaka, where Parliament was silent until 2013.
Safeguards and the shift

The Court now says PIL must be bona fide , with real public interest and not personal or political gain. Courts increasingly issue continuing mandamus and monitor implementation. Judgments recently stress constitutional morality ( Navtej Johar , 2018; Joseph Shine , 2018, adultery), and the earlier 'positive' rights reading for socio-economic rights (Part IV).
India's judicial role today

Examples to cite: Kesavananda Bharati (1973, basic structure), Puttaswamy (2017 privacy), Right to food (PUCL), environment (Forest cases, Vellore Citizens , 1996, 'polluter pays'), electoral bonds struck down (15 February 2024). Also relevant: the 'Judicial vs executive' friction over appointments, with Law Ministry and the Collegium.
How UPSC asks this

"Judicial activism is a necessary supplement to democracy but not a substitute. Discuss." "Examine the role of PIL in expanding access to justice in India." "Distinguish judicial activism from judicial overreach with examples." Structure: definition, origins, landmark cases, Art. 21, appointments, critique, safeguards, examples. Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) is a classic example: the Court laid down guidelines on sexual harassment at the workplace until Parliament acted.
73rd and 74th Amendments
Democracy at the third level

India's Constitution was first written with two levels of government: the Union and the states. Villages and towns were left to state law, with only a weak Directive Principle ( Article 40 ) asking the State to organise village panchayats. The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) changed this by giving rural and urban local bodies a constitutional base. They came into force on 24 April 1993 (73rd, panchayats) and 1 June 1993 (74th, municipalities). About 2.5 lakh panchayats and several thousand urban bodies now work under them, with over 30 lakh elected representatives, of whom roughly 1.4 million are women. Examiners ask: Why were these amendments needed? What are their main features? Have they made democracy real at the grassroots? The best answers compare ideals (Gandhi, Ambedkar, J.S. Mill, Tocqueville) with performance and name the weak spots: money, functions, officials, women's proxy rule.
Four thinkers on local self-government

Gandhi In Hind Swaraj (1909) and later writings, he pictured India as a set of self-governing villages, "oceanic circles" in which each village is a republic and power flows from the bottom up. B.R. Ambedkar In the Constituent Assembly (4 November 1948) he asked what the village is but "a sink of localism, a den of ignorance, narrow-mindedness and communalism". He feared local elites and caste hierarchy. This is why the Constitution did not make panchayats a core feature. J.S. Mill and Tocqueville Mill ( Considerations on Representative Government , 1861) saw local institutions as schools of citizenship. Tocqueville ( Democracy in America , 1835) held that local liberties teach people how to use freedom. Jayaprakash Narayan, Reconstruction of Indian Polity (1959) Proposed a partyless, village-based pyramid of councils. Also Robert Putnam's Making Democracy Work (1993) links local associations to social capital and good government.
The road to 1992

Community Development Programme (1952) and National Extension Service (1953): top-down, officials led. Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957): a three-tier system, with block as the key. Rajasthan launched it at Nagaur on 2 October 1959. Ashok Mehta Committee (1977): two tiers, with the district as the main unit; political parties' role; reserved seats for SC/ST; a social audit. G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985): bureaucratised planning ("grass without roots"); suggested the district as the unit. L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986): recommended constitutional status and financial resources. The 64th Amendment Bill (1989) passed the Lok Sabha but failed in the Rajya Sabha. The Narasimha Rao government passed the 73rd and 74th in 1992.
The 73rd Amendment: panchayats (Part IX)

Gram Sabha (Article 243A): all adult voters of the village. The base of the system. Three tiers , except in states with a population below 20 lakh, which may skip the middle tier. Direct elections to all seats; five-year term; fresh elections within six months if dissolved. Reservation: seats for SC/ST in proportion to population; at least one-third for women (including within the SC/ST seats); states may reserve for OBCs. Many states raised women's reservation to 50%; Bihar did so first in 2006. State Election Commission (Article 243K) runs the polls; State Finance Commission (243I) reviews finances every five years. Eleventh Schedule: 29 subjects such as agriculture, health, education, drinking water, rural housing. Exempt: Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram, some hill areas of Manipur and Darjeeling (Article 243M).
The 74th Amendment: municipalities (Part IXA)

Three types (Article 243Q): Nagar Panchayat for a transitional area, Municipal Council for a smaller urban area and Municipal Corporation for a larger one. Wards committees in cities with a population above three lakh. Reservation for SC/ST and one-third for women; five-year term; State Election and Finance Commissions, as for panchayats. Twelfth Schedule: 18 functions, including urban planning, regulation of land use, roads and bridges, water supply, public health, slum improvement and urban poverty alleviation. District Planning Committee (Article 243ZD) to consolidate plans of panchayats and municipalities; Metropolitan Planning Committee (243ZE) for cities above a million. Notice a key difference: the Twelfth Schedule functions are broader and more technical, but city mayors in many states are weak, elected indirectly or for one year, and parastatal agencies (development authorities, water boards) hold real power.
PESA (1996) and tribal self-rule

The 73rd Amendment did not apply to Fifth Schedule areas unless Parliament extended it. After the Bhuria Committee (1995), Parliament passed the Provisions of the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) . The Gram Sabha is central: it approves plans and safeguards community resources, customs and culture. Consultation before land acquisition and mining leases; ownership of minor forest produce; control over local markets and money-lending. The Forest Rights Act, 2006 gave Gram Sabhas a role in recognising rights over forests. In Orissa Mining Corporation v. Ministry of Environment (the Niyamgiri case, 2013), the Supreme Court told Gram Sabhas of the Dongria Kondh to decide on the bauxite project, which rejected it. PESA applies in ten states (Andhra, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan). Critics say that many states have not made rules in full and that PESA is weakly applied.
Money: the weak link in local government

State Finance Commissions (Articles 243I and 243Y) must recommend how state taxes are shared with local bodies, and what grants they get. Many states set them up late, and the reports are often not acted upon. Central Finance Commission: since the 11th FC, it has recommended grants to supplement local bodies' funds based on the State Finance Commissions' reports. The 15th FC gave over four lakh crore rupees to rural and urban local bodies for 2021-26, partly tied to conditions like property-tax reform and accounts. Own revenue: panchayats raise little, and urban bodies depend on property tax, which is under-collected. Octroi and entry taxes were removed with GST (2017), leaving cities with fewer independent sources. Other tools: municipal bonds in a few cities, user charges, and central schemes channelled through local bodies. Principle of subsidiarity: tasks should rest with the lowest level that can do them well. The Second ARC (2005-09) also urged that local bodies be given clear functions and the funds that go with them.
What went right and wrong

Achievements: Regular elections; a large cohort of elected women (about 46% of panchayat members according to government data), SC/ST and OBC representatives. Studies by Esther Duflo and Raghabendra Chattopadhyay (2004) found that women leaders invest more in public goods like drinking water. Kerala's People's Plan Campaign (1996) transferred about 35-40% of the state's plan funds to local bodies. Weaknesses: The "3 Fs": functions, funds and functionaries are not devolved fully; the Eleventh Schedule is "may" not "shall". States hold the real power. Low own revenue; dependence on grants (the 15th Finance Commission recommended over ₹4 lakh crore for local bodies in 2021-26). Proxy rule by "sarpanch-pati" for women representatives. Caste and elite capture; irregular Gram Sabhas. Delayed urban elections; weak mayors. Parallel bodies and schemes managed by departments.
Reforms and recent cases

Supreme Court on OBC reservation: in Vikas Kishanrao Gawali (2021) the Court required a "triple test" (an empirical commission, proportion to data, and the 50% cap) before OBC quotas in local bodies. Digital: eGramSwaraj portal, SVAMITVA property cards (2020), Gram Panchayat Development Plans and the annual People's Plan Campaign. Proxy rule: a committee under the Ministry of Panchayati Raj studied the problem in 2023, and states are tightening rules. Finance: grants to local bodies recommended by the 15th and 16th Finance Commissions. Urban: Smart Cities Mission (2015) and AMRUT have been criticised for working through special-purpose bodies instead of municipalities. J&K: after 2019, the 73rd and 74th Amendments apply; District Development Council elections were held in December 2020.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine the 73rd and 74th Amendments. Have they strengthened grassroots democracy?" "Why have panchayats failed to become institutions of self-government in practice?" "Discuss the role of women in local government after reservation." "Assess the PESA Act." Structure: ideas (Gandhi, Ambedkar, Mill); committees from Balwant Rai Mehta to Singhvi; features of the 73rd and 74th Amendments with the Schedules; PESA and Forest Rights Act; achievements; the 3 Fs gap; proxy representation; reforms (devolution, own revenue, State Finance Commission follow-up, training); conclude that constitutional recognition is only the first step.
Grassroots Movements
When citizens do democracy between elections

The first lesson in this unit was about institutions: panchayats and municipalities. This one is about citizens' movements : people organising on their own to protect land, forests, wages, information and dignity. Why do these belong under grassroots democracy? Because they deepen it. They give voice to people the parties miss and push the state to make laws such as the Right to Information Act (2005) and MGNREGA (2005). Scholars give them different labels: non-party political formations (Rajni Kothari), new social movements (Gail Omvedt) or movements of the political society (Partha Chatterjee). In exams you are asked to explain their nature, give examples and judge their impact. For environmental and women's movements in detail, see the final unit of this paper; here the focus is on how movements widen democracy.
Frameworks to analyse movements

Old and new social movements Old movements (labour, peasants) fought for class and economic gains and often worked through parties. New social movements (Touraine, Melucci) are about identity, culture, environment and quality of life, and rely on civil society. Resource mobilisation and political opportunity McCarthy and Zald stress organisation and funds; Sidney Tarrow stresses the political openings that allow protest to succeed. Rajni Kothari, "The Non-Party Political Process" (1984) Argued that as parties lost touch with the poor, voluntary groups and local movements began to fill the gap. He saw them as a new "non-party political formation". Partha Chatterjee, The Politics of the Governed (2004) Distinguishes civil society (the middle class, who use rights and law) from political society (the poor, who negotiate with the state through collective claims). Gail Omvedt, Reinventing Revolution (1993) Treats Dalit, women's, farmers' and environmental movements as India's new movements, aiming to redefine the idea of social change.
From Gandhian roots to the JP movement

Bhoodan (1951): Vinoba Bhave began it at Pochampalli (then Hyderabad State) after a landlord offered land to the landless. It grew into the Gramdan idea of village ownership. Success in numbers was modest; in moral terms it was large. Sarvodaya and the Gandhian constructive work tradition. Navnirman Andolan (Gujarat, December 1973 to 1974): students and middle class against corruption and price rise forced the state government to resign. Bihar Movement and JP's "Total Revolution" (1974): Jayaprakash Narayan led students against corruption. The Allahabad High Court's verdict (June 1975) and the Emergency (25 June 1975) followed. The Janata Party victory in 1977 grew out of this. These movements showed that street politics could unseat governments, and the Emergency showed how fragile civil liberties were. They fed into the human rights groups of the late 1970s (PUCL, PUDR).
Movements that changed the law

MKSS (Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan): formed in 1990 in Rajasthan by Aruna Roy, Nikhil Dey and Shankar Singh. From the mid-1990s it held jan sunwai (public hearings) where villagers compared muster rolls with real work. It started the demand for information, which became the RTI Act, 2005. Right to Food: the petition in PUCL v. Union of India (2001) led to orders on midday meals and the Public Distribution System; later the National Food Security Act (2013). MGNREGA (2005) includes a statutory social audit ; Andhra Pradesh pioneered an independent social audit unit. Land acquisition: protests in Singur and Nandigram (2006-07) fed the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013.
Livelihood and organisation: SEWA, farmers and tribal groups

SEWA (Self-Employed Women's Association, Ahmedabad, 1972, founded by Ela Bhatt): a union of women in the informal sector with its own bank, cooperative and training. A model of organising where labour law barely reaches. Farmers' movements: the Shetkari Sanghatana (Sharad Joshi, Maharashtra) argued that price policy was biased against "Bharat" in favour of "India". The Bharatiya Kisan Union (Mahendra Singh Tikait, western Uttar Pradesh, 1980s) and the Samyukta Kisan Morcha (2020-21) are later forms. Tribal movements: the Jharkhand movement led to the state in 2000; Niyamgiri (Dongria Kondh, 2013) showed the Gram Sabha's power; PESA and the Forest Rights Act (2006) are the legal fruit. Dalit movements: Dalit Panthers (1972), BSP and recent campaigns on atrocities (Una 2016). Anti-arrack movement (Andhra Pradesh, 1992): rural women forced a ban on liquor sales.
People's planning in Kerala

The People's Plan Campaign (1996), launched by the Left Democratic Front government with T.M. Thomas Isaac as a key architect, gave local bodies 35-40% of the state's plan funds. Ward and Gram Sabhas held development seminars, volunteers prepared local plans and task forces drew in experts. The Kerala Sastra Sahitya Parishad (KSSP, 1962) supplied thousands of volunteers with science and literacy skills. It is often called a people's science movement. Why it matters: it shows how movements and institutions can work together. Putnam's idea of social capital ( Making Democracy Work , 1993) helps explain it, as Kerala has dense associational life and high literacy. Critics note that political party rivalry later weakened the experiment, and funds were not always maintained. Other examples: participatory budgeting in Pune; Mohalla Sabhas in Delhi (2015); Kudumbashree (Kerala, 1998) for poverty alleviation through women's neighbourhood groups.
Tools of social accountability

Movements have left behind practical tools that ordinary people can use: Right to Information: an application to any public authority, with a 30-day reply time; first appeal; appeal to the Information Commission. Social audit: villagers check records against reality, as in MGNREGA (Section 17 of the Act). Meghalaya was the first state to pass a Social Audit law (2017). Jan sunwai: public hearing where officials answer questions in front of villagers. Citizens' Charters: introduced in 1997 after a conference of Chief Ministers; critics say they lack legal force. Gram Sabha: the legal forum under Article 243A that can approve beneficiary lists and plans. Public interest litigation: relaxed standing since the late 1970s (Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer). Upendra Baxi called this "social action litigation". Lokpal and Lokayuktas: the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013; the first Lokpal was appointed in March 2019. These tools show that grassroots democracy is both a structure (panchayats) and a practice (asking questions).
Strengths and limits of movement politics

Strengths: they widen participation, bring marginal issues to agenda, and often produce laws. Limits and criticisms: Fragmentation: many local struggles with no common platform. Co-optation and NGO-isation: donor money can turn movements into project-driven bodies. The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 (amended in 2020) tightens foreign funds, and critics say it is also used to pressure dissenting groups. Elite leadership: leaders are often middle class and urban; the poor may be followers. State response: police action, cases under the UAPA or preventive laws, internet shutdowns, and bans on assembly. Institutional gains can be undone: the RTI Act was amended in 2019 (tenure and pay of Information Commissioners) and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 changed the personal-information exemption in section 8(1)(j); activists say this weakens transparency. Exclusive demands: some movements (nativist, caste or communal) can threaten others' rights.
Movements to cite from recent years

Farmers 2020-21 : repeal of the three farm laws (November 2021) and the demand for legal MSP (Delhi Chalo, 2024). Anti-CAA protests (2019-20) including Shaheen Bagh, which led to a Supreme Court ruling that public roads cannot be blocked indefinitely. Ladakh: demands for statehood and Sixth Schedule protection, with protests in September 2025 that turned violent in Leh. Activist Sonam Wangchuk was detained under the National Security Act on 26 September 2025, after the Leh protests. The detention was revoked in March 2026. Hasdeo Aranya (Chhattisgarh) against coal mining on forest land, and Great Nicobar project concerns. Labour codes (November 2025): trade union protests. RTI: a rise in pending appeals in Information Commissions and vacancies are repeated complaints. Digital activism and citizen journalism extend the older repertoire.
How UPSC asks this

"Grassroots movements have deepened Indian democracy. Illustrate." "Discuss the role of non-party political formations." "How did the MKSS movement lead to the RTI Act?" "Evaluate the achievements and limits of social movements in India." Structure: define and place movements within civil society; theory (Kothari, Chatterjee, Omvedt); Gandhian and JP legacy; movements that produced laws (RTI, MGNREGA, FRA, Lokpal); livelihood and people's planning (SEWA, Kerala); critique (NGO-isation, state response, rollback); recent examples; conclude that movements and institutions need each other.
ECI, CAG, Finance Commission, UPSC
Guardians built into the Constitution

A democracy needs referees that the government of the day cannot easily control. The Constitution creates several: the Election Commission of India (Article 324), the Comptroller and Auditor General (Articles 148-151), the Finance Commission (Article 280) and the Union Public Service Commission (Articles 315-323). Each guards something different: free elections, honest spending, fair sharing of money between Union and states, and merit in public jobs. UPSC asks about their independence , their effectiveness and recent controversies: the 2023 law on appointing election commissioners, the Special Intensive Revision of rolls, CAG reports on big scams, and the 16th Finance Commission. For each body, learn four things: its Article, how members are appointed and removed, what it does, and the main criticism.
Election Commission: structure
