Article 324 vests the "superintendence, direction and control" of elections to Parliament, state legislatures, President and Vice-President in the Commission. It was a single-member body until 1989; briefly three members in 1989-90; permanently multi-member since 1993. Today: a Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners, deciding by majority. Removal: the CEC only like a Supreme Court judge (Article 324(5)); other Commissioners only on the CEC's recommendation. Appointment: in Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2 March 2023) the Supreme Court said that, until Parliament made a law, a panel of the PM, the Leader of the Opposition and the Chief Justice should choose. Parliament then passed the CEC and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023 : a selection committee of the PM, the Leader of the Opposition and a Union Cabinet minister named by the PM. Critics say this gives the government a 2-1 majority. Gyanesh Kumar became CEC in February 2025, the first under the new law.
Election Commission: powers and record

Prepares electoral rolls, conducts polls, recognises parties and allots symbols (Symbols Order, 1968), and enforces the Model Code of Conduct (a consensus code, not a law). T.N. Seshan (CEC 1990-96) made the Code real and pushed voter ID cards. EVMs used across the country since 2004; VVPAT added from 2013. In April 2024 the Supreme Court refused to order 100% VVPAT matching. Symbol disputes: it gave the Shiv Sena name to the Eknath Shinde faction (February 2023) and the NCP name to the Ajit Pawar faction (February 2024). Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of rolls began in Bihar in 2025 and spread to other states. The Supreme Court upheld the Commission's power to conduct it in May 2026, citing Article 324 and the Representation of the People Act, 1950. Criticism: slow action on hate speech by leaders, the timing of poll schedules, and questions over the SIR's effect on poor and migrant voters. Praise: it runs the world's largest elections, with nearly 98 crore registered voters in 2024.
Comptroller and Auditor General

Ambedkar called the CAG probably the most important officer under the Constitution, since he guards the public purse. Article 148: appointed by the President; removed only like a Supreme Court judge. Term six years or age 65. Not eligible for further government office. Article 149 and the CAG (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 : audits the Union, states and bodies they fund. Article 151: reports go to the President or Governor, who place them before the legislature. The Public Accounts Committee examines them. Kinds of audit: compliance, financial and performance audit (value for money). Famous reports: 2G spectrum (2010, a "presumptive loss" of ₹1.76 lakh crore) and coal block allocation (2012). They shaped politics before the 2014 election, but critics said the loss figures were speculative. K. Sanjay Murthy took office as CAG on 21 November 2024. Weaknesses: appointment by the executive alone, delays in tabling reports, and fewer audit reports in recent years, as critics note.
Finance Commission

Article 280: set up by the President every five years. A chairman with public-affairs experience and four members (Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951). Duties: recommend the share of Union taxes for states ( vertical devolution) and how it is divided among states ( horizontal ), grants-in-aid under Article 275, and measures to augment local bodies' funds. Recommendations are advisory, but the Union has generally accepted the devolution share. Recent commissions 14th (Y.V. Reddy): raised the share to 42% (2015-20). 15th (N.K. Singh): 41% for 2021-26, as J&K became a Union Territory; it added demographic performance as a criterion. 16th (Arvind Panagariya): report tabled on 1 February 2026; kept 41% for 2026-31, which the government accepted, though many states had asked for 50%. Debates: southern states say criteria reward population and penalise good performance; states object to cesses and surcharges outside the pool; the Planning Commission's end in 2015 increased the Finance Commission's weight.
Union Public Service Commission

Articles 315-323. Chair and members appointed by the President; six-year term or age 65. Half the members should have at least ten years in government service. Removal (Article 317): by the President for misbehaviour after a Supreme Court inquiry, or for insolvency, outside employment or infirmity. Functions (Article 320): conducts exams for Union services; advises on recruitment rules, promotions and disciplinary matters. Advice is not binding, but departures are reported to Parliament (Article 323). State Public Service Commissions mirror this. Debates: the long, costly exam and its urban bias; the shift to Paper II CSAT as qualifying (2015); lateral entry (advertised in 2024, then cancelled after objections over reservation); verification scandals (the 2024 case of a probationer's fake disability and caste claims led UPSC to cancel her candidature); and leaks in state commissions and other exams. The Kothari Committee (1976) and the Baswan Committee (2016) reviewed the exam.
Theory: why independent bodies?

Separation and checks: Montesquieu's idea that power must check power. Modern writers add "fourth branch" institutions: electoral bodies, auditors and ombudsmen. Guillermo O'Donnell (1998) called this horizontal accountability : state agencies checking other state agencies, in addition to vertical accountability through elections. Pratap Bhanu Mehta and Devesh Kapur , editors of Public Institutions in India (2005), showed how these bodies' performance depends on leadership and norms, not just law. In India, the Supreme Court has repeatedly linked independence of such bodies to the basic structure. In Anoop Baranwal it said an Election Commission that is not independent can damage democracy itself.
Are they independent enough?

Weak spots: Appointments rest with the executive. Only the ECI got a committee, and even that has a government majority. Post-retirement jobs (as governors, MPs, ministers) can tempt officers. No fixed budgets: most depend on the ministry for staff and money. Delay in action and in tabling reports. Strengths: Constitutional protection against removal. Strong individuals (Seshan; CAG reports of 2010-12) show what is possible. Courts back them when attacked. Reforms suggested: collegium-type selection with the Chief Justice (the Dinesh Goswami Committee, 1990, and the Law Commission's 255th Report, 2015, on the ECI); a ban on post-retirement posts; a charged budget from the Consolidated Fund for the ECI; time limits for tabling CAG reports.
Four bodies, four Articles
Each body has its own constitutional article, and each is meant to work free of day-to-day government control. Begin any answer with the Article.
Latest developments

2023 Act on ECI appointments : challenges pending in the Supreme Court; Gyanesh Kumar appointed CEC (February 2025). SIR of electoral rolls : Bihar (2025), more states in 2025-26; upheld in May 2026. 16th Finance Commission : 41% share for 2026-31; tabled 1 February 2026. GST Council : not one of these four, but another federal body whose recommendations, per Mohit Minerals (2022), are persuasive, not binding. CAG : K. Sanjay Murthy (from November 2024). One Nation, One Election : the 129th Amendment Bill would give the ECI the task of synchronised polls; it is with a JPC.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine the role of the Election Commission in ensuring free and fair elections. Is its independence under threat?" "The CAG is the guardian of the public purse. Discuss." "Evaluate the role of the Finance Commission in fiscal federalism." "Assess the working of the UPSC." Structure: Article and composition; appointment and removal; functions; landmark episodes (Seshan, 2G, 15th and 16th FC); theory of horizontal accountability; critique and reforms; recent issues (2023 Act, SIR).
The Commissions: NHRC, NCW, NCSC, NCST, NCM, NCBC
Watchdogs for rights and for vulnerable groups

Besides courts, India has a set of commissions to protect rights and particular groups: the NHRC (human rights), NCW (women), NCSC (Scheduled Castes), NCST (Scheduled Tribes), NCM (minorities) and NCBC (backward classes). Some are constitutional (NCSC, NCST, NCBC); others are statutory (NHRC, NCW, NCM). This difference matters for status and permanence but less for power: all mainly investigate and recommend. The exam question is usually: are they "toothless tigers"? You need their legal basis, composition, powers and examples of success or failure.
Constitutional or statutory: a quick map

Article 338 began as a Special Officer for SC and ST. The 65th Amendment (1990) made a multi-member commission. The 89th Amendment (2003) split it into NCSC (338) and NCST (338A, from 2004). The NCBC was set up in 1993 by law after Indra Sawhney , and given constitutional status by the 102nd Amendment (2018) .
NHRC: structure and powers

Created by the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 , in line with the UN Paris Principles (1993) for national human rights institutions. Chair: a former Chief Justice of India, or (since the 2019 amendment) a former Supreme Court judge. Members include judges and experts; ex-officio members are chairs of other national commissions. Appointment: by the President on the advice of a committee of the PM, Speaker, Home Minister, Leaders of the Opposition in both Houses and the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman. Powers: inquire into violations (on complaint or on its own), powers of a civil court for summons, visit jails, intervene in court cases, recommend compensation or prosecution. Limits: its recommendations are not binding; it cannot look at complaints older than one year; on the armed forces it can only seek a report from the government (Section 19). Justice V. Ramasubramanian became chairperson in December 2024. State Human Rights Commissions follow the same Act.
NHRC: record and criticism

Positive record: guidelines on custodial deaths (to be reported within 24 hours), encounter killings (inquiry procedure), bonded labour, and the Gujarat riots of 2002, where it moved the Supreme Court for transfers of cases. Criticisms: Critics often call it a "toothless tiger", since it can only recommend. Mostly retired judges and officers; few civil society members. Staff and investigators come from the police. The Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions (GANHRI) deferred its "A" status review in 2023 and 2024, citing issues of pluralism, independence and the role of police in investigations. Thinkers to cite: Upendra Baxi ( The Future of Human Rights , 2002) on the gap between the rhetoric and the "politics of suffering".
NCSC and NCST

Composition: chairperson, vice-chairperson and three members, appointed by the President. Duties (Articles 338, 338A): investigate safeguards, inquire into complaints, advise on development, and report to the President, who lays reports before Parliament with an action-taken memorandum. Powers: of a civil court in inquiries. The NCST also has duties on forest rights, displacement and the protection of tribal lands. Context: they monitor the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 and reservation. Problems: reports are often tabled years late, and many posts have stayed vacant for long periods. The commissions lack their own investigators. Debates: creamy layer and sub-classification after Davinder Singh (2024); Dalit Christians and Muslims' demand for SC status (examined by the K.G. Balakrishnan commission set up in 2022).
NCBC and the OBC question

The NCBC Act, 1993 created it after Indra Sawhney to advise on inclusion and exclusion in OBC lists. The 102nd Amendment (2018) repealed the Act and made it constitutional under Article 338B, with powers like the NCSC's to look into OBC grievances. Article 342A gave the President power to notify OBC lists. In Jaishri Patil (Maratha case, May 2021), the Court read this as taking away states' power to identify OBCs. The 105th Amendment (2021) restored the states' power to keep their own lists. The Rohini Commission (2017-2023) studied sub-categorisation of central OBC lists. Debates: which castes to include (Jats, Marathas, Patidars), creamy layer income limit (₹8 lakh since 2017), and the coming caste data from Census 2027.
NCW and NCM

National Commission for Women Set up in January 1992 under the NCW Act, 1990 . A chairperson and five members (at least one from SC/ST). Reviews safeguards for women, inquires into complaints, recommends changes in law. It has influenced laws on dowry, domestic violence (2005) and sexual harassment at work (POSH Act, 2013). Critics say it reacts selectively and is close to the ruling party. National Commission for Minorities Statutory under the NCM Act, 1992 . Six notified minorities: Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis and Jains (Jains added in 2014). Monitors safeguards and inquires into complaints. Grew out of the Minorities Commission of 1978. Critics point to vacancies and weak follow-up. The National Commission for Minority Educational Institutions (2004) deals with Article 30 rights. Related: the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (2005 Act, set up 2007).
Toothless or useful?

Why "toothless": Recommendations are advisory; government can ignore them. Appointments are made by the executive, often from ruling party circles. Delays, vacancies, and dependence on ministries for staff and money. Overlap: several commissions may handle the same complaint. Why still useful: They create public records, guidelines and pressure. They give victims a cheaper, quicker forum than courts. Parliamentary reporting forces some response. Reforms: binding powers on compensation, independent investigation teams, pluralist membership, fixed budgets, time limits on action-taken reports, and merging overlapping bodies. The Second ARC (2005-09) made similar points.
Recent context

Manipur (2023-26): commissions were criticised for slow responses to ethnic violence and sexual assault cases; the Supreme Court set up its own committee of former judges (August 2023). NHRC accreditation: GANHRI's deferrals (2023-24) became a reputational issue. Caste census: Census 2027 data will matter for NCBC and NCSC work. Waqf Act 2025 and minority rights claims before the NCM and courts. Custodial deaths and encounter cases continue to reach the NHRC.
How UPSC asks this

"National commissions are toothless tigers. Critically examine with reference to the NHRC." "Compare the constitutional and statutory status of the commissions for SCs, STs and backward classes." "Evaluate the role of the National Commission for Women." Structure: map of bodies and their legal basis; NHRC composition and powers with Paris Principles; record and limits; NCSC, NCST, NCBC with amendments (65th, 89th, 102nd, 105th); NCW, NCM; critique and reforms; recent cases; balanced conclusion.
Constitutional Provisions and Centre–State Relations
Federalism: the most-asked theme in Section B

Federalism is asked in Paper I almost every year. The usual question is a version of one puzzle: is India really federal? The Constitution never uses the word "federation". Article 1 says India, that is Bharat, is a Union of States . Yet it has two levels of government, a written constitution, a Supreme Court that settles disputes and a Seventh Schedule that divides powers. It also lets Parliament redraw state boundaries, lets the Centre dismiss a state government and gives the Centre the residuary power. So scholars have called it quasi-federal , federal with a unitary bias , or a system of bargaining between levels. This lesson covers the constitutional design: legislative, administrative and financial relations, and the commissions that reviewed them. The next two lessons cover regional demands and inter-state disputes.
Federal and unitary features side by side

The Constitution is not a copy of any one model. Ambedkar explained in the Constituent Assembly (4 November 1948) that it set up a dual polity , but that the Union was not the result of an agreement among states. So no state can secede. His phrase was that the Union is indestructible , while the units are not: Parliament can change their borders and names under Article 3 . The Court affirmed the same reading in Berubari Union (1960) and, more sharply, in State of West Bengal v. Union of India (1963), where it said states do not have sovereign status.
Four thinkers on the nature of Indian federalism

K.C. Wheare, Federal Government (1946) A strict federation needs co-ordinate, independent governments. By that test India is quasi-federal : a unitary state with subsidiary federal features. Granville Austin, The Indian Constitution (1966) India's founders built cooperative federalism . Units are not rivals. They are "agencies" for national goals, bound by shared administration and money. W.H. Morris-Jones Described Indian federalism as a bargaining system. Real outcomes come from negotiation between Centre and states, not from constitutional text alone. Rajni Kothari, Politics in India (1970) The dominance of the Congress "system" held the units together. When the party weakened after 1967, the federal side of the Constitution began to matter more. Ambedkar's own defence was practical: the Constitution can be "both unitary as well as federal" according to the times. In normal times it works federally, in emergencies it turns unitary.
Legislative relations: three lists and the Centre's reach

Articles 245-255 divide lawmaking. The Seventh Schedule has the Union List (98 entries), the State List (59) and the Concurrent List (52). The Centre holds residuary power (Article 248, Entry 97 of the Union List). That is the opposite of the United States, where residuary power lies with states. The 42nd Amendment (1976) moved five subjects to the Concurrent List: education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice. If a Union and a state law clash on a Concurrent subject, the Union law prevails ( Article 254 ), unless the state law got Presidential assent. Parliament can legislate on State List subjects in five cases: Article 249: Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds, in the national interest (valid one year, renewable). Article 250: while a Proclamation of Emergency is in force. Article 252: two or more state legislatures request it. Article 253: to implement treaties. Article 356: during President's Rule.
Administrative relations

Articles 256-263 and 355 shape the working partnership. States must use their power so that Union laws are obeyed ( Article 256 ) and must not block the Union's executive power ( Article 257 ). Article 355 makes it the Union's duty to protect states from external aggression and internal disturbance. All India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS) are created under Article 312 . Officers serve in states but are controlled by the Centre. Many see this as a bridge; others as a leash. The Governor is the key link. Appointed by the President ( Article 155 ), holding office during the President's pleasure ( Article 156 ), he acts on ministerial advice ( Article 163 ) except where the Constitution gives discretion. He can reserve bills for the President ( Article 200 ), and send reports that start President's Rule. Article 262 lets Parliament settle river water disputes. Article 263 creates the Inter-State Council , set up in 1990 on the Sarkaria Commission's advice. Zonal Councils are statutory, set up by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
Financial relations

Articles 268-293 split the money. States have most spending duties (health, police, agriculture) but the Centre has the best taxes. This gap is the vertical imbalance . It is closed through three channels: Tax devolution (Article 270): after the 80th Amendment (2000), the Finance Commission recommends the share of all Union taxes given to states. The 15th Commission gave 41%. The 16th, chaired by Arvind Panagariya, kept it at 41% for 2026-31, as reported at its tabling on 1 February 2026, though many states had asked for 50%. Grants-in-aid (Article 275, and 282 for discretionary grants). Borrowing (Article 293): states need Union consent when owing it money. Cesses and surcharges are not shared, which states complain about. The 101st Amendment (2016) brought GST : Article 246A gives both levels power to tax goods and services, and Article 279A creates the GST Council . The Centre has one-third of the votes and states two-thirds together; decisions need three-fourths. In Mohit Minerals (2022) the Supreme Court held the Council's recommendations are persuasive, not binding. In September 2025 the Council moved to two main rates, 5% and 18%, with 40% on a few luxury and sin goods.
The commissions that reviewed the design

Rajamannar Committee (appointed by Tamil Nadu in 1969): wanted Article 356 and the All India Services trimmed and a permanent Inter-State Council. Sarkaria Commission (1983, report 1988): did not seek big changes. It backed cooperative federalism, a strong Centre and a standing Inter-State Council. Use of Article 356 should be a "last resort". NCRWC (Venkatachaliah, 2002): suggested a stronger Inter-State Council and limits on Article 356. Punchhi Commission (2007, report 2010): Governors should have a fixed five-year tenure, with removal only through a resolution of the state legislature; consult the Chief Minister on appointment; allow localised use of emergency powers rather than dismissing a whole government.
Article 356, the Governor and the courts

Article 356 lets the President impose rule when a state's government cannot work according to the Constitution. It was used for political ends often, from Kerala in 1959 to the dismissals of 1977 and 1980. Landmark cases: State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977): courts can review only for mala fide or absent grounds. S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994, nine judges): the proclamation is judicially reviewable . Majority must be tested on the floor of the House, not by the Governor's opinion. Federalism and secularism are part of the basic structure . After Bommai, use of Article 356 fell sharply. Rameshwar Prasad (2006): dissolving the Bihar assembly in 2005 was unconstitutional. Nabam Rebia (2016): Governor cannot call the assembly on his own against the Speaker and the cabinet; Arunachal's earlier government was restored. In 2025, the Supreme Court in State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor (8 April) fixed time limits on Governors for bills. In November 2025, a five-judge bench answering a Presidential reference under Article 143 said courts cannot fix such deadlines or recognise "deemed assent", though prolonged inaction can still be questioned in limited ways.
Is India federal? Arguments on both sides

It is federal because: The Court polices the division of powers, and states have won cases, as in Bommai . Amendments touching federal provisions need ratification by half the states (Article 368(2)). Regional parties now shape national coalitions. Since 1989, the Centre has needed state-level partners. The Constitution has special arrangements for Northeast and Fifth/Sixth Schedule areas (asymmetric federalism). It is not fully federal because: States cannot protect their territory: Parliament can redraw them (Article 3). Telangana was carved out in 2014; Jammu and Kashmir was reduced to a Union Territory in 2019 and Ladakh separated. The Governor, Article 356, All India Services and Planning/Finance control keep states dependent. Delhi's elected government has been limited by the Centre's laws on services (2023). The Rajya Sabha represents states by population, not equally, unlike the US Senate. Fair conclusion: India is a flexible, union-centred federation . The text leans unitary; practice swings with party politics.
Federal flashpoints in 2023-2026

Governors and bills: Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Punjab and West Bengal complained of Governors holding bills. See Tamil Nadu v. Governor (April 2025) and the 2025 Presidential reference opinion. Delhi: Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018, and 11 May 2023) gave the elected government control of services. Parliament then passed the GNCTD (Amendment) Act, 2023, which created a National Capital Civil Service Authority and reversed this. GST and money: the 56th GST Council (3 September 2025) moved to two main slabs. States worry about revenue loss now that compensation has ended and about the 16th Finance Commission's 41%. One Nation, One Election: the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024 sits with a Joint Parliamentary Committee. Critics say it cuts into state assemblies' fixed terms. Delimitation: The seat freeze lasts until the first census after 2026 (Article 82 proviso). Southern states fear losing weight. The Lok Sabha defeated the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 on 17 April 2026, which would have expanded the House to 850 seats and allowed a quicker delimitation. Census 2027 is under way. Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025: a Concurrent List subject (Entry 10); the Supreme Court stayed some provisions in September 2025.
How UPSC asks this

"Is the Indian Constitution federal or unitary? Examine in the light of recent trends." (a staple in various forms) "Discuss the changing nature of Centre-State relations. Do Governors and Article 356 weaken federalism?" "Cooperative federalism is more a slogan than a reality in India." Comment. "Examine the role of GST Council and Finance Commission in fiscal federalism." Structure: Article 1 and Ambedkar's "Union of States"; federal vs unitary features; Wheare, Austin, Morris-Jones; legislative, administrative and financial relations; commissions (Sarkaria, Punchhi); Bommai ; recent cases and GST. Conclude with a balanced verdict: flexible, bargaining federation, tilting with party politics.
Integration and Regional Aspirations
A country many said would break up

In 1947, India had two problems at once: a Partition that killed lakhs and displaced millions, and over 560 princely states that could join India, join Pakistan or stand alone. Many outsiders expected the country to fragment. Selig Harrison wrote India: The Most Dangerous Decades (1960) predicting exactly that. It did not happen. India today has 28 states and 8 Union Territories (2020 count after Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu merged). Why did a diverse country hold together while still facing repeated demands for new states, autonomy or independence? The answer lies in how it integrated the princely states, drew its internal borders, and made room for regional identity in the Constitution. This lesson asks you to explain both the successes and the failures. Examiners like the question "How has Indian federalism accommodated regional aspirations?"
Integrating the princely states

The British paramountcy lapsed on 15 August 1947. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel , with his secretary V.P. Menon , led the States Department. Their tools were: The Instrument of Accession : states handed over defence, external affairs and communications. Persuasion and the fear of popular movements within the states. Later merger and integration : small states merged into provinces or formed unions (such as PEPSU or Rajasthan); larger ones such as Mysore and Hyderabad became Part B states under the 1950 Constitution. Generous privy purses in return, which Indira Gandhi's government ended through the 26th Amendment (1971) after the Supreme Court had struck down her derecognition order in 1970. Three cases were hard. Junagadh : its Nawab acceded to Pakistan; a plebiscite in February 1948 favoured India. Hyderabad : the Nizam refused, then the army moved in during Operation Polo (September 1948). Jammu and Kashmir : Maharaja Hari Singh signed accession on 26 October 1947 during the tribal invasion. See V.P. Menon's The Story of the Integration of the Indian States (1956).
Other territories joined later

Pondicherry: French rule ended in 1954; added to the Constitution by the 14th Amendment (1962). Goa, Daman and Diu: liberated from Portugal in December 1961 (Operation Vijay). Goa became a state in 1987. Sikkim: a protectorate; merged in 1975 through the 36th Amendment as a full state. Northeast: hill peoples were never fully ruled by princes. The Sixth Schedule covered them from the start. The Constitution lets Parliament admit or form new states by Articles 2 and 3 . In Article 3 the state legislature is only consulted ; Parliament decides. This is why Telangana (2014) and J&K (2019) could be created without state consent.
Linguistic reorganisation: from fear to acceptance

The Congress had promised linguistic provinces since the 1920s. After Partition, leaders feared a second break-up. The Dar Commission (1948) and the JVP Committee (Nehru, Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya, 1949) advised against language as the basis. The mood changed after Potti Sriramulu died on 15 December 1952 after a fast for a Telugu state. Andhra was formed on 1 October 1953. The States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali, K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru, report 1955) accepted language as a main basis, but stressed unity and the needs of finance and defence. The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 made 14 states and 6 Union Territories.
How states multiplied after 1956

1960: Bombay state split into Maharashtra and Gujarat after the Samyukta Maharashtra movement. 1963: Nagaland. 1966: Punjab split into Punjab and Haryana (Punjabi-speaking state demand by Akali Dal; Shah Commission). Himachal got statehood in 1971. 1972: Meghalaya, Manipur and Tripura became states (North-Eastern Areas Reorganisation Act). 1987: Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa. 2000: Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand, carved out peacefully on grounds of governance and tribal identity, not language. 2014: Telangana , the 29th state, under the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014. 2019: The J&K Reorganisation Act turned the state into two Union Territories: J&K (with a legislature) and Ladakh (without). Today, language is no longer treated as dangerous. Many scholars say that giving language its place strengthened the Union.
Thinkers on India's diversity and unity

Selig Harrison, The Most Dangerous Decades (1960) Predicted that language and regional loyalties would break India apart. History proved him wrong. Paul Brass, Language, Religion and Politics in North India (1974); The Politics of India since Independence (1990) Ethnic and linguistic groups are not natural. Elites build identity and use it to win resources. This is the instrumentalist view. Myron Weiner, Sons of the Soil (1978) Migration and job competition produce nativist movements, as seen in Assam and Maharashtra. Stepan, Linz and Yadav, Crafting State-Nations (2011) India is a state-nation , not a nation-state: it respects many cultural identities and builds loyalty to the state through democracy, federal accommodation and multiple languages. Unlike France, it did not force a single identity. Atul Kohli, Democracy and Discontent (1990) Argued India faced a "crisis of governability" as institutions weakened and demands rose.
Patterns of regional demand

Not every regional demand is the same. Sort them into four types: Secession or sovereignty: Naga National Council under A.Z. Phizo; Mizo National Front under Laldenga (1966); Khalistan militancy; Kashmir insurgency (from 1989). The DMK's early call for a Dravida Nadu led to the 16th Amendment (1963) , which allows restrictions on speech and requires an oath to uphold sovereignty and integrity. Statehood within the Union: Telangana, Vidarbha, Gorkhaland, Bodoland, Harit Pradesh. Autonomy and language rights: anti-Hindi agitation in Tamil Nadu (1965), Anandpur Sahib Resolution (1973), West Bengal and Tamil Nadu demands for more power. Nativism or "sons of the soil": Assam Movement (1979-85), Shiv Sena in its early phase. India used accords with the main insurgent groups to bring them into democratic politics: the Punjab Accord (Rajiv-Longowal, July 1985), Assam Accord (August 1985), Mizo Accord (1986, Mizoram statehood in 1987).
Constitutional tools of accommodation

Fifth and Sixth Schedules (Article 244) for tribal areas. The Sixth Schedule gives Autonomous District Councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Special provisions, Articles 371 to 371J: Nagaland (371A, 13th Amendment 1962: Parliament cannot override Naga customary law without Assembly consent), Assam (371B), Manipur (371C), Andhra and Telangana (371D, 371E), Sikkim (371F), Mizoram (371G), Arunachal (371H), Goa (371I) and Hyderabad-Karnataka (371J, 98th Amendment 2012). Eighth Schedule: 22 languages. The 92nd Amendment (2003) added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali. Article 370 gave J&K special status until it was revoked on 5 August 2019. Autonomous councils by accord: Bodoland Territorial Council (2003, revised accord January 2020), Gorkhaland Territorial Administration (2012). This is asymmetric federalism : different units hold different powers.
Success story or fragile peace?

The success view (Stepan, Linz, Yadav; Ashutosh Varshney in Battles Half Won , 2013): democracy, flexible borders and language recognition tied peripheries to the centre. Most separatist movements ended in accords, not partition. The critical view: Accords are not always carried out. Naga talks (Framework Agreement 2015) remain unresolved. AFSPA and long militarisation in the Northeast and J&K have hurt rights and trust. New states create new minorities within, such as Gorkhas in Bengal or Kuki-Zo groups in Manipur. Unequal development fuels demands (Vidarbha, Bundelkhand). The Centre sometimes ignores regional voices: the 2019 J&K change was made without a state assembly. A balanced answer says India has been good at accommodation but weaker at resolution .
Live cases to cite

J&K and Ladakh: the Constitution Bench in In re: Article 370 (11 December 2023, CJI Chandrachud) upheld the revocation, accepted that J&K had no internal sovereignty, and asked for statehood to be restored "at the earliest". Assembly elections were held in 2024 and Omar Abdullah became Chief Minister. As of late 2026, statehood had not been restored. The J&K Assembly passed a resolution demanding it in September 2026. Ladakh saw protests in September 2025 for statehood and Sixth Schedule status. Manipur: Meitei-Kuki violence began in May 2023. President's Rule ran from 13 February 2025 and was revoked on 4 February 2026, when Yumnam Khemchand Singh took office as Chief Minister. Language: disputes over the three-language policy in NEP 2020 and over Hindi in states like Tamil Nadu and Maharashtra. Delimitation: southern states fear that a post-Census 2027 seat adjustment could reduce their weight in Lok Sabha. Bodo and Karbi accords (2020, 2021) show the accord route continues.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the factors that contributed to the linguistic reorganisation of states. Has it strengthened or weakened national unity?" "Regional aspirations are an integral part of Indian federalism." Examine. "Critically assess the demand for smaller states." "Trace the integration of the princely states and role of Patel." Structure: start from 1947 fears (Harrison); princely states; Dar/JVP to SRC and the 1956 Act; later states; types of demands; constitutional accommodation (Schedules, Article 371, accords); Stepan-Linz-Yadav's state-nation; critique (AFSPA, Manipur, Ladakh); a balanced conclusion.
Inter-State Disputes
When two states claim the same river

Inter-state disputes test whether federalism is a partnership or a tug of war. Water is the oldest and hardest issue. The rivers cross state lines, but water is a State List subject (Entry 17), while inter-state rivers fall under the Union List (Entry 56). Disputes also arise over borders, capitals, sharing of power projects and migration. Examiners ask three kinds of question: the legal machinery, the main cases (Cauvery, Krishna, Ravi-Beas) and whether the system works. Remember the core tension. A state sees its river water as a matter of life and votes. The Union has to act as neutral referee. When parties see the Union as partisan, trust falls. Mind map of this lesson Water: Art. 262 and the 1956 Act. Courts: Art. 131. Talk: Art. 263 and Zonal Councils. Borders: Belagavi and Northeast. Fix: commissions and the 2019 Bill.
Four constitutional doors for dispute resolution

Article 262: Parliament may by law provide for settling disputes over inter-state rivers and may bar courts from hearing them. Parliament used this in the Inter-State Water Disputes Act, 1956 and the River Boards Act, 1956 (never used). Article 131: the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction in disputes between the Union and states, or between states. A proviso keeps out disputes arising from certain pre-Constitution treaties and agreements. Article 263: the President can set up an Inter-State Council to inquire into disputes and advise. It was created in 1990 after the Sarkaria Commission. Zonal Councils (States Reorganisation Act, 1956): five zones, chaired by the Union Home Minister. Their talk can settle border and power-sharing issues. The North Eastern Council (1971) serves the Northeast. Other tools: Article 307 (an inter-state trade commission, never created) and Articles 301 to 304 on free trade within the country.
How the water tribunal route works

The 1956 Act says: the Centre first tries negotiation. If that fails, it can set up a tribunal . The 2002 amendment set a three-year target (extendable by two years) and made the award as binding as a Supreme Court order. Article 262 bars courts from hearing the dispute, yet the Supreme Court has still heard challenges as special leave petitions (Article 136), and in Cauvery (2018) it modified the award.
Cauvery: the longest-running water dispute

The conflict goes back to treaties of 1892 and 1924 between Madras Presidency and Mysore. After independence, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu disagreed. 1990: Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal formed. An interim order in 1991 led to riots in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. 1991-93: Karnataka's ordinance against the order was held void in In re: Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal (1993), a reference under Article 143. 2007: Tribunal's final award; Kerala and Puducherry also got shares. 16 February 2018: the Supreme Court reduced Tamil Nadu's share, raised Karnataka's by 14.75 TMC to 284.75 TMC, and declared the river a national asset . It also ordered a Cauvery Water Management Authority (set up June 2018). Distress years, when the monsoon fails, remain the flashpoint. Karnataka's Mekedatu reservoir plan is another trigger.
Krishna, Ravi-Beas, Narmada, Mahadayi, Mullaperiyar

Krishna: KWDT-I (Bachawat, 1976) and KWDT-II (Brijesh Kumar, 2010, further report 2013) among Maharashtra, Karnataka and undivided Andhra. After Telangana's creation (2014), Andhra and Telangana quarrel over sharing; the Centre referred it to the existing Tribunal. Ravi-Beas: 1981 agreement among Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan; Eradi Tribunal 1986. Punjab passed the Termination of Agreements Act, 2004 . A Presidential reference (Article 143) led the Supreme Court in 2016 to find it invalid. The SYL canal remains unfinished. In 2025 Punjab and Haryana again clashed over Bhakra water releases. Narmada: tribunal award of 1979 across Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Rajasthan. The Narmada Bachao Andolan opposed Sardar Sarovar on displacement grounds. Mahadayi: Goa, Karnataka and Maharashtra; tribunal award 2018. Mullaperiyar: Kerala and Tamil Nadu over a 1886 lease; Supreme Court allowed 142 ft storage in 2014.
Boundary and other disputes

Belagavi: Maharashtra claims this Karnataka district. The Mahajan Commission (1966) favoured Karnataka's hold. Maharashtra rejected it. Chandigarh and Punjab-Haryana: shared capital since 1966. The Rajiv-Longowal Accord (1985) promised transfer to Punjab, still unmet. Assam's borders with Nagaland, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Arunachal. The worst clash was Assam-Mizoram on 26 July 2021, when six Assam police personnel died. Assam and Meghalaya signed a deal on 29 March 2022 to settle six of twelve disputed areas, and Assam and Arunachal reached an agreement in 2023. Ladakh, Telangana, Andhra: division of assets after bifurcation (Schedules 9 and 10 of the 2014 Act). The Centre has no clear tool to redraw borders by agreement; Article 3 gives power to Parliament, but political consent is needed.
Reform ideas and thinkers

Sarkaria Commission (1988) Wanted a standing Inter-State Council under Article 263 and early consultation, so conflicts need not reach the courts. Punchhi Commission (2010) Urged that Zonal Councils and the Inter-State Council be used more actively and that disputes be settled faster. Ramaswamy R. Iyer, Water: Perspectives, Issues, Concerns (2003) Argued that water should be treated as a shared resource and that basin-wide negotiation is better than quarrel over shares. Inter-State River Water Disputes (Amendment) Bill, 2019 Proposed a permanent tribunal with several benches and a dispute resolution committee to try negotiation first. The Lok Sabha passed it in 2019, but the Rajya Sabha did not, so it lapsed with the 17th Lok Sabha. I could not confirm a fresh bill since then.
Why the system struggles

Delays: Cauvery took 17 years in the tribunal and 11 more to a final Supreme Court ruling. Compliance: states defy orders when public anger is high, as Karnataka did in 1991 and Punjab in 2004. Politics: the Centre acts as a party when the same party or alliance rules different states. Opposition states call it biased. Legal gaps: Article 262 is awkward since the Court still gets involved. A single permanent tribunal might solve this but also centralises power. Climate and data: unreliable water data and climate stress make "equitable apportionment" harder. A cooperative answer: a technical basin authority, real-time data and compensation for the losing state, instead of one-time awards.
Current examples to use

Cauvery in lean years: disputes returned in September 2023 when Karnataka was short of rain and the CWMA ordered releases. Krishna: the Centre referred a Telangana-Andhra reallocation request to KWDT-II in October 2023. Punjab-Haryana water (2025) and the Bhakra Beas Management Board. Indus Waters Treaty: India put it "in abeyance" after the Pahalgam attack on 22 April 2025. This is an international dispute, but it shows the same principle: a river is shared. Northeast borders: Assam-Meghalaya, Assam-Arunachal agreements show talk can work. Federal ties: the Supreme Court's 2025 rulings on Governors and the GST Council show the broader theme of Centre-state trust.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine the constitutional and institutional framework for resolving inter-state river water disputes." "Inter-state water disputes threaten cooperative federalism. Suggest reforms." "Discuss the role of the Inter-State Council and Zonal Councils." "Comment on the Cauvery dispute and the 2018 Supreme Court verdict." Structure: define the issue (State List vs Union List); Articles 262, 131, 263 and the 1956 Act; Cauvery, Krishna and Ravi-Beas as examples; limits of the system (delay, defiance, politics); Sarkaria and Punchhi suggestions; permanent tribunal; end with basin-level cooperation.
Nehruvian and Gandhian Perspectives
Two visions of how India should develop

At independence India was poor, mostly rural and dependent on imports of machinery. Leaders agreed on ending poverty but disagreed on how. Two broad answers competed. Nehru's answer: planned, state-led industrialisation, with heavy industry and science, inside a democratic framework. Gandhi's answer: village self-reliance, small-scale production, limited wants and moral economy. The Nehruvian model won in policy, but Gandhian ideas survived in the Directive Principles (Articles 40, 43, 47, 48), in khadi and village industries, and in later debates on sustainability. UPSC asks you to compare the two, to judge the planning era, and to explain why planning gave way to the market after 1991.
Gandhi's economic thought

Hind Swaraj (1909): modern industrial civilisation multiplies wants and destroys moral life. Machinery should serve people, not replace them. Swadeshi and khadi: local production and self-reliance; the charkha as a symbol of dignity and employment. Trusteeship: the rich should hold wealth as trustees for society, a non-violent alternative to both capitalism and class war. Sarvodaya (welfare of all), from his reading of Ruskin's Unto This Last . Village republics and decentralisation. J.C. Kumarappa, Economy of Permanence (1945) Gandhi's economist argued for an economy that lives within nature's limits. Shriman Narayan Agarwal's Gandhian Plan (1944) put these ideas into a plan: cottage industry, agriculture first and village self-sufficiency. Later echoes: E.F. Schumacher's Small is Beautiful (1973) and today's environmental critiques of growth.
Nehru's vision

Influenced by Fabian socialism and Soviet planning, but committed to parliamentary democracy and civil liberties. Mixed economy: a public sector in the "commanding heights" (steel, power, heavy machinery) alongside private enterprise. Socialistic pattern of society: adopted at the Avadi session of the Congress (1955). Science and technology: IITs, atomic energy, and dams which Nehru called the "temples of modern India" (Bhakra Nangal, 1954). Self-reliance: import substitution and building domestic capacity. Nehru disagreed openly with Gandhi in their 1945 letters: he thought village India could not escape poverty without industry and modern science, while Gandhi held to Hind Swaraj .
The planning machinery

Pre-1947 plans: the Bombay Plan (1944, industrialists), the Gandhian Plan (1944), the People's Plan (M.N. Roy, 1944) and the Sarvodaya Plan (J.P. Narayan, 1950). Planning Commission set up on 15 March 1950 by a Cabinet resolution, with the PM as chair. It was extra-constitutional. The National Development Council (1952) brought in Chief Ministers. Industrial Policy Resolutions of 1948 and 1956: reserved key sectors for the State. First Plan (1951-56): agriculture. Second Plan (1956-61): the Mahalanobis model , with priority to heavy industry. Twelve Five-Year Plans in all (1951-2017). The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015.
Assessing the Nehruvian model

Achievements: an industrial base, public institutions (IITs, ISRO's forerunners), dams and power, a democratic framework and modest but steady growth after colonial stagnation. Failures: Growth of about 3.5% a year from 1950 to 1980, which Raj Krishna called the " Hindu rate of growth ". Neglect of agriculture and primary education; mass poverty persisted. A "licence-permit raj" (a phrase linked to C. Rajagopalachari, who founded the pro-market Swatantra Party in 1959). Inefficient public enterprises and rent-seeking. Key critics and analysts Jagdish Bhagwati and Padma Desai , India: Planning for Industrialization (1970): controls choked efficiency. Sukhamoy Chakravarty , Development Planning: The Indian Experience (1987): a balanced insider view. Francine Frankel , India's Political Economy, 1947-1977 (1978): planners wanted radical aims but avoided conflict with landed elites.
Political economy explanations

Pranab Bardhan, The Political Economy of Development in India (1984) Three dominant proprietary classes (industrial capitalists, rich farmers and professionals including bureaucrats) competed for subsidies. The State became a broker of their claims, leaving little for investment. Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph, In Pursuit of Lakshmi (1987) India had a "weak-strong state". They distinguished command polity (state-led, as in the Nehru and Indira years) from demand polity (where voters and groups press the State). They also spoke of " bullock capitalists ": middle farmers who became a political force. Atul Kohli, State-Directed Development (2004) Compared India with Korea and Brazil; India's state was "fragmented-multiclass", not focused enough to drive fast growth.
Was Gandhi's path ever practical?

For the Gandhian view: it protected employment and the environment; it fits ideas of sustainable development and decentralisation; it valued dignity and limited wants. Kumarappa's "economy of permanence" anticipated ecological economics. Against: with a large and growing population, village industry alone could not create enough jobs or defence capacity. Ambedkar rejected village romanticism, and Nehru thought it would lock India in poverty. Middle ground: Gandhian influence lasted in the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (1957), small-scale reservation (until it was phased out in the 2000s), the panchayats (73rd Amendment), MGNREGA's local works, and today's support for MSMEs and the "vocal for local" call.
Gandhian and Nehruvian models
This is the quickest way to frame the comparison question. Note that India's actual path was a mix, with Gandhian ideas surviving in the Directive Principles and in panchayati raj.
Planning today

NITI Aayog (2015): a think tank, not an allocator of funds. Its Governing Council includes all Chief Ministers; it prepares indices (SDG India Index, Export Preparedness) and the "Viksit Bharat 2047" vision. The end of Five-Year Plans in 2017; the Finance Commission and ministries now handle transfers. Atmanirbhar Bharat (2020) and production-linked incentives revive the language of self-reliance, but through private industry rather than the public sector. Gandhian echoes : natural farming, millets, khadi sales and climate-sensitive growth. Debate: some states and economists argue for a body like the old NDC to make planning more federal.
How UPSC asks this

"Compare the Gandhian and Nehruvian models of development." "Critically evaluate the planning era in India." "Explain Bardhan's thesis of dominant proprietary classes." "Is NITI Aayog a better institution than the Planning Commission?" Structure: context of 1947; Gandhi (Hind Swaraj, trusteeship, Kumarappa); Nehru (mixed economy, Mahalanobis, Avadi); planning machinery; achievements and failures; political-economy explanations (Bardhan, Rudolphs, Frankel); legacy today (NITI Aayog, Atmanirbhar).
Green Revolution and Land Reforms
Land and food: the base of rural politics

In 1950, about 70% of Indians worked on land, much of it owned by zamindars and cultivated by tenants and landless labourers. Two policies tried to change this: land reforms (redistribute rights) and the Green Revolution (raise output with technology). The first was about equity , the second about productivity . Both reshaped rural politics: they created a class of owner-farmers who became a political force, and left landless Dalits largely behind. UPSC asks: Why did land reforms have limited success? What were the political consequences of the Green Revolution? How do these explain today's farm protests?
Four stages of land reform

Abolition of intermediaries (zamindari): done in most states in the 1950s. The First Amendment (1951) added Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule to shield these laws from court challenge. Tenancy reform: security of tenure, fair rent, and ownership for tenants. Ceilings on landholding and redistribution of surplus land. National guidelines came in 1972. Consolidation of fragmented holdings, most successful in Punjab, Haryana and western UP. Land is a State List subject, so results varied widely by state.
Where reforms worked and why

Kerala: the 1957 Communist government began, and the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969 abolished tenancy, giving ownership to tenants from 1970. West Bengal: Operation Barga (from 1978) registered sharecroppers (bargadars) and secured their share. Jammu and Kashmir: the Big Landed Estates Abolition Act (1950) redistributed land without compensation under Sheikh Abdullah. Common factor: strong peasant movements and Left or reform-minded parties. Where they failed: in much of north India, landlords used benami transfers, fake partitions and court cases to evade ceilings. Officials and legislators often came from landed castes. Of land declared surplus, only a small fraction (a few million acres nationally) was ever distributed. Vinoba Bhave's Bhoodan (from 1951) collected pledges of land, but much of it was poor or never distributed.
Scholars on land reform

Francine Frankel, India's Political Economy (1978) The Congress depended on dominant rural castes to mobilise votes, so it could not push radical reform against them. Planners accommodated rather than confronted. Daniel Thorner, The Agrarian Prospect in India (1956) Showed how the reforms were weakened by loopholes and landlord resistance. P.S. Appu, Land Reforms in India (1996) A former official's account of the gap between law and implementation. Atul Kohli, The State and Poverty in India (1987) Explained West Bengal's success by a disciplined, left-of-centre party with an organised rural base.
The Green Revolution

After droughts in 1965-66 and dependence on US wheat under PL-480, the government under Agriculture Minister C. Subramaniam adopted a new strategy. Scientist M.S. Swaminathan brought in high-yielding wheat developed by Norman Borlaug in Mexico. Institutions: the Food Corporation of India and the Agricultural Prices Commission (both 1965; the latter now CACP) for minimum support prices and procurement. Results: wheat output more than doubled within a few years, and India became self-sufficient in food grains by the 1970s.
Political consequences

Rise of a farmer class: middle peasants (Jats, Yadavs, Kurmis, Patidars) gained wealth. The Rudolphs called them " bullock capitalists ". They became politically assertive. Charan Singh built the Bharatiya Kranti Dal (1967-69) on this base and became PM in 1979. Farmers' movements of the 1980s (Sharad Joshi, Mahendra Singh Tikait) demanded higher prices and cheaper inputs, the "India vs Bharat" argument. Regional inequality: gains concentrated in irrigated north-west regions. Class and caste conflict: landless labourers, often Dalits, gained less. Violence such as the Kilvenmani massacre (Tamil Nadu, 1968) was linked to wage disputes. The Punjab crisis of the 1980s has been linked in part to Green Revolution tensions. Francine Frankel , India's Green Revolution: Economic Gains and Political Costs (1971), predicted these social tensions.
Ecological and social critiques

Vandana Shiva , The Violence of the Green Revolution (1991): monoculture, chemicals and water use destroyed ecology and fed conflict in Punjab. Groundwater: free power and paddy cultivation have drained aquifers in Punjab and Haryana. Debt and distress: rising input costs and price risk; farmer suicides became a policy issue from the late 1990s. Nutrition: a focus on wheat and rice displaced pulses and millets. Defence: it ended famine fears, lowered food prices for the poor, and gave India strategic independence. M.S. Swaminathan himself called for an "evergreen revolution" that is productive and sustainable.
From 1960s to the 2020s

Farm laws 2020 and repeal (November 2021): farmers in Punjab and Haryana, Green Revolution heartlands, feared the end of MSP-based procurement. MSP debate: the National Commission on Farmers (Swaminathan, 2004-06) suggested MSP at cost of production plus 50%. Demands for a legal guarantee continue. Bharat Ratna (2024) for M.S. Swaminathan and Charan Singh, both symbols of this history. Land: the Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013; digital land records (DILRMP) and SVAMITVA property cards; Bihar's Bandyopadhyay Land Reforms Commission (2008) report was largely shelved. Crop diversification and millets (UN International Year of Millets, 2023).
Land, caste and power today

Land ownership remains unequal. Agricultural census data show that small and marginal farmers (below 2 hectares) are over 85% of holdings but own under half the area. Dalits remain largely landless. This links to caste politics: dominant landowning castes (Jats, Marathas, Patidars) now demand OBC quotas as farming becomes less profitable. Land conflicts underlie tribal movements against mining and dams. Thinkers to connect: Ambedkar argued for state ownership of agricultural land in States and Minorities (1947), as collective farming would end landlessness. His proposal was not adopted.
How UPSC asks this

"Why did land reforms in India achieve only limited success?" "Discuss the political consequences of the Green Revolution." "Examine the rise of farmers' movements in India." Structure: context; four stages of land reform; successes (Kerala, West Bengal) and failures; scholars (Frankel, Thorner, Kohli); Green Revolution and its institutions; political impact (bullock capitalists, Charan Singh, farmer movements); ecological critique (Shiva); links to 2020-21 protests; conclusion.
Liberalisation and Economic Reforms
1991: the turn from plan to market

In mid-1991 India nearly defaulted on its foreign debt. Foreign exchange reserves had fallen to cover only a few weeks of imports. The government pledged gold abroad to raise funds. In this crisis, the new government of P.V. Narasimha Rao , with Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister, launched reforms. The reforms replaced the licence raj with a market-friendly economy. Growth rose, poverty fell, but inequality grew. Political science asks distinct questions: how did a democracy carry out reform without a mandate? Who gained and who lost? How did reforms change the State, parties and federalism? The UPSC regularly asks about the "politics of economic reforms".
What changed in 1991 and after

New Industrial Policy (24 July 1991): licensing ended for most industries; MRTP restrictions eased; public sector reserved list cut. Budget of 24 July 1991 : devaluation (earlier that month), tariff cuts, and the start of tax reform. Foreign investment: automatic approval in many sectors. Financial sector: the Narasimham Committee (1991) led banking reforms; SEBI got statutory powers (1992). India joined the WTO in 1995.
How democracy managed reform

Rob Jenkins, Democratic Politics and Economic Reform in India (1999) Reform by stealth : leaders presented changes as continuity, used federalism to push hard choices to states, and paid off losers. Democratic institutions helped, not hindered, reform. Ashutosh Varshney, "Mass Politics or Elite Politics?" (1999) Reforms that touch elites (trade, industry) passed easily; reforms touching mass politics (labour laws, farm subsidies, power tariffs) were hard, since voters care about them. Atul Kohli, Poverty Amid Plenty in the New India (2012) The State moved to a pro-business alliance with big capital from the 1980s, before 1991. Growth came, but with weak job creation and inequality. Bhagwati and Panagariya vs Drèze and Sen (2013) Why Growth Matters stresses growth to fund welfare; An Uncertain Glory stresses public investment in health and education.
Outcomes

Growth: average growth rose to about 6-7% a year from the 1990s to the 2010s. Poverty: fell sharply. By the Tendulkar method, poverty fell from about 37% (2004-05) to about 22% (2011-12). Services and IT boomed; a middle class grew. Inequality rose; manufacturing jobs lagged ("jobless growth"). Agriculture grew slowly; rural distress persisted. Regional gaps : western and southern states gained more than many northern and eastern ones. Political effects: states became competitors for investment; Chief Ministers' role in economic policy grew; coalitions limited big-bang reform; the welfare state expanded through rights-based laws (RTI, MGNREGA, RTE, NFSA) in 2005-13.
Reforms after 2014

Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016) . Demonetisation of ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes on 8 November 2016. GST from 1 July 2017 (101st Amendment), with GST Council. In September 2025, the Council simplified it to two main rates (5% and 18%) from 22 September 2025. Direct benefit transfer through the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan, Aadhaar, mobile). Production-linked incentives (2020) and Atmanirbhar Bharat . Corporate tax cut (2019). Farm laws (2020), repealed in 2021 after protests. Four labour codes , in force from 21 November 2025. Pattern: reforms with concentrated losers (farmers, unions) remained the hardest, confirming Varshney's mass-elite distinction.
Debates about liberalisation

Supporters: reforms raised growth, cut poverty, modernised industry, and integrated India with the world. Bhagwati and Panagariya argue growth is the main poverty-fighting tool. Critics: Left: crony capitalism, privatisation of public assets, weakening of labour rights. Kohli: pro-business, not pro-market; the State favours big firms. Drèze and Sen: neglect of health and education keeps India behind East Asia. Environmental critics: fast growth damaged forests and rivers. Federal concern: GST reduced states' fiscal autonomy. A balanced answer: reforms were necessary and successful in growth, but the social and institutional side (education, health, jobs, regulation) needed equal attention.
Liberalisation and Indian politics

Party convergence: all major parties accepted reforms in office, even if they opposed them in opposition. Yogendra Yadav and Suhas Palshikar noted a convergence on economic policy. Welfare politics: parties now compete through targeted schemes and cash transfers. Regulatory state: new regulators (SEBI, TRAI, CCI, electricity commissions) replaced direct control. Business and politics: election funding debates (electoral bonds, struck down in 2024). Federalism: states compete for investment; Finance Commission and GST Council become central forums.
Reform milestones
The first wave in 1991 opened industry and trade. Later reforms built the rules of the market: regulators, bankruptcy law and a national tax.
Points for current answers

India's share of the world economy and status among the largest economies; debate on whether growth creates enough jobs. GST 2.0 (September 2025) and compensation questions for states. Labour codes (November 2025) and union protests. 16th Finance Commission (2026-31). Viksit Bharat 2047 goals through NITI Aayog. Trade negotiations and tariffs in a protectionist world.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the politics of economic reforms in India since 1991." "Liberalisation has created a pro-business rather than pro-market state." Examine. "Assess the impact of economic reforms on Indian federalism." Structure: 1991 crisis; main measures; Jenkins, Varshney, Kohli; outcomes; later reforms (GST, IBC, labour codes); critiques; links to parties, welfare and federalism; balanced conclusion.
Caste in Indian Politics
Caste is central to Paper I Section B

Caste and politics is asked almost every year. The question is rarely "what is caste?" It is "how do caste and democracy shape each other?" Two slogans help. Rajni Kothari said: it is not casteism in politics but the politicisation of caste . Politicians use caste to organise votes, but in doing so they also change caste itself, as groups form associations, make alliances and demand shares of power. M.N. Srinivas (the dominant caste), the Rudolphs (caste associations), Kothari (politicisation) and Jaffrelot (the OBC rise) are the core names. Add the legal story: reservation, the Mandal Commission, Indra Sawhney (1992), the EWS quota (2019) and SC sub-classification (2024). The latest chapter is the decision to include caste in Census 2027.
Four scholars on caste and politics

M.N. Srinivas In Religion and Society among the Coorgs of South India (1952) he gave Sanskritisation : lower castes imitate the customs of upper castes to rise. In "The Dominant Caste in Rampura" (1959), and later essays, he defined the dominant caste : numerous, owning land and ritually respectable, such as Vokkaligas, Jats, Patidars and Yadavs. They dominate local politics. Rajni Kothari, Caste in Indian Politics (1970) Caste is a resource and a ladder in competitive politics. Politics draws caste into a secular role, so caste becomes more about interest than ritual rank. Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph, The Modernity of Tradition (1967) Caste associations make traditional loyalty a tool for democracy. They also described three modes of political mobilisation: vertical, horizontal and differential. Louis Dumont, Homo Hierarchicus (1966) Caste is a system of ritual hierarchy based on purity and pollution . Critics say his model ignores power and politics.
Ambedkar, Phule and the Dalit challenge

Jotirao Phule ( Gulamgiri , 1873) attacked Brahminical domination. Periyar E.V. Ramasamy led the Self-Respect Movement from 1925. B.R. Ambedkar is central. In Annihilation of Caste (1936), he argued that caste is not just division of labour but a division of labourers, and that it cannot be reformed without destroying the authority of the shastras. In Castes in India (1916) he called it an "enclosed class" shaped by endogamy. He demanded separate electorates; the Poona Pact (1932) with Gandhi gave reserved seats within general electorates instead. The Constitution abolished untouchability ( Article 17 ) and allowed reservation. After 1956, Ambedkar's followers built political groups, from the Republican Party of India to the Dalit Panthers (Maharashtra, 1972) and the BSP (1984, Kanshi Ram), which pushed bahujan unity.
Constitutional and legal framework

Article 15(4), 16(4): special provisions and reservation in jobs for backward classes. 15(5) (93rd Amendment, 2005): reservation in educational institutions, including private unaided ones. Article 17: untouchability abolished. Laws: Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955; SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 . Articles 330 and 332: reserved seats for SC and ST in the Lok Sabha and Assemblies; 243D, 243T: in local bodies. Article 335: claims of SC/ST in services consistent with administration efficiency. Article 340: commission on backward classes. 102nd Amendment (2018): National Commission for Backward Classes (NCBC) given constitutional status (Article 338B). Articles 341 and 342: President lists Scheduled Castes and Tribes. 103rd Amendment (2019): 10% reservation for the economically weaker sections (EWS) among those not covered by existing quotas (Articles 15(6), 16(6)).
The timeline of reservation

Kaka Kalelkar Commission (1953-55): first Backward Classes Commission; not acted upon. Mandal Commission (set up 1979 under B.P. Mandal; report 1980): OBCs about 52% of the population; recommended 27% reservation so the total stays under 50%. V.P. Singh announced implementation on 7 August 1990. This led to protests and the rise of OBC politics. Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (16 November 1992, nine judges): upheld 27% for OBCs; creamy layer excluded; 50% ceiling (with narrow exceptions); no reservation in promotion. Parliament overrode the last through the 77th Amendment (1995), adding Article 16(4A).
Phases of caste in electoral politics

Congress era: upper castes, Dalits and Muslims in a "catch-all" coalition. In Gujarat, Madhavsinh Solanki's KHAM strategy (1980s) combined Kshatriyas, Harijans, Adivasis and Muslims. Backward-caste upsurge (from 1967, strong after 1990): Lohia's socialist call for 60% preference for backward groups; Charan Singh's peasant base; Mandal brought SP, RJD, JD(U). Dalit assertion: BSP won power in Uttar Pradesh four times, with Mayawati as Chief Minister. Fragmentation and sub-castes: the BJP's "social engineering" courts non-dominant OBCs and non-Jatav Dalits; Nitish Kumar built a base of Most Backward and extremely backward groups. Welfare plus identity: parties now mix caste, religion and benefits. Jaffrelot called the rise of lower castes into power a "silent revolution". Critics say it has benefited dominant sub-castes more than the most disadvantaged.
Recent legal and political developments

EWS quota: upheld 3-2 in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (7 November 2022). Maratha quota: the Court struck down the 2018 law in Jaishri Patil (May 2021) for breaching the 50% cap. The 102nd Amendment was read to remove state power to list OBCs; the 105th Amendment (2021) restored it. Maharashtra passed a fresh 10% Maratha law in February 2024. Sub-classification: in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (1 August 2024), a seven-judge bench (6:1) overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004) and said states may sub-classify Scheduled Castes if based on data on inadequate representation. Some judges urged a creamy layer for SCs and STs; the Union Cabinet said it would not apply it. Bihar: the 2023 caste survey found OBCs and EBCs near 63% of the population; the state raised quotas to 65%, but the Patna High Court struck this down in June 2024. OBC sub-categorisation: the Rohini Commission (2017, report 2023). Caste in the census: the Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs approved this on 30 April 2025. Census 2027's population phase (February 2027) includes a caste question; the last full count was in 1931.
Is caste fading or hardening?

Caste is declining: Dipankar Gupta , in Interrogating Caste (2000), argued that hierarchy has weakened and caste today is "difference", not rank. Urbanisation, education and market jobs reduce ritual hierarchy. Caste is persisting or being reinvented: Atrocities continue (Khairlanji 2006, Una 2016, Hathras 2020). Marriage remains largely within caste; surveys show little inter-caste marriage. Nicholas Dirks, Castes of Mind (2001), argued colonial census and law hardened caste identities. The 2027 count may do so again. Class cuts across caste: a growing "creamy layer" benefits from quotas, and poor upper castes feel left out (the EWS argument). A strong answer says caste has changed from ritual rank to political and economic identity , but remains a resource and a source of exclusion.
Using present-day cases

Caste census: 30 April 2025 decision and the 2027 count could reshape reservation debates and constituency politics; opposition parties argue for removal of the 50% ceiling. State surveys: Bihar (2023), Karnataka and Telangana (2025) held their own surveys, which the Union argued should be done by census alone. Davinder Singh: the SC sub-quota debate in Punjab, Haryana and Telangana. Atrocities Act: after the Supreme Court diluted arrest rules in 2018, protests led Parliament to restore them by amendment (2018). Maratha, Patidar, Jat, Kapu groups: dominant castes seeking OBC status. Panchayats: reserved seats shape village politics.
How UPSC asks this

"Caste is both a source of exclusion and a resource for political mobilisation." Discuss. "Examine the impact of the Mandal Commission on Indian politics." "Has the reservation policy achieved its objectives? Examine the issues of creamy layer and sub-classification." "Explain Srinivas's Sanskritisation and the dominant caste." Structure: Kothari's "politicisation of caste"; scholars (Srinivas, Rudolphs, Dumont, Ambedkar, Jaffrelot); constitutional provisions; Mandal and Indra Sawhney ; EWS and Davinder Singh ; political phases (Congress, Mandal, BSP, BJP engineering); critique (Gupta vs Dirks); end with the 2027 census as the next turning point.
Religion and Ethnicity in Politics
Faith and identity in a plural democracy

India has every major religion and hundreds of ethnic and tribal groups. Its founders chose a secular state, yet religion has shaped politics since Partition. Questions come on secularism , communalism , minority rights and ethnic conflict. Keep three ideas apart: Secularism: the state's stance towards religion. Communalism: the belief that people of one religion share political interests opposed to those of others, and the politics based on it. Ethnicity: identity based on language, descent, tribe or region. Good answers combine theory (Bhargava, Bipan Chandra, Varshney), constitutional law (Articles 25-30, Bommai , Shah Bano , Ayodhya) and current cases (Waqf Act 2025, Places of Worship Act, UCC, Manipur).
Indian secularism: not a Western copy

The Constitution's Preamble has the word "secular" from the 42nd Amendment (1976) , but the idea is there from 1950. Articles 25-28: freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality and health; no tax for a religion; no religious instruction in state-funded schools. Articles 29-30: cultural and educational rights of minorities. Articles 15 and 16: no discrimination on religion. Article 44 (Directive Principle): a Uniform Civil Code. Rajeev Bhargava , in Secularism and its Critics (1998) and The Promise of India's Secular Democracy (2010), calls the Indian model principled distance : the state is neither hostile nor identical with religion. It may engage with religion to protect equality, as with temple entry for Dalits (Article 25(2)(b)) or reforms in personal law. In S.R. Bommai (1994) the Supreme Court held that secularism is part of the basic structure .
Debates about secularism

T.N. Madan, "Secularism in its Place" (1987) Secularism is a Western idea ill-suited to a deeply religious society, and it fails to bring peace. Ashis Nandy, "An Anti-secularist Manifesto" (1985) State secularism has worsened conflict. Better to draw on India's traditions of religious tolerance. Rajeev Bhargava Replies that Indian secularism is distinct, with its own values of equal respect, and allows state intervention in religion for reform. The Hindu-nationalist critique Calls Congress-style secularism "pseudo-secularism", saying it appeases minorities. The counter-charge is that this view treats the majority culture as the nation's culture.
Understanding communalism

Bipan Chandra , in Communalism in Modern India (1984), argued that communalism is a modern ideology, not an ancient hatred. It arose under colonialism through economic competition for jobs and power, and through the colonial state's policies of counting and separate electorates. He gave three stages: Liberal communalism: the belief in a distinct religious interest in cultural and social affairs. Moderate communalism: religious interests are political and separate from the nation's. Extreme communalism: other communities are enemies. Violence follows. Gyanendra Pandey , in The Construction of Communalism in Colonial North India (1990), argued that colonial writing helped to build the idea of fixed communal identities. The historical sequence: separate electorates (1909), the Lucknow Pact (1916), Hindu Mahasabha, Muslim League and RSS, Partition (1947).
Why riots happen, and why they do not

Ashutosh Varshney, Ethnic Conflict and Civic Life (2002) Compared Hindu-Muslim relations in six cities. Cities with associational ties across communities (business groups, unions, professional bodies) stayed peaceful; cities without them saw riots. Everyday contact helps, but organised bridges matter more. Paul Brass, Theft of an Idol (1997); The Production of Hindu-Muslim Violence (2003) Riots are produced by "institutionalised riot systems" of local politicians, police and activists. Steven Wilkinson, Votes and Violence (2004) Violence is less likely where state governments depend on minority votes and so must protect them.
Law, courts and the minority question

Shah Bano (1985): Muslim woman's right to maintenance under s.125 CrPC. The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 limited it. Seen as a case of political concession. Shayara Bano v. Union of India (22 August 2017): instant triple talaq held unconstitutional (3:2). Parliament criminalised it in the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019. Ayodhya ( M. Siddiq v. Mahant Suresh Das , 9 November 2019): unanimously, a Constitution Bench gave the disputed site to the deity (Ram Lalla) for a temple and directed five acres elsewhere for a mosque. Places of Worship (Special Provisions) Act, 1991: freezes the character of places of worship as on 15 August 1947 (except Ayodhya). Challenges are pending; in December 2024, the Supreme Court restrained courts from registering fresh suits or passing effective orders on surveys while it hears them. Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019: fast track for non-Muslim minorities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Pakistan. Rules were notified in March 2024.
Ethnicity, tribe and region

Tribal peoples (about 8.6% of the population in 2011) are protected by the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, the PESA Act (1996), and the Forest Rights Act (2006). Disputes arise over mines, dams and forest land, as in Niyamgiri (Odisha). Northeast: ethnicity underlies Naga, Mizo, Bodo, Karbi and Meitei-Kuki politics. See the lesson on regional aspirations. The May 2023 violence in Manipur displaced tens of thousands. Language groups: anti-Hindi movements, Eighth Schedule status, three-language debates. Sons of the soil: Myron Weiner's term for nativist movements (Assam, Mumbai). Donald Horowitz's Ethnic Groups in Conflict (1985) explains ethnic parties through group rivalry and competitive fear. Kanchan Chandra's view is that ethnic categories are chosen by parties and voters. Both help in analysing Indian cases.
Religion in electoral politics

Early phase: the Congress presented itself as secular, with Muslim, Dalit and upper-caste support. 1980s-90s: the Shah Bano case, the opening of the Babri lock (1986), the Ram Janmabhoomi movement, the demolition of the Babri Masjid on 6 December 1992 and riots. The Liberhan Commission (report 2009) investigated. Hindutva rise: V.D. Savarkar's Essentials of Hindutva (1923) is its text. Christophe Jaffrelot traces it in The Hindu Nationalist Movement in India (1996). In Modi's India (2021) he describes a drift to an "ethnic democracy" in which minorities have a lesser place. Minority representation: reports note that Muslims are about 14% of the population but only about two dozen of 543 Lok Sabha members after 2024. Sachar Committee (2006) found Muslims behind in education, jobs and credit; the Ranganath Misra Commission (2007) suggested quotas for minorities.
Majoritarianism, appeasement and the middle path

Critics of current practice say: State and party closeness to one religion, as in temple events, violates principled distance. Laws such as the CAA, anti-conversion laws and the cow-protection laws target minorities. A Uniform Civil Code may impose majority norms. Uttarakhand's 2025 law, the first by a state since Independence (Goa has a Portuguese-era civil code), was criticised and defended on these lines. Defenders say: The State must treat all alike, and personal laws that discriminate against women require reform (Shayara Bano). Past politics gave symbolic concessions to conservative leaders (Shah Bano) over real development for minorities (Sachar). Bhargava's answer: neither aggressive secularism nor majoritarian nationalism. The best test is equal citizenship and protection of the weak inside every community.
Latest developments for your answer

Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025: passed in April 2025. The Supreme Court on 15 September 2025 refused to stay the whole Act but put on hold some provisions, including the rule that only a person practising Islam for five years can create a waqf (until rules are framed) and the Collector's power to decide on government land claims. The case is still pending. Places of Worship Act: pending petitions on mosque surveys (Gyanvapi, Sambhal). Uttarakhand UCC (2025): the first such law since Independence; debate on a national UCC and the Law Commission's 2018 view that a UCC was neither necessary nor desirable at that stage. Manipur: Meitei-Kuki violence since May 2023; President's Rule from 13 February 2025 to 4 February 2026. SIR of electoral rolls and citizenship scrutiny in 2025-26, upheld by the Supreme Court in May 2026, raised fears for minority and migrant voters. Caste and religion in the 2027 Census.
How UPSC asks this

"Is Indian secularism a Western import? Discuss with reference to the Indian model." "Communalism is a modern phenomenon rooted in colonial policy." Examine.
