"Examine the role of religion in Indian politics since the 1980s." "Ethnic conflicts threaten national integration. Suggest remedies." Structure: define secularism, communalism, ethnicity; constitutional provisions; Bhargava's principled distance vs Madan and Nandy; Bipan Chandra's stages; Varshney, Brass and Wilkinson on riots; key cases (Bommai, Shah Bano, Shayara Bano, Ayodhya); ethnic flashpoints; recent issues (Waqf Act, UCC, Manipur); conclude with equal citizenship and civic engagement.
National and Regional Parties
India's party system keeps changing shape

The party system is a favourite in Paper I. It is asked as a question on trends : from Congress dominance to coalitions to the BJP's rise, and on regional parties . A party system is the pattern of competition among parties: how many matter, how strong they are and how they relate. Political scientists use it to describe stability and change. India is unusual. It has a first-past-the-post system, which Duverger said favours two parties. Yet it has had one dominant party, a multi-party coalition era and, since 2014, a new dominant party with strong regional rivals. This lesson gives you the phases, the key scholars and the facts on recognition of parties. The next lessons cover coalitions, pressure groups and voting behaviour.
Four phases of the party system

These phases follow the framework of Yogendra Yadav and Suhas Palshikar , who split the party system into stages: a Congress-dominant period; a period of challenge after 1967; a competitive multi-party period after 1989; and a new phase after 2014, which Palshikar called India's second dominant party system .
Kothari and Morris-Jones on the Congress system

Rajni Kothari, "The Congress System in India" (1964) In the 1950s and 60s the Congress was both government and a wide umbrella. It held within it many factions that bargained among themselves. Opposition parties were "parties of pressure" that influenced the Congress from outside. Competition took place within the dominant party. Congress was the "party of consensus"; the rest were "parties of pressure". W.H. Morris-Jones Described the system as one dominant party with several opposition parties of different kinds. Opposition's role was limited but real. Why Congress dominated: it led the freedom movement, had a national organisation, social coalitions of upper castes, Dalits and Muslims, and the first-past-the-post system, which converted 45% of votes into about 75% of seats. Why it broke: the 1967 election (Congress lost power in many states), the 1969 split, and later the Emergency (1975-77), after which the Janata Party won in 1977.
Duverger's law and the Indian puzzle

Maurice Duverger , in Political Parties (1951), said that a plurality (first-past-the-post) system tends to produce two parties. India has many more. Why? Pradeep Chhibber and Ken Kollman , in The Formation of National Party Systems (2004), argued that Duverger's effect works at the constituency and state level , where usually two or three parties compete. But the national system has many parties because the number of states with a strong regional party varies. As power moved to the states, parties became more regional. So the national picture is a collection of different state-level contests: Congress-BJP in Gujarat and Rajasthan, DMK-AIADMK in Tamil Nadu, BJP-SP in Uttar Pradesh, and so on. Other reasons for multi-party politics: caste and linguistic diversity, a federal structure, and the end of one party's national hold.
How the ECI recognises national and state parties

The Election Commission recognises parties under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 . It reviews them after each general election. Recognised parties get a reserved symbol, free airtime on public media and electoral roll copies. National party: (a) it wins 2% of Lok Sabha seats (11) from at least three states; or (b) it secures at least 6% of votes in four states and wins four Lok Sabha seats; or (c) it is recognised as a state party in four states. State party (some tests): 6% of votes in the state and two assembly seats; or 3% of seats or three seats, whichever is higher; or 8% of votes. On 10 April 2023, the ECI withdrew national status from the TMC, NCP and CPI and gave it to the AAP . The six national parties then were BJP, Congress, BSP, CPI(M), NPP and AAP. I found no report of a later change.
Why regional parties rose

Language and identity: the DMK (1949, C.N. Annadurai) and the Akali Dal (founded 1920). Regional pride: the Telugu Desam (1982, N.T. Rama Rao) and the Asom Gana Parishad (1985). Social justice and Mandal: the SP, RJD and BSP built on OBC and Dalit voters after 1989. Congress decline: the vacuum was filled by locals. After 1967, many states went to non-Congress parties. Splits from national parties: TMC (1998), NCP (1999), YSR Congress (2011), BJD (1997). Economic reforms and federal bargaining: after 1991, states competed for investment and regional parties dealt with the Centre. Regional parties became kingmakers in coalition governments from 1996 to 2014. In 2024, the TDP and JD(U) helped the NDA reach a majority.
Strengths and weaknesses of this pattern

Strengths: Regional parties give voice to local identities and make a diverse country feel represented. They keep the Centre accountable; the NDA and UPA both needed their consent. They push states' interests on finance, language and water. Criticisms: Personality and dynasty: Kanchan Chandra's Democratic Dynasties (2016) shows that where parties lack institutions, family succession becomes common. Oligarchy: Robert Michels's "iron law of oligarchy" in Political Parties (1911) applies, with little intra-party democracy. Pragmatic alliances weaken ideology; leaders switch sides. Regionalism can obstruct national policy, such as river or Centre-state fiscal talks. Money and criminalisation (see lesson on electoral behaviour).
The BJP era and the shape of competition

Scholars such as Suhas Palshikar note that BJP dominance after 2014 differs from Congress dominance. It rests on a strong organisation, a leader with a direct link to voters and a Hindutva-plus-welfare appeal, yet it faces strong rival parties in many states. It did not erase regional politics, and its dominance is uneven. Key moments: 2014: BJP won 282 seats, the first single-party majority since 1984. 2019: BJP 303. 2024: BJP 240 and NDA 293; Congress 99. The BJP fell short of 272 and relied on allies, so the coalition feature returned. Other trends: a rise in welfare politics (direct benefit transfer), and growth of " third force " parties that are neither Congress nor BJP in the states.
What the latest elections say

Lok Sabha 2024: BJP 240, Congress 99, SP 37, TMC 29, DMK 22, TDP 16, JD(U) 12. NDA 293 against the INDIA bloc's 234. Delhi 2025: BJP defeated the AAP, ending its decade in power. Bihar, November 2025: the NDA won 202 of 243 seats, with BJP 89 and JD(U) 85. The Mahagathbandhan was reduced to the mid-thirties. May 2026: reports show the BJP winning West Bengal for the first time, the Congress-led UDF returning in Kerala, and Vijay's new party TVK emerging as the largest party in Tamil Nadu (108 of 234 seats), with the DMK falling to 59. Check the final results and ministries before using exact seat numbers. Lesson for answers: the national picture is the sum of different state contests, and incumbency and welfare matter more than ever.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the changing nature of the Indian party system since Independence." "Do regional parties strengthen or weaken Indian federalism?" "Examine the Congress system and its decline." "Is India moving to a one-party dominant system again?" Structure: define party system; Kothari and Morris-Jones for the first phase; the 1967 shock; coalition era after 1989; Chhibber-Kollman on why Duverger fails nationally; 2014 and 2024 results; regional party roles and flaws; ECI recognition rules; balanced conclusion.
Coalition Politics
Coalitions: from crisis to a normal way to govern

No party won a Lok Sabha majority between 1989 and 2009. Governments were formed by coalitions , and states had them even earlier. The 2024 election returned the country to a coalition government at the Centre: the BJP won 240 seats, short of the 272 needed, and the NDA formed the government with allies such as the TDP and JD(U). A coalition is a government made of two or more parties that agree to share office and a programme. In parliamentary systems, it is born when no party has a majority. Examiners ask: are coalitions good or bad for India? Do they cause instability? How did the constitution and courts adapt? Your answer should combine theory, a timeline and constitutional rules.
A timeline of Union coalitions

Key points: the Janata Party was a merger, not a coalition. In 1989, V.P. Singh's National Front governed with the BJP and Left giving outside support. The 1996 Vajpayee government lasted 13 days. The 1998 NDA government lost a vote of confidence by one vote in April 1999 after the AIADMK withdrew support, but the 1999 NDA, with over twenty parties, completed a full term. UPA I (2004) lost Left support in 2008 over the Indo-US nuclear deal.
Theories of coalition formation

William Riker, The Theory of Political Coalitions (1962) The size principle : parties form coalitions just large enough to win, since extra partners only dilute rewards. Minimum winning coalitions are most likely. Robert Axelrod, Conflict of Interest (1970) Parties prefer partners close in ideology, forming minimal connected winning coalitions. Why India often breaks these rules Indian coalitions are often oversized (NDA 1999 with 24 parties) or minority governments (Rao 1991). Reasons: pre-poll alliances at constituency level, state-level interests, and the benefit of the winning alliance in first-past-the-post. E. Sridharan has argued that coalition politics is a product of India's parliamentary federalism, with state parties as key players. Another key notion: coalitions can be pre-poll (seat-sharing before the election, favoured under FPTP) or post-poll (formed after results). Outside support is when a party backs a government without joining it.
How coalitions run: programmes and managing partners

Common Minimum Programme: UPA's 2004 CMP; the NDA's National Agenda for Governance (1999). These set out what partners agree on and leave out contentious items such as Ayodhya (for the NDA). Coordination bodies: NDA's convener, UPA's chairperson and the National Advisory Council (2004-14) chaired by Sonia Gandhi. "Coalition dharma": Vajpayee's phrase for respecting allies' interests. Cabinet size: the 91st Amendment (2003) capped the Council of Ministers at 15% of the House (Article 75(1A)). It stopped jumbo cabinets built to please allies. Collective responsibility (Article 75(3)) is tested when ministers belong to different parties. Parties have sometimes treated it flexibly. Managing allies shaped policy: regional parties gained railway, agriculture or telecom ministries, and states won funds.
The law of defection and the Governor's role

Instability came from defection ("Aya Ram, Gaya Ram" in Haryana, 1967). The 52nd Amendment (1985) added the Tenth Schedule : a legislator is disqualified if he voluntarily gives up party membership or defies a whip on a vote. The 91st Amendment (2003) removed the exemption for splits, leaving only a two-thirds merger exemption. The Speaker decides. In Kihoto Hollohan (1992), the Supreme Court upheld the law and said the Speaker's decision is open to judicial review. In Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020), it asked Speakers to decide petitions within three months. In a hung House, who is invited? The Sarkaria Commission advised: first, the pre-poll alliance with a majority; then the largest party or group. S.R. Bommai (1994) says the floor of the House, not the Governor's view, tests the majority. In Subhash Desai (May 2023), on Maharashtra's 2022 crisis, the Court held that the Governor had no basis to call a floor test and that the Speaker's whip appointment was illegal, but did not restore the previous government since the Chief Minister had resigned.
Do coalitions help or harm?

Arguments for: They include many regions and social groups; policy needs wider consent. They force consultation and restrain dominance. Rao (1991-96) delivered the economic reforms from a minority; Vajpayee pursued disinvestment and the Golden Quadrilateral; UPA I introduced MGNREGA (2005), RTI (2005) and RTE (2009). Arguments against: Bargaining by small allies for portfolios, and the difficulty of acting against a partner's ministers. Critics linked UPA II's corruption scandals to this. Delay in decisions; 'policy paralysis' charges for the second UPA. Instability in 1989-99 (six Prime Ministers in ten years). Opportunism, horse-trading and defections at state level (resort politics). Verdict: the issue is less coalition itself than a weak party culture and the lack of binding programmes. India's stability from 1999 to 2014 shows coalitions can last.
Coalitions and federalism

Coalition politics changed Centre-state relations. Regional parties in the ruling alliance could bargain for their states, so the Centre could no longer ignore them. Use of Article 356 fell sharply after Bommai (1994) and the coalition era began. The United Front's Common Minimum Programme (1996) promised greater devolution of funds to states. States won more say in finance: the Finance Commission share of central taxes rose from 32% (13th FC) to 42% (14th FC) and settled at 41% (15th and 16th FC). The Inter-State Council was revived (1990) and later the GST Council (2016) made states partners in tax decisions. Scholars therefore link the coalition era to the rise of cooperative and bargaining federalism . With a single-party majority from 2014 to 2024, many saw a return to a stronger Centre, while in 2024 the dependence on allies returned.
Reform proposals: stability without losing representation

Constructive vote of no-confidence (as in Germany): a government can be removed only if the House simultaneously elects a new leader. The Law Commission's 170th Report (1999) and the NCRWC (2002) both recommended it. Fixed terms: proposals for fixed Lok Sabha terms, linked to the debate on simultaneous elections. Stricter defection law: taking decisions out of the Speaker's hands. The NCRWC and Election Commission suggested the President or Governor, on the Election Commission's advice, should decide disqualification. Pre-poll alliance rules: give the pre-poll alliance priority when forming a government. Party law: regulate internal democracy and funding. Opponents of reform argue that stability must not be bought by silencing smaller voices. Most commentators accept that coalitions are a feature of a plural society.
State coalitions and the 2024 case

Kerala: the LDF and UDF alternate; in 2026 the UDF returned. West Bengal: the Left Front ruled for 34 years (1977-2011) with the CPI(M) dominating partners. Bihar: the NDA's 2025 landslide shows the power of a well-managed pre-poll alliance. Maharashtra: the 2019 post-poll crisis, the Maha Vikas Aghadi, the 2022 Shiv Sena split and the 2024 Mahayuti win. Union, 2024: BJP 240 and NDA 293. The TDP (16) and JD(U) (12) hold key positions. The INDIA bloc, formed in 2023, won 234 but has found state-level seat-sharing difficult. Remember the lesson: when alliances are pre-poll and ideological, the government is stable; when they are post-poll and opportunistic, it is fragile.
How UPSC asks this

"Coalition governments have become a necessity in India. Discuss the merits and demerits." "Examine the impact of coalition politics on Indian federalism." "Assess the working of the anti-defection law." "What role does the Governor play when no party has a majority?" Structure: define; timeline 1977-2024; Riker's size principle and why India differs; working arrangements (CMP, 91st Amendment, collective responsibility); defection law and cases; Governor and floor test; pros and cons; 2024 case and balanced conclusion.
Pressure Groups
Power outside the ballot box

Elections give citizens a vote every five years. Pressure groups give them a voice every day. A pressure group is an organised body that tries to influence government policy without seeking to hold office itself. That is what separates it from a political party : a party contests elections and wants to form the government. Pressure groups, such as trade unions, business chambers, farmers' unions and caste associations, only want to shape decisions. In practice, the line is blurry. Many groups are linked to parties, and some groups become parties (the Dravidar Kazhagam gave rise to the DMK; Shetkari Sanghatana fought elections). Terms to separate: interest group (shares a common interest), pressure group (actively presses the government) and lobby (works directly on legislators and officials). The UPSC asks about types, methods, role and effects on democracy.
Theories: why groups matter

Arthur Bentley, The Process of Government (1908) Politics is the struggle of groups. Government is the arena where their pressures balance. David Truman, The Governmental Process (1951) Groups form to protect shared interests and make government responsive. Overlapping membership moderates conflict. Robert Dahl, Who Governs? (1961) Many groups compete in the New Haven case study. Power is spread out (pluralism). Mancur Olson, The Logic of Collective Action (1965) Large groups struggle to organise because of free riders . Small, concentrated groups, such as business, often organise better than broad groups, like consumers or the poor. C. Wright Mills, The Power Elite (1956) The elite in business, the military and politics dominate. This is the elitist reply to pluralism. Schmitter, "Still the Century of Corporatism?" (1974) In corporatism, the state recognises a few peak bodies and bargains with them.
Types of groups (Almond and Powell)

Gabriel Almond and G. Bingham Powell , in Comparative Politics: A Developmental Approach (1966), gave these four types of interest groups. In India, add issue-based or movement groups : Narmada Bachao Andolan, the Chipko movement, and campaigns for the Right to Information.
Who are the main Indian groups

Business: FICCI (1927), ASSOCHAM (1920), CII (its origin dates to 1895). They shape tax, tariff and licensing policy through pre-budget meetings and committees. Labour: AITUC (1920), INTUC (1947), HMS (1948), BMS (1955), CITU (1970). Most are tied to parties: INTUC to Congress, AITUC to CPI, CITU to CPI(M), BMS to the RSS family. Agrarian: All India Kisan Sabha (1936), the Bharatiya Kisan Union (Tikait), Shetkari Sanghatana (Sharad Joshi, Maharashtra). Professional: Indian Medical Association, Bar Councils, teachers' and bank employees' associations. Students: ABVP, NSUI, AISF, SFI. Student movements helped to start the Assam Movement and the 1974 Bihar movement. Caste and community: Kothari saw caste groups as channels of politics. The Rudolphs, in The Modernity of Tradition (1967), argued that caste associations adapted a traditional form to modern democracy. Civil society and NGOs: MKSS (Aruna Roy), NCPRI, ADR.
Methods and the right to protest

Lobbying legislators, ministers and officials; submissions to parliamentary committees; funding parties. Petitions and memoranda , delegations, media campaigns. Protest: dharna, rally, march, strike, hunger strike, chakka jam . Litigation: public interest litigation (PIL) since the late 1970s. Direct action: boycotts, road blockades. The legal base is Article 19(1)(a), (b) and (c) (speech, assembly, association), subject to reasonable restrictions under 19(2) to (4). The Supreme Court held in Communist Party of India v. Bharat Kumar (1998) that a forced bandh is not protected. In Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (2018) it recognised a right to protest at designated places, and in Amit Sahni (2020) on Shaheen Bagh it said public roads cannot be occupied indefinitely. India has no law regulating lobbying , unlike the United States. The 2010 Radia tapes controversy highlighted this gap.
Groups that changed law and policy

RTI Act, 2005: the MKSS campaign in Rajasthan in the 1990s and NCPRI pushed the law. Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013: the India Against Corruption campaign under Anna Hazare (2011) led to it. MGNREGA (2005): Right to Food and employment campaigners and the National Advisory Council. Three farm laws repealed: farmers, led by the Samyukta Kisan Morcha, camped at Delhi's borders from November 2020, and the government repealed the laws in November 2021. The demand for a legal guarantee of MSP continues. Four labour codes: effective from 21 November 2025, they merged 29 laws. Ten central trade unions protested on 26 November 2025. The BMS stayed out. Reservation demands: Patidar, Jat and Maratha agitations show caste groups pressing the state. Electoral bonds: petitions by the Association for Democratic Reforms led to the Supreme Court striking down the scheme on 15 February 2024.
Groups, parties and the state: three relationships

Group inside the party family: the union or student wing is an arm of a party (INTUC, BMS, ABVP, NSUI). The party gets a base; the group gets access. Risk: the group follows the party line even against its members' interests. Group that becomes a party: the Dravidar Kazhagam gave rise to the DMK; the Assam student union AASU gave rise to the Asom Gana Parishad (1985); Anna Hazare's movement led to the AAP (2012). Independent group: NGOs, professional bodies and chambers deal with all parties. They keep leverage but have less party backing. Rajni Kothari observed that Indian groups often work through party and caste networks , not through formal lobbies. That is why the line between a pressure group and a party is thin in India, unlike in the United States. Tip for the answer: show that a group's power depends on resources (money, numbers, organisation), access (to ministers and officials), public sympathy and the ability to disrupt.
Do pressure groups help or harm democracy?

Positives: They give voice to groups that parties ignore, and bring expert views into policy. They hold government accountable between elections. They broaden participation, making democracy deeper than voting. Negatives: Unequal access: business and the educated middle class are better organised than the landless or informal workers. Olson's logic shows why. Narrow interests can beat the public interest. The "crony capitalism" debate. Dependence on parties: many unions follow party lines, so they cannot act as independent checks. Violence and coercion: bandhs and blockades harm others' rights. Opacity: no disclosure of lobbying. Fair conclusion: pressure groups are needed in a plural democracy, but India needs transparency rules , internal democracy in groups and wider access for the poor.
How to use examples in your answer

Farmers 2020-21: an organised, long-lasting group won a repeal, but the demand for a legal MSP is still alive. Labour codes 2025: unions versus the Centre. The government says reform; unions say it weakens job security. The state/Union split matters because labour is a Concurrent List subject. Maratha quota agitations (2023-25) show how caste groups press state governments within and against the 50% ceiling. Business: CII and FICCI shape budget and GST rate talks. Civil society: ADR on candidate affidavits and funding; PUCL on rights. Digital: hashtag campaigns and online petitions now supplement dharnas.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the role of pressure groups in Indian politics. Are they effective?" "Distinguish between political parties and pressure groups with examples." "Examine how business and labour groups influence policy in India." "Should lobbying be regulated in India?" Structure: define and distinguish from parties; theories (Bentley, Truman, Olson, Mills); Almond-Powell types with Indian examples; methods and constitutional basis; cases of policy impact (RTI, farm laws, labour codes); critique (unequal access, no lobbying law); recommendations.
Electoral Behaviour and Legislators' Profile
Why does India vote the way it does?

Electoral behaviour asks what moves voters: caste, religion, class, leaders, performance, money or fear? It matters because India is the world's largest electorate, and because several myths about it are wrong. One myth is that Indians vote only by caste. Another is that they vote only on development. The real picture is mixed and changes over time and place. The second half of the topic is the profile of legislators : wealth, criminal cases, gender and education. Data from the Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) is quoted in many answers. UPSC asks about trends (turnout, identity, anti-incumbency), the criminalisation of politics, money in elections, and electoral reforms. Prepare each with scholars, data and cases.
Three schools and the Indian studies

Three classical models Columbia school (Lazarsfeld): social groups shape votes. Michigan school (Campbell et al., The American Voter , 1960): party identification. Rational choice (Anthony Downs, An Economic Theory of Democracy , 1957): voters weigh benefits and costs. Eldersveld and Ahmed, Citizens and Politics (1978) An early survey study of India. It found voting often followed local networks and caste leaders, but voters also knew issues. CSDS-Lokniti National Election Studies Surveys since 1996 (Yogendra Yadav, Suhas Palshikar, Sanjay Kumar) track voting by caste, class, gender and age after each general election. They are the base for most claims about Indian voters. Rajni Kothari argued that caste worked as a means of political mobilisation, not simply as a force of tradition.
What shapes the vote

Identity. Caste, community and region. Kanchan Chandra , in Why Ethnic Parties Succeed (2004), links this to the patronage democracy : where the state gives jobs and benefits, voters back leaders of their own group who will deliver. Welfare and performance. Voters judge schemes. A new voter group, the labharthi (beneficiary), has been noted in recent elections. Leaders and party. National elections have become more leader-focused. Local networks, money and mobilisation.
Big shifts in Indian voting

Mandalisation: Christophe Jaffrelot's India's Silent Revolution (2003) describes how lower castes and OBCs moved from voting to ruling, rising in the Hindi belt after the 1990 Mandal reservation. Rising turnout of the poor: Yadav called this the "second democratic upsurge" in the 1990s: the poor, lower castes and Muslims vote at least as much as the rich. Women: turnout has risen. In 2019 women voted at a slightly higher rate than men for the first time in a general election. Anti-incumbency was strong in the 1990s-2000s, then weakened as governments tied elections to welfare delivery. Turnout: about 67.4% in 2019 and about 66% in 2024. Ideology and identity: Hindutva politics and welfare combine; Congress and regional parties respond with social justice and caste-census claims. Local matters too: the 2024 mandate in Uttar Pradesh (SP 37 seats) showed voters can choose differently in Lok Sabha than expected.
Money in elections

Candidate spending far exceeds legal limits; parties have no spending cap in practice. Committees: Dinesh Goswami (1990) on electoral reforms; Indrajit Gupta (1998) on state funding of elections; Law Commission 170th Report (1999). Transparency by courts: in ADR v. Union of India (2002) and PUCL v. Union of India (2003) the Supreme Court made candidates disclose criminal cases, assets and education. Electoral bonds (2018 scheme) allowed anonymous donations. In ADR v. Union of India (15 February 2024) a five-judge bench struck them down as unconstitutional, holding that anonymity violates the voter's right to information. The SBI was told to disclose the buyers. Donations: parties still get funds from corporate donors through electoral trusts. Scholars ask: if funding is secret, are policy favours possible? The Court's answer is that voters need to know.
Criminalisation of politics

Milan Vaishnav , When Crime Pays: Money and Muscle in Indian Politics (2017), explains why voters elect candidates with criminal cases. Parties need money, so they pick wealthy candidates. Voters in areas with weak state institutions see such a candidate as strong enough to deliver, and as a protector of their community. That is why candidates with cases often win. The legal framework: Vohra Committee (1993) found a nexus of crime and politics. Representation of the People Act, 1951, s.8: disqualification on conviction. Lily Thomas (2013): conviction with two years or more disqualifies immediately; the automatic protection for sitting legislators was struck down. PUCL v. Union of India (2013): NOTA option introduced. Public Interest Foundation (2018): Parliament should take steps; parties must publish candidates' records. In 2020-21 the Court told parties to give reasons for choosing candidates with cases.
The profile of the 2024 Lok Sabha

Criminal cases: 251 of 543 winners (46%) declared cases, up from 43% in 2019 and 34% in 2014. Serious cases: 170 (31%). Wealth: 504 of 543 (93%) were crorepatis, compared with 88% in 2019. Women: 74 MPs, about 14%, similar to 2019. Chance of winning: ADR found about a 15% chance for candidates with declared cases, against about 4% for those with clean records. Source: ADR's analysis of the 2024 affidavits. The profile also includes age (most MPs are above 50) and education (a large majority are graduates), and a continuing under-representation of women and religious minorities. Women's reservation: the Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) reserves one-third of Lok Sabha and state assembly seats (including within SC/ST quotas) for women. It came into force on 16 April 2026, but the seats apply only after delimitation. The next day, the Lok Sabha defeated the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 (298 for, 230 against, short of the two-thirds needed), which would have enlarged the House and allowed quick delimitation. So the quota did not apply in 2024 and its start date is now uncertain.
The reform agenda

Disqualification of charged persons: Law Commission 170th Report and the Election Commission proposed barring candidates charged with serious offences by a court. Parliament has not agreed. Fast-track courts for cases against legislators (Supreme Court orders from 2017). State funding (Indrajit Gupta Committee) to cut dependence on donors. Simultaneous elections: the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024 is with a Joint Parliamentary Committee; its report was still awaited in the latest reports I found. Roll integrity: the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, upheld by the Supreme Court in May 2026, raises questions of inclusion of poor and migrant voters. EVM and VVPAT: the Supreme Court in April 2024 declined to order 100% VVPAT matching. Appointments: the 2023 Act on the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners replaced the Chief Justice with a Union minister on the selection panel, after the Court's Anoop Baranwal (March 2023) direction.
Examples to carry into the exam

Bihar 2025: an NDA landslide with women voters and welfare cash transfers widely discussed, plus a controversy over the SIR of electoral rolls. West Bengal, Kerala and Tamil Nadu in 2026: a change in each, showing the pull of anti-incumbency in southern and eastern states, and a new party (TVK) entering a Dravidian-dominated field. Haryana and Maharashtra 2024: surprise results against exit polls. Caste census: approved by the CCPA on 30 April 2025; Census 2027 includes a caste question. Expect pressure on voting patterns and quotas. Digital campaigns and direct benefit transfers change how parties reach voters.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine the major determinants of electoral behaviour in India." "Criminalisation of politics is a threat to democracy. Suggest measures." "How has the role of caste in elections changed since 1990?" "Evaluate the electoral reforms of the past decades." Structure: theoretical models (Columbia, Michigan, rational choice); Indian studies (Lokniti, Eldersveld, Chandra, Jaffrelot); determinants (identity, welfare, leader, money); trends (turnout, women); legislators' profile with ADR numbers; criminalisation (Vaishnav, cases); reforms (electoral bonds judgment, state funding, disqualification); conclude with a balanced view.
Anti-Defection Law
Loyalty versus conscience

Defection by legislators toppled governments in the 1960s and still does. The Tenth Schedule (1985) tried to stop it, and its working is still debated: does it protect stability or kill dissent? It is a core polity topic and often turns up in current affairs.
Aya Ram, Gaya Ram

After the 1967 elections, over 400 defections occurred in states within a year. In Haryana, MLA Gaya Lal changed party three times in one day in 1967, giving us 'Aya Ram Gaya Ram'. The Chavan Committee (1968) studied it, and the Rajiv Gandhi government passed the 52nd Amendment in 1985 , adding the Tenth Schedule.
Grounds for disqualification
Exceptions: merger of the original party if two-thirds of the legislature party agree (para 4), and the Speaker or Chairman resigning to stay neutral. Decisions are by the Presiding Officer .
91st Amendment (2003)

The original law allowed a split if one-third members left. This led to mass defections, so the 91st Amendment removed the split provision and kept only the two-thirds merger. It also capped Councils of Ministers at 15 per cent of the House (minimum 12 in a state) and barred defectors from holding ministerial office or paid political posts until re-elected.
The courts

Kihoto Hollohan (1992) upheld the law, but held the Speaker's decision is a tribunal-like act and subject to judicial review (para 7, ouster of jurisdiction struck down). Rajendra Singh Rana (2007) on the Speaker's duty. Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020) urged Parliament to consider an independent tribunal and said Speakers should decide within three months . Subhash Desai (2023, Shiv Sena split) discussed whips and the Speaker's role.
The whip and the free vote

A whip is a party instruction on how to vote; a three-line whip is the strongest. Under the Tenth Schedule, defying it can cost a member the seat, though the party can condone it within 15 days. That makes legislators follow the party on every vote, not just on confidence. Burke's ideal of the representative as trustee exercising judgement fits badly. Parties may let members vote freely on conscience issues (a free vote ). Related: Rajya Sabha elections now use an open ballot (2003 amendment to the RPA; Kuldip Nayar 2006) so that cross-voting can be traced.
Problems

Speaker's partisanship : delay, selective action. Whip applies to all votes, not only confidence motions: stifles free debate and the 'Burke trustee' ideal. Merger loophole : whole groups (for example, Goa Congress MLAs in 2019 and 2022) merge with another party, and 'resort politics'. Defectors often re-elected after resigning.
Reform proposals

Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) and the Law Commission (170th Report, 1999): limit disqualification to confidence and money votes. Election Commission as decision-maker on Governor's advice (Goswami, Venkatachaliah 2002). Second ARC : disqualification for confidence and budget votes. Independent tribunal headed by a retired judge. UK, Germany: no such law, party discipline by convention.
Today's relevance

Defection reshaped Maharashtra (2022), Madhya Pradesh (2020), Karnataka (2019) and others. Elected members who change sides through resignation and by-election (the 'Operation Lotus' pattern) avoid disqualification. The debate links to party democracy , Speaker neutrality and the Rajya Sabha cross-voting rule (open ballot for party agents).
How UPSC asks this

"The Anti-Defection Law has curbed defection but damaged legislative freedom. Discuss." "What loopholes remain in the Tenth Schedule after the 91st Amendment?" "Who should decide disqualification: the Speaker or an independent authority?" Structure: history, grounds, 91st Amendment, judgments, problems, reforms, examples. Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992) upheld the Tenth Schedule but held that the Speaker's decisions are subject to judicial review.
Electoral Reforms
Cleaning the machinery of democracy

India holds the world's largest elections, yet money, muscle, caste and misinformation distort them. Electoral reform is one of the most repeated topics in GS and PSIR. Know the committees , the Supreme Court rulings and the live proposals such as simultaneous polls. The Election Commission was set up in 1950 under Article 324, and T.N. Seshan, Chief Election Commissioner from 1990 to 1996, made it a visible and assertive institution.
Legal framework

Art. 324-329 : Election Commission and elections. RPA 1950 : rolls, seats. RPA 1951 : conduct, disqualification, corrupt practices. Model Code of Conduct (convention, no statutory force). Tenth Schedule: defection. 61st Amendment (1988): voting age 18. The system is first-past-the-post (FPTP): simple, but winners can have under 50 per cent votes, and seats and votes can diverge.
Major committees
Later: NCRWC (2002), Second ARC (2007), Law Commission 255th Report (2015).
Criminalisation and disclosure

ADR v Union of India (2002) and PUCL v Union of India (2003): voters have a right to know criminal, financial and educational backgrounds of candidates, via affidavits (Art. 19(1)(a)). Lily Thomas (2013): a legislator convicted with two or more years' jail is disqualified at once. The Court has asked parties to publish candidates' criminal records and reasons for selecting them. Fast-track courts for MP-MLA cases ( Ashwini Upadhyay , 2016 onward).
Money and funding

Spending ceilings apply to candidates but not parties. The Electoral Bonds scheme (2018) allowed anonymous donations through banks. In ADR v Union of India (15 February 2024) a five-judge Bench unanimously struck it down as violating the voter's right to information (Art. 19(1)(a)) and ordered disclosure. Proposals: state funding in part (Indrajit Gupta), a National Election Fund, audit of party accounts, and tax-based transparency.
Institutional and technology reforms

NOTA (PUCL, 2013), a right to negative vote, with no electoral effect. EVMs and VVPAT : in April 2024 the Court rejected a demand for 100 per cent VVPAT counting. EC appointments : Anoop Baranwal (2023) set a panel of PM, Leader of Opposition and CJI; the 2023 Act replaced the CJI with a Union minister, and this is contested. Voter rolls : the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) began in Bihar in 2025 and spread to 12 states and UTs from late 2025. The Court allowed it, and critics fear exclusion of genuine voters. Check the latest.
Live proposals

One Nation, One Election : the 129th Constitution Amendment Bill and a UT-laws bill were introduced in December 2024 and sent to a Joint Parliamentary Committee, whose term was extended in 2026. Arguments: lower cost, steady governance. Against: federalism, and shortening of state-assembly terms (as of 2026 under study). Women's reservation : the 106th Amendment (2023) gives 33 per cent in Lok Sabha and assemblies, effective after the Census and delimitation. Proportional or mixed systems; ranked voting; ban on candidates contesting two seats.
Evaluation

Supporters: disclosure and NOTA gave voters tools. Critics: the Model Code is toothless; criminals still win; money grows; the EC is seen as less independent; digital misinformation, deepfakes and paid news are new threats. Think of reform as four fronts : candidates, parties, the EC and the voters.
Comparisons and the way forward

Compare with the UK (state limits on party spending), Germany (mixed-member proportional), and Brazil (compulsory voting). A sensible package: independent EC appointments, internal party democracy, transparent funding, swift trial of election offences, and voter education. The Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998) recommended state funding of elections, a suggestion still debated today. The Law Commission's 255th Report (2015) also proposed changes to electoral finance, such as a state funding mechanism.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine the need for electoral reforms in India." "Evaluate the case for simultaneous elections." "How far have judicial interventions improved electoral democracy?" Structure: problem, committees, court rulings, funding, EC and tech, live proposals, evaluation. Lily Thomas v. Union of India (2013) and the 2002 ADR case on candidate affidavits are standard examples of judicial steps in electoral reform. The 2003 PUCL v. Union of India case on voters' right to know about candidates shows how courts shape electoral choice.
Comparative Politics: Nature and Major Approaches
Why compare?

Comparative politics studies how political systems work by setting them side by side: states, regimes, parties, elections, institutions. It is the base of Paper II Section A, and it gives you tools you can use all over the optional. The central question is simple: why do similar-looking countries end up different, and different ones alike? Why did India stay democratic after 1947 while most new states did not? Why do some economies become rich through state-led plans? The syllabus asks for two things in this lesson: the nature of the field, and its major approaches . You need to know the comparative method, and a clear timeline of approaches: traditional, behavioural, structural-functional, political culture, political development, institutionalism and rational choice. Examiners like thinkers with titles and years: Aristotle, Montesquieu, Almond, Easton, Lijphart, Sartori, Huntington, Skocpol. Add India as a case.
What is comparative politics?

Comparative politics is the study of domestic politics across countries, using systematic comparison. International relations deals with relations between states; comparative politics asks about politics inside them. Roy Macridis described the traditional field as "comparative government", which listed the formal institutions of countries one by one. The modern field asks causal questions, using concepts and evidence. Aims Describe political systems accurately. Classify them: democracies, autocracies, presidential or parliamentary systems. Explain outcomes: regime change, revolutions, party systems, welfare states. Predict and test theories across cases. Learn from others' experience (policy lessons). Its roots are old. Aristotle's team studied the constitutions of 158 city-states (the Constitution of Athens survives). Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws (1748), linked laws to climate and society. Alexis de Tocqueville wrote Democracy in America (1835, 1840). James Bryce wrote Modern Democracies (1921).
The comparative method

Arend Lijphart, "Comparative Politics and the Comparative Method" ( American Political Science Review , 1971), named four ways to test ideas: experimental , statistical , comparative and case study . The comparative method suits few cases but many variables. This is the "small N" problem. J.S. Mill's System of Logic (1843) gave the logic. Adam Przeworski and Henry Teune, The Logic of Comparative Social Inquiry (1970), turned it into most similar and most different systems designs.
Traditional approach and the behavioural revolution

Traditional (institutional-legal) approach. Before the 1940s, scholars described constitutions, legislatures and courts, mostly in Europe and the US. Herman Finer, Theory and Practice of Modern Government (1932), is an example. Criticisms: formal, descriptive, Eurocentric, silent on behaviour and society, and unscientific. Behavioural revolution (1950s-60s). After the war, American political scientists turned to people's actual behaviour, with surveys and statistics. Their claims (David Easton): politics has regularities, theory should be tested, values and facts should be kept apart, and research should be systematic and use quantitative methods. New states in Asia and Africa needed analysis. Old institutional tools did not fit them. Gabriel Almond led a committee on comparative politics in the Social Science Research Council (1954). Post-behaviouralism. Easton's 1969 American Political Science Association address, "The New Revolution in Political Science", argued for relevance and action : the field must tackle real problems, not just method.
Systems and structural-functionalism

David Easton, The Political System (1953) and A Systems Analysis of Political Life (1965), saw politics as a system. Demands and support enter as inputs. The system converts them into decisions and policies (outputs). Feedback returns to the system. Gabriel Almond, in "A Functional Approach to Comparative Politics" (in The Politics of Developing Areas , 1960), asked what functions every system must perform. G. Bingham Powell joined him in Comparative Politics: A Developmental Approach (1966). Almond's functions Input: political socialisation and recruitment, interest articulation, interest aggregation, political communication. Output: rule-making, rule application, rule adjudication. A system is judged by its capabilities : extractive, regulative, distributive, symbolic and responsive. Strength: a common frame to compare all countries, including new ones. Weaknesses: conservative (bias toward stability), vague, and it takes a Western system as the model.
Political culture and political development

Political culture. Almond and Sidney Verba, The Civic Culture (1963), surveyed five countries (US, UK, West Germany, Italy, Mexico). They identified three types of orientation: Parochial: little awareness of the national system. Subject: aware, but passive. Participant: active citizens. A stable democracy needs a mix, the civic culture , with participation balanced by deference. Critics: circular logic, and it ignores power and inequality. Ronald Inglehart revived culture studies with The Silent Revolution (1977) on postmaterial values. Political development and modernisation. S.M. Lipset, "Some Social Requisites of Democracy" (1959): wealthier countries are more likely to be democratic. Daniel Lerner, The Passing of Traditional Society (1958); W.W. Rostow, The Stages of Economic Growth (1960). Samuel Huntington, Political Order in Changing Societies (1968): rapid change without strong institutions creates instability. Order matters more than regime type.
Bringing history and the state back in

From the 1960s, historical and Marxist-influenced comparativists challenged modernisation theory. Barrington Moore Jr. , Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy (1966): the routes to the modern world depend on how landlords, peasants and the bourgeoisie interact. "No bourgeois, no democracy." Theda Skocpol , States and Social Revolutions (1979): revolutions in France, Russia and China arose from state breakdown under international pressure plus peasant revolt. Bringing the State Back In (Evans, Rueschemeyer and Skocpol, eds., 1985): the state is an actor with its own interests, not just a reflection of society. Dependency and world-system writers (Frank, Wallerstein, Cardoso) argued the national case cannot be understood without the international economy. This is the historical-structural tradition. It focuses on a few big cases, long time spans, and "critical junctures" (also path dependence). Its weakness: few cases, so the findings are hard to generalise.
Institutionalism and rational choice

New institutionalism James March and Johan Olsen, "The New Institutionalism" (1984), revived attention to institutions. Peter Hall and Rosemary Taylor (1996) separated three schools: historical (path dependence), rational choice (institutions as rules for strategic actors) and sociological (norms and cultural frames). Douglass North, Institutions, Institutional Change and Economic Performance (1990), defined institutions as "the rules of the game". Rational choice Individuals pursue their interests. Anthony Downs, An Economic Theory of Democracy (1957): parties and voters act like firms and consumers. Mancur Olson, The Logic of Collective Action (1965): large groups struggle to organise. George Tsebelis, Veto Players (2002): policy change depends on how many actors can block it. Critiques of rational choice: unrealistic assumptions; neglect of culture and history; "Green and Shapiro" ( Pathologies of Rational Choice Theory , 1994) said it explains little. Today scholars mix methods: comparative-historical analysis, statistics, case studies and experiments.
India as a case in comparative politics

The puzzle of Indian democracy. India became a democracy as a poor, diverse, mostly illiterate country, against Lipset's expectations. Lijphart, "The Puzzle of Indian Democracy: A Consociational Interpretation" ( APSR , 1996), argued that power-sharing among groups (coalitions, federalism, minority rights) explains it. Congress system. Rajni Kothari (1964) described a dominant-party system with competition inside the party. W.H. Morris-Jones saw "three idioms" of politics: modern, traditional and saintly. State and society. Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph, The Modernity of Tradition (1967), argued that caste adapted to democracy. Atul Kohli and Pranab Bardhan studied the Indian state and its limits. Federal comparison. India is compared with the US, Canada and Nigeria on federalism and with Brazil on development. Post-colonial lens. Partha Chatterjee's "political society" and Mahmood Mamdani on the colonial state challenge Western categories. India fits few single theories, which makes it a favourite "hard case".
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the nature and scope of comparative politics." "Examine the contribution of the behavioural revolution to comparative politics." "Critically evaluate the structural-functional approach of Almond." "Compare the traditional and modern approaches to the study of comparative politics." Structure: define the field, with the aims and roots (Aristotle, Montesquieu). Explain the comparative method (Mill, Lijphart, most similar/most different). Present approaches in order, each with a thinker, a book and one critique: traditional, behavioural, systems, structural-functional, political culture, political development, historical-structural, institutionalism and rational choice. Add India as a case (Lijphart 1996). A timeline table gives a neat, high-scoring finish.
Political Economy, Political Sociology and the Limits of Comparison
Money, society and the limits of comparison

This lesson covers three linked ideas. Political economy asks how politics and the economy shape each other. Political sociology asks how social groups, classes, cleavages and culture shape politics. And the limits of comparison asks the honest question: how far can we trust cross-country comparisons? Together they move you from "what do institutions look like?" (the previous lesson) to "why do they look that way, and what are the limits to what we know?" For the exam, learn a handful of anchor works with years: Polanyi (1944), Esping-Andersen (1990), Hall and Soskice (2001), Lipset and Rokkan (1967), Putnam (1993), Sartori (1970). Add India: Bardhan, Rudolph and Rudolph, Varshney. A top answer ends with the limits: small number of cases, selection bias, concept stretching, and Eurocentrism.
What is political economy?

Political economy studies how states and markets interact: who gets what, when and how, and who decides. There are several traditions. Classical liberal. Adam Smith ( The Wealth of Nations , 1776) and David Ricardo. Free markets create wealth. The state should be limited. Marxist. Karl Marx ( Capital , 1867): the economic base shapes politics. The state serves the dominant class. Statist and nationalist. Friedrich List, The National System of Political Economy (1841): protect infant industries. Keynesian. John Maynard Keynes ( The General Theory , 1936): governments should manage demand. Institutionalist. Institutions shape economic results (Douglass North). Public choice. Politicians and bureaucrats follow self-interest (James Buchanan, Gordon Tullock). Anne Krueger (1974) coined rent-seeking . Karl Polanyi , The Great Transformation (1944): markets are not natural. They are created by states. Unregulated markets trigger a "double movement" as society pushes back to protect itself. Markets must stay embedded in society.
Varieties of capitalism and welfare regimes

Varieties of Capitalism Peter Hall and David Soskice (eds.), Varieties of Capitalism (2001). Firms solve coordination problems differently. In liberal market economies (US, UK) markets and competition do the work. In coordinated market economies (Germany, Japan, Nordic) institutions like unions, banks and employer groups coordinate. Each has comparative advantage: radical innovation versus incremental, high-quality production. Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism Gosta Esping-Andersen (1990). Decommodification is the degree to which people can live without selling their labour. He found three regimes: liberal (US: means-tested aid), conservative-corporatist (Germany, France: social insurance linked to jobs) and social-democratic (Sweden, Denmark: universal benefits). Critiques: they ignore the Global South, the family and gender (feminists such as Ann Orloff and Jane Lewis), and the role of finance.
The state and development

Gerschenkron , Economic Backwardness in Historical Perspective (1962): late developers need the state and banks to push industry. Developmental state. Chalmers Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle (1982); Alice Amsden on South Korea ( Asia's Next Giant , 1989); Robert Wade on Taiwan ( Governing the Market , 1990). A competent bureaucracy guides firms, protects them for a while, and demands export performance. Embedded autonomy. Peter Evans, Embedded Autonomy (1995): the state needs ties to business, but also independence from it. Compare predatory states (Zaire under Mobutu). Corporatism. Philippe Schmitter, "Still the Century of Corporatism?" (1974): peak organisations of labour and business bargain with the state, as in Austria and Sweden. This contrasts with pluralism . Institutions and growth. Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson, Why Nations Fail (2012): inclusive institutions create prosperity; extractive ones do not. They won the 2024 Nobel in economics, with Simon Johnson.
Political sociology: cleavages and parties

Seymour Martin Lipset and Stein Rokkan, in Party Systems and Voter Alignments (1967), argued that Western European party systems "froze" around four cleavages produced by two revolutions: the National Revolution (centre-periphery, state-church) and the Industrial Revolution (land-industry, owner-worker). Lipset's earlier Political Man (1960) linked democracy to economic development and social conditions. Ronald Inglehart's postmaterialism ( The Silent Revolution , 1977) added a new value cleavage: security versus self-expression.
Civil society, social capital and elites

Social capital. Robert Putnam, Making Democracy Work (1993), compared regional governments in Italy. Northern regions, with dense civic associations and trust, did better than the south. Bowling Alone (2000) argued that civic life in the US was declining. Civil society. Tocqueville praised associations. Gramsci saw civil society as the arena of hegemony. Post-1989 scholars saw it as a force against authoritarianism. Elite theory. Gaetano Mosca and Vilfredo Pareto: every society is ruled by an organised minority. Robert Michels's " iron law of oligarchy " ( Political Parties , 1911) argued that even democratic parties become oligarchic. C. Wright Mills, The Power Elite (1956), described a military-industrial-political elite. Robert Dahl's Who Governs? (1961) replied with pluralism. Participation and mobilisation. Voting, protest and social movements (Charles Tilly; resource mobilisation theory). Class and identity. Ethnicity, religion, gender, caste and region as bases of politics.
The limits of comparison

Comparison is powerful, but it has well-known limits. Many variables, few cases. Lijphart's "small N" problem. Dozens of factors, only a handful of countries. Concept stretching. Giovanni Sartori, "Concept Misformation in Comparative Politics" (1970): a concept like "party" or "democracy" gets stretched to fit different contexts until it loses meaning. His "ladder of abstraction" shows that broader concepts cover more cases but say less. Selection bias. Choosing cases because they had a certain outcome (revolutions only) distorts causal claims. Galton's problem. Cases are not independent. Ideas and institutions spread by diffusion and colonialism. Context and equivalence. The same institution (a parliament, a vote) works differently in different settings. Data may not be comparable. Ethnocentrism. Concepts drawn from Western experience may not suit the Global South. Values. Choice of topic and standard reflects the researcher's views. Prediction. Social systems are open: people learn and change.
How scholars respond

Scientific route Gary King, Robert Keohane and Sidney Verba, Designing Social Inquiry (1994): qualitative research should follow the logic of statistical inference. Increase the number of observations and be careful about selection. Qualitative route Henry Brady and David Collier, Rethinking Social Inquiry (2004), and Charles Ragin's The Comparative Method (1987) with Qualitative Comparative Analysis: case knowledge and process tracing give causal insight even with few cases. Mixed methods and area studies Combine large-N data with deep case studies. Use "nested analysis". Respect area expertise. Post-colonial and critical Question whose categories count. Partha Chatterjee, Mahmood Mamdani and Edward Said ask us to read non-Western politics on its own terms. The answer for the exam: comparison remains valuable, but use cautious claims, clear concepts and multiple methods.
Political economy and society in India

Pranab Bardhan , The Political Economy of Development in India (1984): the state is shaped by three dominant proprietary classes : industrial capitalists, rich farmers and the professionals and bureaucrats. Their rivalry slowed public investment and growth. Rudolph and Rudolph , In Pursuit of Lakshmi (1987): India's political economy has a "command polity" of the state and a "demand polity" of groups. Atul Kohli , Democracy and Discontent (1990): the crisis of governability. State-Directed Development (2004) compared India, South Korea, Brazil and Nigeria. Reforms. The 1991 liberalisation shifted India from state-led to market-led growth, while keeping a strong welfare agenda (MGNREGA, 2005; food security law, 2013). Society. Ashutosh Varshney, Ethnic Conflict and Civic Life (2002), applied Putnam's logic to Hindu-Muslim riots. Towns with inter-communal civic associations saw less violence than towns without them. Cleavages. Caste, religion, language and region define India's party system, unlike Europe's class cleavages (Chandra, Yadav). Comparative limits are clear in India: concepts like "class" or "civil society" need adjustment (Chatterjee's "political society").
How UPSC asks this

"What are the limitations of the comparative method in political analysis?" "Discuss the political economy approach to the study of comparative politics." "How do social cleavages shape party systems? Illustrate." "Compare the developmental state with the neoliberal state." Structure: start with a definition. For political economy: traditions (liberal, Marxist, Polanyi), then Varieties of Capitalism and Esping-Andersen in boxes, and the developmental state. For political sociology: Lipset and Rokkan's cleavages, Putnam, elite theory. For limits: small N, concept stretching (Sartori), selection bias, Galton's problem, ethnocentrism, and the responses (mixed methods). Close with India: Bardhan, Varshney, Chatterjee. Show you can criticise the tools you learn.
The State in Capitalist, Socialist, Developed and Developing Societies
The state is not the same everywhere

Every country has a state, but states differ widely. A Swedish welfare state, a Soviet party-state, a developmental Korean state and a fragile state in the Sahel all claim to be "the state", yet they do very different things. This lesson compares the state across capitalist, socialist, developed and developing societies. It builds on your Paper I work on theories of the state (liberal, Marxist, pluralist, post-colonial and feminist) and applies them across cases. Expect questions that ask you to compare, such as "Distinguish between the state in developed and developing societies" or "Has globalisation weakened the state?" A strong answer uses a few typologies, thinkers with books and years (Weber, Tilly, Mann, Alavi, Migdal, Evans), and a quick set of country examples. Always finish with India, which sits between categories: a democratic, developmental and welfare-seeking state in a poor, diverse society.
What is the state?

Max Weber, in "Politics as a Vocation" (1919), defined the state as the human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory. Four features most scholars list Territory with borders. Population. Government : institutions that make and enforce rules. Sovereignty : supreme authority inside, independence outside. Keep three terms apart: the state is the permanent apparatus, the government is the team in office, and the nation is a community of identity. How states formed. Charles Tilly, "War Made the State, and the State Made War" (1975) and Coercion, Capital, and European States (1990): European rulers fought wars, so they raised taxes and built bureaucracies. In much of the Global South, states came from colonial rule or a negotiated independence, with weaker links between state and society. Michael Mann (1984) separated despotic power (rulers acting without consent) from infrastructural power (the ability to reach into society and implement policy).
Mann's two kinds of state power

Mann's four types are a helpful map. Western liberal democracies sit in the bureaucratic box: limited by law but able to tax, register and serve citizens. Many developing states have a gap. They look strong on paper (a big army, wide laws) but cannot enforce rules across the territory.
Theories of the state in brief

Liberal and pluralist. The state is a neutral umpire between groups (Dahl, Who Governs? , 1961). Marxist. Marx and Engels: "The executive of the modern State is but a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie." Instrumentalist view: Ralph Miliband, The State in Capitalist Society (1969), pointed to business links with state elites. Structuralist view: Nicos Poulantzas, Political Power and Social Classes (1968): the state has relative autonomy and serves capital's long-term needs. Gramsci: the state is hegemony protected by the armour of coercion. Elite theory. Mosca, Pareto: an organised minority rules. State-centred. Theda Skocpol, Bringing the State Back In (1985): the state has interests and capacities of its own. Feminist. The state reflects patriarchal power (Catharine MacKinnon, Carole Pateman). Post-colonial. Hamza Alavi and Partha Chatterjee: the colonial inheritance shapes the state. These theories are covered in depth in Paper I. Here we use them as lenses for comparison.
The state in capitalist societies

Capitalist states protect property and contracts, support markets, and usually combine this with welfare and regulation. Over time, the pattern shifted. Laissez-faire/liberal state (19th century): minimal state, "night-watchman" (an image used by Lassalle in 1862 and made famous by Nozick). Keynesian welfare state (1945-70s): full employment, health, education and social insurance. Beveridge Report (1942) and the UK NHS (1948) are landmarks. The Nordic social-democratic model went furthest. Neoliberal state (from the 1980s): Thatcher and Reagan. Privatisation, deregulation, lower taxes, cuts in welfare, an independent central bank. Government became a regulator and facilitator. Post-2008 and post-2020 state. Bailouts, pandemic spending, industrial policy and strategic controls on technology and trade, in the US and EU. Tariffs and subsidies in 2025-26 show that even market economies use the state to steer the economy. Varieties exist: the US state is fragmented and market-oriented; the German state is coordinated; the French is more centralised and interventionist ( dirigisme ).
The state in socialist societies

Socialist states, in the Marxist-Leninist model, claim to represent the working class. Lenin , The State and Revolution (1917): the state is a tool of class rule. After revolution, a dictatorship of the proletariat would suppress the old class and then "wither away". In practice : a one-party state with a vanguard party , a command economy, public ownership, central planning, and heavy control of media and society. The USSR from the 1920s and Eastern Europe after 1945. Critique from within. Milovan Djilas, The New Class (1957): a party bureaucracy became a ruling class. The Soviet nomenklatura system gave privileges to party loyalists. Achievements: literacy, health, industrialisation, and gender equality in law. Failures: shortages, low innovation, repression and the stifling of dissent. Collapse. 1989-91 ended the Soviet model in Europe. Debates on its nature: Trotsky called the USSR a "degenerated workers' state"; others called it "state capitalism" or bureaucratic collectivism.
Market socialism and state capitalism

Surviving socialist-led states changed course. China. Deng Xiaoping's reforms (from 1978) opened the economy: household farming, special economic zones, WTO entry (2001). The Communist Party retains political control, calling it "socialism with Chinese characteristics". The state owns large firms and banks, directs investment, and uses industrial plans (Made in China 2025). Rapid growth lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty. Vietnam. Doi Moi (1986) brought market reforms under one-party rule. Cuba and North Korea remain more closed. Ian Bremmer, The End of the Free Market (2010), called such models state capitalism : the state acts as the main economic actor for political gain. Critics note that corruption, local debt and weak private rights are risks. Supporters point to speed and strategy. Scholars debate whether there is a "Beijing Consensus" (Joshua Cooper Ramo, 2004), an alternative to the Washington Consensus.
The state in developing societies

Overdeveloped state. Hamza Alavi, "The State in Post-Colonial Societies: Pakistan and Bangladesh" (1972): colonial rulers built a large civil-military apparatus before local classes were strong. After independence, the state is relatively autonomous and dominated by a bureaucratic-military oligarchy, which stands above competing local classes. Soft state. Gunnar Myrdal, Asian Drama (1968): the state cannot enforce its own rules and policies. Quasi-states. Robert Jackson, Quasi-States (1990): in Africa, states exist because of external recognition of sovereignty, without strong internal capacity. Weak states and strong societies. Joel Migdal, Strong Societies and Weak States (1988): local strongmen and chiefs challenge the state's rules. Neo-patrimonial state. Nicolas van de Walle and Michael Bratton (1997): public office is used for private gain, through patronage. Failed and fragile states. Robert Rotberg, When States Fail (2004): Somalia, Afghanistan, and others. Today's lists include Sudan, South Sudan, Yemen and Haiti.
Developmental, predatory and rentier states

Developmental state South Korea, Taiwan, Japan, Singapore. A competent bureaucracy, close but autonomous ties with business (Peter Evans's embedded autonomy ), export discipline, land reform and education first. Chalmers Johnson (1982), Alice Amsden (1989), Robert Wade (1990). Predatory state Rulers extract wealth for themselves and their circle. Zaire under Mobutu is Evans's classic case ( Embedded Autonomy , 1995). Rentier state The state lives on external income, such as oil, so it does not need to tax citizens. Hossein Mahdavy (1970); Michael Ross, "Does Oil Hinder Democracy?" (2001). Saudi Arabia, Venezuela, Nigeria. Why they differ Colonial legacy, natural resources, geopolitics (Cold War aid), social structure (land reform, ethnic divisions), and leadership. Dani Rodrik and others stress policy and institutions.
Globalisation and the changing state

Do states matter less today? The debate: Retreat. Susan Strange, The Retreat of the State (1996): markets, firms and global finance limit what governments can do. Kenichi Ohmae spoke of the "end of the nation state" (1995). Adaptation. The state is changing form, not shrinking. Governments regulate global firms, sign trade deals and manage borders. Linda Weiss, The Myth of the Powerless State (1998). Return of the state. After 2008 and the pandemic, then the tariffs, subsidies and sanctions of 2022-26, states play a bigger economic role. National security now shapes trade and technology policy. New pressures. Digital platforms, AI, migration, climate, and non-state armed groups all test state capacity. Conclusion for exams: the state is not withering away. It is changing: from provider to regulator and security manager, with big differences between strong and weak states.
The Indian state in comparative perspective

Type. A democratic, developmental, welfare-seeking state in a poor and diverse society. It combines liberal-democratic form with a developmental purpose. Phases. Nehruvian state (Planning Commission, 1950; mixed economy; public-sector "commanding heights"). The 1991 reforms made the state more of a regulator (SEBI, TRAI, CCI). Since 2014 the Planning Commission has been replaced by NITI Aayog (2015) and the state has used digital delivery (Aadhaar, UPI, DBT). Welfare. A rights-based turn: MGNREGA (2005), RTI (2005), RTE (2009), National Food Security Act (2013). Analyses. Bardhan: held back by the rivalry of dominant proprietary classes. Rudolph and Rudolph: a "command" and a "demand" polity. Atul Kohli: a "democratic developmental" state with mixed results. Partha Chatterjee: The Politics of the Governed (2004), political society : the poor negotiate with the state outside formal civil society. Sudipta Kaviraj on the "dialectic" of the Indian state. Capacity gaps. A strong centre and army, but uneven delivery in health, policing and courts. This is the soft-state critique.
How UPSC asks this

"Compare the nature of the state in developed and developing societies." "Has globalisation weakened the state? Examine with reference to developing countries." "Explain the 'overdeveloped' state thesis of Hamza Alavi." "Distinguish between a developmental state and a predatory state." Structure: define the state (Weber), note Mann's two powers. Give brief theories of the state. Then compare four types in a table: capitalist (liberal, welfare, neoliberal), socialist (Soviet, Chinese), developed (strong infrastructural power, welfare), developing (Alavi, Migdal, Jackson, developmental versus predatory). Add the globalisation debate. Close with India. A two-column table (developed versus developing) is efficient and scores well.
Democracy and Human Rights
Two big ideas, often in conflict

Democracy and human rights are two of the great "norms" of the modern world. States are expected to hold elections and to protect basic freedoms. Yet the world often fails these tests, and the great powers apply them unevenly. For UPSC, the theme asks four things. What are the ideas? How did they spread? Where do they clash with sovereignty? And what is happening now: democratic backsliding, the Responsibility to Protect (R2P), and the strain on global institutions? The topic joins easily with other parts of the syllabus: the UN (Council, ICC), Western political thought (rights, Locke), and Indian Constitution (Part III). It also runs through India's foreign policy debates on human rights and intervention. Aim to show both sides in every answer. Universal values, and local contexts. Rights, and sovereignty. Promotion, and imposition.
What is democracy, and how do we measure it?

There are narrow and wide definitions. Minimal (procedural). Joseph Schumpeter, Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942): democracy is a method in which leaders win power through competitive elections. Polyarchy. Robert Dahl, Polyarchy (1971): free and fair elections plus inclusive suffrage, freedom of expression, alternative information and freedom of association. Substantive. Amartya Sen, Development as Freedom (1999), and "Democracy as a Universal Value" (1999): democracy gives voice, prevents famines and is valued everywhere. Real democracy needs social and economic equality too. Rankings help. V-Dem (Sweden) separates liberal democracies, electoral democracies, electoral autocracies and closed autocracies. Freedom House (US) scores political rights and civil liberties. The EIU Democracy Index uses categories from "full democracy" to "authoritarian". Their methods differ, and governments, including India's, often dispute them.
Waves, promotion and setbacks

Samuel Huntington, The Third Wave: Democratization in the Late Twentieth Century (1991), counted three waves of democratisation, each followed by a "reverse wave". Huntington's waves First: 1828 to 1926 (the long wave, from the US and Europe). Second: 1943 to 1962 (post-war, and decolonisation). Third: from 1974 (Portugal, Spain, Latin America, East Asia, then Eastern Europe after 1989). Francis Fukuyama's "The End of History?" (1989) and book (1992) argued liberal democracy had won the argument. Western states then promoted democracy through aid, election monitoring and conditionality (the EU's Copenhagen criteria, 1993). The results were mixed. The 2003 Iraq invasion was partly justified as democracy-building, and it left a poor record. The Arab Spring (2010-11) brought hope, but only Tunisia held on for a time, and it too has seen backsliding. Critics say democracy cannot be imposed from outside.
Democratic recession

Larry Diamond called it a "democratic recession" (2015). Many see it as a shift from open coups to executive aggrandisement : elected leaders slowly weaken courts, media, civil society and opposition. The V-Dem Democracy Report 2026 counted 92 autocracies and 87 democracies at the end of 2025. It was the second year in a row in which autocracies outnumbered democracies. The report said the average world citizen enjoys democracy at a level last seen around 1978. Typical signs Pressure on the media and on NGOs. Capture or weakening of the judiciary and election bodies. Use of emergency or security laws against opponents. Disinformation and polarisation online. Even established democracies face strain, including the US. Defenders of each government dispute such labels. V-Dem has classed India as an "electoral autocracy", while the Indian government rejects the ratings as biased. Quote the rating but give the government's reply too.
Human rights: the framework

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) was adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948 . It is not binding, but it is the base of later law. 48 states voted yes; none opposed; 8 abstained. The ICCPR and ICESCR (both adopted in 1966, in force 1976) made the rights binding. With the UDHR they form the International Bill of Rights. Karel Vasak's three generations (1979): civil-political; economic-social-cultural; collective or solidarity rights (development, environment, peace). The Declaration on the Right to Development (1986) belongs to the third. The Vienna Declaration (1993) said rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent and interrelated.
Universalism or relativism?

Universalists Rights belong to humans as humans. Jack Donnelly, Universal Human Rights in Theory and Practice (1989). They point to the UDHR, signed by states from every region, and to Hansa Mehta of India, who is credited with changing the draft wording from "all men" to "all human beings". Relativists Rights reflect cultures. Some leaders in Asia, including Lee Kuan Yew of Singapore and Mahathir Mohamad of Malaysia, argued in the 1990s for " Asian values ": community and order over individual rights, and development first. The Bangkok Declaration (1993) put the case. Others stress that rights talk grew out of Western liberalism and was used to justify colonial rule. Middle ground Amartya Sen argued Asian traditions also value tolerance and liberty, and that rights and development reinforce one another. Rawls's The Law of Peoples (1999) proposed a shorter list of "urgent" rights for all societies. The Vienna Conference (1993) stated the common view: cultural particularities must be borne in mind, but states must protect all rights regardless of their systems.
Institutions that enforce rights

Human Rights Council (Geneva). It replaced the Commission on Human Rights in 2006 (UNGA resolution 60/251). It has 47 members. Its main tool is the Universal Periodic Review (UPR), in which every UN member is reviewed by peers every few years. OHCHR , led by the High Commissioner, set up in 1993. Treaty bodies monitor conventions such as CEDAW, CAT, CERD and CRC. International criminal justice. The tribunals for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY, 1993) and Rwanda (ICTR, 1994) led to the Rome Statute (1998). The International Criminal Court (The Hague) began work in 2002. It tries genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression. India, the US, China and Russia are not parties. ICJ hears disputes between states, for example Gambia v. Myanmar (2019) under the Genocide Convention. Recent strain: the ICC issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin (March 2023) and for Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (November 2024). The US has sanctioned ICC officials, and it announced in 2025 that it was withdrawing from the Human Rights Council.
Intervention and the Responsibility to Protect

Rwanda (1994) and Srebrenica (1995) showed the world's failure. NATO's bombing of Kosovo in 1999 happened without UN Security Council approval. Kofi Annan asked: if humanitarian intervention is an unacceptable assault on sovereignty, how should we respond to such crimes? Canada set up the ICISS , whose 2001 report The Responsibility to Protect (chairs Gareth Evans and Mohamed Sahnoun) said sovereignty means responsibility. R2P at the 2005 World Summit (paras 138-139) States have the responsibility to protect their populations from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity . The international community should help, and, if a state manifestly fails, act collectively through the Security Council under the Charter. The Secretary-General's 2009 report framed three pillars: state responsibility, international assistance, and timely and decisive response. Libya (2011). Resolution 1973 authorised "all necessary measures" to protect civilians. India, Brazil, China, Russia and Germany abstained. NATO's campaign led to regime change, and critics said R2P was misused. Brazil offered " responsibility while protecting " (2011). Russia and China later vetoed action on Syria.
Double standards and selectivity

Selectivity. Powerful states shield allies and target rivals. Critics of the West point to Iraq (2003), to the treatment of Gaza and to arms sales to rights abusers. Sovereignty. The Westphalian norm of non-interference is still strong. China, Russia and many in the Global South see "human rights" as a lever of Western pressure. Geopolitics.
