Council vetoes by the P5 block action: Russia and China on Syria, the US on Israel-related drafts, Russia on Ukraine. Weak enforcement. The ICC depends on states to arrest suspects. Rights versus order. Governments cite terrorism and national security to limit liberties. Retreat of the leaders. The US has cut funds and left the Human Rights Council and announced its exit from UNESCO (effective 31 December 2026), and in January 2026 announced exits from dozens of international organisations. Defenders say imperfect enforcement does not make norms useless. Norms change what states feel they must justify.
India's constitutional and diplomatic record

Constitution. Part III (Articles 12-35) lists Fundamental Rights; the Directive Principles add social-economic rights. Article 21 has been expanded to cover privacy ( K.S. Puttaswamy , 2017), dignity, health and a clean environment. In Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), the Supreme Court used CEDAW to fill a gap and issued guidelines against sexual harassment at work. Institutions. The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 created the NHRC (October 1993) and state commissions. Treaties. India ratified the ICCPR and ICESCR in 1979. It signed the Convention against Torture in 1997 but has not ratified it. It is not a party to the Rome Statute. Foreign policy. India helped draft the UDHR (Hansa Mehta was a key figure). It led the UN attack on apartheid. It generally opposes country-specific resolutions, prefers dialogue, and is wary of R2P as a cover for regime change. India abstained on Libya in 2011. Democracy. Largest electoral democracy, but ratings by V-Dem and Freedom House are questioned by India's government. Constitutional courts, a free press and civil society are the usual points of debate.
How UPSC asks this

"Human rights and state sovereignty are in conflict. Discuss." "Examine the Responsibility to Protect doctrine. Has it been a success?" "Is democracy promotion a moral duty or a form of interventionism?" "The universality of human rights is a Western construct." Comment. Structure: define terms (Schumpeter, Dahl, Sen). Trace human rights: UDHR 1948, covenants 1966, Vienna 1993, Rome Statute 1998, R2P 2005, HRC 2006. Put the debates in boxes: universalism or relativism, sovereignty or intervention. Give two or three current examples, such as the ICC warrants, Libya 2011 and the global democratic recession. End with India: Part III, NHRC, Hansa Mehta, the cautious stance on R2P and the ICC. Always include a "way forward": strengthen the UN's legitimacy, reform the veto and avoid double standards.
Environment and Gender Justice
Problems that do not stop at borders

Climate change, biodiversity loss and gender inequality are problems no single state can solve. They also split the world, between rich and poor states, between past and future polluters, and between men and women inside every society. The environment is a regular Paper II topic: Stockholm, Rio, Kyoto, Paris, "common but differentiated responsibilities" (CBDR), climate finance and India's stand. Gender justice appears less often, but it links to feminist IR, CEDAW, Beijing and women in peace and security. This lesson covers both. Treat environment as one half and gender as the other half of the answer, and connect them where you can: women are hit harder by climate impacts, and women's knowledge and leadership matter in natural-resource politics. The current-affairs layer changes every year. Learn the logic of the negotiations, then add the latest COP in one or two lines.
From Stockholm to Paris

Stockholm, June 1972. The first UN conference on the human environment. It led to UNEP. Indira Gandhi's speech said poverty is the greatest polluter. Brundtland Commission, 1987. Our Common Future defined sustainable development as meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. Rio Earth Summit, 1992. The UNFCCC, the Convention on Biological Diversity, Agenda 21 and the Rio Declaration. Principle 7 states CBDR. Kyoto Protocol. Adopted 1997, in force 2005. Only developed (Annex I) countries had binding cuts. Copenhagen, 2009. Failure to agree a binding deal. A goal of $100 billion a year in climate finance was set. Paris Agreement. Adopted 12 December 2015, in force November 2016.
The Paris Agreement and its logic

The Paris Agreement shifted from a top-down to a bottom-up design. Every country puts forward its own pledge, called a Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) . Main features Goal: keep warming well below 2 degrees C above pre-industrial levels, and pursue efforts for 1.5 degrees C . NDCs are updated every five years, each more ambitious (the "ratchet"). A global stocktake every five years. The first concluded at COP28 (2023). Article 6 on carbon markets. Article 8 on loss and damage . Finance, technology and capacity building for developing countries. Applies to all, but keeps CBDR "in the light of different national circumstances". The weakness: pledges are not legally enforceable, and current pledges fall short. 2024 was the warmest year on record, at about 1.5 degrees C above pre-industrial levels by WMO's estimate.
Recent COPs: Glasgow to Antalya

COP26, Glasgow (2021). First mention of phasing down unabated coal. India announced its Panchamrit targets and net zero by 2070. COP27, Sharm el-Sheikh (2022). Agreement to set up a loss and damage fund . COP28, Dubai (2023). First global stocktake. The "UAE Consensus" called for transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems. COP29, Baku (2024). The New Collective Quantified Goal: developed countries to lead mobilising at least $300 billion a year by 2035 , within a wider call to reach $1.3 trillion from all sources. Developing countries called it too low. COP30, Belem (November 2025). The "Global Mutirao" package called for tripling adaptation finance by 2035. The final text did not carry a formal fossil-fuel roadmap, which a large coalition had sought. Brazil's presidency took that work forward outside the formal decision. COP31, Antalya (9-20 November 2026). Hosted by Turkiye, with Australia leading the negotiations. It is under way at the time of writing. The US withdrew from the Paris Agreement; the exit took effect in January 2026.
North and South: who pays?

The Global South's case Rich countries caused most historical emissions . So under CBDR and respective capabilities (CBDR-RC) they must cut first, and provide finance and technology . The right to develop is real. Per capita emissions of many developing states are low. The developed world's case Emissions growth now comes from large emerging economies, such as China and India. China is the largest emitter today, though its per capita and historic figures are lower than the US. So all major emitters should share the burden. Flash points Finance. The $100 billion promise was met late. Adaptation and loss-and-damage funding remain small. Carbon border taxes. The EU's CBAM began its definitive phase on 1 January 2026. India and others call it unfair trade protection. Equity. Concept of a carbon budget shared fairly between countries. Norms like "polluter pays" and the "precautionary principle" (Rio Principle 15) support the South's case. The "tragedy of the commons" (Garrett Hardin, 1968) explains why collective action is hard.
Gender justice in world politics

Gender justice means fair treatment, voice and resources for all genders. It covers rights, safety, work, health, education and political power. Feminist IR asks "where are the women?" Cynthia Enloe, Bananas, Beaches and Bases (1989), showed how international politics depends on women's often unseen labour, from diplomats' wives to factory and sex workers. J. Ann Tickner, Gender in International Relations (1992), argued that realism's idea of power is shaped by male experience. Later work (Jean Elshtain, Women and War , 1987; Laura Sjoberg) looked at war, security and the state. Key global instruments 1975 Mexico City: first UN World Conference on Women. CEDAW (1979, in force 1981): the international bill of rights for women. Beijing 1995: the Fourth World Conference. The Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action made gender mainstreaming central. UNSC Resolution 1325 (2000): Women, Peace and Security. SDG 5 (2015): gender equality. UN Women (created 2010).
Women, environment and ecofeminism

The link between gender and environment has a long history. Ecofeminism. Vandana Shiva, Staying Alive: Women, Ecology and Development (1988), and Maria Mies and Shiva, Ecofeminism (1993). They argued that the domination of nature and of women are linked, and that modern "development" ignores women's knowledge and subsistence work. Chipko movement (1970s, Uttarakhand). Women villagers, famous through Gaura Devi at Reni (1974), hugged trees to stop felling. It is a core example of a women-led environmental movement. Wangari Maathai and the Green Belt Movement in Kenya (founded 1977). She won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2004. Climate impacts are gendered . Women, especially in poor rural areas, depend more on water, fuel and farming. They bear more of the burden after floods and droughts. UN climate talks have therefore adopted a Gender Action Plan . Critics of ecofeminism say it can treat women as "closer to nature", which is a stereotype. Others call it too general across classes and cultures.
Gaps and critiques

Weak enforcement. Both climate and gender norms rely on voluntary pledges and reporting. There is no world court for climate compliance. Finance gap. Money for adaptation, loss and damage is far below needs. US retreat. Withdrawal from Paris and cuts in development aid weaken collective action. Funding for gender programmes was also hit by aid cuts in 2025. Fossil fuel lock-in. COP28 and COP30 could only agree on language, not a binding phase-out. Backlash. Women's rights face pushback in some states, for example in Afghanistan under the Taliban. Intersectionality. Black and post-colonial feminists (Kimberle Crenshaw, 1989; Chandra Talpade Mohanty) say "women" is not one group. Class, caste, race and place shape experience. Green colonialism? Some say climate rules (CBAM, conservation zones) bring new burdens on the South. Positive signs: the cost of solar and wind has fallen sharply, and gender parity in girls' primary schooling has largely been reached.
India on climate and on women

Climate. India's stand: climate justice , CBDR-RC and the right to development. Its per capita emissions are far below the global average. Glasgow 2021: Panchamrit and net zero by 2070 . Updated NDC (approved by Cabinet on 25 March 2026): about 47% cut in emissions intensity of GDP from the 2005 level by 2035, about 60% of installed power capacity from non-fossil sources, and an added carbon sink of 3.5-4 billion tonnes. Confirm the final numbers in the filed document. International Solar Alliance (2015), Mission LiFE (announced at COP26, 2021), and the National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023). Constitution: Article 48A and 51A(g) (42nd Amendment, 1976); Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; National Green Tribunal Act, 2010. Gender. Constitution: Articles 14, 15(3) and 39(d); 73rd and 74th Amendments reserve one-third of local seats for women. Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam (106th Amendment, 2023) reserves one-third of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats, to take effect after the next census and delimitation. India ranked 131 of 145 in the WEF Global Gender Gap Index 2026, doing best in political empowerment. Peacekeeping: India sent the first all-women UN formed police unit to Liberia (2007).
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities in climate negotiations. How has India upheld it?" "Evaluate the Paris Agreement as compared to the Kyoto Protocol." "Does climate action impinge on the right to development of the Global South?" "Explain the contribution of feminist perspectives to the study of international relations." Structure for climate: milestones (Stockholm, Rio, Kyoto, Paris), CBDR, North-South debate, recent COPs in a line each, India's stand and NDC. End with a way forward: finance, technology transfer, adaptation. Structure for gender: feminist IR (Enloe, Tickner), CEDAW and Beijing, UNSCR 1325, links to environment (Chipko, ecofeminism), Indian laws and the 106th Amendment. Keep a balanced conclusion: global goals need both justice and ambition.
Terrorism and Nuclear Proliferation
Two threats that touch India directly

Terrorism and nuclear weapons are the two security issues that bring global politics closest to India's borders. India faces cross-border terrorism from Pakistan and is surrounded by nuclear-armed neighbours, China and Pakistan. Both topics also test the international order. There is no agreed UN definition of terrorism. The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) has been called discriminatory, and its 2026 review conference ended without agreement. Expect questions that ask you to compare the global response with India's stand, to assess the NPT regime, and to link nuclear policy to deterrence (see the lesson on balance of power and deterrence). Learn the dates. Terrorism: 1999 Resolution 1267, 2001 Resolution 1373, 2006 Global Strategy. Nuclear: 1968 NPT, 1996 CTBT, 1998 Pokhran-II, 2008 civil nuclear waiver, 2026 New START expiry and NPT RevCon.
What is terrorism? The definition problem

Terrorism is violence or the threat of it against civilians, used to spread fear and push a political goal. Bruce Hoffman's Inside Terrorism (1998) stresses that it is political, aims at psychological effect and is carried out by a group or network. But there is no agreed legal definition at the UN. Disputes: whether to include state action, and whether to exempt "freedom struggles" against occupation. "One person's terrorist is another's freedom fighter" is the common quip. India proposed a Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism (CCIT) in 1996. It remains stuck in the General Assembly's Sixth Committee. Forms of terrorism Home-grown, and cross-border or state-sponsored. Religious, ethno-nationalist, left-wing, right-wing. Lone-wolf, cyber and online radicalisation. Use of drones and cryptocurrency for financing. David Rapoport's "four waves" (2004) of modern terrorism: anarchist (1880s), anti-colonial, new left, and religious (from 1979).
From 9/11 to ISIS and the Taliban's return

11 September 2001. Al-Qaeda's attacks on the US. The US launched the "war on terror" and invaded Afghanistan in October 2001. The Iraq war followed in 2003. 2014. The Islamic State (ISIS) declared a "caliphate" in Iraq and Syria. It was territorially defeated by 2019 but its franchises continue in Africa and Asia. August 2021. The Taliban retook Kabul after the US withdrawal. Concerns grew over groups like Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed finding space. Africa's Sahel has become a leading region for deadly attacks in recent years. Robert Pape's Dying to Win (2005) argued that suicide attacks respond mostly to foreign military occupation, not religion alone. Huntington's "clash of civilizations" thesis (1993; book 1996) is the contrary frame often cited. Scholars debate whether the war on terror made the world safer, or whether it fuelled radicalisation (Iraq, Guantanamo).
The global counter-terrorism architecture

UN Security Council Resolution 1267 (1999) and successors: a sanctions regime on the Taliban, then Al-Qaeda and ISIL. The list freezes assets and bans travel and arms. Listing of Masood Azhar (Jaish-e-Mohammed) was blocked by China's "technical hold" for years until it was listed on 1 May 2019. Resolution 1373 (2001) , passed after 9/11, binds all states to criminalise terror financing and deny safe haven. It set up the Counter-Terrorism Committee. Other pieces UN Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy (2006), with four pillars including root causes, prevention and human rights. The UN Office of Counter-Terrorism was set up in 2017. FATF (1989) sets rules on money-laundering and terror financing. Pakistan was on its grey list from 2018 to October 2022. Regional: SCO's RATS, the Global Counterterrorism Forum, the Quad, BRICS and G20 statements. Gaps: no definition, politicised listings, vetoes, and uneven action against state sponsors.
India and terrorism

India has been a target for decades: the 2001 Parliament attack, the Mumbai attacks of 26 November 2008 (26/11), Uri (2016) and Pulwama (2019). India's doctrine in action 2016: after Uri, "surgical strikes" across the Line of Control (29 September). 2019: after Pulwama, an air strike at Balakot (26 February). 2025: after the Pahalgam attack (22 April), India launched Operation Sindoor on 7 May. A ceasefire followed on 10 May. India declared that terror attacks would be treated as acts of war and that it would not distinguish between terrorists and their sponsors. Law. UAPA (1967, amended 2004, 2008, 2019), NIA Act 2008 (after 26/11), and NATGRID. Diplomacy. Calls for the CCIT; "zero tolerance"; pressure at FATF and the UN; extradition of 26/11 accused Tahawwur Rana from the US (April 2025). Indus Waters Treaty placed in abeyance (April 2025) as a lever, a move Pakistan rejects. Critics ask about the escalation risk between two nuclear-armed states, and whether deterrence by punishment works.
Nuclear weapons and the NPT

The NPT opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970. It was extended indefinitely in 1995. It has about 190 parties. The five nuclear-weapon states (NWS) are those that tested before 1 January 1967. They promise not to help others get weapons and to pursue disarmament (Article VI). All others promise not to acquire them, in return for access to peaceful nuclear technology (Article IV), under IAEA safeguards . Outside: India, Pakistan, Israel (undeclared) and South Sudan. North Korea announced withdrawal in 2003 and has tested since 2006. Review conferences are held every five years. The 2015, 2022 and 2026 conferences all ended without a consensus final document. The 2026 one (27 April to 22 May) ended on 22 May 2026 with no final document, the third failure in a row; Iran and disarmament were the main splits.
The wider regime and arms control

CTBT (1996): bans all nuclear test explosions. It is not in force, as key states (the US, China, and others, plus India, Pakistan and North Korea) have not ratified. India has not signed. FMCT: a proposed ban on producing fissile material. Talks are stuck at the Conference on Disarmament. Export controls: the Nuclear Suppliers Group (1975, born after India's 1974 test), the MTCR (1987), the Wassenaar Arrangement and the Australia Group. India joined the MTCR (2016), Wassenaar (2017) and the Australia Group (2018), but not the NSG, where China resists. Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (2017, in force January 2021). Nuclear states and their allies, India included, stay out. Nuclear-weapon-free zones such as Tlatelolco (Latin America) and Rarotonga. US-Russia arms control is unravelling The ABM Treaty ended in 2002 and the INF Treaty in 2019. New START (2010), the last limit on strategic forces, expired on 5 February 2026 , leaving no treaty cap for the first time in decades.
Proliferation hotspots

Iran. The 2015 JCPOA limited its programme. The US left it in 2018. Israel and the US struck Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025, and fighting broke out again from 28 February 2026. IAEA access has been badly limited, and Iranian lawmakers have talked of leaving the NPT. The situation remains fluid, so check the latest. North Korea. Six nuclear tests between 2006 and 2017. It has ballistic missiles and rejects denuclearisation. Pakistan. Its programme grew with help from the A.Q. Khan network, which also supplied Libya, Iran and North Korea. Success stories. South Africa gave up its bombs (1989-91). Ukraine, Belarus and Kazakhstan returned Soviet weapons after 1991. Libya gave up its programme in 2003. Ukraine's loss of territory after giving up weapons (the 1994 Budapest Memorandum) is cited by some as a lesson that giving up weapons is risky. The Budapest Memorandum gave assurances, not a binding guarantee. Theory. Kenneth Waltz ("The Spread of Nuclear Weapons: More May Be Better", 1981) held that more nuclear states can bring stability through deterrence. Scott Sagan (the Sagan-Waltz debate, 1995) replied that organisational accidents and bad decisions make spread dangerous.
Is the nuclear order fair?

The case against the NPT It divides the world into nuclear "haves" and "have-nots" by a date (1967), creating what India called nuclear apartheid . The five powers have not met Article VI, and modernise their arsenals. Enforcement is selective: friends such as Israel face no penalty, while rivals face sanctions. The case for it Without it, many more states might have the bomb. John F. Kennedy once feared 15 to 25 nuclear states by the 1970s. Today there are nine. The NPT set a strong norm (the "nuclear taboo", Nina Tannenwald, 2007). Wider questions Does deterrence keep peace or risk catastrophe? Is a world without nuclear weapons realistic? The TPNW says yes, nuclear states say no. Nuclear dangers also rise with new technology: hypersonic weapons, AI in command systems, and weak limits in space and cyber.
India's nuclear journey and doctrine

1974. Pokhran-I, a "peaceful nuclear explosion". The NSG was created in response. 1998. Pokhran-II (Operation Shakti, 11 and 13 May). India declared itself a nuclear-weapon state. Pakistan tested on 28 and 30 May. Doctrine. Draft doctrine in 1999; the Cabinet Committee on Security approved the operational framework in January 2003: credible minimum deterrence , no first use (against nuclear weapons, but with a right to respond to chemical or biological attack), massive retaliation if attacked, and civilian control through the Nuclear Command Authority. India-US civil nuclear deal. The 123 Agreement (signed October 2008). The NSG gave India a waiver on 6 September 2008, and India agreed on safeguards for its civilian reactors. Positions. India has long called for universal, time-bound disarmament (the Rajiv Gandhi Action Plan, 1988), but refuses to join the NPT as a non-nuclear state or sign the CTBT. It keeps a voluntary moratorium on testing. After Operation Sindoor, India's leaders said they would not accept "nuclear blackmail".
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the challenges to the global nuclear non-proliferation regime. How has India dealt with them?" "Examine the NPT as a discriminatory regime." "Terrorism is the greatest challenge to global peace, yet the world has not defined it." Discuss. "Evaluate India's response to cross-border terrorism." Structure for terrorism: the definition problem and CCIT; forms; UN framework (1267, 1373, 2006 Strategy), FATF; limits (vetoes, state sponsors); India's response (laws, strikes, diplomacy). Structure for nuclear: NPT bargain and three pillars; wider regime (CTBT, NSG, TPNW); the unravelling of arms control (New START ended); hotspots (Iran, North Korea); critiques; India's doctrine, 2008 waiver, and the way forward (dialogue, risk reduction).
Human Security
From state security to people's security

For decades 'security' meant defending borders. Human security turns the question around: secure from what, and whom? Hunger, disease, violence at home, repression and climate shocks kill more people than wars. It links Paper II's global concerns with development and rights. The UNDP Human Development Report of 1994 introduced the term and gave it wide circulation through its list of seven dimensions of security.
The 1994 UNDP idea
It grew from Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen's human development work and the end of the Cold War 'peace dividend'.
Seven categories

Economic : assured income, jobs. Food : access to enough food. Health : freedom from disease. Environmental : clean air, water, climate stability. Personal : safety from violence, crime, abuse. Community : cultural identity, protection from ethnic violence. Political : civil and political rights. Critics such as Roland Paris say the breadth of this list makes the concept hard to apply in policy.
Commission on Human Security (2003)

Co-chaired by Sadako Ogata and Amartya Sen , its report Human Security Now (2003) defined the aim as protecting the 'vital core' of all lives, through protection (top-down: states and institutions) and empowerment (bottom-up: people's capabilities). It links to Sen's capability approach. The UN General Assembly's 2012 resolution 66/290 agreed that human security should guide policy without creating new legal obligations or new rights.
Policy tracks

Canada (Lloyd Axworthy) pursued 'freedom from fear': the Ottawa landmines treaty (1997), the ICC (1998), child soldiers. Japan stressed 'freedom from want', with the UN Trust Fund for Human Security (1999). The R2P doctrine (ICISS 2001; adopted at the 2005 World Summit) covers genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity. UNGA resolution 66/290 (2012) set a common understanding.
New threats, new tests

Recent crises test the concept. Pandemics (COVID-19, 2020-22) showed health as a security matter. Climate change displaces millions and strains food and water. Cyber threats , forced migration and refugees, and conflict-linked hunger add pressure. Human security thinking says the response must combine early warning, social protection and local participation, and not rely on force alone. Note that threats are interlinked : drought raises food prices, which feed unrest.
Critiques

Too broad : Roland Paris (2001) called it a vague, 'hot air' concept that cannot guide policy. Securitisation : calling poverty a security issue can justify military or intrusive action. Intervention : used by powerful states selectively (Libya 2011, Iraq 2003). State vs people : states can be the main threat, but they also deliver protection. Realists: security remains about states and force.
Human security and other ideas

Compare: Human development (growth of capabilities), human rights (legal claims), R2P (a narrower, force-linked doctrine), feminist security (everyday safety), Sustainable Development Goals (2015). Human security adds downside risk and vulnerability to development thinking. Human security is broader than the Responsibility to Protect (2005 World Summit), which applies only to four mass atrocity crimes: genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity.
India's position

India accepts people-centred development but is wary of the language of intervention and R2P, stressing sovereignty . Domestic expressions: MGNREGA (2005), National Food Security Act (2013), Right to Education (2009), Ayushman Bharat, disaster management, and Maoist and insurgency-affected area policies. India's COVID vaccine diplomacy (Vaccine Maitri, 2021) is a human-security story at the international level.
How UPSC asks this

"What is human security? How does it differ from traditional security?" "Critically examine the concept of human security and R2P." "Assess India's approach to human security." Structure: origin, seven dimensions, 2003 report, policy tracks, critique, India. India's own tools include Ayushman Bharat (2018) for health cover and the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (2014) for bank access, which are often cited as human security measures.
Parties, Pressure Groups and Movements Compared
How citizens reach the state

In a large society, people cannot govern directly. They act through representatives , and they organise through parties , pressure groups and social movements . These are the main channels linking society to the state. This lesson compares the three across countries. It also prepares you for Paper I Section B (Indian party system, pressure groups, social movements), where the same ideas get applied to India. The comparative questions are usually of this kind: "How do electoral systems shape party systems?", "Distinguish pressure groups from parties", "How are new social movements different from old ones?" You need a few anchor thinkers: Pitkin, Duverger, Sartori, Lijphart, Bentley and Truman, Schmitter, Tilly, Touraine and Melucci. As usual, close with India and with the present: declining trust in parties, populism, digital campaigns and street protest.
What is representation?

Hanna Pitkin, in The Concept of Representation (1967), separated four meanings. Formalistic: authorisation by elections, and accountability to voters. Descriptive: the legislature mirrors society (women, minorities). Symbolic: the leader or flag stands for the people. Substantive: representatives act in the interests of the represented. The old question: is the representative a delegate (follows instructions) or a trustee (uses judgement)? Edmund Burke's speech to the electors of Bristol (1774) is the classic trustee argument. There is also the mandate view (parties win a programme) and the responsible party government model. Issues: whether women and minorities need reserved seats (see Anne Phillips, The Politics of Presence , 1995); how direct democracy (referendums, citizens' assemblies) can complement representation.
Electoral systems and party systems

Maurice Duverger, Political Parties (1951), put forward what are called Duverger's law and hypothesis: single-member plurality voting tends toward a two-party system; proportional representation tends toward multi-partism. It is a tendency, not a law. India has FPTP but many parties because of regional concentration of support. Arend Lijphart, Patterns of Democracy (1999), contrasted majoritarian democracies (the UK) with consensus democracies (Switzerland, Belgium), using ten dimensions including the party system and electoral rules. Germany uses a mixed system (mixed-member proportional) with a 5% threshold for list seats.
Types of parties

Cadre (elite) party versus mass party (Duverger, 1951). Cadre parties are run by notables. Mass parties recruit large paying memberships (socialist parties). Catch-all party (Otto Kirchheimer, 1966): parties drop firm ideology to win every group. Cartel party (Richard Katz and Peter Mair, 1995): major parties merge with the state, share public funding and limit competition. Programmatic, clientelistic, charismatic parties. Herbert Kitschelt studied clientelism and programme. Michels's iron law of oligarchy (1911): all parties tend to be run by an inner circle. Vanguard party (Lenin): a disciplined party of professional revolutionaries, the model for communist states. Functions of parties Aggregating interests, recruiting leaders, organising government, mobilising voters, setting policy agendas, and linking people to the state. Compare the Communist Party of China (a party-state, nearly 100 million members) with the Republican and Democratic parties of the US, which are loose, decentralised electoral machines.
Party systems: Sartori's classification

Giovanni Sartori, Parties and Party Systems (1976), classified systems by the number of relevant parties and their ideological distance. His main types One-party (China, Cuba). Hegemonic party (others are allowed but cannot compete, as in Mexico under the PRI until 2000). Predominant party (one party wins repeatedly in free elections, such as Congress in India until 1967 and the LDP in Japan for most of 1955-93). Two-party (the UK, US). Limited (moderate) pluralism (3 to 5 parties, Germany). Polarised pluralism (many parties and extremes: Weimar Germany, Fourth Republic France, Chile before 1973). Atomised. Counting rule: only parties with coalition or blackmail potential are "relevant". Critique: it counts parties without regard to voter strength. Laakso and Taagepera (1979) proposed the "effective number of parties" index.
Pressure groups: types and theories

A pressure (interest) group tries to influence government policy without seeking to govern. Parties contest elections; groups do not. Sectional (interest) groups: trade unions, business chambers, professional bodies. Cause (promotional) groups: Amnesty, Greenpeace. Insider groups have access to officials; outsider groups lobby from outside (Wyn Grant). Anomic and associational groups (Almond): spontaneous protest versus organised. Theories Pluralism: Arthur Bentley, The Process of Government (1908); David Truman, The Governmental Process (1951); Robert Dahl: politics is bargaining between many groups, so power is dispersed. Collective action: Mancur Olson (1965): small, concentrated interests organise better than large, diffuse ones. Neo-pluralism: Charles Lindblom: business has a "privileged position". Corporatism: Philippe Schmitter (1974): the state licenses a few peak associations and bargains with them. Marxist: business dominates.
Pressure groups compared

United States (pluralist). Many competing lobbies, strong access through Congress and committees. Political action committees and super PACs, after Citizens United v. FEC (2010), raise vast sums. The Lobbying Disclosure Act (1995) requires registration. Austria, Sweden, Germany (corporatist). Peak organisations of labour and employers help set wages and social policy with the government. The EU uses "social partners" too. European Union. Thousands of lobbyists in Brussels target the Commission and Parliament. A transparency register exists. China and other one-party states (state corporatism). Groups exist as state-sponsored associations (such as the All-China Federation of Trade Unions), not independent bargainers. Developing countries. Groups often work through patron-client networks, caste, ethnic or religious associations, and direct protest. Common concerns: unequal resources, money in politics, and regulatory capture, where industry shapes its regulator.
Social movements: theories

A social movement is sustained collective action by people outside formal institutions, to push for or resist change. Charles Tilly and Sidney Tarrow call it "contentious politics". Collective behaviour (older view): movements arise from strain and grievance. Resource mobilisation (McCarthy and Zald, 1977): organisation, money and leadership matter, not just grievance. Political process (Doug McAdam, 1982; Tarrow): movements grow when political opportunities open. Framing (David Snow): how issues are given meaning. New social movements (Alain Touraine, Alberto Melucci, Claus Offe): since the 1960s, movements for peace, environment, gender and identity focus on quality of life and identity rather than class and wages. They are often decentralised, middle-class led and use cultural methods. Old versus new Old: labour, class-based, hierarchical, economic aims. New: identity or values, networked, symbolic and lifestyle aims.
Movements around the world

US civil rights movement (1950s-60s): marches, boycotts, the Civil Rights Act (1964). Solidarity in Poland (1980): a trade union that became a mass movement and helped end communist rule in 1989. Greens in Germany (party formed 1980) grew from environmental and peace movements. Arab Spring (2010-11): social media and street protest toppled rulers in Tunisia and Egypt, but only Tunisia held a democratic course for some years. Occupy (2011) and Black Lives Matter (2013; mass protests in 2020). Fridays for Future (2018): school climate strikes started by Greta Thunberg. #MeToo (2017 viral). Digital media lowers the cost of mobilisation, but Zeynep Tufekci's Twitter and Tear Gas (2017) notes that fast-built movements may lack the organisation to bargain. States respond with surveillance and internet shutdowns. Movements can turn into parties (Greens, Podemos in Spain, India's AAP) or push existing parties .
A crisis of representation?

Falling trust and membership. Party membership has fallen across Europe. Russell Dalton writes of partisan dealignment . Populism. Cas Mudde defines populism as a thin ideology pitting the "pure people" against a "corrupt elite". It has risen on both left and right in Europe, the US, Latin America and elsewhere. Polarisation and fragmentation of party systems, and online echo chambers. Money and lobbying distort representation. Under-representation of women and minorities. Women are about a quarter of legislators worldwide (Inter-Parliamentary Union). Authoritarian use. One-party regimes use "consultative" groups to look participatory. Democratic backsliding often starts by weakening opposition parties, media and courts (see the democracy lesson). Reform ideas: proportional or ranked-choice voting, party finance rules, quotas, citizen assemblies, and digital participation.
India in comparative view

Electoral system. FPTP in single-member constituencies, yet a multi-party system with strong regional parties. The Election Commission recognises national and state parties by vote share and seats. Under the ECI order of 2023 the national parties are the BJP, INC, AAP, BSP, CPI(M) and NPP. Party system phases. The Congress dominance (Kothari's "Congress system"), the coalition era (1989-2014), BJP dominance (282 seats in 2014, 303 in 2019), and a return to coalition politics in 2024 (BJP 240; NDA 293; Congress 99). Defection law. 52nd Amendment (1985), Tenth Schedule; tightened by the 91st Amendment (2003). Money. The Supreme Court struck down the electoral bonds scheme in February 2024. Pressure groups. FICCI (1927), CII, ASSOCHAM; unions (AITUC 1920, INTUC); farmer groups; caste and religious associations; NGOs under the FCRA. Movements. Chipko, the Narmada Bachao Andolan (1985), the India Against Corruption movement (2011) that led to AAP (2012), and the farmers' protest of 2020-21 that led to repeal of three farm laws in November 2021. Representation. Reserved seats for SC and ST; one-third seats for women in local bodies (73rd and 74th Amendments) and, in the 106th Amendment (2023), in Parliament once delimitation follows the next census.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine the relationship between electoral systems and party systems." "Distinguish between pressure groups and political parties. How do they influence policy?" "Compare old and new social movements." "Parties are in decline and movements are on the rise." Discuss. Structure: define representation (Pitkin). Electoral systems and Duverger's law with a small table. Party types and Sartori's systems. Pressure groups: types, theories (pluralism versus corporatism) and country examples. Movements: theories and old versus new, with examples. Then a critique on the crisis of representation. End with India: FPTP with many parties, the 2024 coalition outcome, FICCI and the farmers' protest. Use a three-column table (party, pressure group, movement) to compare aims, methods and accountability.
Globalisation: Developed and Developing Responses
A force that everyone argues about

Globalisation is the process by which economies, societies and politics become more closely linked across borders. Trade, finance, technology, ideas and people all move faster and farther than before. It is one of the most-asked topics in Paper II. The question is nearly always the same: does globalisation help or hurt? And for whom: developed states, developing states, or both? The syllabus asks you to compare developed and developing responses . The best answers do three things: define the term with a scholar, show the debate (hyperglobalists, sceptics, transformationalists), and give a balanced verdict with Indian examples. The topic has also changed fast. In 2025-26 the US raised tariffs sharply, the Supreme Court struck down part of them, and talk of "deglobalisation" grew. Your answer should show you know the story did not end in 2008.
What is globalisation?

Anthony Giddens, in The Consequences of Modernity (1990), described it as the intensification of worldwide social relations that link distant places, so that local events are shaped by events far away. David Held, Anthony McGrew, David Goldblatt and Jonathan Perraton, Global Transformations (1999), defined it as growth in the extent, intensity, speed and impact of global connections. Its dimensions Economic: trade, investment, multinational firms, global finance, supply chains. Political: rise of international organisations and global rules (WTO, IMF, UN), and a debate on state sovereignty. Cultural: global media, brands, language, migration. Technological: internet, containers, digital platforms and, today, AI. Ecological and health: climate change, pandemics. Marshall McLuhan's "global village" (1962) is the early image. Roland Robertson ( Globalization , 1992) added glocalisation : global things adapt to local settings.
Three schools

Held and McGrew's work is the source of this three-way split. Hyperglobalists see a new age where the nation-state is obsolete. Kenichi Ohmae, The Borderless World (1990) and The End of the Nation State (1995). Thomas Friedman, The Lexus and the Olive Tree (1999) and The World Is Flat (2005). Sceptics say integration was as high before 1914 and is mostly regional. Paul Hirst and Grahame Thompson, Globalization in Question (1996). Transformationalists say globalisation is real but is reshaping, not ending, state power.
The case for: gains from openness

Supporters point to evidence. Jagdish Bhagwati , In Defense of Globalization (2004): trade and open markets lift incomes and cut poverty, and globalisation has a "human face" when combined with good policy. Friedman : countries must wear a "Golden Straitjacket", meaning free-market rules that reward discipline and punish bad policy. East Asia (South Korea, Taiwan, then China) grew fast through exports. Extreme poverty worldwide fell sharply from 1990. The Washington Consensus The term was coined by John Williamson in 1989 for ten policies: fiscal discipline, trade liberalisation, privatisation, deregulation, openness to FDI and others. The IMF and World Bank used them as conditions for loans ( structural adjustment programmes ) in the 1980s-90s. The WTO was set up in 1995 to lock in the rules. China joined the WTO in December 2001 and became the "factory of the world".
The case against: costs and discontents

Joseph Stiglitz , Globalization and Its Discontents (2002): IMF policies and the way markets were opened hurt poor countries. He cites the 1997 Asian crisis. Dani Rodrik , The Globalization Paradox (2011): the trilemma . You cannot have deep global integration, national sovereignty and democratic politics together. Pick two. Dependency and world-system writers (Amin, Wallerstein): globalisation deepens core-periphery inequality. Inequality. Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2013 in French; English 2014) documents rising wealth concentration. The "elephant curve" (Lakner and Milanovic, 2013; Milanovic's Global Inequality , 2016) suggests the lower middle class in rich countries gained little. Environment and culture. Race-to-the-bottom worries, McDonaldisation (George Ritzer, 1993) and Benjamin Barber's Jihad vs. McWorld (1995). State retreat. Susan Strange, The Retreat of the State (1996).
How developed countries responded

Rich states wrote the rules and gained, but not evenly inside each country. Early response: push free trade and capital mobility. The US, EU and Japan shaped GATT and the WTO. They kept protection in sensitive areas, such as farm subsidies. Costs at home. Factory jobs moved to Asia. The 2008 financial crisis spread through global banks and hurt many. Backlash. Brexit (the vote in June 2016, exit on 31 January 2020), the 2016 US election, and the rise of populist parties. The slogan became "take back control". New tools. Industrial policy, such as the US CHIPS Act and Inflation Reduction Act (2022), "friend-shoring", export controls on technology, and sanctions after Russia's invasion of Ukraine (2022). Tariffs. In 2025 the US raised tariffs sharply. In February 2026 the US Supreme Court ruled in Learning Resources v. Trump that the emergency law (IEEPA) did not allow tariffs. The administration then used other laws, such as Section 122 and Section 301. The paradox: the main architect of globalisation is now its biggest doubter.
How developing countries responded

There is no single "developing world" response. East Asia: managed openness South Korea and Taiwan used a developmental state : subsidies, export targets and protection of young industries, then opened up. China did similarly after 1978, with special economic zones. Latin America and Africa: hard lessons The 1980s debt crisis brought IMF programmes and austerity. Many countries became more reliant on raw-material exports. The 1990s brought mixed results. Collective bargaining Developing countries formed the G-77 (1964) and pressed for NIEO. In the WTO, they formed blocs like the G-20 on agriculture at Cancun (2003) to resist farm subsidies. BRICS and the New Development Bank (2014) are newer efforts. Common features: concern for policy space , food security, technology transfer and fair rules. Today many ask for reform of the IMF quota system and debt relief, and for climate finance.
Rise, peak and slowdown

Commentators speak of slowbalisation : trade grew slower than GDP after 2008, though digital flows kept rising. The COVID-19 pandemic (2020) exposed fragile supply chains. War in Ukraine and tension in West Asia added shocks. The WTO's March 2026 outlook put world merchandise trade growth for 2026 at about 1.9 percent, down from about 4.6 percent in 2025, a year boosted by importers rushing ahead of higher tariffs. The multilateral system is under strain. At the WTO's 14th ministerial conference in Yaounde (March 2026), members failed to agree on extending the moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions, and the Appellate Body remained unrestored.
India and globalisation

India's path shows a late-but-strong embrace. 1991 crisis. A balance-of-payments emergency, with foreign exchange reserves covering only a few weeks of imports. Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh began LPG reforms (liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation). In July 1991 the rupee was devalued, industrial licensing was largely scrapped, and FDI rules were eased. Results. A services and IT boom, higher growth, and a larger middle class. India was a founder-member of the WTO (1995). Worries. Farm distress, jobs, jobless growth, and inequality. Stance at the WTO. India defends farm subsidies and public stockholding for food security, as a developing-country voice. New turn. "Make in India" (2014), Atmanirbhar Bharat (2020) and PLI schemes aim at manufacturing. At the same time India signs trade pacts. The India-UK CETA came into force on 15 July 2026, the India-EU FTA was concluded in January 2026, and India and the US announced an interim trade framework in February 2026, after tariffs on Indian goods had risen to 50% in 2025. Check the latest status before quoting rates.
How UPSC asks this

"Globalisation has strengthened rather than weakened the nation-state." Discuss. "Examine the responses of developed and developing countries to globalisation." "Is the world moving towards deglobalisation? Comment." "Discuss the impact of globalisation on developing countries with special reference to India." Structure: define (Giddens, Held), list dimensions. Present the three schools in a box. Give gains (Bhagwati) and costs (Stiglitz, Rodrik's trilemma, Piketty). Separate developed and developing responses with 3 points each, including backlash, tariffs, East Asian model and G-77. Add the current picture: slowbalisation, 2025-26 tariffs, WTO MC14. End with India: 1991, WTO stance, Atmanirbhar Bharat plus FTAs. Finish with a balanced judgement: globalisation is being reshaped, not reversed.
Idealism and Liberal Institutionalism
Where IR theory begins

International Relations (IR) theory starts with a simple question: why do states fight, and can they ever live in lasting peace? Idealism says yes. It grew out of the horror of the First World War (1914-18), which killed about ten million soldiers. Its leaders believed war could be prevented by law, public opinion and a world organisation. Its modern descendant is liberal institutionalism , also called neoliberal institutionalism. It says states can cooperate even in anarchy, if institutions make cooperation easier. This is the opening topic of Paper II Section A. Examiners ask about the idealist-realist debate, Wilson and the League, E.H. Carr's critique, the democratic peace, and Keohane and Nye on interdependence. Tie each of these to a year and a book, and you will score well.
What liberals believe

All liberal IR thought rests on a few shared beliefs. Human nature is not fixed in conflict. People can reason and cooperate. War is not natural. It comes from bad institutions, secret diplomacy and autocratic rulers, and it can be reduced. Harmony of interests. Nations gain more from trade and peace than from conquest. Law and organisation can tame anarchy. International law, arbitration and a standing body can replace the "law of the jungle". Public opinion and democracy restrain war. Realists reject nearly all of this. That clash is called the first great debate of IR, held in the 1930s and 1940s between idealists and realists. Note the label. "Idealism" was a name given by critics, mostly by Carr. The idealists thought of themselves as practical reformers.
Kant's Perpetual Peace (1795)

Immanuel Kant wrote Perpetual Peace: A Philosophical Sketch (1795). It is the oldest source of liberal IR theory. Kant's three definitive articles The civil constitution of every state should be republican . Citizens, not kings, decide on war, so they will hesitate. The law of nations should rest on a federation of free states . This is not a world state but a league of peace. Cosmopolitan right is limited to universal hospitality. Strangers must not be treated as enemies. Kant also argued that trade would slowly bind nations together. His thinking shapes the democratic peace thesis and the idea of a league of nations. Other early liberals: Hugo Grotius ( De Jure Belli ac Pacis , 1625) on international law, Jeremy Bentham on a code of international law, and Richard Cobden on free trade as the path to peace.
Wilson, the Fourteen Points and the League

US President Woodrow Wilson is the face of idealism. On 8 January 1918 he announced the Fourteen Points : open diplomacy, freedom of the seas, free trade, arms reduction, fair settlement of colonial claims, self-determination, and a general association of nations. The League of Nations was set up in 1920 with its seat at Geneva. Its Covenant was part of the Treaty of Versailles. Article 10 protected members' territorial integrity. Article 16 provided economic and military sanctions against an aggressor. The League was built on collective security : an attack on one is an attack on all.
Why the League failed

The League had real weaknesses. The United States never joined . The Senate refused to ratify the Treaty of Versailles in 1919-20. Unanimity rule. Council decisions needed everyone's consent. No army. Sanctions depended on members' will. Germany and the Soviet Union were outside at first. Germany joined in 1926 and left in 1933. The USSR joined in 1934 and was expelled in 1939. Then came the tests. Manchuria (1931). Japan seized it. The Lytton Commission condemned Japan, and Japan left the League in 1933. Abyssinia (1935). Italy invaded Ethiopia. Sanctions were weak and oil was never banned. Other signs of failure: the Rhineland (1936) and Munich (1938). The Kellogg-Briand Pact (1928) had outlawed war as a tool of policy, but it had no enforcement. The League formally ended in 1946. Its lessons shaped the UN Charter.
E.H. Carr's attack

E.H. Carr, a British historian and diplomat, wrote The Twenty Years' Crisis, 1919-1939 (1939). It is the founding text of modern realism and the main attack on idealism. Carr's main points Idealists were utopians . They mistook wishes for facts. The " harmony of interests " is not real. It is an ideology of the satisfied powers who want to keep the status quo. Power and morality both matter. Politics needs both utopia and reality. Ideas of international "justice" often reflect the interest of the strong. The Second World War seemed to prove Carr right. For three decades after it, realism dominated IR, led by Hans Morgenthau ( Politics Among Nations , 1948). Fair note: Carr did not reject morality. He said pure realism, like pure idealism, is sterile.
Complex interdependence

Liberalism revived in the 1970s. Oil shocks, multinational firms and the spread of trade made states depend on each other. Robert Keohane and Joseph Nye wrote Power and Interdependence (1977). Complex interdependence has three features Multiple channels link societies: governments, firms, NGOs, individuals. States are not the only actors. No fixed hierarchy of issues. Security does not always come first. Trade or climate can top the agenda. Military force is less useful among interdependent states. They also showed that interdependence is unequal. Sensitivity is how fast a change in one country hurts another. Vulnerability is how costly it is to escape. The less vulnerable party has more bargaining power. Nye later coined soft power ( Bound to Lead , 1990).
Keohane and the institutionalist argument

Keohane's After Hegemony: Cooperation and Discord in the World Political Economy (1984) is the key text of neoliberal institutionalism . His puzzle: if realists say cooperation depends on a dominant power (hegemonic stability), why did cooperation continue after US dominance declined in the 1970s? His answer: international regimes . Stephen Krasner's definition (1982-83) of regimes: sets of principles, norms, rules and decision-making procedures around which actors' expectations converge. GATT and the IMF are examples. What institutions do Cut transaction costs of making deals. Share information and reduce cheating. Create repeated games , so a state values its reputation. Robert Axelrod's The Evolution of Cooperation (1984) showed "tit for tat" works in repeated dealings. Keohane accepts the realist base: anarchy, and states as rational actors. He argues only that cooperation is still possible.
Democratic peace and commercial peace

Other liberal arguments focus on the type of state. Democratic peace. Michael Doyle, in "Kant, Liberal Legacies, and Foreign Affairs" (1983), noted that liberal democracies almost never fight each other. Bruce Russett's Grasping the Democratic Peace (1993) tested it with data. Commercial peace. Trade makes war costly. This goes back to Montesquieu, Cobden and Norman Angell's The Great Illusion (1910). End of history. Francis Fukuyama's essay (1989) and book (1992) saw liberal democracy as the final form of government. Andrew Moravcsik (1997) built a general liberal theory : state preferences come from domestic society, not just from the international structure. Critiques Democracies do fight non-democracies (Iraq 2003). Mansfield and Snyder (1995) found democratising states are war-prone. Trade did not stop war in 1914. Realists see only chance, or US power behind the "peace".
Neorealists versus neoliberals

The 1980s-90s "neo-neo debate" (David Baldwin edited Neorealism and Neoliberalism , 1993) was narrower than the first debate. Both sides accept anarchy and rational, self-interested states. The gap: relative versus absolute gains . Joseph Grieco (1988) argued that states ask "who gains more?" and so fear cooperation. Liberals say states ask "do I gain?" John Mearsheimer's "The False Promise of International Institutions" (1994-95) says institutions have little independent effect. Liberals reply with evidence from trade, arms control and the EU.
Nehru's idealism and India's liberal streak

India was an original member of the League of Nations (1920) and a founding member of the UN (1945). Jawaharlal Nehru brought a strong idealist tone: peaceful coexistence, Panchsheel (1954), anti-colonialism and support for disarmament. India is among the largest contributors of troops to UN peacekeeping. It champions the Global South inside the UN and the WTO. The liberal side shows up today in: The International Solar Alliance , launched with France at the Paris climate summit in 2015. India's G20 presidency in 2023. The New Delhi Declaration was adopted by consensus, and the African Union became a permanent member. Its theme, "One Earth, One Family, One Future", draws on Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam . But India is also a realist. After the 1962 war with China and the 1998 Pokhran tests, it blends the two traditions. It is wary of institutions that limit its sovereignty, such as the NPT.
How UPSC asks this

"Critically examine the idealist approach to international relations." "Explain liberal institutionalism. How does it differ from neorealism?" "Does the democratic peace thesis hold? Discuss." "Why did the League of Nations fail?" Structure: start with the WWI context and Kant's roots. Then Wilson and the League, with 3 reasons for failure. Add Carr's critique. Move to the modern turn: Keohane and Nye (complex interdependence), regimes and cooperation, democratic peace. Give the neo-neo debate in a short table. Finish with India: Nehru's idealism, UN peacekeeping and the ISA, and its limits. Show balance. Say idealism did not vanish. It returned in new form.
Realism and Neorealism
The most-asked IR theory

Realism is the oldest and most dominant theory of international relations. For most of the Cold War it was the default way to read world politics. UPSC asks about it nearly every year, often in comparison with liberalism, Marxism or constructivism. The favourite topics are Morgenthau's six principles, Waltz's structural theory, the security dilemma, balance of power, and the split between defensive and offensive realism. The core claim is short: the world is anarchic (no authority above states), states are the main actors, and they seek power and security . So conflict is normal and cooperation is fragile. This lesson covers classical realism (Morgenthau), neorealism (Waltz), their variants and the critics. Learn the thinkers with book and year, and add Kautilya for the Indian link.
The five realist assumptions

Most realists share five ideas. Statism. The state is the key actor. Firms, NGOs and institutions matter less. Anarchy. No world government exists. Each state must rely on itself. This is called self-help . Survival. The first goal of any state is to survive. Rationality. States weigh costs and benefits and act to protect their interests. Power. Power, especially military power, decides outcomes. Power is a means for some, and a goal for others. Realists also treat the national interest as the guide to foreign policy, and morality as a limited guide. The roots are old: Thucydides on the Athenians and the Melians, Machiavelli's The Prince (written 1513), Hobbes's Leviathan (1651) with its state of nature, and Kautilya's Arthashastra .
Morgenthau and classical realism

Hans Morgenthau, a German-born American scholar, wrote Politics Among Nations: The Struggle for Power and Peace (1948). It made realism the leading IR theory. An earlier book, Scientific Man vs. Power Politics (1946), set out his case. For Morgenthau, politics is governed by laws rooted in human nature . Humans have an urge to dominate (animus dominandi). So states pursue power. His six principles (in short) Politics follows objective laws rooted in human nature. Interest defined as power is the key signpost. Interest is not fixed forever. Its content changes with context. Universal moral principles cannot be applied abstractly to states. A nation's moral aspirations are not the moral laws of the universe. The political sphere is autonomous, like law or economics. He saw balance of power, international law and diplomacy as the main limits on power. Reinhold Niebuhr ( Moral Man and Immoral Society , 1932) and George Kennan (containment, 1947) belong to the same school.
Waltz and neorealism

Kenneth Waltz wanted a scientific theory. In Man, the State, and War (1959) he asked: where are the causes of war? He listed three images: human nature, the state, and the international system. He found the third the deepest. Theory of International Politics (1979) built neorealism , also called structural realism . Power is not an end. States want security. Behaviour is shaped by structure , not by human nature. Three parts of structure Ordering principle: anarchy. Differentiation of units: states are alike in function, whatever their ideology. Distribution of capabilities: how many great powers exist (polarity). Only the third changes. Waltz argued bipolarity was more stable than multipolarity, because fewer actors means fewer miscalculations. He also held that the system makes states balance against strong powers and copy each other's success (socialisation).
From classical realism to neorealism

The table shows the main shift. Classical realists look at why humans seek power . Neorealists look at how the system forces states to behave . For neorealists, even peaceful leaders are pushed into rivalry, because anarchy makes every state's security uncertain. This links to the security dilemma , covered next.
The security dilemma

John Herz coined the security dilemma in 1950 ("Idealist Internationalism and the Security Dilemma"). Robert Jervis developed it in "Cooperation under the Security Dilemma" (1978). The idea: in anarchy, steps a state takes to feel safe make others feel unsafe. They respond in kind. All end up less secure. Example: State A builds missiles for defence. State B reads them as a threat, builds its own, and so on. This is an arms race or spiral , even though neither side wants war. Jervis said the dilemma is sharper when weapons are hard to tell apart as offensive or defensive, and when offence has the advantage. It is milder when defence is easier. Nuclear weapons, in his view, make conquest suicidal, which softens it. The dilemma explains why good intentions are not enough: states cannot read each other's minds.
Defensive and offensive realism

Defensive realism Waltz, Jervis, Stephen Walt, Jack Snyder. States want enough power for security . Too much power triggers balancing against them. So moderate, status-quo strategies pay. Walt's The Origins of Alliances (1987) says states balance against threat , not just power. Offensive realism John Mearsheimer, The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (2001). Great powers can never be sure of rivals' intentions, so the safest course is to become the strongest. The ideal is to be a regional hegemon , with no rival nearby. Oceans limit global hegemony (the "stopping power of water"). Mearsheimer predicted a rising China would clash with the US, as it would seek regional hegemony in Asia. Other variants: neoclassical realism (Gideon Rose, 1998) adds domestic politics and leaders' perceptions; hegemonic stability and power transition theories by Robert Gilpin ( War and Change in World Politics , 1981) and A.F.K. Organski (1958) say war can come when a rising power catches up with the leader.
What critics say

Missed the end of the Cold War. Neorealism did not predict the Soviet collapse (1991) or its peaceful end. Liberals point to institutions, trade and the democratic peace, which realism underrates. Constructivists (Wendt, 1992) say anarchy has no fixed logic: "Anarchy is what states make of it". Identities change interests. Marxists and Robert Cox (1981): realism is a "problem-solving theory" that defends the existing order. Richard Ashley called neorealism a "poverty" of ideas (1984). Feminists (J. Ann Tickner, Gender in International Relations , 1992): the realist idea of power and "human nature" is male-coded. English School (Hedley Bull): states form an "international society" with shared rules. Unfalsifiable. Any outcome can be explained after the fact. Defenders say realism is a parsimonious theory that still explains great-power rivalry well, and the return of power politics in Ukraine and Asia supports it.
Kautilya and Indian realism

Kautilya's Arthashastra (c. 4th century BCE to 3rd century CE in its present form) is India's classic realist text. Mandala theory The vijigishu (would-be conqueror) is at the centre. His neighbour is the natural enemy ( ari ). The neighbour's neighbour is a natural friend. Further rings include the middle ( madhyama ) and neutral ( udasina ) powers. Six-fold policy (shadgunya) Peace ( sandhi ), war ( vigraha ), neutrality ( asana ), marching ( yana ), alliance ( samsraya ), and double policy ( dvaidhibhava ). Modern India shows realist moves too. Pokhran-II (May 1998) was a response to the China-Pakistan threat. India's 2003 nuclear doctrine adopted no first use and credible minimum deterrence. India balances China through the Quad , defence ties with the US, France and Russia, and border infrastructure. Its policy of strategic autonomy is a hedging strategy that realists would recognise.
How UPSC asks this

"Neorealism has been successful in explaining the persistence of conflict but not cooperation." Discuss. "Compare classical realism with neorealism." "Explain the security dilemma and its relevance to South Asia." "Is Kautilya's mandala theory relevant to understanding modern Indian foreign policy?" Structure: define realism with its five assumptions. Give Morgenthau (1948) and his principles. Move to Waltz (1959, 1979), with the three parts of structure. Add defensive versus offensive realism with Mearsheimer (2001). Then critiques: Cold War's end, liberal and constructivist replies. End with India: Kautilya, Pokhran-II, strategic autonomy. A simple table comparing classical and neorealism earns marks.
Marxist and Dependency Approaches
The view from the bottom of the system

Realists see states competing for power. Liberals see states cooperating. Marxists ask a different question: who gains from the international system, and who pays? For Marxist and dependency thinkers, world politics is shaped by capitalism and class . The rich "core" grows rich by drawing wealth from the poor "periphery". Rivalry between states is a side effect of competition between capitalists. This approach matters for the exam because it explains imperialism, underdevelopment, the Global South's demands (NIEO, UNCTAD) and India's own colonial experience. It is also the best theory to cite when asked about inequality in globalisation. Expect questions on Lenin, Wallerstein's world-system, dependency theory (Frank, Prebisch, Amin), and neo-Gramscian ideas (Cox). A critique card at the end shows you can weigh the theory.
The Marxist starting point

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels ( The Communist Manifesto , 1848) argued that history moves through class struggle . Capitalism spreads across the globe to find markets, cheap labour and raw materials: "it creates a world after its own image". Marx did not write a full theory of international relations. Later Marxists did. Their shared ideas: Economics comes first. The base (the mode of production) shapes politics, the state and war. The state is a tool of the ruling class (or at least tied to it). The unit of analysis is class and the world capitalist system, not the nation-state. Capitalism produces inequality between and within countries. Real change needs a change in the system. Reform within it is limited.
Hobson, Lenin and imperialism

J.A. Hobson, a British liberal economist, wrote Imperialism: A Study (1902). He said imperialism arose from underconsumption at home. Rich investors needed outlets abroad. V.I. Lenin took this up in Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (1916). It is the central Marxist text on IR. Lenin's argument Competitive capitalism turns into monopoly capitalism . Banks and industry merge into finance capital . Rich countries have surplus capital. They export capital to colonies, where profits are higher. Cartels and great powers divide the world . Capitalism develops unevenly, so rivals demand a redivision. So WWI was an inter-imperialist war . Imperialism also gives the working class of the core a share ("labour aristocracy"), which delays revolution. Others: Rosa Luxemburg ( The Accumulation of Capital , 1913), Nikolai Bukharin ( Imperialism and World Economy , 1915). Karl Kautsky disagreed and predicted "ultra-imperialism": a peaceful joint rule by the great powers.
Dependency theory: Prebisch to Frank

After 1945, Latin American thinkers asked why the poor stayed poor. Raul Prebisch, head of the UN Economic Commission for Latin America (ECLA) and later first Secretary-General of UNCTAD (1964), and Hans Singer argued in 1949-50 that the terms of trade turn against primary exporters. Prices of raw materials fall relative to manufactures. Their remedy was import-substitution industrialisation . Andre Gunder Frank In "The Development of Underdevelopment" (1966) and Capitalism and Underdevelopment in Latin America (1967), Frank said poverty is not a stage before development. It is created by integration into the world market. He described a chain of metropolis and satellite , where surplus flows upward. His remedy: break links with the core. Samir Amin An Egyptian economist. Unequal Development (1973) described a periphery with a distorted economy, built to serve the core. He called for "delinking". Paul Baran ( The Political Economy of Growth , 1957) and Walter Rodney ( How Europe Underdeveloped Africa , 1972) share this line.
Cardoso and Galtung: softer versions

Not all dependency thinkers wanted a full break from the world market. Fernando Henrique Cardoso and Enzo Faletto , Dependency and Development in Latin America (written 1967-69; English edition 1979), argued that dependency does not rule out growth. They described associated-dependent development : local elites, multinationals and the state build industry together, but on terms set by the core. Cardoso later served as President of Brazil (1995-2002). Johan Galtung , "A Structural Theory of Imperialism" (1971), said the world is a set of centres and peripheries, and each country has its own centre (the elite) and periphery. Imperialism rests on a harmony of interest between the elite in the centre and the elite in the periphery, and on a disharmony between the masses. This is why dependency is called structural : it is a relationship, not just a policy.
Wallerstein's world-system

Immanuel Wallerstein, The Modern World-System (vol. 1, 1974), argues that since the "long sixteenth century" there has been one capitalist world-economy . It has a single division of labour, many states and no world empire. Core: strong states, advanced industry, high wages. Gets the surplus. Periphery: weak states, raw materials, low-wage labour. Semi-periphery: in between. It gets exploited by the core and exploits the periphery. It keeps the system stable. Countries can move between zones, but the system as a whole keeps the structure. Hegemons (Dutch, British, American) rise and fall in long cycles. Wallerstein said the system would eventually reach a crisis.
Gramsci, Cox and critical theory

Antonio Gramsci ( Prison Notebooks , 1929-35) stressed hegemony : ruling classes keep power through consent, culture and ideas, not only force. Robert Cox , "Social Forces, States and World Orders" (1981), used this in IR. His famous line: "Theory is always for someone and for some purpose". He split theory into problem-solving (accepts the order, as realism does) and critical (asks how the order came about and how it can change). Cox's three forces Material capabilities, ideas, and institutions. They combine into a historic bloc . A world order becomes hegemonic when its ideas are widely accepted, as US-led liberalism after 1945 was. International organisations help spread them. Others in this line: Stephen Gill, on the "new constitutionalism" of free-market rules, and the Frankfurt School thinkers Adorno, Horkheimer and Habermas. In IR, Andrew Linklater ( Men and Citizens , 1982) took critical theory to questions of community and emancipation.
Strengths and weaknesses

What it explains well Imperialism, colonial extraction and unequal trade. Why many poor states stay stuck in raw-material exports. Debt, structural adjustment, and the demand for NIEO. The link between economic power and political power. What it struggles with East Asian success. South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore grew rich within the world market. China too, after 1978. It is economically reductionist : it ignores security, culture, identity and domestic politics. It underrates the role of local elites and bad governance. Robert Brenner (1977) attacked Wallerstein for putting trade ahead of production relations. Bill Warren (1980) argued capitalism actually develops the periphery. The Soviet bloc, supposedly anti-capitalist, also built empires. A balanced answer: the approach is strong on structure but weak on agency.
Drain theory, NIEO and the Global South

India's own thinkers had a dependency-like view long before Frank. Dadabhai Naoroji 's Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901) set out the drain of wealth : Britain took resources out of India without return. R.C. Dutt 's The Economic History of India (1901-03) documented de-industrialisation. After independence, Nehru built a state-led, import-substituting economy, close to Prebisch's advice. India helped found UNCTAD (1964) and the G-77 (1964), and pushed the NIEO (1974). Today, India speaks as a voice of the Global South. During its G20 presidency (2023) it held the "Voice of Global South Summit", and the African Union joined the G20. It argues for debt relief, climate finance and fair trade rules at the WTO. But India is no longer a pure periphery. Its software exports, new economy and middle-income status mean a mix of core-like and periphery-like traits, which fits Wallerstein's "semi-periphery". Critics also note India's own domestic inequality.
How UPSC asks this

"Critically examine the Marxist approach to international relations." "Explain Lenin's theory of imperialism." "Dependency theory has lost its relevance in the age of globalisation." Discuss. "Explain Wallerstein's world-system theory. How useful is it for understanding North-South relations?" Structure: core assumptions (class, capitalism, structure). Then the three families: classical (Lenin, Hobson), dependency (Prebisch, Frank, Amin, Cardoso) and world-system (Wallerstein), plus Gramsci and Cox. Give the core-periphery diagram. Then critique: East Asia, reductionism. Close with India: Naoroji's drain, NIEO, India as semi-periphery. Write the thinkers with titles and years. This is where marks are won.
Functionalism and Neofunctionalism
Peace by doing things together

Realists say states grab for power. Functionalists say: let them build things together instead. Functionalism argues that peace grows from cooperation in practical, technical tasks such as post, health, transport and trade. As people see the benefits, they trust each other and a web of ties forms. Politics gets pushed to the side. Neofunctionalism adds politics. It explains how the European Union began and why it deepened. This topic links directly to the next unit on regional groupings (EU, ASEAN, SAARC). Exam questions ask you to explain "spillover", to compare functionalism with federalism, to test neofunctionalism on the EU, and to contrast it with intergovernmentalism. It also underpins how we think about the UN's specialised agencies. Know Mitrany, Haas, the Schuman Declaration and the EU treaties in order.
David Mitrany and functionalism

David Mitrany, a Romanian-born British scholar, wrote A Working Peace System (1943), in the middle of the Second World War. He was unhappy with both the League model of a grand political organisation and with world federation. Borders are political. Needs are technical. So build bodies around functions . Mitrany's key ideas Form follows function. Create an agency to handle a specific job, whatever its borders. Rivers, health and airlines cross frontiers. Ramification. Success in one area leads people to want cooperation in the next. Habits of cooperation spread. Technocrats over politicians. Experts, not diplomats, should run these bodies. Welfare over sovereignty. Loyalty will shift to bodies that deliver. No need for a single world state. Models: the Universal Postal Union, the International Telecommunication Union and the ILO. Mitrany's thinking lies behind the idea of UN specialised agencies.
Ernst Haas and neofunctionalism

Ernst Haas, a German-American scholar, wrote The Uniting of Europe: Political, Social, and Economic Forces, 1950-1957 (1958). Leon Lindberg ( The Political Dynamics of European Economic Integration , 1963) and Philippe Schmitter built on it. Neofunctionalists kept the idea that cooperation grows step by step, but added three changes. Integration is a political process , driven by interest groups, parties and supranational officials. The key concept is spillover . Elites shift their loyalty and expectations to a new centre. Haas defined integration as a process in which actors in several national settings are persuaded to shift their loyalties, expectations and political activities toward a new centre whose institutions have jurisdiction over the existing states. Where Mitrany wanted to avoid politics, Haas put politics at the centre. The European Coal and Steel Community was the model.
How spillover works

Haas and Lindberg described three kinds of spillover . Functional: integrating one sector creates problems that need integration of related sectors. A common market needs common standards and then a common currency. Political: interest groups and parties turn to the European level, because that is where decisions are made. Cultivated: supranational institutions, such as the Commission, push the process along. Jean Monnet's method is the model.
The EU story, in order

9 May 1950: Robert Schuman, French foreign minister (inspired by Jean Monnet), proposes pooling coal and steel. This is the Schuman Declaration , still celebrated as Europe Day. 1951: Treaty of Paris creates the ECSC (France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg). In force 1952. 1957: Treaties of Rome set up the EEC and Euratom (in force 1958). 1965-66: De Gaulle's "empty chair" crisis. The Luxembourg Compromise (1966) kept a national veto on vital interests. 1986-87: Single European Act: single market by 1992. 1992-93: Maastricht Treaty makes the European Union , with plans for the euro. 1999-2002: Euro launched, with notes in 2002. 2007-09: Lisbon Treaty. 2020: UK leaves (Brexit). 2026: Bulgaria joins the euro on 1 January, as its 21st member. The EU has 27 members. This path, steady and sectoral, looked like neofunctionalism.
Stanley Hoffmann and the stall

De Gaulle's veto of British entry (1963 and 1967) and the empty chair crisis (1965) shook neofunctionalism. Stanley Hoffmann , in "Obstinate or Obsolete? The Fate of the Nation-State and the Case of Western Europe" (1966), made the main challenge. He drew a line between "low politics" (economy, welfare) and "high politics" (defence, foreign policy, identity). States will cooperate on the first, but guard the second. Spillover stops at high politics. This became intergovernmentalism . Haas himself wrote "The Obsolescence of Regional Integration Theory" (1975), admitting that the theory did not fit. Other critiques: It was Eurocentric . Attempts in Africa, Latin America and South Asia did not follow the pattern. It underrates outside shocks , such as the Cold War and the US role. It assumes integration is a one-way ratchet. Brexit reversed it.
Liberal intergovernmentalism and other rivals

Liberal intergovernmentalism Andrew Moravcsik, The Choice for Europe (1998). Integration is the result of bargains between governments .
