National leaders respond to domestic business and farm interests, bargain with each other, and set up institutions to keep promises credible. The EU is a tool of states. Not an independent force. Supranational governance Alec Stone Sweet and Wayne Sandholtz (1998): rising cross-border exchange creates demand for rules, and the European Court of Justice and the Commission respond. This revives neofunctionalism. Others Karl Deutsch, Political Community and the North Atlantic Area (1957): a security community arises through dense communication and transactions. Constructivists study how European identity forms. Federalists, such as Altiero Spinelli, want a European federation. Neofunctionalism returned after the euro crisis (2010-12) and Brexit as scholars debated "failing forward".
Functionalism versus federalism versus realism

Students often mix these up. Here is the contrast in plain terms. Functionalism Cooperate on technical tasks. Skip big politics. Peace comes from below. No world government. Neofunctionalism Same step-by-step logic, but led by elites and institutions. Politics matters. Spillover pushes toward a supranational centre. Federalism Make a constitutional union at once, with a central government. Peace comes from above. Examples: Spinelli, Kant's federation. Realism and intergovernmentalism States guard sovereignty. Cooperation reflects state interests. Integration stops at high politics. The Monnet method is functionalist in spirit. The aim was political (a federation) while the route was economic.
Functional cooperation in India's neighbourhood

Functionalist logic appeals to South Asia, where political quarrels block grand projects. SAARC (founded in Dhaka, 1985) began with "integrated programmes of action" in agriculture, health, telecom, and rural development. SAFTA (signed 2004, in force 2006) followed. But political disputes froze the group; its last summit was in Kathmandu in 2014. BIMSTEC (1997) works through sectors: transport, energy, trade, fisheries. International Solar Alliance (2015) is a functional body on one technical issue. The BBIN Motor Vehicles Agreement (2015) tried to connect Bangladesh, Bhutan, India and Nepal by road. The Indus Waters Treaty (1960) is a famous functional success: it survived wars. But in April 2025 India put it in abeyance after the Pahalgam attack. Pakistan says it stays in force, and a Court of Arbitration said in August 2026 that it does. India rejects that ruling. It shows the limit: spillover fails when high politics intrudes, as Hoffmann said.
How UPSC asks this

"Explain the functionalist and neofunctionalist approaches to international integration." "What is spillover? Is it a useful concept to understand regional integration?" "Compare functionalism with federalism." "Neofunctionalism is not able to explain the setbacks to European integration." Discuss. Structure: define functionalism (Mitrany, 1943: form follows function, ramification). Then neofunctionalism (Haas, 1958: spillover types, elites, supranational bodies). Apply to the EU timeline with 4-5 dates. Critique: Hoffmann's high versus low politics, Moravcsik's intergovernmentalism, Brexit. Conclude with South Asia: SAARC, BIMSTEC, Indus Waters Treaty. Draw the spillover chain. It is quick and scores well.
Systems Theory and Constructivism
Two ways to see the whole system

This lesson joins two approaches that look at the system as a whole. Systems theory borrows from science and treats international politics as a system with parts, inputs, outputs and feedback. It tries to find patterns in how states interact. Constructivism asks a different question: what is the system made of? Its answer: ideas, norms and identities, not just guns and money. It arrived in the early 1990s, just as the Cold War ended, and it explained what realism and liberalism could not. The syllabus does not name constructivism explicitly in the unit title, but the exam asks about it often. Examiners look for three scholars: Alexander Wendt , Martha Finnemore and Kathryn Sikkink , and Peter Katzenstein . Learn each one with a book, a year and a core idea.
Systems theory in IR

A system is a set of parts that interact, with a boundary separating it from its environment. Apply that idea to world politics and you get a few shared ideas. The international system has units (states and others) and a structure (how power is spread). The system responds to inputs and sends out outputs , with feedback . David Easton developed this for domestic politics in The Political System (1953) and A Systems Analysis of Political Life (1965). The system tends toward equilibrium . Shocks cause adjustment. Behaviour depends on the system's type, not only the units' wishes. Other contributors: James Rosenau on linkage politics (1969), which links domestic and external politics, and Karl Deutsch on communication and cybernetics ( The Nerves of Government , 1963). Kenneth Waltz's neorealism is itself a systemic theory.
Morton Kaplan's six systems

Morton Kaplan, System and Process in International Politics (1957), is the most famous systems work in IR. He described six ideal-type systems. Know the names and one line each. Kaplan's six models Balance of power: five or more great powers, shifting alliances (Europe, 18th-19th century). Loose bipolar: two blocs plus non-aligned and universal actors (early Cold War). Tight bipolar: two rigid blocs, no neutrals. Universal: a strong world body, for example a universal actor holding great powers in check. Hierarchical: a world state or empire. Unit veto: every state can destroy all others, so none dares attack (a nuclear-armed world). For each, Kaplan set out rules of behaviour. In the balance-of-power system, for example, states try to raise their capabilities but prefer talks to war, fight if a chance to gain is otherwise lost, and avoid wiping out another essential power. The rules differ in each system.
Strengths and limits of systems theory

Why it helps Gives a big picture : polarity, alliances, balance. Shows how a change in one part affects the whole. Pushes IR toward scientific method. Why it was criticised Static and conservative. It stresses equilibrium, so it struggles to explain deep change, like decolonisation or the Soviet collapse. Too abstract. Kaplan's models were not tested against history. Ignores domestic politics and leaders' choices, treating states as black boxes. Mechanical. Borrowing from biology and engineering does not fit politics, where people choose and interpret. Systemic thinking survives in neorealism, in world-system theory, and in Hedley Bull's The Anarchical Society (1977), which spoke of an "international society". Constructivism, next, keeps the system but puts meaning inside it.
Why constructivism arose

The Cold War ended in 1989-91 without a shot between the superpowers. Neither realism (which stressed material power) nor liberalism (which stressed institutions) had predicted it. Constructivists said: ideas changed. Gorbachev's "new thinking" altered how the USSR saw the world. Roots go further back. Nicholas Onuf coined the word "constructivism" in World of Our Making (1989). Friedrich Kratochwil ( Rules, Norms and Decisions , 1989) and John Ruggie, who wrote Constructing the World Polity (1998), worked on rules and meaning. Social theory (Berger and Luckmann's The Social Construction of Reality , 1966, Giddens's structuration) shaped them. Core claims The world is socially constructed . Structures are made of shared ideas, not only material things. Identities shape interests , which shape action. Agents and structures make each other (mutual constitution). Norms matter. States ask "what is appropriate?" as well as "what pays?"
Alexander Wendt

Wendt, a German-American scholar, is the leading constructivist. His works: "The Agent-Structure Problem in International Relations Theory" (1987). "Anarchy Is What States Make of It: The Social Construction of Power Politics", International Organization (1992). Social Theory of International Politics (1999). "Anarchy is what states make of it." Wendt, International Organization, 1992 He accepts that the system is anarchic and that states are the main actors, like the neorealists. But he argues anarchy has no single logic. Its meaning depends on shared ideas . His example: 500 British nuclear weapons worry the US less than 5 North Korean ones, because of the meaning each carries, which is friendship versus enmity. Self-help is not given by anarchy. It results from processes of interaction. If states treat each other as enemies, they build a self-help world. If they interact differently, identities and interests can change. Wendt calls his view structural or "thin" constructivism, as it keeps a state-centred, scientific outlook.
Wendt's three cultures of anarchy

In Social Theory of International Politics (1999), Wendt says anarchy can take three forms, depending on the role states assign each other: enemy, rival or friend. States can move along the line. He names three levels of internalisation : through force, through self-interest, and through legitimacy, where the norm becomes part of a state's own identity. Only the last gives a stable culture. Wendt's point: the modern state system moved from Hobbesian to Lockean (after Westphalia, 1648) and may be moving towards Kantian in some regions, such as Western Europe.
Martha Finnemore

Martha Finnemore, in National Interests in International Society (1996), argued that states do not know their interests in advance. They learn them through interaction in international society . She showed how international organisations act as teachers of norms. Three cases: UNESCO pushed states to create national science bureaucracies, even in countries that had no use for them. The Red Cross and the Geneva Conventions spread the idea of rules in war. The World Bank changed its view of development: from big projects in the 1950s-60s to a focus on poverty alleviation under McNamara in the 1970s. The lesson: interests are not given by material power or by domestic politics alone. They are shaped by global norms . Later work: Finnemore's The Purpose of Intervention (2003) traced how the reasons states give for humanitarian intervention changed over time.
Finnemore and Sikkink: the norm life cycle

Finnemore and Kathryn Sikkink, "International Norm Dynamics and Political Change", International Organization (1998), is the key text on norms. Emergence: norm entrepreneurs (NGOs, activists, individuals) persuade others, using an organisational platform. Norm cascade: after a tipping point (about a third of states), others join through socialisation, pressure for legitimacy, reputation and esteem. Internalisation: the norm is taken for granted, built into law and bureaucracy. Examples: women's suffrage, the ban on landmines, anti-slavery, the human rights norm. They also contrast the logic of appropriateness with the logic of consequences . Sikkink's The Justice Cascade (2011) applied it to human rights trials. With Margaret Keck she wrote Activists Beyond Borders (1998) on the "boomerang effect".
Peter Katzenstein and the culture of security

Peter Katzenstein edited The Culture of National Security: Norms and Identity in World Politics (1996). It is the leading collection that applied constructivism to security. His claim: security policy is shaped not just by threats and capabilities, but by cultural-institutional context : domestic and international norms, and national identity. His cases Japan: an "anti-militarism" norm after 1945, written into Article 9 of its constitution. Japan's defence policy stayed restrained long after its power grew. Germany: a culture of restraint and multilateralism after the Nazi past. Realism predicted both would rearm and seek great-power status. They did so slowly, because their identities pointed another way. Katzenstein later led work on "analytic eclecticism" and on world regions ( A World of Regions , 2005). The title is worth citing along with the 1996 volume. Related studies: Nina Tannenwald on the nuclear taboo (2007) and Richard Price on the chemical-weapons taboo (1997).
Varieties and critiques of constructivism

Varieties. Conventional (Wendt, Katzenstein, Finnemore) uses scientific methods. Critical constructivists (Kratochwil, Onuf, Hopf, Weldes) focus on language and discourse. Emanuel Adler's "Seizing the Middle Ground" (1997) described constructivism as a bridge between rationalism and post-modernism. Critiques Realists (Mearsheimer, 1994-95): ideas can matter but cannot overcome fear and power. Wendt's version is state-centric and stays within positivism, so critical theorists call it too close to mainstream theory. It is better at explaining how things change after the fact than at predicting. Where do norms come from? The theory often treats Western liberal norms as the "good" ones. Not all norms are good: norms of racism and colonialism also spread. It underplays power and material interests , and who gets to be a norm entrepreneur. Feminists note it is often silent on gender. Defenders: constructivism is not a theory of politics but an approach, which sits with other theories.
Identity and norms in Indian foreign policy

Constructivism helps read India's behaviour. Non-alignment was an identity as much as a policy. A newly independent, post-colonial state saw itself as a leader against colonialism and bloc politics. Norm entrepreneur. India raised the treatment of Indians in South Africa at the first UN General Assembly in 1946 and was among the earliest to impose trade sanctions on the apartheid regime. It pushed decolonisation and disarmament norms. Panchsheel (1954) was an attempt to set norms for relations among states. Nuclear restraint and identity. India holds a no-first-use doctrine and rejected the NPT as discriminatory, seeing it as a "nuclear apartheid". Enmity and rivalry. India-Pakistan ties look Hobbesian at times, with a shared past turned into rival identities. India-China moved between "Hindi-Chini bhai bhai" and rivalry. Civilisational identity. " Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam " and the claim to be a vishwa mitra (friend of the world) are attempts to project an identity. Critics add that identity talk can hide interests, a realist reply.
How UPSC asks this

"Constructivism has opened up new ways to understand international relations." Discuss with reference to Wendt, Finnemore and Sikkink, and Katzenstein. "Anarchy is what states make of it." Explain. "Examine the norm life cycle." "Is systems theory still useful for understanding the international system?" Structure: (1) systems theory in short: Easton, Kaplan's six models, one critique. (2) The rise of constructivism after the Cold War. (3) Core claims. (4) Wendt (1992, 1999: three cultures). (5) Finnemore (1996) and Finnemore and Sikkink (1998: emergence, cascade, internalisation). (6) Katzenstein (1996: Japan, Germany). (7) Critiques from realists and critical theorists. (8) India: non-alignment identity, nuclear taboo, norm entrepreneurship. Always give the author, year and title. Draw the norm life cycle and the three cultures.
Feminist IR
Where are the women in world politics?

Feminist IR began as a simple question by Cynthia Enloe: 'Where are the women?' Traditional IR studies states, wars and markets, yet gender shapes all three. The approach is now a regular Paper II topic, with the Women, Peace and Security agenda, and Indian examples.
Main claims
Sex is biological; gender is the social meaning of masculinity and femininity, which is unequal.
Schools of feminist IR
Tickner's Gender in International Relations (1992) re-reads Morgenthau's six principles as masculine.
Enloe and the personal as international

In Bananas, Beaches and Bases (1989) Cynthia Enloe shows how women's labour, domestic work, military wives, sex workers and diplomatic spouses support international politics. 'The personal is international'. Her method: follow women through supply chains and bases to see hidden power. Enloe's Maneuvers (2000) extends this to the US military, showing that bases and missions depend on unpaid domestic and emotional labour.
War, security and the body

Feminists redefine security : not just the state's borders, but safety at home and in society. They study sexual violence as a weapon of war (Bosnia and Rwanda in the 1990s, the Rome Statute 1998), militarised masculinity, and women as combatants and peace-builders. Carol Cohn's 'Sex and Death in the Rational World of Defense Intellectuals' (1987) shows how nuclear strategy talk is gendered.
Women, Peace and Security

UN Security Council Resolution 1325 (2000) urged women's participation in peace processes and protection from violence. It was followed by later resolutions (1820, 2122 and others), and many states made National Action Plans. Research (for example by UN Women) suggests peace agreements are likelier to last when women take part.
Feminist foreign policy

Sweden declared a feminist foreign policy in 2014; Canada, France, Mexico and others followed with feminist aid or diplomacy. Sweden dropped the label in 2022 after a change of government; several others have scaled back since, so treat this as contested. Three Rs: rights, representation, resources.
Critiques

Mainstream realists: gender is not central to state behaviour. Essentialism: assuming women are naturally peaceful. Western feminism may ignore the voices of Southern women (Mohanty). Hard to test empirically. Defenders: it widens the questions IR can ask. Ann Tickner's Gender in International Relations (1992) was an early full treatment of the subject, and it argued that gender must be part of how security is defined.
India and gender in IR

Gandhi linked non-violence with women's strength. India sent the first all-women Formed Police Unit to a UN mission, in Liberia in 2007 . The Supreme Court ( Babita Puniya , 2020) allowed permanent commission for women in the Army, and Parliament passed the 106th Amendment (2023). Critics note that India has not adopted a formal National Action Plan on 1325 (verify current status).
How UPSC asks this

"Explain how feminist approaches challenge mainstream IR." "Examine the Women, Peace and Security agenda." "Is a feminist foreign policy possible and desirable?" Structure: problem, gender concept, schools, Enloe and Tickner, security, UNSCR 1325, critique, India. UNSCR 1325 (October 2000) was the first Security Council resolution to link women's participation with peace and security, and it is a standard reference. Sweden adopted a feminist foreign policy in 2014, a useful example for the last part of the question.
Postcolonial IR
The discipline looked from Europe

Mainstream IR was written mostly in the US and Britain, about the great powers. Postcolonial and Global IR ask: whose history counts? What if the world is seen from Delhi, Lagos or Lima? It is an emerging UPSC theme with links to Third World approaches.
Core claims
Said, Fanon, Spivak

Edward Said , Orientalism (1978): the West created the 'Orient' as backward, which justified rule. Frantz Fanon , The Wretched of the Earth (1961): colonialism wounds the mind, and decolonisation needs a new humanism. Gayatri Spivak , 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988): elites speak for the powerless. Homi Bhabha : hybridity and mimicry.
Critique of Eurocentrism

Textbook IR starts with the 1648 Westphalia peace, as if states began in Europe. Critics note that sovereignty was unequal : colonies lacked it, and 'standards of civilisation' decided who was a full state. John Hobson, The Eurocentric Conception of World Politics (2012) shows how racial hierarchy shaped Western IR. The Berlin Conference (1884-85) divided Africa without Africans. Racism is thus a hidden structure of international order.
Global IR and non-Western theory

Acharya and Buzan, 'Why is there no non-Western IR theory?' (2007), found rich ideas that had not been theorised: Kautilya's mandala , Chinese tianxia and 'harmony', Islamic and African traditions. Amitav Acharya's Global IR (ISA address, 2014) asks for a discipline grounded in world history, diverse theories and regional worlds, instead of replacing the West with the rest.
Third World security

Mohammed Ayoob 's subaltern realism (1995) says that for the Third World, state-making and internal security come first, unlike the North's external focus. Dependency and world-systems ideas (Prebisch, Frank, Wallerstein) and TWAIL (Third World Approaches to International Law) argue that international law serves imperial interest. Bandung 1955 and the NAM, NIEO appear as Southern agency.
Critiques

Realists: power politics is universal, not Western. Risk of replacing one essentialism ('the West') with another. Elites in the Global South can also be Eurocentric; the Third World is not one voice. Obscure language; weak policy guidance. Defenders: it exposes silent assumptions and widens the field.
Postcolonialism and other approaches

Compare: Marxism (class and capital; postcolonialism adds race and culture), constructivism (ideas matter; postcolonialism asks whose ideas), feminism (gender; shares critique of the 'universal' subject). It also links with decolonial thought from Latin America (Quijano, Mignolo). Edward Said's Culture and Imperialism (1993) and Homi Bhabha's The Location of Culture (1994) give the textual tools that postcolonial IR borrows. Dipesh Chakrabarty's Provincializing Europe (2000) asks how Europe's history came to stand as universal history for everyone.
India's voice

Nehru's anti-colonial IR, NAM, India's stance on Palestine, apartheid, and NIEO, and demands for a reformed UNSC all carry postcolonial concerns. India's civilisational ideas ( Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam , Panchsheel, Kautilya) feed Global IR. Scholars: Ranajit Guha, Dipesh Chakrabarty ( Provincializing Europe , 2000), and Kanti Bajpai. Remember to note the risks of using civilisational pride to cover national interest.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine how postcolonial approaches challenge the Eurocentrism of IR." "What is Global IR?" "Assess the contribution of non-Western ideas to IR theory." Structure: problem, thinkers, Eurocentrism, Global IR, Third World security, critique, India. Amitav Acharya's 2014 article 'Global IR and Regional Worlds' makes the case for a plural IR that recognises regional and non-Western theories. Sanjay Seth's Postcolonial Theory and International Relations (2013) argues that the discipline still carries colonial assumptions.
National Interest and Power
The two oldest words in IR

Every state says it acts for the national interest . Every theory of IR has a view on power . These are the building blocks of foreign policy analysis, and they appear in almost every answer you write. The problems are real. What exactly is the national interest? Who decides? Is power just guns, or also money, ideas and attraction? Can power be measured? UPSC likes both direct and indirect questions: "Explain national interest as a determinant of foreign policy", "Distinguish hard and soft power", "Is soft power enough?" You should know Morgenthau, Nye, Lukes and Strange with their books, and be able to link India's examples such as Kautilya, yoga, the diaspora and the nuclear arsenal. Treat this lesson as a toolkit: definitions first, thinkers next, then the Indian case.
National interest: meaning and types

The national interest is what a state believes it must protect or pursue in its dealings with the world. It is often described in terms of security, prosperity, and values. Charles Beard, The Idea of National Interest (1934), studied how the phrase was used in US history. Hans Morgenthau made it central: "interest defined as power" guides a rational foreign policy. Arnold Wolfers (1952) called "national security" an ambiguous symbol: it means different things to different groups. Joseph Frankel, National Interest (1970), split it into aspirational, operational and explanatory uses. Donald Nuechterlein (1976) offered four interests: defence, economic well-being, favourable world order, promotion of values , each with four intensities: survival, vital, major, peripheral. Stephen Krasner, Defending the National Interest (1978), argued that interest is set by the state's central decision-makers. Types often listed Vital (core) and secondary; permanent and variable; general and specific.
Who defines the national interest?

Realists: It is objective: survival and power. A wise leader finds it. Liberals: It comes from the preferences of domestic groups, such as business and voters (Moravcsik, 1997). Constructivists: It is shaped by identity and norms. Martha Finnemore, National Interests in International Society (1996), shows states learn interests from international society. Marxists: It hides class interest. The "national" interest often means the ruling class's interest. Critics say the phrase can be a slogan to justify anything, from conquest to secrecy. Bureaucratic politics (Graham Allison, Essence of Decision , 1971): different agencies see different interests. In a democracy, the interest is debated in parliament, the media and courts. In a closed system, a small group decides. Good answers say: the national interest is real but contested. Moral claims (human rights, climate) increasingly enter it.
What is power?

Power is the ability to get others to do what they would not otherwise do (Robert Dahl, 1957). But thinkers have added layers. Three faces of power Decision-making (Dahl): who wins open conflicts. Agenda-setting (Bachrach and Baratz, 1962): who keeps issues off the table. Preference-shaping (Steven Lukes, Power: A Radical View , 1974): who shapes what people want. Four kinds of power in IR Michael Barnett and Raymond Duvall (2005): compulsory (direct force), institutional (control through rules), structural (positions in the system, like creditor and debtor) and productive (shaping identities through discourse). Susan Strange States and Markets (1988): structural power sits in four structures: security, production, finance and knowledge. Kenneth Waltz used a simple scale: power is the combined capabilities of a state. Mearsheimer separates latent power (wealth, population) from actual power (army).
Elements of national power

Morgenthau listed nine elements in Politics Among Nations (1948). Morgenthau's nine Stable: geography, natural resources. Changing: industrial capacity, military preparedness, population. Intangible: national character, national morale, quality of diplomacy, quality of government. He thought the quality of diplomacy was the most important factor. He called it the "brains" of national power, and national morale its "soul". Other measures: The Correlates of War Composite Index of National Capability (J. David Singer): iron and steel, energy, military spending, personnel, urban population and total population. China's comprehensive national power approach. Ray Cline's formula (1975) added "strategic purpose and will". Remember the limits: a large country is not always strong (India, 1962), and a smaller one with will and technology may do well (Israel, Vietnam against the US).
Joseph Nye: hard, soft, smart power

Joseph Nye, in Bound to Lead (1990), coined soft power . He developed it in Soft Power: The Means to Success in World Politics (2004). Hard power : the ability to coerce through military force and pay through economic incentives. Soft power : the ability to attract and get others to want what you want. Its sources: culture, political values and foreign policies that others see as legitimate. Smart power : a mix of the two (Nye, The Powers to Lead , 2008; Hillary Clinton used the phrase in 2009). Sharp power is a newer term (Christopher Walker and Jessica Ludwig, 2017) for authoritarian influence by manipulation and censorship, used for China and Russia. Nye's later book The Future of Power (2011) argued that power is diffusing from states to non-state actors and from West to East. Criticisms Soft power is hard to measure and slow. It works through civil society, not governments. Realists doubt it counts without military backing. It can also backfire if a government's policies contradict its image.
The spectrum of power

This is Nye's scale, from command (hard) to co-option (soft). Most real policies mix them. Examples: the Marshall Plan (economic power plus attraction), US-led sanctions (economic coercion), Hollywood and universities (soft), Chinese Belt and Road (economic inducement with soft aims), India's yoga diplomacy (soft).
Instruments of national power

States turn power into policy through a set of tools. A common list uses the letters DIME : diplomatic, informational, military and economic. Diplomacy: negotiation, treaties, alliances, mediation, summitry. Military: deterrence, compellence, war, arms transfers, training, peacekeeping. Economic statecraft: aid, trade deals, tariffs, sanctions, investment, control of technology and supply chains. In 2025-26 tariffs and export controls became the most visible tools of great powers. Information and culture: broadcasting, education, cyber operations, public diplomacy. Law and institutions: using rules at the UN, WTO and IMF. Thomas Schelling's distinction is useful. Deterrence aims to stop someone from acting. Compellence aims to make them act or stop acting ( Arms and Influence , 1966). Compellence is harder. The real art is the mix. Using only force can create resistance. Using only attraction leaves a state open to threats.
Limits of power

Power is not always convertible into results. Power paradox. Strong states lose wars against weaker rivals when the weak have more at stake. Andrew Mack's "Why Big Nations Lose Small Wars" (1975) is a classic study. Examples: Vietnam, Afghanistan. Fungibility. David Baldwin argued power is specific to an issue and context. Military strength does not help on climate or trade rules. Nuclear weapons. They give great destructive power but limited usable power. Interdependence. Keohane and Nye: the less dependent actor holds more power. Legitimacy. Power seen as illegitimate invites resistance (Iraq 2003). Time. Power shifts. Power-transition theory (Organski, 1958) says war risk peaks when a rising power nears the leader. Graham Allison's "Thucydides Trap" ( Destined for War , 2017) applies this to the US and China. For the exam, show that power is relational (over whom?), contextual (on what?), and changing (for how long?).
Kautilya, national interest and Indian power

Kautilya treated the state's interest ( rajya-hita ) as supreme. His saptanga theory lists seven elements of the state: swami (king), amatya (ministers), janapada (territory and people), durga (fort), kosha (treasury), danda (army) and mitra (allies). He also named three powers: utsaha (energy), prabhu (military and treasury) and mantra (counsel and diplomacy). Modern India. Nehru told the Constituent Assembly in 1947 that the art of conducting foreign policy lies in finding what is most advantageous to the country. Article 51 (a Directive Principle) sets goals of peace and international law. Core interests: territorial integrity, energy and food security, development, strategic autonomy, a safe diaspora. Hard power: a nuclear triad, a large army, and rising defence indigenisation. India is among the top five military spenders. Soft power: the International Day of Yoga (21 June, UN resolution of December 2014), Buddhism, Bollywood, ICCR scholarships, ITEC training, Vaccine Maitri (2021), UPI as a digital public good. Economic power: among the world's five largest economies by nominal GDP.
How UPSC asks this

"Explain the concept of national interest. Is it a useful guide for foreign policy?" "Distinguish between hard power and soft power. Which is more important for India?" "Examine Morgenthau's elements of national power." "How does Kautilya's saptanga theory relate to national power?" Structure: define the term and cite Morgenthau, Nuechterlein and Finnemore. Present who defines the interest (realists, liberals, constructivists). Move to power: Dahl, Lukes, Strange, Barnett and Duvall. Elements of power (Morgenthau's nine). Nye's hard, soft and smart power. Close with India: Kautilya, yoga, diaspora, nuclear and economic capacity. Always give one critique and one Indian example.
Balance of Power and Deterrence
Two ways states try to stay safe

How do states protect themselves in an anarchic world? Two classic answers: balance of power (match your rival's strength) and deterrence (make attack too costly). Both are central to realism. Both also shape India's security today, from its response to China's rise to its nuclear posture towards Pakistan. UPSC asks for meanings, techniques, and critiques. A typical question: "Is balance of power still relevant?" or "Nuclear deterrence has kept the peace. Do you agree?" To answer well, you need Morgenthau, Waltz, Walt and Schelling, a few Cold War examples, and the Indian cases: Kautilya's mandala, the 1998 tests, the stability-instability paradox in South Asia, and the 2025 India-Pakistan conflict. First we take balance of power, then deterrence.
Balance of power: what does it mean?

The term is slippery. Ernst Haas, in "The Balance of Power: Prescription, Concept or Propaganda?" (1953), found eight meanings. Inis Claude, Power and International Relations (1962), grouped them as: a situation (a rough equality of power), a policy (acting to prevent any state from dominating) and a system (a way the international order works). Core idea If one state grows too strong, others will join to check it. The result is that no one dominates, and the independence of states survives. History offers examples: Europe against Louis XIV, Napoleon and Hitler. Assumptions: states are the key actors, they want to survive, power can be measured, and alliances can shift freely. Morgenthau (1948) listed methods: divide and rule , compensations (territorial trades), arms build-up , alliances , and a " holder of the balance ", a swing power like Britain in Europe.
Waltz, Walt and the modern debate

Waltz ( Theory of International Politics , 1979): balancing is not a policy choice but a result of the system. Anarchy makes states balance, as firms in a market compete. Balances form whether or not anyone intends them. Internal and external balancing. Internal: build up your own economy and army. External: ally with others. Stephen Walt ( The Origins of Alliances , 1987): states balance against threat , not just power. Threat depends on aggregate power, geography, offensive capability and perceived intent. Weak states may bandwagon (join the stronger side). Mearsheimer sees a role for the offshore balancer : a power like the US that stays away from Eurasia but intervenes if a regional hegemon rises. Soft balancing (Robert Pape and T.V. Paul, 2005): using diplomacy and institutions, not alliances, to constrain a strong state. Example: opposition to the 2003 Iraq war. Balance of interests (Randall Schweller): not all states balance, some bandwagon for profit.
Balance of power in history

1648. Peace of Westphalia: sovereign states and the idea of a balance. 1713. Treaty of Utrecht names the balance of power as its aim. 1815. The Concert of Europe after Napoleon (Vienna, Metternich, Castlereagh). 1871-1890. Bismarck's alliance system. 1914. Rigid alliances (Triple Entente and Triple Alliance) turned a Balkan crisis into a world war. 1945-91. Bipolar balance between NATO and the Warsaw Pact. The lesson from 1914: balancing can fail when alliances are rigid. Alliance entrapment, miscalculation and arms races can turn a balance into a war.
Balance of power: criticisms

Vague. It has too many meanings to be a testable theory. Not automatic. States often fail to balance, or balance late. In the 1930s, Britain and France appeased Germany. Others "buck-pass". Dangerous. It rests on calculating power, and misjudgements lead to war (1914). It does not stop arms races. Amoral. Small states were often used as tokens, as in the partitions of Poland. Liberals: institutions and trade, not balance, keep peace. Collective security (next lesson) seeks to replace it. Constructivists: balances depend on perceptions. Wendt: 500 British weapons are less threatening to the US than five North Korean ones. Hard to measure in a world of cyber, finance and technology. Defenders point to repeated balancing against would-be hegemons, and to the way the Quad, AUKUS (September 2021), NATO's growth (Finland 2023, Sweden 2024) and Russia-China ties are explained by balancing logic.
Deterrence: the logic

Deterrence means persuading an adversary not to act by threatening unacceptable costs. It works on the adversary's mind. Bernard Brodie , The Absolute Weapon (1946): since atomic bombs, the aim of military force must be to avert wars, not win them. Albert Wohlstetter , "The Delicate Balance of Terror" (1959): deterrence needs a secure second-strike capability , the ability to retaliate after being hit. Thomas Schelling , The Strategy of Conflict (1960) and Arms and Influence (1966): threats must be credible ; commitment and signalling matter; "the threat that leaves something to chance". Glenn Snyder (1961): deterrence by punishment (threaten retaliation) versus deterrence by denial (make the attack fail). Conditions for success Capability (can you do it?), credibility (will you?), communication (does the adversary know?), and a rational adversary.
Mutually assured destruction and the Cold War

By the 1960s each superpower could destroy the other even after absorbing a first strike. This was mutual assured destruction (MAD) , the policy named in US debates under Defense Secretary Robert McNamara. The nuclear triad : land-based missiles, submarine-launched missiles and bombers, to protect the second strike. Flexible response (NATO, 1967): options between surrender and holocaust. Extended deterrence : the US "nuclear umbrella" covering allies. Arms control followed: the ABM Treaty and SALT I (1972), INF (1987), START. Stability-instability paradox (Glenn Snyder, 1965): nuclear stability at the top makes limited conventional or sub-conventional conflict more likely below it. Did deterrence keep the peace? Supporters: no direct US-Soviet war. Critics: luck (Cuba 1962, the Able Archer scare in 1983), and the risk of accidents. Daniel Ellsberg and Scott Sagan point to near-misses. Today, new tech (hypersonics, missile defence, cyber, AI) tests the old logic, and New START expired on 5 February 2026.
Does deterrence work?

It works Waltz: nuclear weapons make war irrational, so more states with weapons can mean less war. India-Pakistan have not fought a full war since Kargil (1999), and even the 2025 conflict ended in days. It does not always work Rational-actor assumptions may fail: leaders can misread, panic or be fanatical. Credibility is uncertain. Would a state risk its cities for an ally? Terrorists and non-state actors are hard to deter. Cyber attacks are hard to attribute. Sagan: accidents, bad command-and-control, and organisational failure. Moral objection: threatening mass killing is wrong. The 2017 Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons rests on this. Conventional deterrence also matters. Ukraine had given up its Soviet weapons in 1994 and was invaded in 2014 and 2022, and many cite it as a lesson on the value of deterrence, though the Budapest Memorandum was not a binding guarantee.
India's balancing and deterrence

Kautilya's mandala is an old model of balancing: ally with the neighbour's neighbour. The six-fold policy matches balance of power logic. Internal balancing. A nuclear arsenal after 1998, missile programmes (Agni series; Agni-V tested with multiple warheads in March 2024), and the nuclear triad with INS Arihant (the first deterrence patrol in 2018) and INS Arighaat (commissioned 2024). External balancing. The Quad (revived 2017, leaders level from 2021), the 2+2 dialogues, defence pacts with the US (LEMOA, COMCASA, BECA), the Malabar exercise and close ties with France, Japan and Australia. Russia remains an arms supplier. Doctrine. Credible minimum deterrence, no first use, and massive retaliation. Pakistan keeps a first-use option and tactical weapons. Stability-instability paradox in South Asia. The 1999 Kargil war, the 2001 Parliament attack, 26/11 (2008), Uri (2016), Pulwama-Balakot (2019) and Pahalgam-Operation Sindoor (2025). India claims it can respond to terror under the nuclear shadow and says it will not accept "nuclear blackmail". Two-front problem from China and Pakistan.
How UPSC asks this

"Balance of power is both a theory and a policy. Explain with examples." "Is the balance of power relevant in a world of nuclear weapons and interdependence?" "Discuss the logic of nuclear deterrence. Has it succeeded?" "Examine India's nuclear doctrine in the context of deterrence." Structure: meanings (Haas, Claude), methods (Morgenthau), Waltz and Walt, critique, then deterrence: Brodie, Schelling, second strike, MAD, triad, stability-instability paradox. Add the debate, with Waltz versus Sagan. End with India's mandala, the 1998 tests, the 2003 doctrine and the Sindoor experience. A balanced finish: balancing and deterrence are tools, not guarantees. Both need diplomacy and arms control alongside.
Collective Security and Transnational Actors
One against all, and actors beyond the state

This lesson joins two ideas that answer different questions. Collective security asks: can states agree to stop aggression together, so that nobody has to arm in fear? It is the liberal answer to the balance of power, and it is the logic behind the League of Nations and the UN Security Council. Transnational actors ask: who else plays in world politics besides states? Multinational firms, NGOs, terror networks, diasporas, religious bodies, experts and now big technology platforms. Both are classic UPSC topics. Questions usually ask you to evaluate collective security's record, to compare it with the balance of power and alliances, and to judge whether non-state actors are weakening the state. Link them in your head: collective security tries to limit state violence, while transnational actors show that states no longer hold all the cards.
What is collective security?

Inis Claude, in Power and International Relations (1962), gave the standard account. The idea is " all against one ": every member promises to oppose an aggressor, whoever it is, and even a friend. Assumptions States agree on what counts as aggression. All members care equally about peace, and will act. No state is so strong that it cannot be stopped. Members can overcome their own narrow interests, including trade or friendship with the aggressor. If these hold, aggression will be deterred because the aggressor faces overwhelming force. Distinguish it from related ideas: Balance of power: flexible alliances against a particular threat. Collective defence: an alliance against an outside enemy, like NATO's Article 5. Cooperative security: dialogue and trust among adversaries, like the OSCE.
From the League to the UN

League of Nations. The Covenant's Article 10 pledged members to respect and preserve territorial integrity. Article 16 allowed economic and military sanctions. But decisions needed unanimity, the US was absent, and it failed in Manchuria (1931) and Abyssinia (1935). United Nations (1945). The Charter tried to fix the flaws. Chapter VII. The Security Council can find a "threat to the peace, breach of the peace or act of aggression" (Article 39), apply sanctions (Article 41), or authorise force (Article 42). Article 43 was to give the Council standing forces from members. It was never implemented, and the Military Staff Committee remains idle. Article 51 preserves the right of individual and collective self-defence until the Council acts. The veto of the five permanent members is the main change from the League. It prevents action against a P5 member or its friends.
The UN's record in practice

Korea (1950). The Council could authorise a UN force because the USSR was boycotting. Later, the General Assembly's Uniting for Peace resolution (1950) gave the Assembly a role when the Council is deadlocked. Peacekeeping (since 1948), developed by Dag Hammarskjold and Lester Pearson in the Suez crisis (1956), is a middle path: consent-based, impartial, minimal force. Kuwait (1991). Resolution 678 authorised "all necessary means". Seen as a model case. Rwanda (1994) and Srebrenica (1995) showed the UN's lack of will. Russia is a P5 member and vetoes action over Ukraine. The US shields Israel on some Gaza drafts.
Why collective security struggles

Veto. The P5 cannot be coerced, which breaks the "all against one" rule. No agreement on aggression. The General Assembly's Definition of Aggression (resolution 3314, 1974) is not binding on the Council. Free riding. Each state hopes others will act. Interests. States apply the principle selectively. Realists (Morgenthau, Carr) say collective security is a utopian dream of the satisfied powers. Costs. Sanctions hurt the enforcers too. Civil wars. Most modern conflicts are within states, where the model fits poorly. Credibility. No standing force. UN missions rely on contributed troops. Defenders say it works partly: the UN legitimises force, restrains some wars, and offers peacekeepers (about a dozen missions today, with troops mostly from South Asia and Africa). Norms against conquest have grown since 1945. Reform ideas: limit the veto (France's proposal, the ACT group's code of conduct), expand the Council, and strengthen regional bodies.
Transnational actors: who are they?

Realism sees only states. Keohane and Nye's edited volume Transnational Relations and World Politics (1972, from a 1971 journal issue) argued that cross-border actors matter. John Burton's "cobweb" model in World Society (1972) saw a web of links rather than billiard balls. Main types Multinational corporations (MNCs): Apple, Toyota, Tata. Some have revenues above the GDP of many states. NGOs and civil society: Amnesty International, Greenpeace, MSF, the Red Cross. Epistemic communities (Peter Haas, 1992): expert networks that shape policy, such as climate scientists (IPCC). Diasporas and migrants. Religious bodies: the Catholic Church, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. Violent networks: Al-Qaeda, ISIS, drug cartels, private military companies. Media and tech platforms: global news networks, social media.
Do transnational actors weaken the state?

Yes, they do Susan Strange, The Retreat of the State (1996): markets and firms now hold power once held by states. Hyperglobalists see a "borderless world". NGOs shaped the landmine ban (1997, the Ottawa Treaty, Jody Williams and ICBL, Nobel Prize 1997), the Rome Statute (1998) and climate norms. Big Tech sets rules for speech and data. Terrorist networks strike across borders. Banks and credit rating agencies discipline governments. No, states still decide Realists (Waltz, Gilpin): states set the rules for firms, give NGOs permission to operate, and fight wars. Firms need state protection. The 2025-26 tariff and sanctions wars show state power over trade. States can also use these actors: sovereign wealth funds, state firms, or private military firms such as Russia's Wagner Group. Balanced view: the state is not dying but sharing space. Governance is now "multi-level", with the state still the central actor.
Collective defence and regional answers

Where universal collective security stalls, groups of states build narrower systems. NATO (1949). Article 5 says an armed attack on one member is an attack on all. It has been invoked only once, after 9/11. This is collective defence : it targets an outside threat. At the Hague summit in June 2025 members agreed to aim at defence-related spending of 5% of GDP by 2035 (3.5% core defence plus 1.5% related). NATO now has 32 members, after Finland (2023) and Sweden (2024). Warsaw Pact (1955-91), the Soviet counterpart. Regional organisations. Chapter VIII of the UN Charter recognises them. The African Union 's Constitutive Act (2000) Article 4(h) gives the Union a right to intervene in grave circumstances such as genocide. ECOWAS has used force in Liberia and Sierra Leone. The OSCE builds cooperative security through monitoring. CSTO (Russia-led) and the SCO (security and counter-terror cooperation). Critics note that these arrangements can raise tensions with outsiders (the security dilemma) and may weaken the universal system.
Peacekeeping: a practical middle path

The Charter did not mention peacekeeping, but practice created it. First generation (1948-88). Unarmed or lightly armed observers, with consent, impartiality and use of force only in self-defence. UNTSO (1948) and the first UN Emergency Force in Suez (1956) are examples. Second generation (1990s). Complex missions in civil wars (Cambodia, Namibia, Bosnia, Somalia), with election monitoring and state-building. Failures at Somalia, Rwanda and Srebrenica led to the Brahimi Report (2000) calling for clear mandates and robust rules of engagement. Third generation. "Robust" or protection-of-civilians mandates, as in the DR Congo (the Force Intervention Brigade, 2013) and Mali. Today. Funding stress and political pushback limit new missions. The UN80 reform drive and US cuts to contributions in 2025 put pressure on peacekeeping budgets. Peacekeepers are not a collective security army. They support peace after a ceasefire, not enforce it by war. India's troops, doctors and police are in many missions.
India and collective security, India and non-state actors

Collective security. India is a founding UN member and one of the oldest and largest troop contributors to peacekeeping, from Korea (1950) onwards, with a long record in Africa and West Asia, and the first all-women police unit in Liberia (2007). India supports a role for the UN, but seeks reform : a permanent seat on the Security Council (with the G4: Brazil, Germany, Japan, India) and limits to the veto. It is also wary of intervention that bypasses the Council. India stays out of military alliances, preferring strategic partnerships. Transnational actors. Diaspora. India has the world's largest diaspora, and receives the largest annual remittances, well over $100 billion a year. Pravasi Bharatiya Divas is held every two years. Indian MNCs: Tata (Jaguar Land Rover, 2008), Infosys, Reliance. NGOs: The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 (amended 2020) regulates foreign funding. Critics say it restricts civil society, while the government cites security. Terror networks: Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed are the main concerns (see the lesson on terrorism). Tech platforms: debates over data localisation and the IT Rules.
How UPSC asks this

"Collective security has failed to ensure peace. Examine." "Compare collective security with balance of power." "Role of non-state actors in international politics." Discuss. "Are multinational corporations a threat to state sovereignty?" Structure for collective security: meaning (Claude: all against one), assumptions; League; UN Charter Chapter VII (Articles 39, 41, 42, 43, 51); record (Korea, Kuwait, Rwanda, Syria, Ukraine); problems; reforms; India's role in peacekeeping and UN reform. Structure for transnational actors: types; theory (Keohane and Nye 1972, Burton, Strange); the "state retreat" debate; examples (landmine ban, MNCs, terror networks); India (diaspora, FCRA, Tata). Conclude: the state remains central, but it shares authority.
Superpowers, Bipolarity and the Cold War
The 45-year contest that shaped the modern world

The Cold War (c. 1947-1991) was a struggle between the United States and the Soviet Union that never became a direct war. It shaped alliances, arms races, decolonisation, the UN and India's own foreign policy. It matters for the exam in three ways. First, it is the base for bipolarity , a key idea in IR theory (Waltz). Second, it explains why India chose non-alignment . Third, its end in 1991 opened the "unipolar moment" and set India's economic reforms. Expect questions on origins, major crises, détente, the end of the Cold War, and the debate among historians. Stay with dates and doctrines: Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, NATO, Warsaw Pact, Cuban Missile Crisis, SALT, Helsinki, INF Treaty. Remember the Indian lens: Nehru, Bandung, the 1971 Indo-Soviet treaty, and the post-1991 recalibration.
Origins: from allies to rivals (1945-1949)

The US and USSR fought together against Nazi Germany, but their systems and goals differed: liberal capitalism and democracy versus Communist one-party rule. Yalta (February 1945) and Potsdam (July-August 1945) : wartime conferences. Disputes over Poland, Germany and Eastern Europe grew. 1946. George Kennan's "Long Telegram" from Moscow (February) urged firm resistance to Soviet expansion. Churchill's " Iron Curtain " speech at Fulton, Missouri (March). 1947. The Truman Doctrine (12 March): US aid to Greece and Turkey, and support for free peoples resisting subjugation. Kennan's "X" article in Foreign Affairs set out containment . The Marshall Plan (announced June 1947) gave about $13 billion in aid to rebuild Western Europe. The USSR formed the Cominform (September) and Andrei Zhdanov described a world of "two camps". 1948-49. Berlin blockade and airlift (June 1948 to May 1949). NATO founded on 4 April 1949 with 12 members.
Crises and the arms race (1949-1962)

1949. USSR tests its first atomic bomb (August). Communists win in China (October). 1950-53. Korean War. A UN force led by the US faced North Korea and China. India chaired the Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission. 1955. West Germany joins NATO; the USSR forms the Warsaw Pact (May). 1956. The USSR crushes the Hungarian uprising. The Suez crisis shows the limits of old European powers; the US and USSR both pressured Britain and France. 1957. Sputnik starts the space race. 1961. The Berlin Wall is built (August). 1962. The Cuban Missile Crisis (October, 13 days): the USSR placed missiles in Cuba, the US imposed a naval "quarantine", and the crisis ended with Soviet withdrawal and a US pledge not to invade Cuba, plus the quiet removal of US missiles from Turkey. It was the closest the world came to nuclear war. Result: a hotline (1963) and the Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963).
Phases of the Cold War

Historians split the era into phases. Each had its own mood, from fear and crisis to cooperation and then a tense revival. Use this as a quick frame in answers. It helps you place events and show you see the pattern: crisis, learning, arms control, relapse, and finally collapse of one side.
Détente and the second Cold War

Détente (1969-79) was a relaxation of tension. 1969-72. Nixon and Kissinger opened ties with China (Nixon's visit, February 1972), and played the "China card". Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik improved West German ties with the East. 1972. SALT I and the ABM Treaty were signed in Moscow. 1975. The Helsinki Final Act (CSCE) accepted post-war borders and added human rights language that dissidents later used. Détente broke down after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (December 1979), the Iranian Revolution and US reaction. Under Reagan, the US raised arms spending, supported mujahideen, and announced the Strategic Defense Initiative (1983), called "Star Wars". This is the "Second Cold War" (1979-85). Meanwhile the Third World saw proxy wars: Vietnam (US withdrew 1973; Saigon fell 1975), Angola, Ethiopia, Nicaragua and Afghanistan.
How and why it ended (1985-1991)

Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in March 1985. He brought glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring), and "new thinking" in foreign policy. December 1987. The INF Treaty eliminated a whole class of US and Soviet missiles. 1989. The USSR withdrew from Afghanistan (February). Eastern European regimes fell. The Berlin Wall opened on 9 November. 1990. German reunification (3 October). July 1991. The Warsaw Pact was dissolved, and START I was signed. December 1991. The Soviet Union dissolved, with Gorbachev resigning on 25 December. Why did it end? Debated answers: Soviet economic stagnation and overreach; US pressure under Reagan; Gorbachev's reforms and choice not to use force; nationalism within the USSR; the power of ideas (constructivists). Realists were surprised, which fed the criticism of neorealism.
How historians explain the Cold War

Orthodox (traditional) Soviet expansion started it and the US responded defensively. Herbert Feis and Arthur Schlesinger Jr. Revisionist US capitalism needed open markets and pushed the USSR into a corner. William Appleman Williams, The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959); Gabriel Kolko; Walter LaFeber. Post-revisionist Both sides contributed, through fear, misperception and domestic politics. John Lewis Gaddis, The Long Peace (1986) and We Now Know (1997), using new Soviet archives, put more weight on Stalin. Melvyn Leffler emphasised US security fears. Why no war? Kenneth Waltz argued bipolarity was stable. Others credit nuclear deterrence, mutual assured destruction (MAD), and rules of the game after Cuba. Gaddis called it the "long peace". Cold War was cold only at the centre. In Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan and Africa, millions died in proxy wars.
Features of bipolarity

Two superpowers far ahead in military power and nuclear arsenals. Blocs and alliances: NATO (1949), Warsaw Pact (1955), SEATO (1954) and CENTO (the Baghdad Pact, 1955). Nuclear deterrence and the arms race. Global stockpiles peaked at over 60,000 warheads in the mid-1980s. Ideological contest: liberal capitalism versus Marxism-Leninism. Proxy wars and spheres of influence: Truman Doctrine; the Brezhnev Doctrine (1968) after the invasion of Czechoslovakia. Economic blocs: Marshall Plan and the OEEC; the Soviet side had COMECON (1949), covered in the next unit. Third World choice: join a bloc or stay non-aligned. The UN Security Council was often paralysed by vetoes. Only a few operations, such as in Korea (1950, helped by a Soviet boycott), went ahead.
India in the Cold War

Non-alignment. Nehru chose independence from both blocs. India stayed out of SEATO and CENTO and criticised pacts. See the next lesson. Korea. India mediated and chaired the Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission (1953), and sent a medical unit and a custodian force. US-Pakistan ties. Pakistan joined SEATO and the Baghdad Pact, and got US arms. India worried. Soviet ties. The USSR vetoed UN action on Kashmir in the 1950s-60s and supported India's industrialisation (Bhilai steel plant). The Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation (August 1971) came as the US and China leaned to Pakistan before the Bangladesh war. 1962. India sought help from the US during the Sino-Indian war, which coincided with the Cuban crisis. 1979-89. India's muted response to the Soviet entry into Afghanistan drew criticism. After 1991. The loss of the Soviet partner, plus the balance-of-payments crisis, pushed India toward economic reform and a "Look East" policy, and improved ties with the US.
How UPSC asks this

"Trace the origins of the Cold War. Which explanation do you find convincing?" "Bipolarity was more stable than the present multipolar world." Discuss. "What were the causes of the end of the Cold War?" "Examine India's response to the Cold War." Structure: context (1945), then origins with Kennan, Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan. Add crisis dates, détente (SALT, Helsinki), second Cold War, and end (INF, 1989, 1991). Put historians in a three-box list. Add Waltz on stability. Close with India: non-alignment, Korea, 1971 treaty, 1991 shift. A timeline diagram with 8 dates adds clarity and saves words.
Non-Alignment: Aims and Achievements
A third way in a two-camp world

When the Cold War divided the globe into two blocs, a group of newly independent states said: we will not join either. That was the Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) . It is one of the most important Indian contributions to world politics. Jawaharlal Nehru was its architect, along with Tito, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah. UPSC returns to it often: its aims, achievements, failures and relevance today. Do not mix up three words: Non-alignment : independent judgement on each issue, with no military bloc membership. Neutrality : staying out of a particular war, a legal status. Isolationism : staying out of world affairs altogether. India was never neutral or isolated. It spoke on Korea, Suez, Hungary, Vietnam and disarmament. A frequent question is whether non-alignment is still useful. A good answer links it to today's "strategic autonomy" and "multi-alignment".
Origins: Asia, decolonisation and the Bandung meeting

1947. Nehru convened the Asian Relations Conference in New Delhi, before independence. He wanted Asia to find its own voice. 1954. The Colombo Powers (Burma, Ceylon, India, Indonesia, Pakistan) met. India and China signed the Panchsheel agreement on Tibet on 29 April 1954. Bandung, 18-24 April 1955. The Asian-African Conference brought together 29 states. It condemned colonialism and racism and issued the ten-point Declaration on the Promotion of World Peace and Cooperation , which built on Panchsheel. Panchsheel, the five principles Mutual respect for each other's territorial integrity and sovereignty. Mutual non-aggression. Non-interference in internal affairs. Equality and mutual benefit. Peaceful coexistence. Bandung was not yet NAM but it created the mood. China's Zhou Enlai attended, and the US and USSR were not invited.
Belgrade 1961: the movement is born

The founding summit was held in Belgrade, 1-6 September 1961 , with 25 member states. The "big five" leaders were Nehru (India), Tito (Yugoslavia), Nasser (Egypt), Sukarno (Indonesia) and Nkrumah (Ghana). A preparatory meeting in Cairo (June 1961) fixed the criteria for membership. They included: an independent policy based on peaceful coexistence and non-alignment; support for national independence movements; no membership of a multilateral military alliance linked to great-power conflict; and no bilateral military pact with a great power. Core aims End colonialism, racism and apartheid. Peaceful settlement of disputes and general disarmament . Respect for sovereignty and equality of states. Economic development, and a fairer economic order. Reform of the UN. Nehru spoke of avoiding the "war of the blocs" and widening the "area of peace". Nehru's own thinking is in The Discovery of India (1946) and in his speeches collected as India's Foreign Policy .
Milestones of NAM

The movement grew from 25 members in 1961 to about 120 today, which makes it the largest group of states outside the UN itself. It has no secretariat or permanent headquarters; a rotating chair coordinates it. India hosted the 7th summit in March 1983, and Indira Gandhi chaired the movement until 1986. The 18th summit was in Baku (2019) and the 19th in Kampala, Uganda (January 2024).
Nehru's idea of non-alignment

Independence of judgement. India would decide each issue on its merits, not on a bloc line. Anti-colonialism and anti-racism. This was a moral and strategic aim from India's own experience. Peace for development. A newly independent poor country needed peace, trade and technology from both sides. Reduce the Cold War. Nehru believed that alliances spread tension. He opposed SEATO and the Baghdad Pact. Strategic autonomy. Keep freedom to act, with the ability to take aid from the US, the USSR and others. It was both principle and interest. Realist critics call it a prudent policy for a weak state to extract gains from both sides. Idealist readers call it a moral stance for peace. Nehru's phrase was a " policy of non-alignment ", not neutrality. He also said that where freedom or justice is threatened, India cannot be neutral.
What NAM achieved

Decolonisation. It gave newly independent states a voice and pushed the UN toward the 1960 Declaration on Granting Independence to Colonial Countries. Anti-apartheid and Namibia. NAM kept pressure on South Africa and supported liberation movements. Reduced bloc pressure. Members like India, Egypt and Yugoslavia could take help from both camps, and avoid being satellites. Economic agenda. The Algiers summit (1973) called for a New International Economic Order . The UN General Assembly's Sixth Special Session adopted the NIEO Declaration in May 1974. NAM worked with the G-77 (1964) and UNCTAD. Disarmament. NAM backed the Partial Test Ban Treaty, the NPT debates and disarmament conferences. Palestine. Consistent support for Palestinian rights. Mediation. In Korea, Indo-China and the Suez crisis, non-aligned diplomacy helped to keep talks open. It also strengthened the idea that small states have a voice in the UN, which is why the UN's membership expansion mattered.
Limits and failures

Internal divisions. Members quarrelled with each other: India and China (1962), India and Pakistan, Iran and Iraq (1980-88). The Egypt-Israel peace treaty of 1979 caused rifts among Arab members. Tilt towards Moscow? Cuba's Fidel Castro, at Havana in 1979, argued that the Soviet bloc was the "natural ally" of the movement. India's 1971 treaty with the USSR and its soft response on Afghanistan (1979) drew the same charge. Weak institutions. No secretariat, no enforcement, decisions by consensus. Hard security gap. Non-alignment did not save India in 1962. Economic weakness. The NIEO call was largely resisted by the North. The 1980s debt crisis divided the South. After 1991. With one bloc gone, critics said NAM lost its reason: "non-aligned with whom?" Many members were drifting into alliances. Defenders reply that NAM still has work: equity in global governance, UN reform, climate justice and freedom from great-power rivalry.
Relevance after the Cold War

Why it still matters The principles (sovereignty, peaceful settlement, anti-colonialism) are timeless. A new US-China rivalry and the Ukraine war push many Global South states to avoid choosing sides. It supports a voice for developing countries on debt, climate and trade. Why it has faded No bipolar structure to stand apart from. Divergent interests of 120 members. India's leaders have preferred forums such as the G20, BRICS, the SCO and the Quad, rather than NAM summits. The 2012 report Nonalignment 2.0 , by a group of Indian strategists (published by the Centre for Policy Research), argued India should keep strategic autonomy, but with a new, more flexible approach: engage all powers, build capabilities, and avoid being tied to any one.
From non-alignment to multi-alignment

Cold War. India took Soviet help on steel, defence and Kashmir diplomacy, and American food aid and loans. The 1971 treaty was framed as a response to a "Washington-Beijing-Islamabad" axis. 1990s. After the Soviet collapse, India reached out to the US, Israel, ASEAN (Look East, 1992) and the EU. Today's phrases. Strategic autonomy , multi-alignment (a term used by Shashi Tharoor and others) and Vishwa Bandhu . External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar's The India Way (2020) explains the approach of engaging many poles at once. Practice. India sits in the Quad with the US, Japan and Australia, but also in BRICS and the SCO with Russia and China. It buys Russian oil and arms, and builds defence ties with the US and France. Global South voice. The "Voice of Global South Summit" (2023), the African Union's G20 membership under India's presidency, and India's BRICS chair in 2026. Critics say multi-alignment is hedging without a firm anchor. Supporters say it fits a multipolar world.
How UPSC asks this

"Non-alignment was a policy of the Cold War, with no place in a post-Cold War world." Comment. "Assess the achievements and failures of the Non-Aligned Movement." "Discuss Nehru's contribution to the philosophy of non-alignment." "How has India's non-alignment evolved into multi-alignment?" Structure: define and separate from neutrality. Origins: Asian Relations Conference 1947, Panchsheel 1954, Bandung 1955, Belgrade 1961. Aims. Achievements (decolonisation, NIEO, disarmament). Failures (divisions, 1962, 1971 treaty criticism, no institutions). Then relevance: Nonalignment 2.0, strategic autonomy, Quad plus BRICS. Keep a balanced verdict: the tool changed, the aim of autonomy remains.
Unipolarity, American Hegemony and Multipolarity
Who runs the world now?

This is the most live question in IR. After the Soviet Union fell in 1991, the US stood alone. Three decades later, China is a peer rival, Russia has gone to war in Europe, and many middle powers act on their own. What kind of order is this? The syllabus title links three ideas: unipolarity (one dominant power), American hegemony (a dominant power that also leads through rules and institutions) and multipolarity (several centres of power). UPSC asks about this theme in many forms: "Is the world multipolar?", "Has American hegemony ended?", "India's place in a multipolar world". It also feeds into Paper II Section B on India-US, India-China and India-Russia relations. This topic changes every year, so learn the concepts and the thinkers, then update with two or three recent facts (tariffs, the war in West Asia, BRICS). Always put the date next to a fact.
Polarity: how many poles?

Polarity counts the great powers that shape the system, judged by their share of military, economic, technological and diplomatic power. Waltz made polarity the main variable in Theory of International Politics (1979). Unipolar: one power far ahead of the rest. Bipolar: two superpowers (1945-91). Multipolar: three or more major powers. A related word, hegemony , means leadership with consent as well as power. Charles Kindleberger and Robert Gilpin argued that an open world economy needs a hegemon to supply public goods. This is hegemonic stability theory . Debate over stability: Waltz thought bipolarity safest, Deutsch and Singer (1964) argued multipolarity is safer, and Wohlforth (1999) said unipolarity is peaceful.
The unipolar moment, 1991 onward

Charles Krauthammer's essay "The Unipolar Moment" ( Foreign Affairs , winter 1990-91) claimed that the US stood alone at the top. He thought the moment might be brief. Key events: 1991 Gulf War. A US-led coalition, authorised by the UN Security Council, expelled Iraq from Kuwait. Bush spoke of a "new world order". 1990s. Interventions in Somalia (1993), Bosnia (1995) and Kosovo (1999, NATO without UN approval). NATO expanded to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic in 1999. Economic lead. US-led institutions (IMF, World Bank, WTO) set the rules. Washington Consensus ideas spread. Idea of "end of history" (Fukuyama): liberal democracy had no rival. William Wohlforth, in "The Stability of a Unipolar World" ( International Security , 1999), argued that the US lead was so large that no rival could challenge it, so the system was peaceful and durable.
Sources of American hegemony

Hard power Unmatched military reach, with hundreds of overseas bases, aircraft carriers and a nuclear triad. SIPRI estimates US military spending in 2024 at nearly $1 trillion, over three times China's estimated figure. Economic power The largest economy for decades (about a quarter of world GDP in nominal terms), and the dollar as the main reserve and trade currency, which gives the US financial sanctions power. Top universities and technology firms. Soft power Joseph Nye, Bound to Lead (1990) and Soft Power (2004): attraction through culture, values and institutions. Institutions and alliances G. John Ikenberry, After Victory (2001) and Liberal Leviathan (2011), argued the US built a rules-based liberal international order that others joined because it was open and constrained US power. NATO and alliances in Asia anchored it.
Overreach after 9/11

The attacks of 11 September 2001 changed US strategy. War in Afghanistan (2001) and the invasion of Iraq (2003) without a clear UN mandate. The 2002 National Security Strategy embraced pre-emption. The costs: trillions of dollars, loss of lives, and damage to legitimacy as no weapons of mass destruction were found. Chaos in Iraq, the rise of ISIS (2014), and the chaotic US exit from Afghanistan (August 2021). The 2008 global financial crisis , which began in the US, hurt the image of the US economic model. The G20 leaders' summit (first held in 2008) recognised that emerging economies had to be at the table. Scholars like Paul Kennedy ( The Rise and Fall of the Great Powers , 1987) warned about "imperial overstretch". Chalmers Johnson ( Blowback , 2000) and others made a similar point on empire's costs.
The rise of the rest

Fareed Zakaria, The Post-American World (2008), described the "rise of the rest": the US is not declining in absolute terms, but others are catching up. Richard Haass called it "nonpolarity" (2008): power is spread among states, firms, NGOs and militias. Amitav Acharya, The End of American World Order (2014), spoke of a "multiplex world". China. From the 2001 WTO entry to the world's second-largest economy. The Belt and Road Initiative (2013), the AIIB (opened 2016) and a modern navy. Russia. Crimea (2014) and the invasion of Ukraine (February 2022). Closer ties with China and North Korea. BRICS (2009), expanded in 2024 with Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE, and Indonesia from 2025. The New Development Bank started in 2015. Middle powers : India, Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Brazil, Indonesia. They hedge and bargain. EU as an economic and regulatory power.
Unipolar, bipolar or multipolar today?

Still unipolar? Stephen Brooks and William Wohlforth, World Out of Balance (2008) and later work: the US still leads in military technology, finance, alliances and universities. No other state has the full set. Bipolar (US-China)? China and the US are far ahead of all others in GDP, technology and defence spending. Yan Xuetong of Tsinghua and others see a coming bipolar competition. John Mearsheimer says China's rise makes rivalry nearly certain. Multipolar? Russia, India, EU, Japan and regional powers shape outcomes. Military power is concentrated in two, but economic and diplomatic power is spread. Disorder? Ian Bremmer's "G-Zero" (2012): no one leads. Some say we have a "multipolar world without multilateralism". Mearsheimer's view in "Bound to Fail" ( International Security , 2019) is that the US-led liberal order was bound to fade, and a realist order, bounded by great-power balance, replaces it.
2025-26: shocks to the order

US trade shock. Heavy tariffs from April 2025, challenged in court. On 20 February 2026 the Supreme Court ruled that the emergency law (IEEPA) did not authorise tariffs. The administration used other laws, such as Section 122 (a temporary 150-day tariff that lapsed in July 2026) and then Section 301 tariffs on dozens of economies. Retreat from institutions. The US left the Paris Agreement (effective January 2026) and WHO, and announced exits from dozens of other bodies in January 2026. War in West Asia. US and Israeli strikes on Iran began again on 28 February 2026. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz was disrupted. Trump and Xi met in Beijing in May 2026. US-China. A trade truce was struck in October 2025 and talks continue. Others. The Ukraine war continues. BRICS and the SCO have drawn more attention. India chaired BRICS in 2026. These show a system with a still-powerful but less predictable US, a rival China, and wider room for middle powers. Treat each fact as of 2026, and re-check before the exam.
India in a multipolar world

India's preference. New Delhi has long said it wants a multipolar world , and a multipolar Asia too. Joint statements with Russia and France use this phrase. Strategic autonomy and multi-alignment. India works with the US (Quad, defence and technology), Russia (energy and arms), France, Japan, Gulf states and the Global South. Pressure test. In 2025 the US imposed tariffs of up to 50% on Indian goods, citing India's Russian oil purchases. India diversified: FTAs with the UK (in force 15 July 2026), the EU (concluded January 2026), and a US interim framework in February 2026. Rates and status are still evolving. China. Improved tone in 2025 (Modi's visit to the SCO summit in Tianjin, August-September 2025), but border and trade issues remain. Platforms. BRICS chair in 2026; G20 presidency in 2023; Voice of Global South summits; Quad; I2U2; IMEC (announced 2023). Risk. Overreliance on one partner, and a gap between aspiration and capability. India's GDP is large, but per capita income and manufacturing remain low.
How UPSC asks this

"The unipolar moment is over. Do you agree?" "Is the world moving towards a multipolar order? What does this mean for India?" "Examine the challenges to American hegemony." "Compare the stability of bipolar and multipolar systems." Structure: define polarity and hegemony (Waltz, Kindleberger, Gilpin). Show the unipolar moment (Krauthammer 1990-91, Wohlforth 1999). Sources of US power and Ikenberry's liberal order. Overreach (Iraq 2003, 2008 crisis). Rise of China, Russia and BRICS (Zakaria, Acharya). Debate: unipolar, bipolar, multipolar. Recent shocks, with dates. End with India: strategic autonomy, multi-alignment, and a call for a reformed multilateral order. Say what you think: "multipolar in economics, bipolar in military power, and increasingly disordered".
Power Transition and the Rise of China
The defining rivalry of the century

The rise of China and the US response shape trade, technology, security and India's choices. Theory frames it: power transition , Thucydides Trap and offensive realism . UPSC links this to the changing world order and India's China policy. Graham Allison's Destined for War (2017) found 16 cases since 1500 where a rising power challenged a ruling one, and 12 of them ended in war.
Power transition theory
A.F.K. Organski , World Politics (1958), and Kugler. Unlike balance of power, it says war is likeliest near parity , not when one side dominates.
Thucydides Trap

Graham Allison, Destined for War (2017), took Thucydides' line that Sparta's fear of rising Athens made war inevitable. In 16 historical cases of a rising power challenging a ruling one, 12 ended in war. Allison says war between the US and China is not inevitable but is more likely than we think . Critics say the sample is selective and nuclear weapons change the logic.
Mearsheimer and the liberal answer

John Mearsheimer , The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (2001): great powers seek regional hegemony , so a strong China will try to dominate Asia and the US will resist. G. John Ikenberry answers that the US-led liberal order is open and rules-based, so China can be integrated, though it is now strained. Joseph Nye 's 'smart power' and the soft power view stress attraction.
China's rise: how

Reform from 1978 (Deng); WTO entry in 2001; world's second-largest economy since about 2010. State capitalism, manufacturing, exports; Made in China 2025 push for technology. Belt and Road (2013), AIIB (2016), BRICS and NDB, Global Development, Security and Civilisation initiatives. PLA modernisation: carriers, missiles, South China Sea bases.
The US response

Obama's pivot to Asia (2011), the 2018 trade war under Trump, export controls on chips, and tariffs. Alliances: Quad (revived 2017), AUKUS (2021), Indo-Pacific strategy. As of 2025, tariff and technology rivalry continues alongside periodic truces, so describe the competition as managed rivalry and 'decoupling' and 'de-risking'.
Peak China? Peaceful rise?

China's official line: 'peaceful development', a 'community with a shared future'. Neighbours see assertiveness: South China Sea, Senkaku, Taiwan, the Himalayan border. Domestic limits: ageing population, property debt, slower growth ('peak China'). Some scholars argue power transition applies poorly: the US is still ahead in alliances and technology, so a multipolar world or a G2 may emerge instead.
