Order and institutions

China wants a bigger say in institutions (IMF quota, UNSC, WTO) and builds alternatives, such as the AIIB and SCO. It does not directly attack the UN system, which it uses. Compare with the Soviet challenge: no ideological export, but a rival model of development (the 'Beijing Consensus').
India's China challenge

India has the 1962 war , Doklam (2017), Galwan (June 2020) , trade deficit, CPEC through PoK, 'string of pearls' in the Indian Ocean. India uses multi-alignment: Quad, I2U2, Russia ties, BRICS and SCO. Since the October 2024 patrolling arrangement and the Modi-Xi meetings (Kazan 2024; Tianjin SCO 2025), there has been a careful thaw, though trust is low.
How UPSC asks this

"Does the power transition theory explain the US-China rivalry?" "Examine the Thucydides Trap and its critics." "Assess the implications of China's rise for India." Structure: theory, Allison, Mearsheimer vs Ikenberry, China's tools, US response, debate, India. John Mearsheimer's The Tragedy of Great Power Politics (2001) predicts that China will seek regional hegemony, which the US will try to contain. Ikenberry's Liberal Leviathan (2011) argues that the US-led order lasts because it is open and rule-based.
Bretton Woods to the WTO
The rules of money and trade

After the Great Depression and the Second World War, the victors built a new set of rules for money and trade. That system, named after a 1944 conference at Bretton Woods , New Hampshire, still shapes the world: the IMF, the World Bank and, through GATT, the WTO. UPSC asks how this system was built, why it changed in 1971, how GATT became the WTO, and why the WTO is now in crisis. India's stand on agriculture, food security, TRIPS and dispute settlement is a regular sub-question. The topic is also live. In 2025-26 the US raised tariffs sharply, the WTO's Appellate Body stayed frozen, and the 14th ministerial conference at Yaounde (March 2026) failed on its main items. Learn the timeline first, then the institutions, then the debates.
Why Bretton Woods was needed

The interwar years were an economic disaster. The gold standard broke down. Countries devalued to win exports, a "beggar-thy-neighbour" race. The Great Depression (from 1929) and protectionism, such as the US Smoot-Hawley tariff (1930), shrank world trade sharply. Economic collapse helped fascism rise. The Bretton Woods conference (July 1944) brought 44 Allied nations together. India, still a British colony, sent a delegation. The two main architects were John Maynard Keynes (UK) and Harry Dexter White (US). Keynes wanted an international clearing union with its own currency (the "bancor"), which would put pressure on surplus countries too. White's plan, which mostly won, gave the US dollar the central role. The aim was embedded liberalism (John Ruggie, 1982): open trade abroad, with room for welfare and full employment at home.
The Bretton Woods system

Fixed but adjustable exchange rates. Currencies were pegged to the dollar; the dollar was convertible to gold at $35 an ounce. The IMF lent to members with short-term balance-of-payments problems. Votes depend on quotas , roughly economic size. The IBRD (World Bank) financed reconstruction and then development. The IDA (1960) gives soft loans to the poorest. A planned International Trade Organization (Havana Charter, 1948) died when the US Congress would not ratify it. GATT , signed in October 1947 by 23 countries, India among them, filled the gap. By convention, an American heads the World Bank and a European heads the IMF.
The collapse of fixed rates (1971-76)

The system rested on confidence in the dollar. As the US spent on Vietnam and social programmes, dollars piled up abroad, and gold reserves could not cover them. Robert Triffin had warned of this in 1960: the Triffin dilemma , where the reserve-currency country must run deficits that undermine trust in its currency. 15 August 1971. President Nixon suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold: the " Nixon shock ". 1971. The Smithsonian Agreement tried new pegs, but they failed. 1973. Major currencies began to float. 1976. The Jamaica Accords amended the IMF Articles to legalise floating rates. The IMF then shifted toward lending to developing countries, especially after the oil shocks (1973, 1979) and the debt crisis that began with Mexico in 1982. Its loans came with conditionality : structural adjustment programmes based on the Washington Consensus. Critics such as Stiglitz say they caused hardship, as in the 1997 Asian crisis.
GATT rounds to the Uruguay Round

GATT worked through negotiating rounds that cut tariffs step by step. Geneva (1947) to the Dillon Round (1960-61): tariff cuts on goods. Kennedy Round (1964-67): large across-the-board cuts and an anti-dumping code. Tokyo Round (1973-79): non-tariff barriers, and the "enabling clause" (1979) allowing special treatment for developing countries. Uruguay Round (1986-94), launched at Punta del Este: the biggest round. It brought agriculture , textiles , services and intellectual property into the rules, and created the WTO. GATT's core principles Most-favoured-nation (MFN): no discrimination between trading partners. National treatment : imports treated like domestic goods once inside. Bound tariffs , transparency and exceptions for regional trade agreements (Article XXIV) and security (Article XXI). Arthur Dunkel's draft text (1991) shaped the final deal, and India had a heated public debate over it.
The WTO: structure and agreements

The Marrakesh Agreement (April 1994) set up the World Trade Organization , which began on 1 January 1995 in Geneva. It has 166 members. Main pillars GATT 1994 for goods, with the Agreement on Agriculture (AoA). GATS for services. TRIPS for intellectual property: patents for 20 years, including on pharmaceuticals. Dispute Settlement Understanding : panels and a seven-member Appellate Body , with binding rulings and "negative consensus" adoption. Trade Policy Review Mechanism. The highest body is the Ministerial Conference , held every two years or so. Decisions are by consensus , which gives every member a veto in practice. The Agreement on Agriculture sorts farm support into boxes: amber (trade-distorting, capped), blue (production-limiting) and green (minimal distortion, allowed). The current Director-General, Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala, is the first woman and first African in the post, now in her second term.
Doha to Yaounde: a stalled agenda

Doha Development Agenda (November 2001): a round meant to help developing countries. It stalled over farm subsidies and market access, with collapses at Cancun (2003) and in 2008. Bali (2013): the Trade Facilitation Agreement (in force 2017), and an interim "peace clause" on food stockholding. Nairobi (2015): agreement to end farm export subsidies. MC12, Geneva (2022): a deal on harmful fisheries subsidies and a limited TRIPS waiver for COVID-19 vaccines. MC13, Abu Dhabi (2024): few results. MC14, Yaounde (26-29 March 2026): no consensus to extend the moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions, which lapsed on 30 March 2026 for the first time since 1998; no fix for the Appellate Body; fisheries talks on overcapacity were sent on to the next conference. Some members have since moved toward a temporary extension of the moratorium. Meanwhile groups of members use plurilateral deals (investment facilitation, e-commerce), which India often opposes as bypassing consensus.
The WTO in crisis

Appellate Body paralysis. Since December 2019 the US has blocked new appointments, so the body cannot hear appeals. Losing parties can appeal "into the void". About 50-odd members use a stopgap, the Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement (MPIA, 2020). India and the US are not in it. Unilateral tariffs. US tariffs in 2025-26, justified by national security (Section 232) and other laws, ignore MFN commitments. The US Supreme Court ruled in February 2026 that one law (IEEPA) did not allow tariffs, but other tariffs continue. China's model. State subsidies and state firms strain rules written for market economies. North-South divide. Disputes over special and differential treatment, farm support and TRIPS. Consensus deadlock among 166 members. Regionalism. Mega-deals such as CPTPP and RCEP (in force 2022) shift rule-making elsewhere. Defenders note that most world trade still runs on WTO tariff bindings, and that the system has prevented a 1930s-style collapse.
Reforming the Bretton Woods institutions

Voice and votes. The US holds about 16.5% of IMF votes, enough to veto decisions needing an 85% majority. China's quota (about 6.4%) is below its economic weight. The 16th quota review (December 2023) raised quotas by 50% but kept shares the same; realignment was pushed to later talks. Leadership convention (American at the Bank, European at the Fund) is criticised by emerging economies. Conditionality and austerity are criticised. Climate and debt. The G20's Common Framework for debt (2020) has been slow. Calls grow for more concessional finance. New bodies. The BRICS New Development Bank (began 2015, Shanghai) and the China-led AIIB (2016, Beijing; India is its second-largest shareholder). Dollar dominance. The dollar remains the main reserve currency, though its share has slowly fallen. Talk of "de-dollarisation" grew after sanctions on Russia in 2022.
India and the global economic order

Founding member of the IMF, World Bank and GATT (1947), and of the WTO (1995). 1991. India took IMF support during its balance-of-payments crisis and began reforms. Agriculture and food security. India defends minimum support prices and public stockholding for food security, protected for now by the Bali peace clause. It seeks a permanent solution. In 2018-19 India became the first country to invoke the peace clause, for rice. TRIPS. India's Patents Act amendment (2005) kept Section 3(d) against "evergreening". The Supreme Court upheld it in Novartis v. Union of India (2013). India and South Africa proposed the COVID-19 TRIPS waiver (October 2020). Fisheries. India seeks room for small and artisanal fishers in subsidy rules. Disputes. India has been both complainant and respondent, including with the US over steel, solar panels and tariffs. IMF and World Bank. India seeks quota realignment. Its IMF quota share is about 2.75%. Trade policy. A mix of multilateralism and new FTAs (UAE 2022, Australia 2022, UK in force July 2026, EU concluded January 2026).
How UPSC asks this

"Trace the evolution of the international economic order from Bretton Woods to the WTO." "Why did the Bretton Woods system collapse in the 1970s?" "Is the WTO in crisis? Examine India's stand on WTO reform." "The Bretton Woods institutions need democratisation. Discuss." Structure: interwar background, Bretton Woods 1944 (Keynes versus White), three pillars, the 1971 Nixon shock and floating rates, the debt crisis and conditionality. Then GATT rounds, the Uruguay Round and the WTO (1995) with its agreements. Then Doha's stall and MC12-MC14. The crisis: Appellate Body, tariffs, China. Reform debates. End with India's positions. A timeline (1944, 1947, 1971, 1986, 1995, 2001, 2019, 2026) gives quick marks.
CMEA and the Demand for NIEO
Two challenges to the Western economic order

The Bretton Woods order was built by the West. Two groups tried other paths. The Soviet bloc set up its own trading system, the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance (CMEA or COMECON) . The newly independent states of the Global South demanded a New International Economic Order (NIEO) . Both failed in their own ways. The CMEA collapsed with communism in 1991. The NIEO was blocked by rich states and undercut by the 1980s debt crisis. Yet the questions they raised, about fair prices, technology, debt and voice in global bodies, are alive today in BRICS, G20 and climate-finance debates. UPSC asks you to explain each, compare them with Bretton Woods, and judge why the NIEO failed. India, a leader of the G-77 and NAM, is central to the NIEO story.
Birth of the CMEA

The CMEA was founded in Moscow in January 1949 by the USSR, Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Poland and Romania. It was Stalin's answer to the Marshall Plan (1947), which Moscow had forbidden its satellites to accept. Albania joined in 1949 but stopped taking part in 1961. East Germany joined in 1950. Non-European members came later: Mongolia (1962), Cuba (1972) and Vietnam (1978). Yugoslavia had an associate status from 1964. Headquarters: Moscow. Its stated aim was planned economic cooperation and a "socialist division of labour" among members. In practice it linked Eastern European economies to the Soviet Union.
How the CMEA worked

Bilateral barter-like trade. Trade was agreed in five-year plans between governments, not through markets. Prices were set by formulas, often based on past world-market prices. Transferable rouble. A unit of account cleared through the International Bank for Economic Cooperation (1963). It was not freely convertible. Energy for goods. The USSR supplied oil and gas, often below world prices after 1973, in exchange for machinery and consumer goods. The Druzhba ("Friendship") pipeline (1960s) is a symbol. Comprehensive Programme (1971) aimed at deeper integration and joint investment. Specialisation dispute In 1962 Khrushchev proposed a supranational planning body that would assign roles to each country. Romania objected, fearing it would be kept as a farm supplier, and the plan was shelved. National sovereignty limited integration, unlike the EEC.
Why the CMEA failed

No price signals. Without markets, prices did not show real costs. Waste and shortages followed. Low quality and technology. Members traded goods that could not compete in the West. Soviet dominance. Members resented the hub-and-spoke structure. The USSR's subsidies were also a political tool. Inconvertible currencies blocked multilateral trade. Debt. Poland and Hungary borrowed heavily from the West in the 1970s. Politics. The 1989 revolutions removed the regimes that made it work. In 1991 members moved to world prices and hard currency. The CMEA was formally dissolved in June 1991 , months before the USSR itself. Compare with the EEC: market-based, rule-bound and supranational, it deepened while the CMEA dissolved. Many former CMEA states later joined the EU (2004, 2007).
Roots of the NIEO

Newly independent states found that political freedom did not bring economic freedom. They still exported raw materials and imported manufactures on unfavourable terms (the Prebisch-Singer thesis ). 1962. UN resolution 1803 on permanent sovereignty over natural resources . 1964. The first UNCTAD in Geneva, led by Raul Prebisch. The G-77 formed on 15 June 1964. 1968. UNCTAD II in New Delhi pushed the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP). 1970. UN target that rich states give 0.7% of GNP as aid. 1973. NAM's Algiers summit called for a new order. That October, the OPEC oil embargo and price rise showed commodity power. Encouraged by OPEC, the South pressed its case at the UN.
The NIEO programme (1974)

The UN General Assembly's Sixth Special Session adopted on 1 May 1974 the Declaration on the Establishment of a New International Economic Order (resolution 3201) and a Programme of Action (3202). In December 1974 the Assembly adopted the Charter of Economic Rights and Duties of States (resolution 3281), over Western objections. Main demands Stable, fair commodity prices , and indexation to the prices of manufactures. The right to regulate and nationalise foreign firms. Technology transfer on fair terms; a code of conduct for multinationals. Preferential, non-reciprocal access to rich markets. More aid and debt relief . Reform of the IMF and World Bank to give the South a bigger voice. Producer associations, like OPEC, for other commodities.
What came of it

UNCTAD IV (Nairobi, 1976) adopted an Integrated Programme for Commodities and a Common Fund , agreed in 1980 but only in force in 1989, far smaller than planned. The EEC's Lome Convention (1975) with African, Caribbean and Pacific states gave trade preferences and STABEX export-earnings support. The Brandt Report , North-South: A Programme for Survival (1980), urged mutual interest and large transfers. The Cancun summit (1981), with Reagan and Indira Gandhi, produced little.
Why the NIEO failed

Northern resistance. The US, UK and West Germany rejected price controls and nationalisation rules. Reagan and Thatcher (from 1979-81) championed free markets. The debt crisis (from Mexico, 1982) shifted power to creditors. The IMF's structural adjustment replaced the NIEO agenda. Divided South. Oil price rises hurt oil-importing developing countries. East Asian states chose export-led growth. Commodity cartels failed beyond oil. Producers of copper, coffee or bauxite could not hold prices. UN votes are not binding. General Assembly resolutions lacked enforcement. Neoliberal turn in ideas: the Washington Consensus (1989). Some analysts (Robert Rothstein, Stephen Krasner's Structural Conflict , 1985) argued the South sought authority-based regimes because it lacked market power.
Legacy: the NIEO today

The NIEO is often called dead, but its themes returned. Voice. G20 (leaders from 2008), IMF quota reform, the African Union in the G20 (2023). Alternatives. BRICS and its New Development Bank, the AIIB. Climate justice. CBDR, loss and damage, and the $300 billion finance goal (2024) echo the call for transfers. Debt. The G20 Common Framework (2020), and calls for a UN debt mechanism. Technology. The COVID-19 TRIPS waiver fight (2020-22). Sovereignty over resources. Critical minerals policies in Indonesia and Africa. Scholars such as Vijay Prashad ( The Darker Nations , 2007) see the NIEO as the high point of a Third World project. Others see the shift to market reform as a better route.
India, CMEA and the NIEO

Rupee trade with the Soviet bloc. India was not a CMEA member, but it traded with the USSR and Eastern Europe through rupee-rouble clearing agreements (from 1953), paying in goods rather than hard currency. Soviet help built Bhilai (steel) and other plants. After 1991. Russia and India settled the old rouble debt in 1993. Rupee trade ideas resurfaced after the 2022 sanctions on Russia, when the RBI allowed trade settlement in rupees (July 2022). NIEO leadership. India hosted UNCTAD II (New Delhi, 1968), was a founding G-77 member, and chaired NAM from 1983. Indira Gandhi championed the NIEO, and attended the 1981 Cancun summit. Today. India speaks for the Global South: Voice of Global South summits (2023 onwards), debt and climate finance, and WTO food security. It chaired BRICS in 2026.
How UPSC asks this

"Why did the demand for a New International Economic Order fail? Is it relevant today?" "Examine the role and failure of COMECON." "Compare the CMEA with the European Economic Community." Structure for CMEA: origin (1949, reply to Marshall Plan), members, working (plans, transferable rouble, Soviet energy), Romania's 1962 dispute, failure and dissolution (June 1991), comparison with EEC. Structure for NIEO: roots (Prebisch, UNCTAD 1964, G-77, OPEC 1973), 1974 Declaration and Charter, demands, outcomes (Common Fund, Lome, Brandt), reasons for failure, legacy today, India's role.
Role and Record of the UN
Eighty years of the world's parliament

The United Nations was founded in 1945 "to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war", in the words of the Charter's preamble. It turned 80 in 2025, in a year of war in Ukraine, Gaza and Sudan, deep budget cuts and a reform drive called UN80 . UPSC asks you to assess its role and record: peace and security, development, human rights, decolonisation. Answers need balance. The UN failed in Rwanda and is blocked over Ukraine, yet it feeds millions, runs peace operations and sets global norms. Learn the Charter's purposes and organs, key articles, landmark successes and failures, and India's contribution. The reform side is in the next lesson.
Founding the UN

Atlantic Charter (August 1941): Roosevelt and Churchill's war aims. Declaration by United Nations (1 January 1942): 26 Allied states, India among them. Dumbarton Oaks (1944) drafted the structure; Yalta (February 1945) agreed the veto. San Francisco Conference (April-June 1945): 50 states signed the Charter on 26 June 1945. Poland signed later as the 51st original member. The Charter entered into force on 24 October 1945 , now UN Day. India, then under British rule, was an original member. Membership today is 193 states, with South Sudan (2011) the newest. Palestine and the Holy See are non-member observer states.
Purposes, principles and organs

Purposes (Article 1) Maintain peace and security; develop friendly relations based on equal rights and self-determination; cooperate on economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems and human rights; be a centre for harmonising actions. Key principles (Article 2) Sovereign equality; peaceful settlement of disputes; Article 2(4) : no threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state; Article 2(7) : no intervention in domestic matters, except Chapter VII enforcement. Six principal organs General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC), Trusteeship Council (suspended since 1994 after Palau), International Court of Justice (The Hague), Secretariat (led by the Secretary-General).
Security Council and General Assembly

The P5 are China, France, Russia, the UK and the US. The Council grew from 11 to 15 members in 1965. The veto has been used most by the USSR/Russia and the US. The Assembly controls the budget, elects non-permanent members, and with the Council appoints the Secretary-General and ICJ judges. The Uniting for Peace resolution (1950) lets it act when a veto blocks the Council. Since 2022, a General Assembly debate must follow every veto (resolution 76/262).
The Secretary-General

The Secretary-General is the "chief administrative officer" (Article 97), appointed by the General Assembly on the Council's recommendation, for five years by convention, renewable. Article 99 lets the SG bring threats to peace to the Council's attention, a power Antonio Guterres used on Gaza in December 2023. Trygve Lie, Dag Hammarskjold (died in 1961 in a plane crash in Africa), U Thant, Kurt Waldheim, Javier Perez de Cuellar, Boutros Boutros-Ghali ( An Agenda for Peace , 1992), Kofi Annan (Nobel 2001), Ban Ki-moon, and Antonio Guterres (2017-2026). Guterres's term ends on 31 December 2026. The 2026 selection used public candidate dialogues and Council straw polls. Women's groups pushed for the first woman SG. As of November 2026 the Council had held several straw polls but not yet made a recommendation. Guterres's term ends on 31 December 2026. Hammarskjold shaped "preventive diplomacy" and peacekeeping. Critics say the SG is "more secretary than general", dependent on the P5.
Peace and security: the record

Successes or partial successes Korea (1950) and the reversal of Iraq's invasion of Kuwait (1990-91). Suez (1956): the first armed peacekeeping force, UNEF. Missions that helped end wars in Namibia (1989-90), Mozambique, El Salvador, Cambodia (UNTAC, 1992-93), Sierra Leone, Liberia and Timor-Leste. No third world war; nuclear and chemical arms treaties negotiated under UN auspices. Failures Paralysis during much of the Cold War. Rwanda (1994): troops were cut while about 800,000 people were killed. Srebrenica (1995). Iraq (2003): war without Council approval. Syria (from 2011), Ukraine (from 2022), Gaza (from 2023) and Sudan: vetoes or weak responses. Peacekeeping: over 70 operations since 1948. The Blue Helmets won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1988.
Beyond security: development, rights and norms

Decolonisation. The 1960 Declaration (resolution 1514) helped about 80 former colonies join. Membership rose from 51 to 193. Human rights. UDHR (1948), the covenants (1966), CEDAW, the Human Rights Council (2006). Development. UNDP, UNCTAD, the Millennium Development Goals (2000-15) and the Sustainable Development Goals (2015-30), 17 goals. Humanitarian work. WFP (Nobel 2020), UNHCR (Nobel 1954 and 1981), UNICEF (Nobel 1965). Environment. Stockholm (1972), UNFCCC (1992), Paris Agreement (2015). Law. UNCLOS (1982), the ICJ, international criminal tribunals. Pact for the Future (September 2024): commitments on Council reform, digital cooperation and future generations. Many scholars say the UN's quiet, everyday work matters more than its high-politics failures.
Theoretical views of the UN

Realists The UN reflects great-power interests; it works only when the P5 agree. Morgenthau and Mearsheimer doubt that it constrains states. Liberals It lowers transaction costs, spreads information and builds habits of cooperation. Imperfect, but better than none. Constructivists It creates and spreads norms: sovereignty, decolonisation, human rights, R2P (Finnemore). Critical and Global South views The veto and the P5 freeze the power map of 1945. Funding by a few rich states shapes priorities. Inis Claude, Swords into Plowshares (1956), and Paul Kennedy, The Parliament of Man (2006), are standard histories.
The UN at 80: crisis

Money. The UN faces a liquidity crisis. The US, which pays about 22% of the regular budget, cut contributions sharply. The 2026 regular budget was cut to $3.45 billion (adopted December 2025, about 15% below 2025), and thousands of posts were cut. Retreat of a founder. The US left WHO, the Paris Agreement and the Human Rights Council, and announced it will leave UNESCO from 31 December 2026, and in January 2026 announced exits from 66 international bodies, 31 of them UN-linked. Council deadlock. Vetoes on Ukraine and Gaza; little action on Sudan. Wars of 2026. Conflict involving Iran, Israel and the US from February 2026 bypassed the Council. Legitimacy. The South asks why Africa and India have no permanent seat. The UN80 Initiative (launched March 2025) aims to cut costs, review mandates and merge bodies. See the next lesson.
India and the UN

Founding member. India signed the 1942 Declaration and the 1945 Charter. Human rights and decolonisation. Hansa Mehta in UDHR drafting; India raised apartheid in 1946. Kashmir. India took the issue to the Council in January 1948; it now insists on bilateralism (Simla Agreement, 1972). Peacekeeping. One of the largest troop contributors since the 1950s (Korea, Congo, Gaza, Lebanon, South Sudan), with the first all-women police unit (Liberia, 2007). Security Council. Elected eight times, most recently for 2021-22. India seeks a permanent seat, working with the G4. Leadership. Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit was the first woman President of the General Assembly (1953). Norms. International Day of Yoga (2014), the International Year of Millets (2023), and India's CCIT proposal (1996).
How UPSC asks this

"Evaluate the role of the UN in maintaining international peace and security." "The UN has failed but it is indispensable." Discuss. "Discuss India's contribution to the United Nations." Structure: founding and purposes (Articles 1, 2(4), 2(7)); organs with the Council and Assembly diagram; Secretary-General's role (Articles 97, 99). Record: peace successes and failures, then development, rights, decolonisation and environment. Theories in brief. Current crisis (funding, US exits, vetoes, UN80). India's role. Conclusion: reform, not abandonment.
Specialised Agencies and UN Reform
The working arms of the UN, and how to fix the whole

Most of what the UN does day to day is done not by the Security Council but by its specialised agencies , funds and programmes: vaccines, food aid, air safety, labour standards, telecom frequencies, weather data. At the same time, the UN is under pressure to reform: its Council reflects 1945, its finances are in crisis, and in 2025 the Secretary-General launched the UN80 Initiative to cut and merge. UPSC asks: what are the specialised agencies and how do they work? What reforms are needed, especially of the Security Council? What is India's case for a permanent seat? This lesson covers both halves. Link the agencies to Mitrany's functionalism , which they embody.
What is a specialised agency?

Under Articles 57 and 63 of the Charter, specialised agencies are autonomous international organisations linked to the UN by agreements with ECOSOC. They have their own members, budgets, governing bodies and heads. They differ from funds and programmes (UNICEF, UNDP, WFP, UNHCR), which are subsidiary bodies of the UN, mostly funded by voluntary donations. The idea comes from functionalism : David Mitrany's A Working Peace System (1943) argued that cooperation on technical tasks would build peace. Some agencies are older than the UN: the ITU (1865), the Universal Postal Union (1874) and the ILO (1919). There are 15 specialised agencies, plus related bodies such as the IAEA and the WTO, which report to the UN but are not specialised agencies.
The main agencies

Examples of their work: WHO declared smallpox eradicated (1980) and coordinated COVID-19 (declared a pandemic in March 2020). The ILO is tripartite , with governments, employers and workers. ICAO sets aviation rules; ITU assigns radio spectrum and satellite slots. Headquarters: WHO, ILO, ITU, WIPO and WMO in Geneva; FAO and IFAD in Rome; UNESCO in Paris; ICAO in Montreal; IMO in London; UPU in Bern; IMF and World Bank in Washington.
Strengths and problems of the agencies

Strengths Technical expertise, global standards, near-universal membership, effective in non-political fields (aviation, post, health data). Problems Politicisation. The US left UNESCO in 1984, rejoined in 2003, left in 2018 after Palestine's admission (2011), rejoined in 2023, and announced withdrawal again in 2025. Funding. Most money is voluntary and earmarked by donors, which distorts priorities. WHO's budget depended heavily on a few donors and foundations. US exit from WHO , effective January 2026, cut a major funder. Overlap. Many bodies work on the same issues (food, health, gender). Great-power rivalry for top posts, such as China's campaigns for agency heads. The WHO Pandemic Agreement (adopted May 2025) showed that agencies can still make new rules, even without the US.
Why the UN needs reform

Security Council reflects 1945: no permanent seat for Africa, Latin America or India; Europe is over-represented. The veto blocks action on mass atrocities and on conflicts involving the P5. Finances. Late or unpaid dues, and overdependence on a few donors. Bureaucracy. Too many mandates and overlapping bodies. Effectiveness. Slow response to crises. Representation of non-state actors and of future generations. Reform history: the Council's 1965 enlargement; Kofi Annan's In Larger Freedom (2005), which led to the Human Rights Council and Peacebuilding Commission (2005-06); Ban's and Guterres's management reforms (2019 development system reform); the Pact for the Future (September 2024); and UN80 (2025).
Security Council reform: the models

Talks are held in the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) of the General Assembly, since 2009. Any change needs a Charter amendment under Article 108 : two-thirds of the Assembly, then ratification by two-thirds of members including all five P5. Main groups G4 (Brazil, Germany, India, Japan): new permanent and non-permanent seats, and a 15-year review of the veto for new members. Uniting for Consensus ("Coffee Club", led by Italy, Pakistan, Argentina, South Korea and others): no new permanent seats, more long-term elected seats. African Union (Ezulwini Consensus, 2005): two permanent seats with veto and five non-permanent seats for Africa. L.69 group of developing countries supports expansion in both categories. The P5 differ: the US, UK, France and Russia have voiced support for India's bid in principle; China is opposed or silent. Veto restraint: the France-Mexico initiative and the ACT code of conduct on atrocities.
UN80: cutting and merging

Guterres launched UN80 in March 2025, amid a cash crunch caused largely by US cuts. Efficiency: cut posts and costs; move staff from high-cost cities (New York, Geneva) to cheaper hubs such as Nairobi and Bonn. For 2026, posts were cut and the regular budget trimmed to $3.45 billion (about 15% below 2025). Mandate review: the General Assembly is reviewing tens of thousands of mandates for overlap. Structural change: proposals include merging UNDP with UNOPS, merging UNFPA with UN Women, and phasing out UNAIDS. The UNFPA-UN Women idea is controversial; women's groups fear loss of focus. Critics say UN80 is cost-cutting driven by donors, not a vision. Supporters say slimming is the only way to survive. The new Secretary-General, from January 2027, will carry it forward.
Why reform is so hard

The P5 veto over reform itself (Article 108). Regional rivalries. Pakistan opposes India, Italy opposes Germany, Argentina and Mexico oppose Brazil, China opposes Japan. Africa's unity on Ezulwini makes compromise difficult. Efficiency versus representation. A bigger Council may be fairer but slower. Money talks. Donors shape agencies through earmarked funds. US ambivalence. A US that is leaving bodies has little interest in strengthening them. Thinkers' views: realists expect no reform without a shift in power; liberals favour incremental change (working methods, veto restraint); Global South scholars see legitimacy as the core issue.
India's case and role

Case for a permanent seat: the world's most populous country (since 2023), a large economy, a founding member, one of the largest peacekeeping contributors, nuclear restraint, and a voice of the Global South. Elected eight times as a non-permanent member, most recently 2021-22; candidate for 2028-29. Diplomacy: works in the G4 and the L.69 group, and supports the African position; calls for text-based negotiations in the IGN. Agencies: active in WHO (vaccines; "pharmacy of the world"), ILO, FAO (International Year of Millets 2023), ITU (hosted the World Telecommunication Standardization Assembly in New Delhi, 2024), and the International Solar Alliance as a new treaty body. Criticisms India faces: its record on certain human rights resolutions and its reluctance to support R2P.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine the role of UN specialised agencies in global governance." "What are the obstacles to Security Council reform? Assess India's claim to a permanent seat." "Is the UN80 Initiative real reform?" Structure: define agencies (Articles 57, 63; functionalism), list key ones with roles, give strengths and problems (politicisation, funding, US exits). Then reform: why needed, history (2005, 2024 Pact), Council models (G4, UfC, Ezulwini, L.69), Article 108 hurdle, UN80. End with India's case and a way forward.
EU and NAFTA/USMCA
Two models of regional integration

Regionalisation means states in a region cooperating more closely, in trade, money or even politics. The two biggest examples in the West are very different. The European Union is the deepest integration project in history: a single market, a common currency for 21 states, shared laws and a parliament. NAFTA (1994), replaced by the USMCA (2020), is a free trade agreement among the US, Canada and Mexico, with no supranational bodies. UPSC asks you to compare them, explain the EU's institutions and crises, and assess what changed from NAFTA to USMCA. The topic links to functionalism, globalisation and India's own FTAs (India-EU, concluded 2026).
Stages of economic integration

Bela Balassa's The Theory of Economic Integration (1961) set out the ladder. Free trade area: no tariffs among members; each keeps its own external tariff (NAFTA/USMCA, SAFTA). Customs union: plus a common external tariff (EU since 1968, Mercosur). Common market: plus free movement of labour and capital. Economic and monetary union: plus a common currency and policies (eurozone). Political union. Jacob Viner (1950) showed that integration can create trade or divert it from cheaper outsiders.
How the EU grew

1951 ECSC; 1957 Treaties of Rome (EEC); 1968 customs union. Enlargements: UK, Ireland, Denmark (1973); Greece (1981); Spain, Portugal (1986); Austria, Finland, Sweden (1995); ten states mostly from Central and Eastern Europe (2004); Bulgaria, Romania (2007); Croatia (2013). 1986 Single European Act; 1992 Maastricht (EU, citizenship, euro plan, three pillars); 1997 Amsterdam; 2001 Nice; 2007 Lisbon (in force 2009: legal personality, permanent European Council President, High Representative, citizens' initiative, Article 50 exit clause). 1995 Schengen in force; 1999 euro launched; 2002 notes and coins. 2020 UK left (the only exit so far). 2026: Bulgaria became the 21st euro member on 1 January. Candidate states include Ukraine and Moldova (status 2022), the Western Balkans and Turkiye (talks frozen). Montenegro and Albania are seen as the front-runners.
EU institutions

European Commission (Brussels): proposes laws, enforces treaties, negotiates trade. One commissioner per state. President: Ursula von der Leyen (second term from 2024). European Council: heads of state or government; sets direction. President: Antonio Costa (from December 2024). Council of the EU: national ministers; co-legislator. Most votes by qualified majority (55% of states with 65% of population); unanimity on foreign policy and tax. European Parliament: directly elected since 1979; 720 members after the 2024 election; co-legislator. Court of Justice of the EU: supremacy and direct effect of EU law ( Van Gend en Loos , 1963; Costa v ENEL , 1964). European Central Bank (Frankfurt): monetary policy for the eurozone. The EU mixes supranational (Commission, Court, ECB, Parliament) and intergovernmental (European Council) features. Scholars call it a sui generis polity.
Crises of the EU

Democratic deficit: distant institutions and low turnout. Eurozone crisis (2010-12): Greek debt, bailouts, austerity; ECB's Mario Draghi pledged "whatever it takes" (2012). Migration crisis (2015) and the 2024 Pact on Migration and Asylum. Brexit (2016 vote; exit 31 January 2020). Rule of law disputes with Hungary and Poland; funds were withheld. Populism and Eurosceptic parties grew in the 2024 elections. War in Ukraine (2022): sanctions, energy shift from Russia, and a defence push (ReArm Europe, 2025). Trade pressure from US tariffs in 2025-26 and from Chinese competition. Yet each crisis has also produced more integration: the NextGenerationEU recovery fund (2020) with joint borrowing, and joint defence spending. Jean Monnet's line that Europe would be forged in crises is often cited.

The North American Free Trade Agreement came into force on 1 January 1994 . It built on the 1988 Canada-US FTA. Removed most tariffs among the US, Canada and Mexico over 15 years. Covered investment (with investor-state dispute settlement, Chapter 11), services and intellectual property. Side agreements on labour and environment. Dispute panels on trade remedies (Chapter 19). Effects. Trade among the three grew several times over. Integrated supply chains, especially in cars, crossed borders many times. Mexico gained factories (maquiladoras) but rural farmers suffered from cheap US corn. US critics blamed it for lost manufacturing jobs; economists found modest net effects. The Zapatista uprising in Chiapas began the day NAFTA took effect.
From NAFTA to USMCA

Donald Trump called NAFTA "the worst trade deal". Renegotiation produced the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (Canada calls it CUSMA, Mexico T-MEC), signed on 30 November 2018 and in force on 1 July 2020 . Key changes Cars: regional value content raised to 75%, and 40-45% of a car made by workers earning at least $16 an hour. Labour: Mexico reformed union laws; a rapid-response mechanism targets factories. Digital trade chapter; longer patent and copyright terms. ISDS largely removed for Canada and limited for Mexico. A "non-market economy" clause aimed at China. Sunset clause: a 16-year term with a joint review after six years.
USMCA in 2025-26

In 2025 the US placed tariffs on Canada and Mexico, citing fentanyl and migration, but exempted goods that met USMCA rules. Steel, aluminium and car tariffs (Section 232) hit both partners. The first joint review fell on 1 July 2026. The US declined to extend the agreement in its current form. That triggers annual reviews ; the deal remains in force until 2036 unless all three agree to extend. Any party may withdraw with six months' notice. US-Mexico talks have covered car rules of origin, steel and economic security. Canada's talks lagged. New US Section 301 tariffs from July 2026 exclude USMCA-compliant goods. The lesson: a free trade area without strong institutions is vulnerable to the power of its largest member. Check the latest before the exam.
EU versus NAFTA/USMCA

Depth EU: customs union, single market, euro, common law. USMCA: free trade area only. Institutions EU: supranational Commission, Parliament and Court. USMCA: a Free Trade Commission of ministers and dispute panels. Power EU: several big states balance each other. USMCA: one dominant member (the US) with about 85% of the combined GDP. Goals EU: peace and political union. USMCA: commerce and supply chains. Theory EU fits neofunctionalism and liberal intergovernmentalism; USMCA fits realist and hegemonic models.
India, the EU and North America

EU. India's largest or second-largest trading partner in goods. Strategic partnership since 2004. The India-EU FTA was concluded on 27 January 2026 after talks that began in 2007; separate investment and geographical-indications deals were negotiated. The EU-India Trade and Technology Council was set up in 2022-23. Friction points: the EU's carbon border tax (CBAM) and its deforestation rules. US. India's largest export market. Tariffs on Indian goods rose to 50% in 2025, then an interim framework in February 2026 aimed at 18%. Status is evolving. Canada. Ties fell sharply in 2023-24 over the Nijjar case and began to thaw in 2025. Mexico is a growing partner in cars and pharma. Lessons for India: the EU shows the value of institutions; USMCA shows the risks of dependence on one market. India prefers FTAs to deep integration.
How UPSC asks this

"Compare the European Union with NAFTA/USMCA as models of regional integration." "Is the EU facing a crisis of integration?" "What are the main differences between NAFTA and USMCA?" Structure: define regionalisation; Balassa's stages diagram. EU: growth, institutions, crises, resilience. NAFTA: aims and effects. USMCA: changes and the 2026 review. Comparison table. India's links: India-EU FTA, US tariffs.
ASEAN, APEC and SAARC
Asia's three regional experiments

Asia has built regional groups very different from the EU. ASEAN is the most successful, a loose but durable community of 11 South-East Asian states. APEC is a trans-Pacific forum of 21 economies that works by voluntary goals. SAARC , India's own neighbourhood grouping, has been frozen for a decade. UPSC asks why ASEAN succeeded where SAARC failed, what the "ASEAN Way" means, why India is outside APEC, and how BIMSTEC is replacing SAARC in India's policy. These link directly to Paper II Section B: Act East, the Indo-Pacific and South Asia. Know the founding dates, members, key agreements and the latest state of each, and be ready to compare.
ASEAN: origins and growth

The Bangkok Declaration of 8 August 1967 founded ASEAN with Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand. It was partly a Cold War bloc against communist spread, and a way to calm quarrels among members (such as Indonesia's "Konfrontasi" with Malaysia). Timor-Leste became the 11th member on 26 October 2025 at the Kuala Lumpur summit. The Philippines chairs ASEAN in 2026.
The ASEAN Way and institutions

The ASEAN Way Consensus ( musyawarah and mufakat ), non-interference in internal affairs, quiet diplomacy, informality and respect for sovereignty. Codified in the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation (1976), which outside powers including India (2003), China and the US have also signed. ASEAN Charter (2007, in force 2008) gave legal personality. Secretariat in Jakarta. ASEAN Community (2015) with three pillars: political-security, economic and socio-cultural. AFTA (1992) and the ASEAN Economic Community. ASEAN centrality: ASEAN hosts wider forums: ASEAN Regional Forum (1994), ASEAN Plus Three (1997), East Asia Summit (2005), ADMM-Plus (2010). RCEP (signed November 2020, in force January 2022): ASEAN plus China, Japan, South Korea, Australia and New Zealand. India left the talks in November 2019. Amitav Acharya, Constructing a Security Community in Southeast Asia (2001), applies constructivism to ASEAN.
ASEAN's limits

Myanmar. After the February 2021 coup, ASEAN's Five-Point Consensus (April 2021) went largely unimplemented. Myanmar's junta leaders were barred from summits. South China Sea. Members split: the Philippines and Vietnam resist China; Cambodia and Laos lean to Beijing. A Code of Conduct with China has been negotiated for years without conclusion. The 2016 arbitral award for the Philippines was rejected by China. Non-interference limits action on human rights. Weak secretariat and slow integration compared with the EU. Great-power pressure from US-China rivalry and US tariffs in 2025-26. Yet ASEAN has kept peace among members for nearly 60 years and shaped the region's architecture. Realists see it as a "talk shop"; constructivists see a nascent security community.
APEC

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum was launched in Canberra in 1989 , proposed by Australian Prime Minister Bob Hawke. It has 21 member economies , including the US, China, Japan, Russia, Australia, ASEAN states, Taiwan ("Chinese Taipei") and Hong Kong. It uses the word "economies" so that Taiwan and Hong Kong can join. Open regionalism: lower barriers voluntarily, without discriminating against outsiders. Non-binding decisions by consensus; leaders' meetings since 1993 (Blake Island, Seattle). Bogor Goals (1994): free and open trade by 2010 for developed and 2020 for developing members. Putrajaya Vision 2040 (2020) replaced them. Korea hosted APEC in 2025 (Gyeongju) and China in 2026 (Shenzhen). Critics call APEC a summit photo-op; supporters say it builds norms and ideas that become trade deals (such as the CPTPP).
India and APEC

India applied to join APEC in 1991. In 1997 APEC froze new membership for ten years; the moratorium lapsed in 2007, but India was not admitted. Why India is outside Geography: India is not on the Pacific rim, though Russia and Peru joined in 1998. Some members saw India's trade regime as too closed. APEC's consensus rule lets any member block new entrants. Fear that a large member would slow the group. The US has at times said it "welcomes India's interest". India's Act East policy, the Indo-Pacific concept and its FTAs (ASEAN 2009, Japan and Korea 2010-11, Australia 2022) partly compensate. Membership would help India join regional supply chains.
SAARC: aims and freeze

The South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation was set up in Dhaka on 8 December 1985 by Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. Afghanistan joined in 2007. The secretariat is in Kathmandu (1987). The idea came from Bangladesh's President Ziaur Rahman. The Charter bars bilateral and contentious issues and needs unanimity . Trade: SAPTA (1993, in force 1995) and SAFTA (2004, in force 2006). Others: SAARC Development Fund, South Asian University (New Delhi, 2010), the SAARC Disaster Management Centre, and the SAARC satellite India launched in 2017 (as the South Asia Satellite, without Pakistan). The last summit was the 18th, in Kathmandu in November 2014. The 19th, due in Islamabad in 2016, was called off after the Uri attack when India and others pulled out.
Why SAARC failed

India-Pakistan hostility and cross-border terrorism. India's size: India accounts for most of the region's GDP and area, which raises fears of domination among neighbours. Low intra-regional trade: only about 5% of South Asia's trade, among the lowest of any region. Pakistan's blocking of connectivity, such as the SAARC motor vehicles agreement (2014). No conflict-resolution role under the Charter. China's rise: China is an observer and a major partner of most members. In June 2025 China, Pakistan and Bangladesh held a trilateral meeting in Kunming. Reports spoke of a possible new grouping without India; Bangladesh denied it was an alliance. No formal bloc has been launched as of this writing. Compare with ASEAN: a shared external threat, no single dominant member, and the habit of setting aside disputes.
India's turn to BIMSTEC and Act East

BIMSTEC (1997, Bangkok Declaration): Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Myanmar, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Thailand. It links South and South-East Asia, and excludes Pakistan. Its Charter was adopted at the Colombo summit (2022). The 6th summit was in Bangkok (April 2025). BBIN (2015) for road and power links. Neighbourhood First policy and lines of credit; power trade with Nepal, Bhutan and Bangladesh. ASEAN. Look East (1991-92) became Act East (2014). India became a sectoral partner (1992), dialogue partner (1995), summit partner (2002), strategic partner (2012) and comprehensive strategic partner (2022). The ASEAN-India goods agreement (2009) is under review because of India's trade deficit. Connectivity: the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway and the Kaladan project.
How UPSC asks this

"Why has ASEAN succeeded where SAARC has failed?" "Explain the 'ASEAN Way'. Is it an asset or a liability?" "Is BIMSTEC a viable alternative to SAARC?" "Examine APEC's open regionalism. Should India seek membership?" Structure: ASEAN origins, members, ASEAN Way, institutions, RCEP, limits (Myanmar, South China Sea). APEC: origin, open regionalism, Bogor, India's exclusion. SAARC: aims, achievements, the 2014-16 freeze and reasons. Comparison table. India: Act East, BIMSTEC, Kunming trilateral concern.
Determinants and Institutions
Who decides, and what shapes the decision?

This opening lesson of Paper II Section B asks two simple questions. What shapes India's foreign policy (the determinants)? And who makes it (the institutions)? The answers explain everything that follows: why India chose non-alignment, why it treats its neighbourhood as a priority, why the PMO and NSA matter so much, and why a state like West Bengal can still block a river deal with Bangladesh. In the exam, this topic often appears as a general question, such as "Discuss the determinants of India's foreign policy", or it is used as the framework for a longer answer. Prepare a clear list and attach an example to each item.
The determinants at a glance

Geography: long land borders (about 15,000 km) with seven neighbours, a 7,500 km coastline, and the Indian Ocean on its flank. K.M. Panikkar's India and the Indian Ocean (1945) argued that India's security depends on the seas. History: colonial rule shaped sovereignty, anti-imperialism and sensitivity to outside intervention. Partition made Pakistan a lasting problem. Economy: energy needs, trade, remittances and technology. After 1991 economic interests grew louder. Security: China, Pakistan, terrorism, the nuclear question.
Ideas, leaders and domestic politics

Ideology and values: Gandhian non-violence, Nehruvian internationalism, and the older ideas of Kautilya (the mandala theory) all appear in Indian thinking. Panchsheel (1954) listed five principles of coexistence. Leadership: Nehru (1947–64) shaped policy personally. Indira Gandhi, Vajpayee, Manmohan Singh and Modi have each left a distinct stamp. Domestic politics: coalition governments (1989–2014) needed consensus; the BJP's majority from 2014 gave the PM freedom. Tamil Nadu (Sri Lanka) and West Bengal (Teesta) play a part. Public opinion and the diaspora matter. International system: the Cold War, then a unipolar moment, now a contested multipolar order. Scholars: A. Appadorai , The Domestic Roots of India's Foreign Policy (1981); Kanti Bajpai on Nehruvian, neo-liberal and hyper-realist schools of thought.
Does India have a strategic culture?

George Tanham (RAND, 1992) In 'Indian Strategic Thought: An Interpretive Essay', Tanham said India lacked a tradition of strategic planning, because of its fatalism, caste and history of invasions. Indian scholars answered that this was a Western lens. Kautilya's Arthashastra The mandala theory: the neighbour is a likely enemy, and the neighbour's neighbour a likely friend. Four methods ( saam, daam, dand, bhed ). Modern writers such as Shyam Saran ( How India Sees the World , 2017) trace links. Kanti Bajpai Three schools: Nehruvian (cooperative security), neo-liberal (economics first) and hyper-realist (power, nuclear weapons).
The constitutional framework

Article 51 (Directive Principles): the State shall promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, and encourage settlement of disputes by arbitration. Union List, Seventh Schedule: Entries 10–14 cover foreign affairs, diplomatic and consular matters, the UN, international conferences and treaties. Entry 97 gives residuary powers to the Union. Article 73: the executive power of the Union extends to matters on which Parliament can legislate. Article 253: Parliament can make any law to implement an international treaty, even on a State subject. This is how treaties override the federal division. Article 246 and Article 245 : legislative competence. Importantly, there is no constitutional requirement that Parliament ratify a treaty. The Executive negotiates and ratifies. Parliament's role is mainly to discuss, question and, where needed, legislate.
What the courts have said

In re Berubari Union (1960): the Supreme Court held that Article 3 cannot be used to cede Indian territory. A constitutional amendment under Article 368 is required. The 9th Amendment (1960) followed. Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India (1969): giving away territory (as in the Rann of Kutch award) requires an amendment, but settling a boundary by demarcation does not. Gramophone Co. of India v. Birendra Bahadur Pandey (1984): rules of international law that do not conflict with municipal law are part of Indian law. Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997): the Court used international conventions (CEDAW) to fill a gap in domestic law. The Land Boundary Agreement with Bangladesh was implemented by the 100th Amendment (2015) for this reason.
Who makes foreign policy?

Prime Minister and the PMO Final authority. The PM sets the broad line and leads summit diplomacy. Modi's personal style is very visible. External Affairs Minister and the MEA The Ministry runs missions and negotiations. The Foreign Secretary is its senior career official. The Indian Foreign Service (IFS) was created in 1946. Cabinet Committee on Security (CCS) and the NSA The National Security Council and the National Security Council Secretariat were set up in 1998. The NSA (Ajit Doval since 2014) coordinates security and has led talks with China as Special Representative. Others Defence, Finance and Commerce Ministries; the RAW (1968); ISRO and DAE; the ICCR (1950) for cultural diplomacy; ITEC for training.
Parliament, states and society

Parliament: question hour, debates and the Standing Committee on External Affairs. The 2008 vote of confidence after the nuclear deal is the biggest case of a foreign policy issue shaking the House. Calls for mandatory parliamentary approval of treaties have been made but not accepted. States: border states shape policy on Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka. The Centre has begun to involve states: for example, through a States Division in the MEA. Think tanks and media: ORF, MP-IDSA, Carnegie India, Gateway House. Business and the diaspora: the diaspora of about 35 million Indians abroad gives soft power and remittances. The Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs was merged into the MEA in 2016. Critics say India's foreign policy is over-centralised and short of diplomats: its IFS cadre is only about a thousand, small for a state of India's size.
Determinants at work in 2025–26

Geography and security: the 2025 Pahalgam attack and Operation Sindoor; the China border thaw. Economy: response to US tariffs by new FTAs (UK, EFTA, EU). Ideas: multi-alignment as the new label for strategic autonomy. Federal politics: West Bengal's role in the Ganga and Teesta talks with Bangladesh. Leaders: summitry with Putin, Xi, Trump and others, as in Delhi, Tianjin and Washington. Use such examples to show that the determinants are live and not just textbook headings.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the determinants of India's foreign policy." (typical) "What is the role of the Prime Minister's Office and the NSA in making foreign policy?" (typical) "Critically examine the role of states in India's foreign policy." (typical) Structure: (1) intro with a sentence from Nehru's or Jaishankar's view; (2) determinants in two groups (external, domestic) with examples; (3) constitutional basis (Art 51, 253, 73, Union List); (4) institutions and their roles; (5) problems (centralisation, weak parliamentary role, cadre shortage); (6) reforms.
Continuity and Change
Is Indian foreign policy new or the same old thing?

The central question is easy to state: has India's foreign policy changed since 1947, or only its style? UPSC asks it almost every few years, often as "continuity and change" or in the form of "Nehru to Modi". The best answers say: core goals remain (sovereignty, security, development, strategic autonomy), while methods and partners have changed (from idealism to pragmatism, from the Soviet Union to many partners, from caution to assertive security action). Use the phases below to structure your answer, and give each phase one date and one example.
Phases of Indian foreign policy
These dates are rough. Some historians argue the real breaks were 1962 (Nehru's idealism was damaged), 1991 (economy) and 1998 (nuclear status).
What has stayed the same

Strategic autonomy: from non-alignment to 'multi-alignment', India wants freedom of decision. Panchsheel and respect for sovereignty (1954 agreement with China). Priority to the neighbourhood: from Nehru's "special relations" to the Gujral Doctrine and Neighbourhood First. Development as a goal: a stable external environment for growth. Nuclear restraint: no first use, credible minimum deterrence, support for disarmament in speeches. Support for the UN and the Global South, and a demand for UN reform. No overseas bases or alliances. A short way to say it: India has been a status quo power in territory and a reformist power in institutions .
What has changed

From idealism to realism: power and national interest are openly stated. From Soviet closeness to multi-alignment: the US, Japan, France, Gulf and Russia all matter. From moral lecture to action: India now acts (surgical strike 2016, Balakot 2019, Operation Sindoor 2025) and sets conditions. From closed to open economy, so trade, energy and technology shape diplomacy. New tools: diaspora events, digital public goods, solar alliance, vaccine diplomacy.
The Modi-era toolkit

Neighbourhood First (2014), Act East (2014), Link West / Think West , SAGAR (2015) and MAHASAGAR (2025). Summit and diaspora diplomacy: Howdy Modi (Houston 2019), Namaste Trump (Ahmedabad 2020), large community events abroad. Development partnerships: lines of credit, Vaccine Maitri (2021), Operation Ganga (2022) and other evacuations. Climate and public goods: the International Solar Alliance, CDRI, Mission LiFE. Economic nationalism with openness: Make in India, Atmanirbhar Bharat, PLI schemes, along with new FTAs. Security doctrine: surgical strikes (2016), Balakot (2019), Sindoor (2025): the claim that India will respond to terror on its own terms, with no distinction between terrorists and sponsors.
The doctrines in short

Nehruvian idealism Non-alignment, anti-colonialism, Asian solidarity, peace through the UN. Indira Doctrine No outside power should intervene in South Asia (a Monroe-style principle), and India will act where needed (Bangladesh 1971, Sri Lanka 1987). Gujral Doctrine (1996–97) Generosity towards smaller neighbours without reciprocity. Vajpayee Nuclear status, outreach to Pakistan (Lahore 1999), strategic partnership with the US. Manmohan Singh Civil nuclear deal; 'strategic autonomy'; G20 and BRICS. Modi Neighbourhood First, Act East, multi-alignment, 'new normal' on terror.
How scholars read the shift

C. Raja Mohan, Modi's World (2015): India has moved from "Nehruvian idealism" to pragmatic realism. Shivshankar Menon, Choices (2016): successive governments made hard choices on China, Pakistan and the nuclear question. Sunil Khilnani and others, Nonalignment 2.0 (2012): India should keep its autonomy but adapt it to a new world. Kanti Bajpai: identifies Nehruvian, neo-liberal and hyper-realist schools that compete in Indian strategic thinking. Tanvi Madan, Fateful Triangle (2020): India has long hedged between the US and China. S. Jaishankar, The India Way (2020): argues that India must be a more confident player in a multipolar world, guided by multi-alignment and national interest.
Is the change fundamental?

Defenders of continuity (such as Menon) say India has always adapted its means. Those who stress change point to Modi's style : personal summit diplomacy, the diaspora, more willingness to use force, and a language of civilisation ('Vishwa Bandhu', 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam'). A balanced view: the objectives are continuous, the method is more assertive , and the world around India has changed more than India's basic aims.
Test cases: 2020–2026

China: from Wuhan and Mamallapuram's summitry to Galwan's confrontation, then cautious re-engagement (Kazan 2024, Tianjin 2025). US: from the nuclear deal and Quad to the shock of the 50% tariff (2025) and the 2026 trade framework. Russia: Ukraine war neutrality; oil; Putin's visit (December 2025). Pakistan: Sindoor and the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance. Global South: G20 2023, BRICS chair 2026. Each case shows both continuity (autonomy) and change (assertiveness, hedging, trade diplomacy).
How UPSC asks this

"Indian foreign policy has shown continuity amid change. Discuss." (typical) "Trace the evolution of India's foreign policy from Nehru to Modi." (typical) "Is 'multi-alignment' a continuation of non-alignment or a break?" (typical) Structure: (1) thesis in one line; (2) phases with dates; (3) continuity list; (4) change list; (5) scholars (Raja Mohan, Menon, Jaishankar); (6) test cases; (7) conclusion: same ends, new means.
India and NAM: Phases and Current Role
The idea India gave the world

Non-alignment is the best-known idea in Indian foreign policy. It means not joining a military bloc, keeping freedom to judge issues on merit, and working for peace and decolonisation. The Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) began at Belgrade in 1961 and grew into a group of about 120 states. India was its founder. Today the question is whether non-alignment is still relevant, or whether it has become strategic autonomy and multi-alignment . UPSC asks about phases, India's changing role and the relevance of NAM after the Cold War. This lesson follows those three themes.
Non-alignment is not neutrality

Nehru said India would not join either camp in the Cold War, but it would take a stand on issues. This is different from neutrality (staying out of conflicts) and from isolationism . Independence of judgement: India voted differently on different issues. No military pacts: India refused to join SEATO or CENTO (US-led) and signed no alliance with the USSR. Peace and disarmament: India supported the UN, a nuclear test ban, and cooperative security. Anti-colonialism and anti-racism: support to freedom movements and a stand against apartheid. Economic independence: self-reliance and aid from both blocs. The 1954 Panchsheel principles (mutual respect for sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and peaceful coexistence) guided the policy.
Birth: from Bandung to Belgrade

The Belgrade summit (September 1961) had 25 members. The five founders were Nehru (India), Tito (Yugoslavia), Nasser (Egypt), Sukarno (Indonesia) and Nkrumah (Ghana) . The Cairo preparatory meeting (1961) fixed criteria such as an independent policy, no membership of military alliances and support for liberation movements. At Bandung (1955) , 29 Asian and African states set out ten principles. It was not yet NAM, but it laid the base.
Phase two and three: setbacks and revival

1962 China war: Nehru's idealism was hurt. India accepted Western arms and still stayed non-aligned. Lal Bahadur Shastri and Indira Gandhi took a more realist line. 1971: the Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation led critics to say India was tilting. India answered that it was a response to US–China–Pakistan ties during the Bangladesh crisis. 1973–74: Algiers summit and the call for a New International Economic Order . 1983: the 7th summit in New Delhi. Indira Gandhi chaired NAM (1983–86). She pushed disarmament and development. Rajiv Gandhi handed over the chair at the 1986 Harare summit. India helped form the Africa Fund against apartheid.
After the Cold War: loss of purpose?

When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, there was no bloc to be non-aligned against. NAM's purpose came into doubt. Critics asked whether the movement was a 'talking shop'. 1991 reforms: India sought Western capital and technology. 1990s: NAM shifted its focus to development, debt, UN reform and human rights. 2003 Kuala Lumpur, 2006 Havana, 2009 Sharm el-Sheikh: routine declarations. 2012 Tehran: Manmohan Singh attended. 2016 Margarita and 2019 Baku: Modi skipped both. India sent the Vice-President. In 2024 (Kampala, 19th summit) India was again not represented by the PM. A key marker: Modi has not attended a NAM summit as PM, and has described foreign policy in new words.
How NAM works, and where it split

Structure: no charter or secretariat. A summit every three years, a rotating chair, a Coordinating Bureau at the UN in New York, and decisions by consensus. Successes: support for decolonisation (Namibia, Zimbabwe), the long campaign against apartheid, the call for a New International Economic Order and for nuclear disarmament, and a joint voice in the UN General Assembly. Splits: at Havana (1979) Fidel Castro argued that the Soviet bloc was the 'natural ally' of NAM. India and Yugoslavia opposed this and kept it autonomous. The Iran–Iraq war (1980–88) and the India–Pakistan and India–China disputes showed that NAM could not settle conflicts among its own members. Size: about 120 members, with observers. An easy way to say it: NAM was strong as a voice but weak as an institution .
From non-alignment to strategic autonomy

Nonalignment 2.0 (2012) A report by Sunil Khilnani, Rajiv Kumar, Srinath Raghavan, Shyam Saran and others. It said India must keep its autonomy but use it for a new world: strengthen internal capacity, build ties with all powers, and treat Asia as a priority. S. Jaishankar, The India Way (2020) Says non-alignment fit a bipolar world. Today India practises multi-alignment , engaging many powers on the basis of interest. Nehru's own view The policy was "not neutrality" but active participation in world affairs without joining blocs, in line with his book The Discovery of India (1946) and speeches in the Constituent Assembly.
Is non-alignment dead?

Supporters say the core idea , independence of judgement, is alive in India's stance on Ukraine (no sanctions, balance with the West) and in the Quad-and-BRICS balance. Critics say that the NAM as an institution has little influence, and that India has moved close to the US on many issues. A fair conclusion: NAM has faded, but non-alignment lives on as strategic autonomy. India's present policy is described by terms such as multi-alignment , issue-based alignment and 'strategic autonomy' .
Examples from today

Ukraine: India abstained at the UN, kept buying Russian oil and also engaged Kyiv. A non-aligned style of conduct. Quad plus BRICS/SCO: membership in both Western and Eurasian groupings. Global South: Voice of the Global South summits since 2023 echo old NAM themes. 2025–26 trade pressure: India resisted US demands on Russia, but concluded an interim framework with the US and signed new FTAs with others. Gaza and Iran: India balanced ties with Israel and the Arab world and Iran.
How UPSC asks this

"Is non-alignment still relevant for India?" (typical) "Trace the evolution of India's role in NAM." (typical) "Distinguish between non-alignment and strategic autonomy." (typical) Structure: (1) meaning and principles; (2) origins: Bandung, Belgrade, five founders; (3) phases: Nehru, 1962–71, 1983 Delhi summit, post-1991; (4) debate on relevance; (5) strategic autonomy and multi-alignment; (6) present examples.
SAARC, BIMSTEC and Regional Cooperation
A region that trades with everyone but itself

South Asia holds about a quarter of humanity. Yet only around 5% of its trade is within the region , compared with over 20% in ASEAN. Border crossings are closed, flights are few and power grids barely connect. This lesson asks why SAARC (1985) stalled, why India now prefers BIMSTEC and sub-regional deals, and what policy tools India uses: the Gujral Doctrine, Neighbourhood First, SAGAR and connectivity projects. UPSC likes the comparison: SAARC versus BIMSTEC, and bilateralism versus regionalism. The theme links to functionalism and regional integration theory from Paper II Section A.
SAARC: the story

The founding members were Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka. Afghanistan became the eighth member in 2007. China, Japan, the US, the EU and others are observers. The Charter (Article X) says decisions need unanimity and that bilateral and contentious issues are excluded . That rule was meant to protect smaller states from India, but it also stops the group from handling its main problem: India–Pakistan rivalry.
Why SAARC stalled

India–Pakistan rivalry: after the Uri attack (September 2016), India and others pulled out of the Islamabad summit. No summit has happened since 2014. Asymmetry: India is about 70% of the region's GDP and land. Neighbours fear dominance. Pakistan's veto: the SAARC Motor Vehicles Agreement failed at Kathmandu in 2014 because Pakistan did not clear it. India then moved to BBIN (Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal), and the BBIN Motor Vehicles Agreement was signed in June 2015. Low trade: SAFTA has many items on sensitive lists, and non-tariff barriers are high. Trust: Pakistan denies India transit to Afghanistan. India denies Pakistan MFN trade status (withdrawn in 2019). The South Asia Satellite (GSAT-9, 2017) was India's gift to the region, but Pakistan opted out.
BIMSTEC: the alternative

The Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation began in Bangkok on 6 June 1997. Myanmar joined in December 1997, and Nepal and Bhutan in 2004. The Secretariat is in Dhaka . It links South Asia and Southeast Asia and leaves Pakistan out . It was boosted by the BRICS–BIMSTEC outreach in Goa (October 2016) and Modi's invitation to leaders to his 2019 swearing-in. Charter: adopted at the 5th summit in Colombo (30 March 2022). 6th summit, Bangkok (April 2025): Modi attended. Bangladesh took the chair. A maritime transport cooperation agreement was signed. Unfinished: the BIMSTEC FTA, begun in 2004, is still not concluded.
India's tools in the neighbourhood

Gujral Doctrine (1996–97) Five principles by I.K. Gujral: no reciprocity demanded from smaller neighbours; no territory used against another; no interference in internal affairs; respect for sovereignty; peaceful settlement of disputes. Neighbourhood First (2014) Modi invited all SAARC leaders to his 2014 swearing-in. Focus on connectivity, trade, lines of credit and quick delivery. SAGAR (2015) and MAHASAGAR (2025) Security and Growth for All in the Region, extended in 2025 to a wider 'mutual and holistic advancement' framework. Other tools: the Colombo Security Conclave (India, Sri Lanka, Maldives, later Mauritius and Bangladesh), the Indian Ocean Rim Association (IORA) and the Mekong–Ganga Cooperation .
Integration theories applied to South Asia

Functionalism (David Mitrany, A Working Peace System , 1943) Cooperate on technical tasks first. Habits of cooperation grow and make war less likely. Neo-functionalism (Ernst Haas, The Uniting of Europe , 1958) Cooperation in one sector 'spills over' into others. Intergovernmentalism (Stanley Hoffmann) States stay in charge and integrate only where their interests match. South Asia fits intergovernmentalism best. Spillover has not happened because the core security rivalry blocks it. Karl Deutsch ( Political Community and the North Atlantic Area , 1957) said integration needs a 'security community' where war is unthinkable. India and Pakistan are far from it.
Can South Asia integrate?

Realists say regional integration cannot succeed while the two largest states are rivals. Functionalists reply that cooperation in low-politics areas such as power, transport and health can build habits of trust. Sub-regionalism gives a middle path: BBIN, the Bhutan–India–Nepal power trade and the India–Bangladesh–Nepal energy deals (Nepal exports hydropower to Bangladesh via India, 2024). In 2025 reports described Chinese-backed talks among China, Pakistan and Bangladesh in Kunming on a possible alternative grouping, showing China's interest in the space.
What India does now

Treats SAARC as dormant and puts BIMSTEC at the centre of its Bay of Bengal policy. Funds roads and rail: Kaladan, the Trilateral Highway, and India–Bangladesh rail links. Offers Vaccine Maitri (2021) and disaster relief across the region, as in the 2015 Nepal earthquake and 2025 Myanmar earthquake relief (Operation Brahma). Links payment systems: UPI in Nepal, Bhutan and Sri Lanka. The tension: India is accused of acting alone while preaching consultation. Big projects still need local politics to line up.
Key facts to memorise

SAARC Founded 8 December 1985, Dhaka. 8 members. Secretariat: Kathmandu. Last summit: 2014. BIMSTEC Bangkok Declaration 1997. 7 members. Secretariat: Dhaka. Charter 2022. Latest summit: Bangkok, April 2025. SAFTA Signed 2004, in force 2006. Tariff phase-down for SAARC goods. BBIN MVA Signed 2015. Bhutan did not ratify, and the others proceeded on their own.
How UPSC asks this

"SAARC has failed to achieve its objectives. Is BIMSTEC a better platform for India?" (typical) "Examine India's Neighbourhood First policy." (typical) "Discuss the challenges to regional cooperation in South Asia." (typical) Structure: (1) SAARC's aims and record; (2) causes of failure: rivalry, asymmetry, unanimity; (3) BIMSTEC's strengths and gaps; (4) India's policy tools (Gujral, Neighbourhood First, SAGAR); (5) sub-regional initiatives (BBIN); (6) way forward: connectivity, trust, trade, working through functional areas.
India–Pakistan
The rivalry that shapes the neighbourhood

India–Pakistan is the most dangerous bilateral relationship in Asia: two nuclear-armed states, one unsettled territorial dispute (Kashmir), cross-border terrorism and a shared river system. The topic is asked in many forms: Kashmir, terrorism, Indus Waters, nuclear stability, confidence-building measures and, since May 2025, Operation Sindoor and its aftermath. A good answer shows the cycle : a terror attack, Indian retaliation, a crisis, third-party concern, then an uneasy calm. And it explains why talks have repeatedly failed to hold.
Wars, accords and attempts at peace

The Simla Agreement (1972) (Indira Gandhi and Z.A. Bhutto) committed both to settle disputes bilaterally and to respect the Line of Control (LoC) of December 1971. India reads it as barring third-party mediation. The Lahore Declaration (February 1999) was signed by Vajpayee and Nawaz Sharif. Months later Pakistan's army occupied heights in Kargil . India recovered them in a limited war, without crossing the LoC.
Kashmir: three positions

India: J&K acceded legally by the Instrument of Accession (26 October 1947). The whole former princely state, including PoK and Gilgit-Baltistan, is Indian. Parliament's 1994 resolution says so. Pakistan: Kashmir is 'unfinished business' of Partition. It points to UN Security Council resolutions (1948–49) on a plebiscite, and calls for self-determination. Kashmiri voices: range from autonomy to independence. Many want to be part of any talks. August 2019: India abrogated Article 370, split J&K into two Union Territories (J&K and Ladakh) and removed special status. The Supreme Court upheld this in In re: Article 370 (December 2023). J&K held assembly elections in 2024. Statehood restoration remained pending as of 2026. Pakistan downgraded diplomatic ties and suspended trade in 2019.
Terror, crisis and the 'new normal'

India says the core problem is cross-border terrorism backed by Pakistan's army and intelligence (ISI). Key attacks: Parliament (2001), Mumbai 26/11 (2008), Pathankot (2016), Uri (September 2016), Pulwama (February 2019) and Pahalgam (22 April 2025) . 2016: after Uri, 'surgical strikes' across the LoC. 2019: after Pulwama, an air strike at Balakot; Pakistan retaliated and an Indian pilot was captured and returned. 2025: after Pahalgam (26 killed, mostly tourists), India launched Operation Sindoor on 7 May, striking nine sites linked to terror groups, then Pakistani military targets. Four days of drone and missile exchanges ended in an understanding on 10 May , reached through the DGMO hotline. Modi laid down a new line: any terror attack will be treated as an act of war, no difference between terrorists and their sponsors, and no tolerance for 'nuclear blackmail'.
After Sindoor: what changed

23 April 2025: India put the Indus Waters Treaty in abeyance , closed the Attari border post, cancelled visas, cut High Commission staff. Pakistan's response: closed airspace to Indian airlines and suspended trade. It threatened to suspend Simla and other bilateral pacts. Mediation dispute: Trump claimed credit for the ceasefire. India said no third party was involved. Pakistan thanked him. Pakistan's military: Gen. Asim Munir was promoted Field Marshal in May 2025. Reports say Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia in September 2025. Trade and travel: still frozen. Cricket contacts limited to multilateral events. India calls Operation Sindoor 'paused', not over. The ceasefire has held on the LoC since May 2025, as of 2026, but there is no formal dialogue.
The Indus Waters Treaty

The Indus Waters Treaty (IWT) was signed in 1960 at Karachi, mediated by the World Bank, by Nehru and Ayub Khan. Eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) go to India. Western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab) go mainly to Pakistan. India may build run-of-river hydropower with design limits. A Permanent Indus Commission, a Neutral Expert and a Court of Arbitration handle disputes (Kishenganga, Ratle). India put the treaty in abeyance in April 2025. In August 2026 the Court of Arbitration at The Hague, in an award India refused to attend, held that the treaty remains in force and cannot be suspended by one side. India rejected the award, calling the court illegally constituted, and maintains that the abeyance continues until Pakistan ends support for terrorism. A Neutral Expert decision on Ratle is expected around mid-2027. Pakistan calls any water stoppage an 'act of war'.
Nuclear deterrence and the stability-instability paradox

Both states tested weapons in 1998 (India 11 and 13 May; Pakistan 28 May). India follows no first use and 'credible minimum deterrence'.
