Pakistan has no no-first-use pledge and a 'full spectrum deterrence' with short-range Nasr missiles. Glenn Snyder (1965) described the stability-instability paradox : nuclear weapons make big wars unlikely, but make smaller conflicts safer to start. Pakistan's use of terrorists under a nuclear shield fits this idea. India's response was limited, conventional, calibrated strikes that show resolve but stay under the nuclear threshold (Cold Start debate, surgical strikes, Balakot, Sindoor). Existing CBMs: the 1988 agreement not to attack nuclear facilities (lists exchanged every 1 January), the 2005 pre-notification of ballistic missile tests and the DGMO hotline.
Engage, isolate or deter?

Doves cite the 2003 ceasefire and 2004–07 Composite Dialogue, when Kashmir violence fell. Hawks argue that every opening was followed by an attack, from Lahore to Kargil and Pathankot to Pulwama. The current Indian line, in the words of the Foreign Ministry, is that talks and terror cannot go together , and that if talks are held they will be on terrorism and PoK. Pakistan wants to discuss Kashmir and water.
What India can and cannot do

Can: isolate Pakistan diplomatically (FATF grey-listing in 2018–22), keep up military pressure, build water infrastructure on the western rivers, and shape UN debates. Cannot easily: change Pakistan's army-driven policy, or stop China's backing (J-10C and PL-15 supplies, CPEC, UNSC shielding). Good practice for answers: link Pakistan with the China factor, the US factor (Trump–Munir), Afghanistan (the Taliban-Pakistan clashes since 2025–26 give India an opening) and domestic Kashmir politics (Omar Abdullah became J&K Chief Minister in October 2024).
How UPSC asks this

"Cross-border terrorism and the Indus Waters Treaty: how should India respond?" (typical) "India's relations with Pakistan: has the policy of 'talks and terror' reached a dead end?" (typical) "Examine the nuclear dimension of the India-Pakistan rivalry." (typical) Structure: (1) wars and agreements: Tashkent, Simla, Lahore; (2) Kashmir and Article 370; (3) terrorism and crises: Mumbai, Uri, Balakot, Sindoor; (4) IWT and the 2025–26 legal contest; (5) nuclear risk (stability-instability); (6) way forward: deterrence, backchannel, CBMs, no third-party mediation.
Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan
Three neighbours, three kinds of problem

Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan all share long open borders with India. Each tests a different side of Indian policy: Bangladesh (water, migration, politics), Nepal (a special treaty, a boundary dispute, China) and Bhutan (a close security partner with a China question). From 2024 to 2026 politics changed in all three. Sheikh Hasina fell in Bangladesh (August 2024), Nepal's government was toppled by youth protests (September 2025), and both held elections in early 2026. The exam wants three things: the treaty framework , the irritants and the current shifts . Write "as of 2026" for anything recent.
Bangladesh: the foundation

The Land Boundary Agreement (1974, ratified in 2015) exchanged 111 Indian enclaves for 51 Bangladeshi ones. The Constitution (100th Amendment) Act, 2015 gave effect to it. India has also given large lines of credit and built rail and road links, and bought power from Bangladesh. Bangladesh is India's largest trading partner in South Asia (about $13 billion in 2023-24, mostly Indian exports). India offers duty-free access to most goods.
Bangladesh: the irritants

Teesta: a sharing deal was nearly ready in 2011 but West Bengal objected. China has offered to fund a Teesta project. Ganga Water Treaty (12 December 1996) runs for 30 years, so it expires in December 2026 . As of late 2026 renewal talks were reported to be at an early stage, and a parliamentary committee in India warned of delay. Border killings, migration and 'push-ins' along the 4,096 km border. Trade barriers: non-tariff barriers, and India's 2025 curbs on some Bangladeshi imports and the withdrawal of a transshipment facility after tough remarks from Dhaka's interim government. Minorities: attacks on Hindus drew Indian concern in 2024–25. Hasina in India: she has lived in India since 5 August 2024. A Bangladeshi tribunal sentenced her to death in absentia in November 2025. Dhaka wants her extradited. India has not agreed.
Bangladesh after the election

The interim government under Muhammad Yunus ruled from August 2024. The Awami League was barred from the 12 February 2026 election, which the BNP won with a two-thirds majority (about 209 of 297 declared seats). Tarique Rahman became prime minister on 17 February 2026. India sent Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri to the swearing-in. Modi invited Rahman to India. Analysts expect a reset but a more 'balanced' Bangladesh that deals with China and Pakistan too. India's agenda: border security, minority rights, extradition questions, transit and connectivity (Akhaura–Agartala rail, Chattogram port access), energy, and a Ganga treaty renewal. Bangladesh's agenda: Teesta, border killings, trade access, a new Ganga deal and a fair visa regime.
Nepal: the special relationship

The 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship allows an open border and free movement of people. Its Article 7 gives Indians and Nepalis reciprocal rights to reside, work and own property. Gorkha regiments in the Indian Army come from Nepal. India is Nepal's biggest trade partner and transit route, since Nepal is landlocked. Hydropower, rail (Jaynagar–Kurtha) and pipelines (Motihari–Amlekhgunj, South Asia's first cross-border petroleum pipeline, 2019) deepen ties. Irritants: The 2015 blockade after Nepal's new Constitution, which Madhesis felt left them out. Kalapani–Lipulekh–Limpiyadhura: in 2020 Nepal published a new map and amended its Constitution to include them. Nepal calls for revision of the 1950 treaty (the Eminent Persons Group report, 2018, was never formally received). The Agnipath scheme (2022) stalled Gorkha recruitment.
Nepal after the Gen Z protests

In September 2025, a ban on social media and anger at corruption set off youth protests. Parliament buildings were burned. PM K.P. Sharma Oli resigned, and former Chief Justice Sushila Karki led an interim government. In the election on 5 March 2026 , the Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) under former Kathmandu mayor Balendra (Balen) Shah won almost two-thirds of the seats. Shah, aged 35, became Nepal's youngest prime minister on 27 March 2026. Early signs are mixed. Modi congratulated him, but reports describe friction over diplomatic protocol, and a wariness about both India and China. Shah has dropped a Chinese-funded industrial park near the Siliguri Corridor from his plans. China's Belt and Road framework (signed December 2024 under Oli) remains a factor. India's aim: stable ties and early delivery on hydropower, rail and trade.
Bhutan: the closest partner

The 1949 Treaty of Friendship was revised in 2007 to remove the clause requiring Bhutan to be 'guided' by India in foreign policy. Now it asks for close consultation on national security interests. Hydropower: India helps build and buys power: Chukha, Tala, Mangdechhu (720 MW, 2019) and Punatsangchhu. It is Bhutan's largest source of revenue. Doklam (2017): India acted to protect Bhutan's claim and its own Siliguri Corridor. China and Bhutan hold boundary talks; India watches any deal on Doklam. Gelephu Mindfulness City: a large special region announced by Bhutan's king in December 2023. India has agreed on rail links to Gelephu and Samtse (approved in 2025) and Modi visited Bhutan in November 2025. Bhutan was the first country to receive Indian vaccines in 2021.
Big brother or good neighbour?

India's neighbours complain of asymmetry : India sets the pace. They also use China as leverage, which scholars call hedging . India's reply, in the 'Neighbourhood First' policy, is to provide public goods quickly and not to interfere in internal politics. The common thread in 2024–26: when India is seen as backing a single ruling group (Hasina in Bangladesh, parties in Nepal), a change of government leads to a backlash. India now stresses people-to-people ties and engages all parties.
India's playbook, and its test in 2026

Connectivity: Integrated Check Posts, Bangladesh rail links, Nepal's rail and pipeline, Bhutan's rail plan. Energy grid: India transmits Nepali and Bhutanese hydropower to Bangladesh through its grid, a rare tri-lateral success (2024). Money and aid: lines of credit, grants and rupee trade. Security: border management, intelligence sharing, defence training for Bhutan and Nepal. Crisis help: the 2015 Nepal earthquake, Covid vaccines, fuel and fertiliser support. The 2026 test is to reset with new governments in Dhaka and Kathmandu without taking sides, to renew the Ganga treaty in time, and to avoid being seen as shielding Hasina. India's quick outreach to Tarique Rahman and Balen Shah shows this approach.
How UPSC asks this

"Evaluate India's relations with Bangladesh after August 2024." (typical) "The India-Nepal relationship is described as 'roti-beti'. Examine its challenges." (typical) "Discuss India-Bhutan ties in the context of China's presence." (typical) Structure for each country: (1) treaty base; (2) cooperation areas; (3) irritants; (4) China's role; (5) 2024–26 developments; (6) way forward. Use a comparison table across the three. Keep the Ganga treaty expiry (December 2026) and Kalapani as your key hooks.
Sri Lanka, Maldives, Myanmar and Impediments to Cooperation
The maritime and eastern neighbours

Sri Lanka and the Maldives lie on the Indian Ocean sea lanes that carry most of India's trade and energy. Myanmar is India's land bridge to Southeast Asia. All three are courted by China. These countries show the limits of Indian influence . India has large aid, culture and security ties with each, but each also shows that small states can bargain between big powers. Politics at home can flip a relationship overnight. The syllabus title ends with "impediments to cooperation" . Prepare a general list (asymmetry, trust deficit, China, domestic politics, delays) and then give country examples.
Sri Lanka: from war to aid

The Indo-Lanka Accord (29 July 1987) , signed by Rajiv Gandhi and J.R. Jayewardene, created Provincial Councils via Sri Lanka's 13th Amendment . The Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) went in, fought the LTTE and left in 1990 at heavy cost. Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated by the LTTE in 1991. J.N. Dixit's Assignment Colombo (1998) is the insider account. After 2009, India pushed for Tamil rights and devolution and was criticised at the UNHRC for abstaining or voting inconsistently.
Sri Lanka today

In the 2022 economic collapse India extended about $4 billion in credit lines, currency swaps and fuel support, and gave early financing assurances that helped Sri Lanka secure an IMF programme. Anura Kumara Dissanayake (NPP, a leftist) won the presidency in September 2024. His first state visit abroad was to India (December 2024). Modi visited Colombo in April 2025 and signed a defence cooperation MoU , plus energy and connectivity deals (a Trincomalee energy hub, a land bridge idea, power grid links). Colombo says its land and ports will not be used against India's security. It has paused visits by Chinese research vessels through a moratorium and rules, though Chinese projects such as the Colombo Port City and a Hambantota refinery continue. Irritants: fishermen arrests in the Palk Strait, Katchatheevu (ceded in 1974 and 1976 agreements; revived as a political issue in Tamil Nadu), Tamil rights.
The Maldives: from 'India Out' to a reset

India has been the Maldives' first responder: Operation Cactus (1988) stopped a coup, and India gave water and aid in crises. 2023: Mohamed Muizzu won on an 'India Out' campaign. Roughly 80–90 Indian military personnel who ran India-gifted helicopters and a Dornier aircraft were replaced by civilians by May 2024. January 2024: a social media spat after Maldivian ministers mocked Modi's Lakshadweep trip. China: a free trade agreement (signed January 2024) and defence cooperation, plus research-vessel visits. India's support: rupee-dirham swap and budget support in 2024 to avert default. Modi attended the 60th Independence anniversary in July 2025, offering a large line of credit and starting free trade talks. Greater Malé Connectivity Project , built with Indian funds, is a flagship. In late 2026 reports said Muizzu visited Pakistan and signed defence MoUs, which Delhi watched closely.
Myanmar: India's gateway to the East

Myanmar matters for the Act East policy and the Northeast. Major projects: Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project: sea from Kolkata to Sittwe, river to Paletwa, then road to Mizoram. Sittwe port operates; the road section is delayed by conflict. India–Myanmar–Thailand Trilateral Highway (about 1,360 km, Moreh to Mae Sot), long delayed. Since the coup of 1 February 2021 , India has avoided isolating the junta, citing the need for border cooperation and a hedge against China. China's pipelines and its Kyaukpyu port are a rival presence. The Arakan Army controls much of Rakhine, near the Kaladan route. India ended the Free Movement Regime (16 km visa-free zone) from 2024 and plans to fence the border, which angers Mizoram and Nagaland. A junta-run election was held in phases from December 2025; in April 2026 the new parliament elected Min Aung Hlaing president, after he gave up command of the army. India gave earthquake relief in March 2025 under Operation Brahma .
Impediments to cooperation: a checklist

Asymmetry: India's size makes neighbours anxious. Trust deficit and India–Pakistan rivalry that freezes SAARC. China's inroads: loans, ports, arms. Domestic politics: 'India Out' campaigns, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal pressing the Centre on fisheries and water. Delays: Indian projects can be slow (Kaladan, the Trilateral Highway). Border issues: migration, smuggling, insurgents, refugees (Rohingya and Chin). Bilateral baggage: boundary and water disputes. Weak regional institutions and low intra-regional trade. For each, add one example and one policy response. This makes answers specific.
South Asia as a regional security complex

Barry Buzan and Ole Wæver ( Regions and Powers , 2003) define a regional security complex : states whose security problems are so linked that they cannot be analysed apart. South Asia is a classic case, centred on the India–Pakistan rivalry. Buzan notes India's problem: small neighbours see India as the threat, and India sees outside powers (China, the US) as threats. This makes India a regional hegemon that cannot fully act as one. Two doctrines are often contrasted. The Indira Doctrine (a Monroe-like belief that no external power should intervene in the region) and the Gujral Doctrine (generosity without reciprocity). Modi's Neighbourhood First combines delivery with a firm line on security.
Hegemon, leader or partner?

India's best argument is geography : it cannot move away from its neighbours, and a stable neighbourhood is in India's interest. Its weakness is execution : late projects and uneven treatment. The 2024–26 pattern shows neighbours do not choose between India and China. They take from both. India's task is to be the more reliable and quicker of the two.
Tools that work

Crisis aid first (Sri Lanka 2022, Maldives swaps, Myanmar quake 2025). Security presence: the Colombo Security Conclave, coastal radar networks, hydrography help. Connectivity with local ownership: Malé bridge, Sri Lanka's energy links, Sittwe port. Digital public infrastructure: UPI in Sri Lanka and the Maldives (RuPay too). Soft power: Buddhism, scholarships, ITEC training. Always link to SAGAR/MAHASAGAR and the Indian Ocean Region. Add that India is the first responder across the region.
How UPSC asks this

"India has been losing ground in its neighbourhood. Critically comment." (typical) "Examine the impediments to regional cooperation in South Asia, with examples." (typical) "Discuss India's strategic interests in Sri Lanka and the Maldives." (typical) Structure: (1) context: Indian Ocean and Act East; (2) country by country: Sri Lanka, Maldives, Myanmar; (3) China factor; (4) the checklist of impediments; (5) India's responses; (6) way forward: faster delivery, consult, balance.
Look East to Act East
Where South Asia meets the Pacific

India's turn to the East began in 1991 . The Cold War ended, the Soviet Union fell, and India needed new markets and partners. East and Southeast Asia were the fastest growing region in the world. The shift from Look East (a mostly economic policy) to Act East (2014, a strategic and security policy) is one of the most asked topics in this part of Paper II. It links to ASEAN, the Indo-Pacific, the Quad and the Northeast. Key phrase for answers: ASEAN centrality . India says ASEAN must remain at the middle of the regional architecture.
From Look East to Act East

Look East had phases: first a focus on ASEAN trade (1991–2002), then widening to East Asia, Japan, Korea and Australia, and a security dimension (joint exercises, maritime talks). Act East adds action : faster delivery, a focus on connectivity, the Northeast, and defence cooperation. Modi announced it at the 12th ASEAN–India Summit in Nay Pyi Taw (November 2014). The Delhi Commemorative Summit (January 2018) saw all ten ASEAN leaders as Republic Day chief guests.
Institutions and agreements

ASEAN–India: Treaty of Amity and Cooperation accession (2003). Free Trade in Goods (signed 2009, in force January 2010), Services and Investment (in force July 2015). AITIGA review: India wants the ASEAN–India Trade in Goods Agreement revised because of a large trade deficit (about $44 billion in 2023-24; total trade about $122 billion). The review had not concluded as of 2026. East Asia Summit (EAS): India a founding member (2005). It now has 18 members. Mekong–Ganga Cooperation (2000) and BIMSTEC link the sub-regions. RCEP: India walked out in November 2019. Newcomer: Timor-Leste became ASEAN's 11th member in October 2025. Philippines chairs ASEAN in 2026.
Connectivity and the Northeast

The Northeast is the heart of Act East: 98% of its borders are international, and it connects India to Myanmar and Bangladesh. Kaladan Multi-Modal Project and India–Myanmar–Thailand Trilateral Highway (see the previous lesson). Agartala–Akhaura rail and Chattogram port access, via Bangladesh. Japan's Act East Forum funds roads and power in the Northeast. Digital and air links: UPI with Singapore (2023) and direct flights. Obstacles: conflict in Myanmar, delays, the closed Myanmar border, and fewer land links via Bangladesh after 2024. Critics say Act East needs less rhetoric and more roads .
Security and the Indo-Pacific

India's defence ties in Southeast Asia have grown fast: Vietnam: a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership (2016). India offered $500 million for defence purchases and trains submarine crews. Philippines: the first export of the BrahMos missile (a $375 million deal signed in January 2022). Indonesia: President Prabowo was chief guest at Republic Day 2025; BrahMos talks followed. Singapore: naval exercise SIMBEX; a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership in 2024. Malaysia, Thailand: exercises and defence talks. India sees the Indo-Pacific as one space and backs the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific (AOIP, 2019) . In November 2019 Modi announced the Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative (IPOI) . Also on freedom of navigation, India backs the 2016 South China Sea arbitration ruling in favour of the Philippines.
Two ways to read the East

C. Raja Mohan, Samudra Manthan (2012) The Indian and Pacific Oceans are becoming one strategic theatre. India must act as a maritime power. Act East is part of that. Amitav Acharya, Constructing a Security Community in Southeast Asia (2001) The 'ASEAN way' of consultation, consensus and non-interference created norms that kept the region at peace. It is a constructivist reading that explains why ASEAN centrality matters. Realists see Act East as balancing China . Constructivists stress shared norms and identity (cultural links such as Buddhism and the Ramayana traditions). Liberals focus on trade and institutions.
Beyond ASEAN: the wider East

Japan: the anchor partner (see the earlier lesson): the Special Strategic and Global Partnership of 2014. South Korea: a Special Strategic Partnership (2015) and a CEPA (2010). Samsung and Hyundai are big investors. Korea's 'New Southern Policy' meets Act East. Australia: a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership (2020), the ECTA trade deal (in force December 2022), and the Quad. Talks on a fuller CECA continued. Pacific Islands: the Forum for India–Pacific Islands Cooperation ( FIPIC ) was started in 2014 at Suva. Taiwan: unofficial ties, with a focus on semiconductors, through economic and cultural offices. The Act East label therefore covers more than ASEAN. It extends the Indian reach from the Bay of Bengal to the Pacific. It is also a counter to China's presence in the same space.
Is Act East delivering?

India is a dialogue partner, not a member , of the main ASEAN economic structures. China is ASEAN's top trading partner; India is far behind. The Indian economy's limited integration into East Asian supply chains is a handicap. Supporters point out that India now matters in ASEAN's security thinking and that bilateral partnerships (Vietnam, Philippines, Singapore, Indonesia) are growing.
Policy for the next phase

Renegotiate the ASEAN trade agreement and tackle non-tariff barriers. Complete the Northeast's land and river links and keep the Sittwe route alive. Use Malabar, the Quad and bilateral partnerships to support freedom of navigation. Expand defence exports (BrahMos, Akash, patrol vessels). Keep ASEAN centrality while joining minilaterals. Example: India reached out to ASEAN at the 2025–26 summits while US tariffs rose. Diversification towards ASEAN and Japan was a clear theme.
How UPSC asks this

"How does the Act East Policy differ from Look East? Examine its achievements." (typical) "Discuss the importance of ASEAN to India's Indo-Pacific strategy." (typical) "India's Northeast is the gateway to Southeast Asia. Analyse." (typical) Structure: (1) 1991 origins; (2) phases; (3) 2014 shift; (4) economic: AITIGA, RCEP; (5) connectivity and Northeast; (6) security: Vietnam, Philippines, Malabar, IPOI; (7) gaps and way forward. Add a one-line comparison table: Look East = economics, ASEAN; Act East = strategy, wider Indo-Pacific.
Africa and Latin America
Two continents, one new focus

Africa and Latin America are the heart of the 'Global South' that India claims to speak for. They offer markets, resources (oil, gold, lithium, pulses), votes at the UN, and a field of competition with China. In the past decade India has opened new embassies, offered large lines of credit and brought the African Union into the G20 (2023). Yet its trade with these regions is still small compared with China's. UPSC asks about the Africa partnership (IAFS, Kampala Principles), Latin America (trade, lithium, Brazil) and a comparison with China. Look for patterns: demand-driven, capacity building, development partnership .
Old links with Africa

India's early role was moral and political. It led the UN campaign against apartheid : it banned trade with South Africa in 1946, and cut diplomatic ties in 1954. It backed independence for Ghana, Kenya, Namibia and Zimbabwe. It sent peacekeepers to Congo. About three million people of Indian origin live in Africa, mainly in South Africa, Mauritius, Kenya and Tanzania. The diaspora is both an asset and, at times (Uganda 1972), a burden.
The modern partnership: IAFS and the Kampala Principles

India–Africa Forum Summit (IAFS): I (New Delhi, 2008), II (Addis Ababa, 2011), III (New Delhi, October 2015) with leaders from all 54 African countries; India announced $10 billion in concessional credit and $600 million in grants. Pan-African e-Network (2009): tele-education and tele-medicine. Kampala Principles (July 2018): in Uganda's Parliament Modi set out ten guiding principles: Africa's priorities come first, demand-driven partnership, local capacity building, no conditionality, and so on. IAFS-IV: planned for New Delhi on 28–31 May 2026, but postponed on 21 May 2026 because of an Ebola outbreak. As of November 2026 no new date had been announced. The African Union became a permanent G20 member at the 2023 Delhi summit.
What India offers Africa

Lines of credit: over $12 billion across many projects. Trade: about $100 billion a year (Africa as a whole). India is among the top partners. Cumulative Indian investment is estimated near $70 billion. Capacity building: the ITEC programme, scholarships, the Pan-African e-Network. Health: low-cost medicines, Covid vaccines (Vaccine Maitri), the Cheetah project with Namibia (2022) and South Africa. Energy and food: ONGC in Mozambique's gas, pulses imported from Africa, solar power through the ISA. Defence and security: training, anti-piracy patrols, Africa-India Field Training Exercise (AFINDEX), Indian troops in UN missions in Congo and South Sudan. Digital: UPI and Aadhaar-like systems. India opened a number of new missions in Africa in recent years.
China in Africa

China is Africa's biggest trade partner (about $280 billion a year, as of recent years) and a major lender through the Belt and Road. It has a naval base in Djibouti (2017) and has largely removed tariffs on African goods. India cannot match China's money. It stresses instead: Democratic values and a shared colonial history. Low-cost, human-centred projects (health, skills, IT). Fewer strings and less debt risk, in contrast with the 'debt-trap' charge against China. Partnerships with Japan (Asia-Africa Growth Corridor, 2017) and the EU. Critics say Indian projects are slow, and credit lines are often delayed. India's trade with Africa is also skewed: oil and gold imports, with exports of pharma, vehicles and machines.
Latin America and the Caribbean

Trade: about $50 billion. India imports crude oil (Brazil, Venezuela, Colombia, Guyana), gold, and vegetable oils; it exports vehicles, pharma, chemicals and IT. Brazil: a partner in BRICS, IBSA and G4. Modi made a state visit in July 2025 after the Rio BRICS summit. Argentina and Chile: lithium. India's KABIL signed deals for lithium blocks in Argentina (2024). A Chile–India PTA exists (2006), widened in 2017. Mercosur–India PTA in force since 2009. Guyana: Modi's visit in November 2024 was the first by an Indian PM in over 50 years. Guyana's new oil is of interest to India. Mexico, Cuba, Caribbean: trade, vaccines and the CARICOM link. In July 2025 Modi toured Ghana, Trinidad and Tobago, Argentina, Brazil and Namibia in one trip, a sign of the Global South focus.
Institutions that tie India to both regions

IBSA (2003) India, Brazil, South Africa. Brasilia Declaration, 2003. A democratic, multicultural South–South forum with a small development fund (the IBSA Fund). BRICS Brazil and South Africa are members. Egypt and Ethiopia joined in 2024. India chaired in 2026. G4 and the UN Brazil is in the G4. Many African and Latin American states back UN reform. Others The G20, G77, WTO coalitions, the International Solar Alliance and the Global Biofuels Alliance (with Brazil, 2023).
Partnership or new influence race?

Realists see India competing with China for influence and resources. Liberals stress mutual gains and institutions. Post-colonial writers ask whether India repeats extractive patterns. India says its model is demand-driven, Africa-led, and without conditions . The 2026 Ebola-related postponement of IAFS-IV shows how health shocks can slow even a prestige event. The key test is whether summit promises become projects.
Practical next steps

Hold IAFS-IV once health conditions allow, with project lists and timelines. Improve credit-line delivery and set up faster project agencies. Build supply chains: critical minerals (lithium, cobalt), pulses and edible oils. Strengthen digital and pharma partnerships, regional manufacturing and vaccine production in Africa. Use shipping and naval presence to guard sea lines to Africa. Make one point with a number: AU in the G20 (2023), Kampala Principles (2018), $10 billion (2015), IAFS-IV postponed (2026).
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the significance of Africa to India's foreign policy." (typical) "India's engagement with Latin America: opportunities and constraints." (typical) "Compare India's and China's approach to Africa." (typical) Structure: (1) historical ties; (2) IAFS and Kampala Principles; (3) offers: credit, capacity building, health, energy; (4) Latin America: trade, lithium, Brazil; (5) China comparison; (6) problems; (7) way forward.
NIEO, WTO and the Voice of the South
The long fight for a fairer economic order

Since the 1960s the developing world (the 'South') has argued that the global economic system favours the rich 'North'. In the 1970s it demanded a New International Economic Order (NIEO) . Today the same fight continues in the WTO , in climate finance and in debt talks. India has been at the centre of this story: a leader of the G77 and NAM, a strong voice in the Uruguay and Doha rounds, and, since 2023, the host of the Voice of the Global South summits. The examiner wants the history (NIEO, UNCTAD), the theory (dependency, unequal exchange), the WTO issues (agriculture, TRIPS, subsidies) and recent events (MC12, MC13, MC14).
How the South organised

The G77 began in 1964 with 77 developing states at the first UNCTAD (United Nations Conference on Trade and Development), led by Raúl Prebisch . It now has over 130 members, and India is a core member. The shock of the 1973 oil embargo showed that raw-material producers could use their leverage. At the Algiers NAM summit (1973) the South called for a new order.
The NIEO declaration, 1974

The sixth special session of the UN General Assembly (April–May 1974) adopted the Declaration and Programme of Action on the Establishment of a New International Economic Order (Resolutions 3201 and 3202 (S-VI)). In December 1974 came the Charter of Economic Rights and Duties of States (Resolution 3281). Permanent sovereignty over natural resources , including the right to nationalise. Fair and stable commodity prices , linked to prices of manufactured imports. Preferential trade access (GSP) and no reciprocity from poor countries. Technology transfer and regulation of multinational firms. Debt relief and more aid (the 0.7% of GNP target). More voice in the IMF and World Bank.
Why the South felt exploited

Prebisch-Singer thesis (1950) Raúl Prebisch and Hans Singer argued that the prices of primary goods fall relative to manufactures over time. Poor exporters lose out. Policy: industrialise by import substitution. Dependency theory André Gunder Frank ( Capitalism and Underdevelopment in Latin America , 1967) and Samir Amin ( Unequal Development , 1973) said that the periphery is kept poor by the core. World-systems theory Immanuel Wallerstein, The Modern World-System (1974): core, semi-periphery and periphery. Stephen Krasner, Structural Conflict (1985) The Third World pushed for authoritative, rule-based allocation against the market-based liberal order. He sees the NIEO as an attempt at "regime change" in global economic rules.
Why the NIEO faded

Northern resistance: the US under Reagan and Britain under Thatcher backed free markets. The 1981 Cancun summit produced little. Debt crisis (1982): Mexico's default began a decade of IMF structural adjustment: the Washington Consensus. Divided South: oil-rich states, East Asian exporters (the 'tigers') and the poorest had different interests. OPEC's price hikes hurt non-oil poor states. Rise of the WTO (1995) and rules the South had little say in. The Brandt Report ( North-South: A Programme for Survival , 1980) and the South Commission ( The Challenge to the South , 1990, chaired by Julius Nyerere) kept the ideas alive. India itself moved from import substitution to liberalisation (1991) . It argued for the South in principle but joined the open system in practice.
India in GATT and the WTO

India was a founding member of GATT (1947/48) and of the WTO (1995). Uruguay Round (1986–94): India opposed TRIPS and services, then accepted the package. It won the principle of special and differential treatment (S&DT) . Doha Round (launched 2001): called a 'development round'. India and Brazil led the G20 coalition (Cancun 2003) against farm subsidies in the rich world, and the G33 for special products and a Special Safeguard Mechanism (SSM) for farmers. Talks stalled. Public stockholding (PSH): India's minimum support prices and food purchases breach WTO caps on subsidy. At Bali (2013) a 'peace clause' protects India until a permanent solution is found. Dispute settlement: the Appellate Body has not worked since December 2019 because the US blocks appointments.
Ministerial conferences, 2022 to 2026

MC12, Geneva (June 2022): a limited TRIPS waiver on Covid vaccines (India and South Africa had pushed for broader), a first Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies (curbing harmful subsidies), and an e-commerce moratorium extension. MC13, Abu Dhabi (Feb–Mar 2024): the e-commerce moratorium was extended to MC14. No permanent PSH solution. MC14, Yaoundé, Cameroon (March 2026): ended without a major deal. There was no consensus to extend the e-commerce customs-duty moratorium, so it lapsed for the first time since 1998. India and African states again asked for a permanent PSH solution; talks on fisheries continue. Investment Facilitation for Development (IFD): a plurilateral deal that India has blocked from joining the WTO rulebook, arguing it goes against consensus. As of 2026 the WTO is under severe strain: unilateral US tariffs, a paralysed Appellate Body and rising plurilaterals.
Spokesperson for the South or a defender of its own interests?

Supporters say India protects 800 million food-subsidy beneficiaries and farmers' livelihoods, and defends policy space for development. Critics say India's position is defensive and blocks deals that could help smaller developing states, and that India's own growth makes it a different kind of actor. India's reply: it is not a spoiler but a champion of consensus and of S&DT . The Voice of the Global South summits are one more effort to bring the South's demands to the G20 and beyond.
What India does now

WTO: defend PSH, S&DT and TRIPS flexibility; resist non-trade issues like labour and environment standards; support restoring the Appellate Body. G20 2023: pushed debt restructuring, reform of multilateral development banks and climate finance; brought in the AU. Voice of the Global South summits (January 2023, November 2023, August 2024) collected views from over 100 countries. FTAs: India now signs bilateral trade deals (UAE, Australia, UK, EFTA, EU) as the WTO stalls. UN: backs reform of the IMF and UNSC for fairer representation.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the New International Economic Order and why it failed." (typical) "India's role in the Doha Round and the WTO: examine." (typical) "How is India working as a voice of the Global South?" (typical) Structure: (1) background: UNCTAD, G77; (2) NIEO demands (1974); (3) theory: Prebisch-Singer, dependency; (4) why it faded: debt crisis, divisions; (5) India in GATT/WTO: S&DT, PSH, G20 and G33; (6) MC12–MC14; (7) Voice of the Global South; (8) assessment.
India–USA
The relationship that decides the rest

India–USA is the most-asked bilateral topic after China. It sits behind almost every other question in Paper II: the Indo-Pacific, Russia, nuclear policy, West Asia and the Global South. The story has three layers. First, estrangement in the Cold War. Second, a strategic turn after 1998 and the 2005–08 nuclear deal. Third, a stress test in 2025–26 when tariffs, Russian oil and Trump's claims about Kashmir and Pakistan hit trust. The best exam answers show both sides: the deep, institutional partnership and the real limits set by India's strategic autonomy . Everything time-sensitive in this lesson is written "as of 2026". Check the latest news before the exam.
Estranged democracies, 1947–1998

Why did two democracies drift apart? The US saw India's non-alignment as pro-Soviet. India saw US military aid to Pakistan as a threat. Nuclear policy added a second wall: the US led the non-proliferation regime India rejected. The hinge was 1991 . The Soviet Union fell and India liberalised. In 1998 the US imposed sanctions after Pokhran-II. But the Jaswant Singh–Strobe Talbott talks that followed began a real strategic dialogue.
From Clinton to the civil nuclear deal

Bill Clinton's visit in March 2000 was the first US presidential visit in 22 years. In 2001 George W. Bush lifted the sanctions. In 2004 came the Next Steps in Strategic Partnership (NSSP) . The July 2005 joint statement (Manmohan Singh and Bush) set up the civil nuclear deal. The US passed the Hyde Act (2006). India and the IAEA agreed a safeguards deal. The Nuclear Suppliers Group gave India a clean waiver on 6 September 2008 . The 123 Agreement was signed on 10 October 2008. The deal ended India's nuclear isolation without India signing the NPT. It cost political capital: the Left withdrew support from the UPA government in July 2008.
Defence: from buyer to partner

US arms sales to India were close to zero in 2000. They have since grown into billions of dollars (P-8I, C-17, C-130J, Apache, Chinook, MQ-9B drones). The US named India a Major Defense Partner in 2016. India signed the foundational agreements : GSOMIA (2002): sharing of classified information. LEMOA (2016): logistics support at each other's bases. COMCASA (2018): secure military communications. BECA (2020): geospatial data for targeting and navigation. Exercises include Yudh Abhyas (army), Malabar (navy, with Japan and Australia) and Cope India (air). A 2+2 ministerial dialogue began in 2018. A new 10-year defence framework was signed on 31 October 2025 in Kuala Lumpur.
Technology, trade and people

The Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology (iCET) began in 2023 under Biden. In 2025 it was folded into the TRUST initiative (Transforming the Relationship Utilising Strategic Technology). Themes: semiconductors, AI, space, quantum and defence co-production such as the GE F414 jet engine. Trade: the US is India's largest trading partner in goods, about $130 billion in 2024. India exported roughly $87 billion in FY2024-25 and runs a surplus. In February 2025 the two leaders set a target of $500 billion in trade by 2030 . People: about five million Indian Americans form one of the richest immigrant groups in the US. Indian students and H-1B workers are a major pillar. A $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions announced in September 2025 hit this pillar.
2025: the year trust cracked

In 2025 the relationship faced its worst stress in decades. Tariffs: a 25% 'reciprocal' tariff took effect on 7 August 2025. A further 25% penalty for buying Russian oil followed on 27 August. Total: 50% , among the highest on any US partner. Ceasefire claims: after Operation Sindoor (7–10 May 2025), Trump repeatedly said he brokered the India–Pakistan ceasefire. India said it was agreed directly between the two DGMOs and rejected any mediation. Pakistan thanked Trump. Pakistan outreach: Trump hosted Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir, and praised Pakistan. India's reply was to keep strategic autonomy: it refused to stop Russian oil on command, hosted Putin in December 2025 and attended the SCO summit in Tianjin in 2025.
Where the trade deal stands

On 6 February 2026 the two governments announced a framework for an interim trade deal. The US said it would cut tariffs on India to 18% and remove the extra 25% Russian-oil penalty from 7 February. Then the courts intervened. In February 2026 the US Supreme Court held that the IEEPA law does not authorise such tariffs. The administration shifted to other laws. The US then used temporary tariffs and opened Section 301 investigations in March 2026. As of late 2026, the final tariff rate and the signing of the deal were still not settled. As of November 2026 there is still no signed treaty text and no entry-into-force date. Sticking points are agriculture and dairy, where India protects small farmers, and digital rules. On Russian oil, Washington says India agreed to cut; trade data show Russian crude still arriving in 2026, though below the 2025 peak.
Ally, partner or hedger?

Realists (such as C. Raja Mohan) argue India must drop its Cold War caution and use the US to balance China. Autonomists (the Non-Alignment 2.0 report of 2012) warn against becoming a junior partner. S. Jaishankar describes the current line as multi-alignment . India works with the US in the Quad and I2U2, with Russia in BRICS and SCO, and with Europe and the Gulf. India calls the US a "partner" but never an "ally": no treaty, no bases, no obligation to fight. Structural irritants: CAATSA sanctions (2017) over the S-400, US positions on human rights, the Pannun plot case (2023), Pakistan, and trade protection.
What India gains and risks

Gains: technology, capital, defence co-production, an Indo-Pacific counterweight to China, a big market for services and a diaspora of about five million Indian Americans. Risks: India becomes dependent on US tech controls. Tariff shocks hit labour-intensive sectors like textiles, gems and shrimp. US policy swings with each presidency. A US–China deal could leave India exposed. India's response in 2025–26: diversify. It signed an FTA with the UK (July 2025), concluded one with the EU (January 2026), closed the EFTA agreement (2024, in force October 2025), and stayed in BRICS. It also kept buying US energy and defence goods to reduce the trade surplus. For the exam, give one hard fact per claim : the 2008 NSG waiver, the 2016 Major Defense Partner label, the 50% tariff of 2025, and the 2026 framework.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the significance of the Indo-US civil nuclear deal for India." (typical) "India–US relations have moved from estrangement to engagement. Critically examine." (typical) "Examine how the Quad and the Indo-Pacific shape India-US strategic convergence." (typical) Structure: (1) Cold War estrangement; (2) post-1998 turn: NSSP, 2005 statement, 2008 deal; (3) pillars: defence, technology, trade, people, Indo-Pacific; (4) 2025–26 strain: tariffs, Russian oil, H-1B, Sindoor claims; (5) assessment: convergence on China, divergence on autonomy; (6) way forward: trade deal, co-production, diversification. Always name at least three dates and two agreements.
India–China: Border and Strategy
The question asked every year

India–China has appeared in the PSIR paper almost every year since 2015. It is the central security question for India. It is also the one with the most dates, treaties and places to remember. This lesson covers the border and strategy : where the dispute lies, how the 1993–2013 agreements tried to manage it, what Galwan changed, and how the 2024–26 thaw works. The next lesson covers economy and multilateral rivalry. Core tension: China wants a stable border so that it can deal with India as one of many partners. India says that peace on the border is the basis of the whole relationship . After Galwan (2020), India made normal ties conditional on restoring the border status quo.
The three sectors of the dispute

The border is about 3,488 km by India's count (China says about 2,000). It is the Line of Actual Control (LAC) , not a settled boundary. The term was used in a 1959 letter from Zhou Enlai and written into the 1993 agreement. The McMahon Line comes from the 1914 Simla Convention. China does not accept it. It calls Arunachal "South Tibet". China also holds the Shaksgam Valley that Pakistan ceded to it in 1963. Both sides have different perceptions of where the LAC runs, so patrols often meet face to face.
From Panchsheel to 1962

Nehru's forward policy (1961) put small Indian posts in disputed territory. China answered with a large attack in October 1962. It declared a unilateral ceasefire in November. India lost the war, and the shock still shapes its military thinking. Ties were restored step by step. Rajiv Gandhi's 1988 visit to Beijing started a "delink" approach: improve other ties while talking about the border.
The agreements that kept the peace

Between 1993 and 2013 India and China built a rulebook for the LAC. 1993 Agreement on Maintenance of Peace and Tranquillity along the LAC. 1996 Agreement on Confidence-Building Measures in the military field. It bars use of firearms and explosives within 2 km of the LAC. This is why Galwan was fought with rods and stones. 2005 Political Parameters and Guiding Principles for settling the boundary. Both sides should keep settled populations in mind. 2012 WMCC (Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination). 2013 Border Defence Cooperation Agreement (BDCA). The Special Representatives (SR) mechanism began in 2003. The SRs are India's NSA and China's Foreign Minister.
Doklam 2017 and Galwan 2020

Doklam (June–August 2017): China began building a road on the Doklam plateau, claimed by Bhutan, near the tri-junction. Indian troops crossed to stop it. The 73-day standoff ended on 28 August with both sides pulling back. Doklam is near the Siliguri Corridor, India's 'chicken's neck'. Galwan (15 June 2020): after Chinese build-up in Eastern Ladakh from May 2020, a violent clash in the Galwan Valley killed 20 Indian soldiers . China later acknowledged four of its own dead. It was the first deadly clash since 1975. China also occupied points at Pangong Tso, Gogra-Hot Springs, Depsang and Demchok . Both sides sent about 50,000–60,000 troops each into the theatre. India responded with a ban on Chinese apps, tighter FDI rules (Press Note 3, April 2020) and a military build-up.
Disengagement, step by step

Talks went through Corps Commander rounds and the WMCC. At several points both sides created buffer zones , where neither patrols. India lost some patrolling rights this way, critics say. The October 2024 agreement let patrols resume at Depsang Plains and Demchok. Disengagement was done; de-escalation and de-induction of troops (pulling back the heavy deployments) are still pending, as of 2026.
The thaw after Kazan

After Kazan the two sides rebuilt step by step. December 2024: 23rd SR talks in Beijing (Doval and Wang Yi). 2025: Kailash Mansarovar Yatra resumed; Wang Yi visited Delhi for the 24th SR round in August; Modi met Xi at the SCO summit in Tianjin (31 August–1 September) and both said they are partners, not rivals. Late 2025: direct flights restarted after five years; border trade through Lipulekh, Shipki La and Nathu La was agreed. August 2026: the 25th SR round in Beijing reportedly agreed more military meeting points and hotlines and a group to delimit the less disputed parts of the border. The next round is due in India in 2027. Analysts call this "normalisation without trust" : a managed truce, not a settlement.
China's pressure points beyond the LAC

Water: China began building a huge dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo (Brahmaputra) near the great bend in 2025. India plans the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project in reply. Renaming: China keeps issuing 'standardised' Chinese names for places in Arunachal. Tibet and the Dalai Lama: China insists on approving his reincarnation. The Dalai Lama said in July 2025 that the institution will continue. India says it takes no position on religious succession. Pakistan: China arms Pakistan (J-10C jets, PL-15 missiles) and backs CPEC through PoK. Indian officials said China gave support to Pakistan during Operation Sindoor in May 2025. Indian Ocean: Chinese research ships, the Djibouti base (2017), Gwadar and Hambantota, the so-called 'string of pearls'. India's counters: the Vibrant Villages Programme , border roads and tunnels (Atal Tunnel, Sela Tunnel 2024), the Andaman and Nicobar command, the Quad and Malabar.
Is the thaw real?

Jaishankar's formula for ties is the three mutuals : mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest. India links progress to peace on the LAC. China prefers to put the border "in its appropriate place" and widen cooperation elsewhere. Scholars differ. Shivshankar Menon ( Choices , 2016) sees management and deterrence. Others, such as Tanvi Madan ( Fateful Triangle , 2020), see India hedging between the US and China.
What India can do

Policy options India uses at once: deterrence (troop posture, infrastructure), diplomacy (SR talks, WMCC), partnerships (Quad, France, Japan, Vietnam, Philippines BrahMos sale) and economic caution (apps, FDI screening). It also keeps both doors open: Modi visited China in 2025 for the SCO while India hosted BRICS in 2026. For the exam, link the border to Tibet policy (India recognised the Tibet Autonomous Region as part of China in 2003; China implicitly accepted Sikkim as Indian in 2003–04 by agreeing to trade through Nathu La), to Bhutan (Doklam) and to Nepal (Lipulekh).
How UPSC asks this

"The India-China border dispute has become a bigger challenge than the economic partnership. Discuss." (typical) "Analyse the disengagement process after Galwan and its limits." (typical) "Examine how China's moves in the neighbourhood affect India's security." (typical) Structure: (1) sectors and the LAC; (2) 1914, 1954, 1962; (3) the 1993–2013 rulebook; (4) Doklam and Galwan; (5) disengagement and the October 2024 pact; (6) 2025–26 thaw and what is unresolved (de-escalation, buffer zones, water, Tibet); (7) way forward. Draw a small sketch of the three sectors.
India–China: Economy and Multilateral Rivalry
Rivals who cannot decouple

India and China are neighbours, Asia's two largest populations and two of its biggest economies. Their trade is large. Their strategic trust is small. That gap is the heart of this lesson. Exam questions ask three things: (1) why India depends on Chinese goods even while distrusting China; (2) how the two compete in the neighbourhood , the Indian Ocean and global institutions; and (3) where they cooperate, as in BRICS, SCO and climate talks. Keep one idea in mind: China treats India as a regional rival that should stay inside South Asia. India wants to be treated as a great power in its own right .
The trade picture

In FY2024-25 bilateral trade was about $128 billion . India's deficit with China crossed $99 billion , its largest with any country (figures as of 2025). China is the key supplier of active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs) , mobile phone parts, solar cells, lithium-ion batteries, tunnel-boring machines and, importantly, rare earth magnets . When China curbed rare earth magnet exports in April 2025, Indian car and electronics makers were hit within weeks. Some licences were later granted to Indian firms. The lesson Indian planners took: dependence on one supplier is a strategic weakness. The answer is PLI schemes , the National Critical Mineral Mission (2025) and supply-chain partnerships with Japan, Australia and the US.
India's economic guardrails

April 2020, Press Note 3: investment from land-border countries needs government approval. It was aimed at stopping opportunistic Chinese takeovers during Covid. App bans from June 2020 (TikTok, WeChat and over 300 others eventually) under Section 69A of the IT Act. RCEP exit (November 2019): India walked out partly over fear of Chinese goods swamping its market. Belt and Road: India is the main large state that refuses to join, saying the China–Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) passes through Indian territory in PoK. As of 2026 the guardrails are being loosened, selectively. The Cabinet approved changes to Press Note 3 on 10 March 2026. Since 1 May 2026, investors from land-border countries can hold up to 10% non-controlling stakes through the automatic route, and some manufacturing sectors get faster approvals. Early approvals were small: about 29 projects worth ₹4,900 crore by August 2026. Analysts call it selective de-risking , not decoupling.
Rivalry in the neighbourhood

The 'string of pearls' idea (from a 2004 US study) describes Chinese-linked ports ringing the Indian Ocean. China says they are commercial. India sees possible military use. China's base at Djibouti opened in 2017. India answers with its own offers: Neighbourhood First (2014), the SAGAR doctrine (2015) which became MAHASAGAR (2025), lines of credit, the Colombo Security Conclave, and port projects at Chabahar and Sittwe. Smaller states play both sides. They take Chinese money and Indian security and trade, and they bargain with each.
Belt and Road versus India's offers

China launched the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) in 2013. India boycotted the Belt and Road Forums of 2017 and 2019. India's answers are mostly connectivity with partners: the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) with Russia and Iran, the Chabahar port in Iran, the Kaladan project in Myanmar, the India–Middle East–Europe Corridor (IMEC) announced at the G20 in 2023, and the Asia-Africa Growth Corridor with Japan. India says its model is demand-driven and respects sovereignty. Critics note that India's own projects are slower, and several (Chabahar, IMEC, Kaladan) have faced delays from war, sanctions and instability.
BRICS, SCO and AIIB: cooperate and compete

Both sit in BRICS (2009), SCO (India joined 2017) and the AIIB (2016, where China is the largest shareholder and India second). Both are in the New Development Bank . BRICS: China wants it as an anti-West bloc and pushes expansion. India supports expansion in a measured way and has said it does not want de-dollarisation. India chaired BRICS in 2026 and the New Delhi summit (12–13 September) adopted a consensus declaration. SCO: India refused to sign the 2018 Qingdao text over BRI. At Tianjin in 2025 the declaration condemned the Pahalgam attack. The 2026 summit was in Bishkek (31 August–1 September). Climate and trade: both back developing-country positions, though India differs from China on loss of its own coal and manufacturing space.
Blocking India at the top table

NSG: China led opposition to India's membership in 2016, insisting on non-NPT criteria applying equally to Pakistan. UN 1267 sanctions: China placed 'technical holds' on listing Masood Azhar until 2019, when he was finally listed. UNSC reform: China backs Africa and Latin America more than a permanent seat for India, and does not endorse India's claim. Standards and values: China pushes its own tech standards, a rival 'Global Development Initiative' and a Global Security Initiative. India offers DPI (UPI, Aadhaar-style models) and the Voice of the Global South summits. Both claim to speak for the Global South. This competition is about leadership , not just trade.
Compete, cooperate or contain?

Hedgers say India should deepen trade with China to grow, while arming and partnering to deter. Hawks say any dependence is a lever China will use, so India should restrict Chinese capital and tech, as in the app bans. A third view, from Shyam Saran ( How China Sees India and the World , 2022), is that India must understand China's own strategic culture and negotiate from strength, not reaction. Structural point: India's manufacturing push (PLI, electronics assembly) still needs Chinese parts. India's electronics exports have grown, yet they rely on Chinese components and sometimes Chinese technicians. Reported 2025 curbs on specialty fertilisers and tunnel-boring machines, along with the rare earth curbs, showed how supply can be used as pressure.
A balanced scorecard for 2026

Where India has gained leverage: it is among the world's top five economies by 2025–26 estimates, a favoured 'China plus one' site (Apple supply chains moved strongly to India in 2024–25), and an FTA partner of the UK, EFTA and the EU (concluded January 2026). Where it is exposed: a deficit near $100 billion, tech and critical-mineral dependence, and a smaller defence-industrial base. Recent steps: loosening Press Note 3 within limits; resuming direct flights and border trade; Modi–Xi meeting at Tianjin; and tariff pressure from the US pushing both Delhi and Beijing to stabilise. A reported China complaint at the WTO against India's EV and battery subsidies in 2025 shows that disputes continue. For the exam, cite one metric (the deficit), one rule (Press Note 3), one forum (BRICS or SCO) and one 2026 change.
How UPSC asks this

"India-China relations are marked by trade growth and strategic rivalry. Discuss." (typical) "What are the implications of China's Belt and Road Initiative for India?" (typical) "Compare India and China's roles in BRICS and SCO." (typical) Structure: (1) trade numbers and dependence; (2) Indian guardrails and their recent easing; (3) BRI, CPEC and the neighbourhood contest; (4) multilateral cooperation and rivalry (BRICS, SCO, AIIB, NSG, 1267); (5) assessment: managed rivalry; (6) way forward: diversify, build capacity, keep dialogue. A short table, cooperation versus competition , scores well.
India–Russia
The oldest strategic partner

Russia (and the Soviet Union before it) has been India's most dependable great-power partner for 70 years. It supplied arms, vetoes at the UN and steel plants. Today the partnership is tested by the war in Ukraine , Russia's closeness to China and US pressure over oil. UPSC asks how India balances this relationship with its growing ties to the US. The answer needs three things: the history , the four pillars (defence, energy, nuclear/space, diplomacy) and the 2022–26 stress points . A neat line for your answer: India–Russia is a special and privileged strategic partnership (2010) built on trust, but today's trade is thin outside oil and arms.
From the Soviet era to the present

The Soviets backed India on Kashmir at the UN, built the Bhilai steel plant and sold arms on easy rupee terms. The 1971 Treaty (Gromyko and Swaran Singh) gave India cover during the Bangladesh war. It contained a security clause (Article IX) short of an alliance. After 1991 trade shrank, and the debt in rupees was settled by 'rupee-rouble' arrangements. The 2000 Declaration on Strategic Partnership restarted ties. Annual summits began in 2000, alternating between the two capitals.
Pillar one: defence

Russia is still a leading arms supplier, but its share has fallen. SIPRI data show Russia's share of India's arms imports at about 36% in 2020–24 , down from over 70% in 2010–14, as India diversified to France, the US and Israel and built more at home. Platforms: Su-30MKI, T-90 tanks, INS Vikramaditya, Kilo submarines, the Kamov helicopters. S-400 Triumf: bought in 2018 for about $5.4 billion despite the US CAATSA threat. Deliveries began in late 2021. BrahMos: the joint venture (1998) that makes the supersonic cruise missile. Co-production: AK-203 rifles at Amethi (Korwa), under Make in India. Weak points: delays, spare-part shortages after sanctions, and cost overruns (the Admiral Gorshkov refit).
Pillar two: energy and nuclear

Nuclear: Rosatom builds the Kudankulam plant in Tamil Nadu. Units 1 and 2 operate and more are under construction. The 1988 agreement was signed before the NSG existed, and Russia backed India for NSG membership. Oil: before 2022 Russia supplied under 2% of India's crude. After Western sanctions and the G7 price cap (December 2022, $60 a barrel), Russia sold at a discount. By 2023–24 Russia supplied about 35% of India's imports. India says it buys where it is cheapest to protect Indian consumers. Space: Rakesh Sharma flew on Soyuz T-11 in 1984. Russia trained Gaganyaan astronaut candidates. Connectivity: the INSTC (2000, with Iran), the Chennai–Vladivostok sea route and an Arctic/Northern Sea Route interest.
India, Ukraine and the West

After the February 2022 invasion, India abstained on the UN resolutions and did not impose sanctions. It said it favoured dialogue and diplomacy and called for respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity. Modi told Putin at Samarkand in September 2022 that today's era is not an era of war. India also engaged Ukraine. Modi visited Kyiv in August 2024 , the first Indian PM to do so. He had visited Moscow a month earlier for the annual summit. India's critics abroad called it a 'free rider'. India's reply is the principle of strategic autonomy , and it points out that European states also kept buying Russian energy for months. India hosted the G20 in 2023 and secured a New Delhi declaration that omitted direct condemnation of Russia, a diplomatic success for the Global South camp.
The sanctions squeeze

August 2025: the US added 25% to its tariff on India for buying Russian oil (total 50%). October 2025: US sanctions on Rosneft and Lukoil. Reliance and other buyers sharply cut purchases from them. July 2025: the EU sanctioned Nayara Energy (Rosneft owns about 49%). 4–5 December 2025: Putin visited New Delhi for the 23rd annual summit. He promised 'uninterrupted' fuel supply. The sides signed a programme for economic cooperation to 2030, a labour mobility agreement and set a trade goal of $100 billion by 2030. February 2026: the US announced it was dropping the 25% penalty after India said it would cut Russian oil. Trade data show a drop from the 2025 peak, but Russian crude still arrives; reports differ on volumes. Bilateral trade was about $69 billion in FY2024-25, mostly Indian oil imports. India's exports to Russia are small, under $5 billion.
Reliable friend or a fading partner?

Russia's 'no limits' partnership with China (February 2022) worries Delhi. Russia also sells arms to Pakistan in small quantities and recognised the Taliban government in July 2025. Supporters argue Russia is a balancing power : India benefits from a multipolar world and a Russia not wholly dependent on China. Sceptics say India overestimates what Moscow can still do. Commentators like C. Raja Mohan describe a 'managed decline' of the old partnership that India must carry without breaking.
How India handles the balance

It diversifies arms: Rafale (France), P-8I, MQ-9B (US), Israeli systems. It keeps Russia in useful forums: BRICS, SCO , the RIC idea (Russia–India–China). It uses rupee and local-currency payments , plus UAE dirham, to avoid dollar exposure. It invests in the Far East (a $1 billion line of credit in 2019). It publicly separates 'Russia' from 'Ukraine war', saying it will support peace efforts. The 2025–26 pressure shows the limits. India can adjust oil volumes but will not cut Russia off. In defence, S-400 and possible Su-57 offers show Russia still pitches high-end hardware.
Key terms to remember

Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership The 2010 upgrade from the 2000 Strategic Partnership. Russia has this label only with India. RELOS A reciprocal logistics exchange agreement, signed in Moscow in February 2025, giving access to each other's facilities. 2+2 Foreign and defence ministers' dialogue. India–Russia held its first in 2021. INSTC A 7,200 km multimodal route linking Mumbai to Russia via Iran and the Caspian.
How UPSC asks this

"India-Russia relations have stood the test of time. Examine in the context of the Ukraine war." (typical) "Evaluate the role of defence cooperation in India–Russia relations." (typical) "How has the changing global order affected India's Russia policy?" (typical) Structure: (1) history: 1955, 1971, 2000, 2010; (2) pillars: defence, nuclear, energy, space, diplomacy; (3) Ukraine: abstentions, Samarkand, Kyiv; (4) 2025–26 pressure: tariffs, Rosneft/Lukoil sanctions, Dec 2025 summit; (5) assessment: strategic autonomy with limits; (6) way forward: diversify, deepen economic ties (INSTC, Far East), keep ties with Russia without losing the West.
India–EU
Europe: India's quiet third pole

The European Union is India's largest trading partner in goods (with the US), a top investor and a source of technology. Yet for decades the relationship was called an 'underperforming partnership'. In 2026 that changed, at least on paper. In January 2026 , at the 16th India–EU summit in New Delhi, the two sides announced the conclusion of a Free Trade Agreement after nearly two decades of off-and-on talks. EU leaders (Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa) were chief guests at Republic Day 2026. The exam angle: why is Europe now more attractive to India, what are the hurdles, and how does the EU fit into India's multi-alignment ?
Slow beginnings, strategic label in 2004

The 2004 partnership and the 2005 Joint Action Plan set broad aims, but results were thin. India found the EU slow and bureaucratic. The EU found India protectionist. The FTA talks (the Broad-based Trade and Investment Agreement) began in 2007 and stalled in 2013 over cars, wine and spirits, services visas, and data protection. The Porto summit (May 2021) and the 2022 relaunch restarted them, together with separate talks on investment protection and geographical indications.
The pillars of the partnership

Trade: about €120 billion in goods in 2023-24, plus large services trade. The EU is India's biggest export market in some years. Technology: the India–EU Trade and Technology Council (TTC) , set up in 2022, covers semiconductors, AI and digital standards. India is only the second TTC partner after the US. Connectivity: the 2021 Connectivity Partnership, the Global Gateway, and IMEC (2023). Climate and energy: green hydrogen, solar and the International Solar Alliance. Security: maritime cooperation, counter-terrorism, and Indo-Pacific engagement. The EU adopted an Indo-Pacific strategy in 2021. Individual members matter too. France has been a strategic partner since 1998 and sells the Rafale. Germany builds submarines with Indian yards (a Project 75I partnership with Mazagon Dock was in progress in 2025–26). Italy , Spain and Netherlands are growing partners.
The FTA: what was agreed

The agreement was concluded on 27 January 2026. As of the latest reports (autumn 2026), it still needs legal scrubbing, formal signing and ratification by both sides, including the European Parliament and the EU Council. Check the latest status before the exam. Industrial goods: big tariff cuts both ways. India lowers duties on cars, wines and spirits in phases, with quotas. Services and mobility: the two sides also agreed to work on easier movement of professionals and students. Protected areas: sensitive farm items like dairy are largely kept out. Rules: chapters on sustainability, services, digital trade and intellectual property. Europe called it a huge deal covering two billion people. India framed it as a way to hedge against US tariff shocks.
What can still go wrong

CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism): the EU's carbon tax on imports of steel, aluminium, cement, fertiliser and others started its definitive phase in January 2026. India says it is unfair to developing countries and violates 'common but differentiated responsibilities'. EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR): compliance costs for Indian farm goods. Data and digital rules: the EU does not give India 'data adequacy' status. Russian oil: the EU sanctioned Nayara in 2025 and banned imports of refined fuels from Russian crude from 2026. This hits Indian refiners exporting to Europe. Values: European Parliament resolutions criticising India on human rights, for example on Manipur in 2023, irritate Delhi. Pace: the EU's ratification process is slow and can be contested by member states and farm lobbies.
The member-state layer

EU policy is made in Brussels, but many results come from individual capitals. France: strategic partner since 1998 . It sold 36 Rafale jets (2016), then 26 Rafale-M for the Navy (agreed 2025), and builds Scorpene submarines in Mumbai. Its support at the UN Security Council has been steady. The Horizon 2047 roadmap (2023) sets long-term goals. France is also in the Indo-Pacific through its overseas territories. Germany: India's biggest European trade partner. It is working on a submarine project (Project 75I) and is a G4 partner for UN reform. Italy, Netherlands, Nordics: technology, shipping, green energy. Brexit also pushed the UK to build a separate track, which led to the 2025 CETA.
Ukraine, Russia and different worlds

The war in Ukraine split Europe and India. Europe saw a threat to the rules-based order. India saw a European war and kept buying Russian oil. In June 2022 Jaishankar told a European audience that Europe must stop thinking its problems are the world's problems, a line widely quoted. Over time Europe accepted India's position and began to see it as a swing power. In 2024–25, European leaders courted India for trade and defence deals. In 2026 the concluded FTA shows how far this has come. Still, Europe watches closely: refined fuels from Russian crude, sanctions on Nayara and the future of S-400 purchases are tests of trust.
Hedge or high hopes?

Optimists see Europe as a partner that, unlike the US or China, has no territorial quarrel with India and no appetite to arm Pakistan heavily. Sceptics recall that two decades of 'imminent' deals went nowhere. Scholars such as Garima Mohan and Jagannath Panda argue Europe needs a bigger security role in the Indo-Pacific, while India needs a clear sense of what it wants from the EU beyond trade. India's other recent FTAs show the pattern: EFTA TEPA (signed March 2024, in force October 2025, with a $100 billion investment pledge over 15 years) and the India–UK CETA (signed July 2025).
What India should seek

Use the FTA to bring exports of textiles, leather, gems, pharma and engineering into a market of 450 million consumers. Seek EU technology in semiconductors, green steel and defence co-production. Negotiate carbon rules (CBAM) in line with the Paris Agreement. Link with Europe in IMEC and Indo-Pacific security (EU naval missions, port calls). Treat France, Germany and Italy as bridges to the EU level. For an Indian student of IR, the lesson is simple. A middle-power India benefits from diversified partners. The EU, Japan and the Gulf are not alternatives to the US. They are insurance against US unpredictability.
How UPSC asks this

"Critically examine the prospects of an India-EU FTA." (typical) "Why is the EU important for India's foreign policy and economy?" (typical) "Assess the impact of CBAM on India's trade." (typical) Structure: (1) background: 1994, 2004, 2007–13, 2022; (2) pillars: trade, technology, connectivity, security; (3) the January 2026 FTA and its status; (4) friction: CBAM, EUDR, data, Russian oil; (5) assessment; (6) way forward: ratify, align standards, link to IMEC and Indo-Pacific. Mention France and Germany to show you know the member-state layer.
India–Japan
Asia's friendliest partnership

India–Japan is often called the least problematic great-power relationship India has . There are no border disputes, no history of war between them, and a shared worry about China's rise. Japan matters for India in four ways: capital (Official Development Assistance and investment), technology (Shinkansen, automobiles, electronics), security (Quad, Malabar) and ideas (the Indo-Pacific concept). The weak point is trade. Bilateral trade is only about $23 billion, small for two of Asia's major economies. Exam questions often ask why the strategic and economic sides do not match.
From sympathy to 'Special Strategic and Global Partnership'

Goodwill dates from Justice Radhabinod Pal , the Indian judge at the Tokyo Tribunal who dissented, and from India's decision not to claim war reparations. India signed a separate peace treaty in 1952. Japan was the first country to give India a yen loan (1958). After the 1991 crisis it was a lender and investor. After 1998 Japan sanctioned India over its nuclear tests, but ties recovered by 2000. Shinzo Abe then made India a priority.
Abe and the Indo-Pacific idea

In August 2007 Abe addressed India's Parliament with a speech titled 'Confluence of the Two Seas' , borrowing a phrase from the Mughal prince Dara Shikoh. He argued the Pacific and Indian Oceans were joining into a 'broader Asia'. This idea fed the first Quad meeting (2007) and later Japan's 'Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP)' strategy, announced at TICAD VI in Nairobi in 2016. India's own Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative (IPOI) followed in 2019. Abe's visit as Republic Day chief guest (2014) and his close friendship with Modi gave the partnership personal momentum. Abe was assassinated in July 2022. Modi declared a day of national mourning.
Security and defence pillar

2008: Joint Declaration on Security Cooperation. 2+2 dialogue (foreign and defence ministers) since 2019. ACSA (2020): Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement for logistics. Exercises: JIMEX (navy), Dharma Guardian (army), Shinyuu Maitri (air), and the Malabar exercise with the US and Australia (Japan a permanent member from 2015). Quad: a core member of the grouping. Technology: talks on defence equipment and technology; Japan's relaxation of its arms-export rules in 2014 made such cooperation possible. The 16th annual summit in New Delhi (1–3 July 2026, with PM Sanae Takaichi) reportedly signed 16 deals, including AI, defence and maritime security. Japan is an Indo-Pacific security partner, though it has no alliance with India.
Economic pillar and infrastructure

The Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) came into force in 2011. Japan is a top-five investor with cumulative FDI over $40 billion. Mumbai–Ahmedabad High Speed Rail (MAHSR): a 508 km Shinkansen-based line, funded largely by a low-interest JICA yen loan. Work is behind schedule; the first section is targeted for the late 2020s. Delhi–Mumbai Industrial Corridor and the Delhi Metro, a showpiece of Japanese aid. Act East Forum: Japanese roads and power in India's Northeast. Maruti Suzuki: the 1983 joint venture made Japan a household name in India. Investment goals rose over time: ¥3.5 trillion (2014–19), ¥5 trillion (2022–27) and a new target of ¥10 trillion over ten years set in 2025 and reaffirmed in July 2026.
The civil nuclear agreement

Japan, the only country attacked with nuclear weapons, signed a civil nuclear cooperation agreement with India on 11 November 2016 . It entered into force on 20 July 2017. It was historic because India is outside the NPT. The deal came with a Japanese statement that cooperation would stop if India conducted a nuclear test. It matters in practice because Japanese firms supply key heavy components for reactors that other countries build. Heavy forgings for reactors worldwide come from Japanese suppliers, so the deal helped US and French reactor projects planned in India.
Africa and the wider region

Japan and India also link in third countries. The Asia-Africa Growth Corridor (AAGC) , announced in 2017, aims at quality infrastructure in Africa as an alternative to Belt and Road. They have discussed joint projects in third countries such as Sri Lanka and Bangladesh. Both support supply-chain resilience . In 2021 India, Japan and Australia launched the Supply Chain Resilience Initiative (SCRI) . The Quad's critical minerals work followed. India, Japan, Germany and Brazil form the G4 , pressing for UN Security Council reform.
Strategic closeness, economic gap

Japan's constitution (Article 9) limits its use of force, so it cannot act as a full military ally. Japanese firms complain of Indian red tape, land acquisition and tax disputes. India is not part of RCEP, which includes Japan and China. Scholars like Purnendra Jain and Rajaram Panda describe the relationship as a ' values-plus-interest ' partnership. Realists see it as balancing against China.
Japan in India's strategy

Japan is a model for capital and quality infrastructure, without political strings. It supports India's bid for a permanent UNSC seat and NSG membership. Japan wants a stable India as a balancer in Asia as China and the US both turn more demanding. The Northeast and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands receive Japanese projects of strategic value. In 2025–26 the US tariff shock pushed India and Japan closer on supply chains, semiconductors and rare earths. Japan's new government under Sanae Takaichi (since October 2025) continued the partnership with a stronger focus on economic security and defence technology.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the strategic dimensions of the India-Japan partnership." (typical) "India-Japan relations are strong strategically but weak economically. Examine." (typical) "What is the significance of Japan's role in the Indo-Pacific for India?" (typical) Structure: (1) history: 1952, 1958, 2000, 2006, 2014; (2) Abe's 2007 speech and the Indo-Pacific; (3) security: 2+2, ACSA, Malabar, Quad; (4) economy: CEPA, MAHSR, ¥10 trillion target; (5) civil nuclear deal (2016); (6) limits and way forward.
Peacekeeping
The blue helmets and India's proudest record

UN peacekeeping is the area where India has paid the highest price and earned the most goodwill. Indian soldiers, police and civilians have served in more than 50 missions since 1948. By India's own count (repeated at the UN in November 2026) over 300,000 personnel have served in total, and well over 180 have died. The topic asks you to know three things: how peacekeeping works and has changed , India's contribution and sacrifices , and India's critique of how mandates are made, which links to its demand for a UNSC seat. Peacekeeping is not mentioned in the UN Charter. Dag Hammarskjöld called it "Chapter VI and a half".
How peacekeeping works

Legal basis: the Security Council authorises missions under Chapter VI (peaceful settlement) or, in robust cases, Chapter VII (enforcement). The term 'Chapter six and a half' is attributed to Hammarskjöld. Three classic principles: consent of the parties, impartiality, and non-use of force except in self-defence and defence of the mandate. Early missions: UNTSO (1948, Middle East) and UNMOGIP (1949, India–Pakistan, Kashmir). The first armed force was UNEF I (1956), after Suez, an idea developed by Lester Pearson and Hammarskjöld. Funding: a separate peacekeeping budget with assessed contributions. Troop-contributing countries (TCCs) are reimbursed at a standard rate. India does not accept that UNMOGIP is relevant after the 1972 Simla Agreement.
Evolving generations

After the Cold War, missions began to do more: elections, human rights, police training and state-building. Failures in Somalia (1993), Rwanda (1994) and Srebrenica (1995) led to reform. The Brahimi Report (2000) asked for clear mandates and enough resources. The Responsibility to Protect (R2P) was endorsed at the 2005 World Summit. The Action for Peacekeeping (A4P) initiative came in 2018. Modern missions face asymmetric threats (Mali, DRC), accusations of sexual exploitation, and a shortage of funds.
Peacekeeping, peacemaking, enforcement, peacebuilding

Boutros Boutros-Ghali's An Agenda for Peace (1992) separated four ideas. Learn them as a ladder. Preventive diplomacy Act before a conflict breaks out: fact-finding, early warning, mediation. Peacemaking Bring warring parties to agreement by peaceful means (Chapter VI). Peacekeeping Deploy UN personnel, with consent, to hold a ceasefire or help implement a deal. Peace enforcement Use force under Chapter VII, even without consent. Post-conflict peacebuilding Rebuild institutions and trust. The Peacebuilding Commission was set up in 2005. India is strong in the third and fifth, and cautious about the fourth.
India's record: places and names

Korea (1950s): India led the Custodian Force for prisoners of war and chaired the Neutral Nations Repatriation Commission; a field ambulance unit served in the war. Indochina (1954): chaired the International Control Commissions in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia. Congo (1960–64): over 6,000 Indian troops.
