Captain Gurbachan Singh Salaria was awarded the Param Vir Chakra, India's only peacekeeper to receive it. Cyprus (1964–): Lt Gen K.S. Thimayya, Force Commander of UNFICYP, died in service in December 1965. Other: Gaza (UNEF), Somalia, Rwanda, Angola, Sierra Leone (UNAMSIL), Namibia (UNTAG, Lt Gen Prem Chand as Force Commander), the former Yugoslavia (UNPROFOR, Lt Gen Satish Nambiar as first Force Commander), Lebanon (UNIFIL), Golan (UNDOF), South Sudan (UNMISS), DR Congo (MONUSCO), Abyei (UNISFA).
Firsts and today's numbers

All-women unit: in 2007 India sent the first all-female formed police unit to Liberia (UNMIL), a major source of inspiration. It served until 2016. Sacrifice: India says over 180 of its peacekeepers have died, the highest toll of any country (the count changes a little each year). Today: India is among the larger contributors of troops in recent years, with a few thousand personnel in UN missions, mainly in South Sudan, Lebanon, DRC, Golan and Abyei. In 2026 about 600 are in UNIFIL, Lebanon. India has said it is the largest cumulative contributor. Training: the Centre for UN Peacekeeping (CUNPK) in New Delhi, set up in 2000, trains Indian and foreign peacekeepers. Leadership: Indian generals have commanded forces in UNTAG, UNPROFOR and MONUSCO.
India's critique and conditions

Say in mandates: TCCs do the dying but have little voice in drafting mandates. India pushes consultations (Resolution 1353, 2001, created consultation meetings). Safety: India led the push for Resolution 2589 (August 2021) , adopted during its UNSC presidency, on accountability for crimes against peacekeepers. Technology and training: India backs digital tools for peacekeepers and offers medical help and training. Rules of engagement: India is cautious about robust enforcement and about missions that become parties to conflict. Consent and sovereignty: India insists on host-state consent and a UN mandate for any deployment. It did not send troops to Iraq (2003) without a UN mandate. The deeper argument: those who contribute most should have a seat at the table.
Do the benefits justify the cost?

Realists say contribution gives little real power: the P5 still decide. Liberals see value in shared norms and leadership in global order. India's argument: peacekeeping is both a moral duty and a case for reform. The UN's financial difficulties and US funding cuts in 2025–26 also threaten missions and reimbursements. Another view, from scholars of peacekeeping: India's choice of safe mission areas with a stable consent environment follows its tradition of respect for state sovereignty.
Current themes

India stresses women, peace and security : more women peacekeepers and a gender-balanced role. It supports technology (digital tools, drones), medical care and training through CUNPK. In November 2026 it called at the UN for better-resourced and better-protected missions. It links peacekeeping to UNSC reform : "those who sacrifice should decide". Peacekeepers also serve under pressure in Lebanon amid the broader West Asia conflict.
How UPSC asks this

"Evaluate India's contribution to UN peacekeeping. How does it relate to India's claim for a permanent UNSC seat?" (typical) "Discuss the challenges facing UN peacekeeping in the 21st century." (typical) "Explain the principles of UN peacekeeping and the Brahimi Report." (typical) Structure: (1) concept and legal basis; (2) principles; (3) evolution and failures; (4) India's contribution: missions, firsts, sacrifices; (5) India's critique and conditions; (6) link to UN reform; (7) way forward.
The Permanent Seat and UN Reform
Why a rising power wants a permanent seat

The UN Security Council (UNSC) still reflects 1945. Five permanent members (P5: US, UK, France, Russia, China) hold a veto. Africa and Latin America have no permanent seat. India, with 1.4 billion people, a top-five economy and a record of peacekeeping, has none either. The campaign for a permanent seat is a pillar of Indian foreign policy. It has been pursued since the 1990s and, as of 2026, has not succeeded. Every year the UN General Assembly decides to continue talks. Exam questions ask for the case for reform, the competing models, the obstacles (Article 108 and the P5), and what India should do.
The rules of the Council

Article 23: the Council has 15 members: five permanent plus ten elected by the General Assembly for two-year terms. The list was written into the Charter in 1945 (11 members). The General Assembly enlarged it to 15 in 1963 (Resolution 1991 (XVIII)), effective 1965. Nothing has changed since. Article 24: the Council has primary responsibility for peace and security. Article 27: nine affirmative votes are needed, including all five permanent members on non-procedural matters (the veto ). Articles 108 and 109: amendments need two-thirds of the General Assembly and ratification by two-thirds of members including all five permanent members . So any P5 state can block reform. India has served as an elected member eight times: 1950–51, 1967–68, 1972–73, 1977–78, 1984–85, 1991–92, 2011–12 and 2021–22.
How the reform debate unfolded

A 1979 General Assembly item on 'equitable representation' started the debate. In 1993 an Open-ended Working Group was formed. In 2005 Kofi Annan's report In Larger Freedom offered Models A and B. The 2005 World Summit pledged early reform, but no deal followed. Since 2009 the process runs as Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) in the General Assembly, based on Decision 62/557. A decision in 2015 passed a 'framework document' to the IGN. Talks have been repetitive, with positions stated but no negotiating text.
The competing groups

G4 (2004): six new permanent seats (two for Africa) and four more non-permanent. Veto issue deferred. Supports each other's claims. African Union (Ezulwini Consensus 2005, Sirte Declaration): two permanent seats with full veto for Africa and five non-permanent. Uniting for Consensus (UfC): led by Italy and Pakistan. Wants a larger Council of elected members only, with longer terms, no new permanent seats. L.69 group: India co-leads this alliance of developing states (it takes its name from a 2007 draft resolution, A/61/L.69). Small island states and others: want a seat rotation.
India's case

Population and economy: the most populous country and one of the largest economies. India overtook Japan in nominal GDP in 2025 (IMF estimates). Peacekeeping record (see the previous lesson). Democratic, nuclear-armed and responsible, with a record of global public goods (ISA, vaccines). Representation: the Council over-represents Europe and under-represents Africa, Asia and Latin America. Legitimacy: a Council from 1945 cannot guide a 2026 world. Indian leaders call the present Council outdated and unrepresentative and urge 'reformed multilateralism'. Support: France, the UK, Russia and the US have said they back India's permanent membership in some form. President Obama said in the Indian Parliament in 2010 that he looked forward to a reformed Council with India as a permanent member. China's language is vague: it says it understands India's aspirations but does not endorse them.
Why it has not happened

The P5 veto over reform (Article 108). Each has its own interests. China: does not want a rival Asian permanent member. It links itself to Japan and India separately. Rivals: Pakistan (with Italy) in UfC, South Korea, Mexico, Argentina and Indonesia, who resist regional leaders. African unity: the AU wants veto for Africa. Other groups reject new vetoes. The 2005 G4 draft put off the veto question for 15 years. India's later line is that if the veto stays, new permanent members should not be second-class. Process: the IGN works by consensus and has no negotiating text. Great-power politics: the US and others slow the talks.
Where India stands now

The General Assembly decided without a vote to continue the IGN in its 80th session and to put the item on the agenda of the 81st session (2026–27). India's line (2026): start text-based negotiations with milestones and timelines. Expand both permanent and non-permanent categories. In the October 2026 IGN debate on the veto, India said the veto should not remain exclusive to the current five, and rejected a separate category of permanent seats, with or without a veto. Pact for the Future (September 2024): for the first time a major UN outcome document committed states to Council reform. Context: the Ukraine war, the Gaza war and the 2026 Iran war showed the Council's paralysis. In 2022 the General Assembly adopted Resolution 76/262 , requiring a debate after any veto. It is called the veto initiative .
Reform or alternatives?

Realists such as Mearsheimer say institutions reflect power and the P5 will not give it up. Liberals argue that legitimacy gaps will push states to build other forums. India's strategy is to hold both: press for reform but also invest in groups where it already has a seat (G20, BRICS, SCO, Quad). Some Indian analysts suggest India should join reform packages that put off the veto question or add a review clause, rather than wait for a perfect deal.
Strategy and the road ahead

Build a stronger coalition with Africa (the AU seat in the G20 helps). Seek P5 support in writing and press China directly. Keep strong peacekeeping, development and disaster relief records. Use non-permanent terms (2021–22) to show leadership. Consider a new elected term. Link reform to the wider push to change the IMF, World Bank and WTO. For the exam, keep a short table: Group, demand, India's stand . Cite Article 108 and the 1963 enlargement.
How UPSC asks this

"India's quest for a permanent seat in the UNSC: assess the prospects." (typical) "Why is UN reform so difficult? What can India do?" (typical) "Discuss the proposals for UNSC expansion." (typical) Structure: (1) structure and the 1945 hangover; (2) Articles 23, 27, 108; (3) reform history and groups (G4, UfC, AU); (4) India's claim; (5) obstacles; (6) 2024–26 developments (Pact for the Future, IGN stalemate); (7) way forward.
Evolution of India's Nuclear Policy
From Bhabha's labs to a nuclear triad

India's nuclear story runs from a peaceful energy programme in 1948 to declared weapons in 1998 and a sea-based deterrent today. It shows the pull between idealism (Nehru's call for disarmament) and security (China's 1964 test, Pakistan). UPSC asks about the phases, the 1974 and 1998 tests, the nuclear doctrine (no first use, credible minimum deterrence) and whether the doctrine still fits after Operation Sindoor (2025).
The phases at a glance
Scholars call the period from 1974 to 1998 one of 'recessed deterrence' or keeping the option open: India had the capability but did not weaponise openly.
Nehru and Bhabha: peaceful atom, open option

Homi J. Bhabha built the programme: the Atomic Energy Commission (1948), the Apsara reactor (1956, Asia's first research reactor) and CIRUS (1960, with Canadian help and US heavy water). He designed the three-stage programme : natural uranium reactors, then fast breeders using plutonium, then thorium, which India has in plenty. Nehru pressed for a ban on nuclear tests (1954 'standstill' proposal) and for disarmament. But he kept the scientific capacity that could later be used for weapons. After China's test in 1964, Bhabha said India could build a bomb in about 18 months. Shastri approved work on a 'peaceful nuclear explosion' study.
Pokhran-I (1974): the 'peaceful nuclear explosion'

On 18 May 1974 , under Indira Gandhi, India tested a device at Pokhran, code-named 'Smiling Buddha'. It called it a peaceful nuclear explosion (PNE) . Canada cut nuclear aid, since CIRUS plutonium was used. The Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG) was set up in 1974–75 to control exports. The US passed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Act (1978) , which ended fuel supply to Tarapur. India then waited for 24 years. Reasons: sanctions, cost, and a hope that global disarmament would come. Pakistan's covert programme under A.Q. Khan and Chinese help to it changed the calculation.
Pokhran-II (1998): becoming a nuclear weapon state

On 11 and 13 May 1998 , under Vajpayee, India tested five devices (Operation Shakti), including a thermonuclear device. Vajpayee wrote to President Clinton citing China as the main threat. Pakistan tested at Chagai on 28 and 30 May. The UNSC passed Resolution 1172 (June 1998) condemning the tests. The US and Japan imposed sanctions. India announced a voluntary moratorium on testing and began the Jaswant Singh–Strobe Talbott dialogue, which led over time to the 2005–08 nuclear deal. K. Subrahmanyam, the father of Indian strategic thinking, had long argued for an open deterrent.
The nuclear doctrine (2003)

The National Security Advisory Board released a Draft Nuclear Doctrine in August 1999. The Cabinet Committee on Security adopted the official version on 4 January 2003 . Credible minimum deterrence. No first use (NFU): nuclear weapons only in retaliation against a nuclear attack on Indian territory or forces anywhere. Massive retaliation to inflict unacceptable damage. Exception: India keeps the option of a nuclear response to a major attack with biological or chemical weapons. No use against non-nuclear states. Civilian control: the Nuclear Command Authority , with a Political Council chaired by the PM and an Executive Council chaired by the NSA. The Strategic Forces Command manages the arsenal. Continued moratorium on tests, strict export controls, and support for a global, verifiable disarmament.
Delivery systems and the triad

Land: the Prithvi and Agni series. Agni-V (over 5,000 km). In March 2024 Mission Divyastra tested Agni-V with MIRV (multiple warheads). Air: nuclear-capable fighter aircraft. Sea: INS Arihant , a nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine, was commissioned in 2016 and completed its first deterrence patrol in November 2018, completing the triad . INS Arighaat followed in 2024. A sea-based force gives a secure second strike, which is essential for a no-first-use doctrine.
Should India drop no first use?

In 2019 Defence Minister Rajnath Singh said that NFU stands, but what happens in future depends on circumstances. Critics such as Bharat Karnad ( Nuclear Weapons and Indian Security , 2002) want a bigger arsenal. Supporters of NFU say it has served India well.
After Operation Sindoor

In May 2025 India struck targets in Pakistan below the nuclear threshold. In his address on 12 May 2025 Modi said India would not tolerate nuclear blackmail . This shows the logic of the stability-instability paradox : limited conventional war under a nuclear umbrella. Civil side: the SHANTI Act (December 2025) replaced the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010, opening nuclear power to private companies under licence. The target is 100 GW of nuclear power by 2047. See the next lesson for the treaties.
How UPSC asks this

"Trace the evolution of India's nuclear policy from Nehru to the present." (typical) "Is India's no-first-use doctrine still relevant?" (typical) "Explain the key features of India's nuclear doctrine." (typical) Structure: (1) Bhabha and Nehru; (2) 1964 trigger; (3) Pokhran-I and the response; (4) the option period; (5) Pokhran-II; (6) the 2003 doctrine; (7) triad; (8) NFU debate and 2025 events; (9) conclusion.
NPT, CTBT, NSG and the Civil Nuclear Deal
Outside the club, but inside the trade

India never signed the NPT or the CTBT . Yet since 2008 it can trade in nuclear fuel and technology, thanks to the NSG waiver and the India–US civil nuclear deal . It has also joined three of the four export-control regimes. UPSC asks why India rejects the NPT and CTBT, how the 2008 deal changed things, and why NSG membership is still blocked.
The NPT and India's objection

The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970. It recognises five nuclear weapon states: those that tested before 1 January 1967 (US, USSR/Russia, UK, France, China). Everyone else must stay non-nuclear. Article VI asks the nuclear states to pursue disarmament in good faith, but sets no deadline. Article X allows withdrawal (North Korea, 2003). India calls the NPT discriminatory : it divides the world into nuclear 'haves' and 'have-nots' for ever. Jaswant Singh called this 'nuclear apartheid' in 1998. India says it will not join as a non-nuclear state.
The CTBT

The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1996. It bans all nuclear explosions. It is not in force, because it needs all 44 states listed in Annex 2 (those with nuclear reactors) to ratify. India, Pakistan and North Korea have not signed; the US and China have signed but not ratified. India blocked the text at the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva in 1996. Its reasons: no time-bound disarmament, and the entry-into-force clause forced India's hand. India keeps a voluntary moratorium on tests since 1998.
Export-control regimes

NSG (1974–75) 48 members who control nuclear exports. India is not a member. MTCR Missile Technology Control Regime. India joined in June 2016. Wassenaar Arrangement Conventional arms and dual-use goods. India joined in December 2017. Australia Group Chemical and biological controls. India joined in January 2018. India's domestic law: the WMD Act (2005) , which bans transfers to non-state actors, in line with UNSC Resolution 1540 (2004).
The road to the 2008 deal

India separated its reactors into civilian (under IAEA safeguards) and military (outside). It promised to keep its test moratorium and strong export controls. In return it received a clean waiver from NSG rules, the only non-NPT state to get one.
What the deal gave India, and what it did not

Gains: imported uranium from Russia, Kazakhstan, Canada, Australia, Uzbekistan and France; deals with France, the US and Japan (2016); recognition as a responsible nuclear state; the end of decades of 'technology denial'. Limits: no new US reactor was built for years, mainly because of the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act (2010) , which let operators claim against suppliers (Section 17(b)). Foreign suppliers feared unlimited liability. 2025 change: the SHANTI Act (December 2025) replaced the 2010 liability law and the Atomic Energy Act, 1962. It caps operator liability, removes the supplier liability that blocked foreign firms, and lets private companies operate plants under licence. Critics say it shifts risk to taxpayers. India ratified the Convention on Supplementary Compensation (CSC) in 2016.
The NSG membership fight

India applied for NSG membership in 2016. At the Seoul plenary (June 2016) , China led opposition, saying non-NPT states need a common, criteria-based approach. That would also bring in Pakistan, which India and many members oppose because of the A.Q. Khan network. Membership requires consensus, so one state can block. As of 2026 India is still outside. In practice the 2008 waiver gives most of the trade benefits; membership would give a voice in making rules.
Rule-taker or rule-maker?

Non-proliferation purists say the 2008 deal rewarded a state that stayed out of the NPT. Supporters reply that bringing India into the system is better than isolating it. India also backs the FMCT (fissile material cut-off) talks in principle but did not sign the 2017 Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons .
Disarmament in India's voice

Rajiv Gandhi Action Plan (1988) at the UN: a timebound plan to eliminate nuclear weapons by 2010. India supports a Nuclear Weapons Convention and a universal, non-discriminatory approach. India–Pakistan CBMs: the 1988 agreement on not attacking nuclear facilities (lists exchanged each 1 January) and the 2005 missile-test notification. Energy goal: 100 GW nuclear power by 2047, small modular reactors and private entry under the SHANTI Act.
How UPSC asks this

"Why has India refused to sign the NPT and CTBT?" (typical) "Assess the significance of the Indo-US civil nuclear deal." (typical) "Discuss India's bid for NSG membership." (typical) Structure: (1) NPT and CTBT and India's objections; (2) export regimes; (3) the 2005–08 deal and waiver; (4) liability issue and the 2025 SHANTI Act; (5) NSG bid and China; (6) disarmament stance; (7) assessment.
Afghanistan
India's old friend and a new test

Afghanistan sits at the crossroads of South and Central Asia. For India it is a source of risk (terror groups, drugs) and an opportunity (a route to Central Asia, a friendly public, a counter to Pakistan's reach). After the Taliban returned on 15 August 2021 , India closed its embassy and watched. From 2022 it moved step by step to a pragmatic engagement . In October 2025 it upgraded its Kabul mission to an embassy. In 2026 the Pakistan–Taliban clashes added a new twist. The examiner wants a balanced view: values versus interests , and engagement without recognition.
India in Afghanistan, 1947–2021

Between 2001 and 2021 India gave over $3 billion in aid, more than any other regional state. Major projects: Zaranj–Delaram highway (218 km, 2009), a route linking to Iran's Chabahar. Salma Dam (Afghan–India Friendship Dam, Herat, 2016). Parliament building in Kabul (2015) and many schools, hospitals and training programmes. Air Freight Corridor (2017) bypassing Pakistan. The 2011 Strategic Partnership Agreement was Afghanistan's first such pact. India's line was 'Afghan-led, Afghan-owned, Afghan-controlled' peace. The book to know is Avinash Paliwal's My Enemy's Enemy: India in Afghanistan from the Soviet Invasion to the US Withdrawal (2017).
From rejection to pragmatism

The 2020 Doha agreement between the US and the Taliban led to the US withdrawal in 2021. India's earlier ban on talking to the Taliban faded. Officials met Taliban leaders in Doha in 2021. June 2022: a 'technical team' returned to the Kabul embassy to coordinate aid. Aid: wheat, medicines, vaccines and earthquake relief, delivered through the UN and directly. Visas and Afghan students: a limited regime; Afghan Sikhs and Hindus given priority. January 2025: the Foreign Secretary met Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi in Dubai. October 2025: India attended the 7th Moscow Format consultations (7 October 2025) and hosted Taliban Foreign Minister Muttaqi in Delhi. Jaishankar announced the upgrade of the Kabul technical mission to a full embassy . January 2026: a Taliban-appointed chargé d'affaires took charge at the Afghan embassy in Delhi. India has not formally recognised the Taliban. As of 2026 only Russia has (July 2025).
India's reasons for engaging

Pakistan: relations between the Taliban and Pakistan have turned hostile over the TTP. Pakistan struck Afghan cities in February 2026 and declared 'open war' on 27 February; a ceasefire proved fragile and clashes continued through 2026. Islamabad accuses Kabul of being 'a colony of India'. India denies backing militants. Terrorism: the Taliban condemned the Pahalgam attack (April 2025) and promised that Afghan soil will not be used against others. Connectivity: access to Central Asia and Chabahar, minerals and markets. China and Russia: both engage the Taliban. India does not want to leave the field. People: Afghans' goodwill towards India remains high. Pakistan's denial of land transit for trade stays a key hurdle. Air and sea routes are used instead.
Geography and the Durand Line

India has no land border with Afghanistan in practice. The Wakhan Corridor touches India's claimed territory in PoK, but Pakistan controls the access. The Durand Line (1893) is the Afghanistan–Pakistan border. No Afghan government has accepted it. This is the root of the Pakistan–Taliban quarrel. Pakistan's idea of 'strategic depth' in Afghanistan has clashed with Taliban nationalism. Routes for India: Chabahar to Zaranj, then the Zaranj–Delaram highway; the INSTC ; and the TAPI gas pipeline (Turkmenistan–Afghanistan–Pakistan–India), which has been stalled for decades. Afghanistan is also a mineral-rich country (copper, lithium, rare earths) and a corridor for Central Asian energy.
The regional chessboard

Pakistan Helped create and shelter the Taliban, but now fights them over the TTP and the Durand Line. China Seeks mines, security for its Xinjiang border and a route for CPEC. Russia and Iran Talk to the Taliban, worried about ISKP. Russia recognised the Taliban in 2025. Central Asian states Want trade and security, and engage Kabul. United States Withdrew in 2021, but still wants counter-terror access and, according to Trump's 2025 remarks, Bagram. India's position: not the biggest player, but a trusted one among ordinary Afghans.
The limits and risks

Women's rights: bans on girls' secondary education and women's work. India raises this in UN forums but ties are not conditional on it. Terror groups: the UN lists several, including al-Qaeda, the Islamic State–Khorasan (ISKP) and Pakistan-focused groups like the TTP. India worries about LeT and JeM havens. Chabahar: the US reimposed sanctions on the port in September 2025, granted a conditional waiver to 26 April 2026, and the position after that was still unclear. Check the latest status. Recognition: a formal step would anger Western and domestic critics, and give Pakistan an argument. Drugs and refugees. US interest in Bagram: Trump said in 2025 he wanted it back.
Principle or pragmatism?

A realist reading: states deal with whoever rules. India's influence in Kabul would vanish if it stayed away. A constructivist reading: India's identity as a democracy and its standing among Afghans (and its position on rights) set limits on how close it can go. Paliwal argues India's policy has always been an anti-Pakistan hedge more than a love for any Afghan ruler. The Taliban-Pakistan rift in 2025–26 supports that view.
What India does

Keeps the humanitarian channel strong: food, medicine, health teams. Builds trade through air corridors and Iran. Insists on an inclusive government and women's rights in statements. Works with Russia, Iran and Central Asia in the Moscow Format and the India–Central Asia Dialogue (2019). Wants a written guarantee against terrorism from Afghan soil. Present tense for the exam: India engages but does not recognise . It has upgraded to an embassy and accepted a Taliban diplomat, which is 'recognition in all but name' to some critics.
How UPSC asks this

"India's Afghanistan policy after the Taliban takeover: continuity or change?" (typical) "Evaluate the regional implications of the US withdrawal from Afghanistan for India." (typical) "Why is Afghanistan important for India's connectivity to Central Asia?" (typical) Structure: (1) history and Indian projects; (2) 2021 shock; (3) pragmatic engagement steps 2022–26; (4) drivers: Pakistan, terrorism, connectivity, Chinese and Russian presence; (5) limits: women's rights, recognition, sanctions; (6) way forward: engage on humanitarian and security, coordinate with regional states.
West Asia and the Gulf
The region India cannot ignore

West Asia (the Gulf, Iran, Israel, Turkey, the Levant) supplies about half of India's crude oil and most of its gas imports. Around 9 million Indians live and work in the Gulf. They sent a large share of India's remittances, which were about $130 billion in 2024 (World Bank). Trade with the GCC is above $150 billion. The region is also unstable. From the Gaza war (October 2023) to the Red Sea attacks and the Iran war of 2026 , India has had to balance Israel, Iran, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and the US. Policy label: 'Think West' (from the 2010s) or 'Link West' , meaning a multi-aligned approach with all sides.
The Gulf partnership: UAE and Saudi Arabia

UAE: Comprehensive Strategic Partnership (2017). The India–UAE CEPA came into force on 1 May 2022 and lifted trade to over $80 billion. The UAE hosts 3.5 million Indians, is a big investor and a partner in I2U2 and IMEC . Rupee–dirham trade and UPI links are in place. Saudi Arabia: Strategic Partnership Council (2019). It is a top oil supplier and a pledged investor. Modi visited in April 2025 and cut the trip short after the Pahalgam attack. Qatar: main LNG supplier. In February 2024 eight former Indian Navy men sentenced to death in Qatar were released. Oman, Kuwait, Bahrain: defence, port and labour ties. The Gulf is no longer only a source of oil and jobs. Its sovereign funds are investing in Indian infrastructure, and India has pushed for an India–GCC FTA .
Iran: Chabahar and sanctions

India has civilisational and energy ties with Iran. Iran once supplied a large share of India's oil. After US sanctions (2018–19), imports ended. Chabahar Port: a 2016 trilateral agreement between India, Iran and Afghanistan. A 10-year operating contract with Iran followed in May 2024. It gives India access to Afghanistan and Central Asia without Pakistan, and anchors the INSTC . Sanctions: the US revoked the port's sanctions waiver in September 2025, then gave a conditional waiver to 26 April 2026. What followed is unclear, as of November 2026. Abstention at the IAEA: India has often balanced Iran's nuclear file with its partnership with the US. The Iran–Israel conflicts are India's hardest balancing act.
The Iran war and the Hormuz shock

All of these are as reported; details differ across sources. In India's case the main effects were: Energy: the Strait of Hormuz carries about a quarter of seaborne oil. Disruption raised prices and strained supplies. Under Operation Urja Suraksha the Indian Navy escorted merchant ships. Citizens: thousands of Indians were evacuated from Iran, as in Operation Sindhu in June 2025. Shipping: Indian-linked vessels were damaged or delayed, as reported. Diplomacy: India urged restraint. The BRICS New Delhi Declaration (September 2026) called for de-escalation but avoided condemning any party. The crisis revived arguments for energy diversification and for IMEC and Red Sea routes.
Israel and Palestine in Indian policy

India recognised Palestine in 1988 and Israel in 1950 but only had full diplomatic ties with Israel from 1992 . Modi was the first Indian PM to visit Israel (July 2017) and visited Ramallah in February 2018. After the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack, Modi condemned terrorism and expressed solidarity with Israel. India has also kept its two-state solution position and sent humanitarian aid. On UN votes: India abstained on the October 2023 UNGA call for a truce, voted for the December 2023 humanitarian ceasefire resolution and again in December 2024, and abstained in June 2025. India welcomed the US-brokered Gaza ceasefire of late 2025 and UNSC Resolution 2803, and attended the first meeting of the US-led Board of Peace as an observer in February 2026.
From Arab sympathy to Link West

In the Cold War India stood with the Arab cause, partly for oil and partly because of its large Muslim population and non-alignment. India voted against the UN partition plan for Palestine in 1947. In 1974 it was among the first non-Arab states to recognise the PLO as the sole representative of the Palestinian people. The 1990–91 Gulf War forced a rethink. India evacuated about 1.7 lakh Indians from Kuwait and Iraq, one of the largest civilian airlifts ever. The end of the Cold War and the 1991 economic crisis led to the 1992 ties with Israel. Since the 2010s, India has treated the Gulf as an extended neighbourhood : bilateral strategic partnerships, defence exercises (with Saudi, Oman, the UAE), and investment.
The Red Sea, Houthis and maritime security

After the Gaza war, the Yemen-based Houthi movement attacked shipping in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden from late 2023. Many ships went around the Cape of Good Hope. Costs and transit times rose, and India's trade to Europe and the US East Coast was affected. The Indian Navy deployed warships in the Arabian Sea and the Gulf of Aden, escorted merchant ships, rescued crews and tracked piracy off Somalia. In 2024 India also worked with partners to board hijacked vessels. These events strengthened two ideas: India as a net security provider in the Indian Ocean, and the need for alternative routes such as IMEC , INSTC and Chabahar. The 2026 Hormuz crisis made the same point more sharply.
Hyphenation or multi-alignment?

India's formula is de-hyphenation (Israel and Palestine treated separately) and multi-alignment (partnership with Israel, Iran and the Gulf at once). It has worked because India offers no bases and does not take sides in the Sunni–Shia or Arab–Israeli contests. Critics say India's silence on Gaza lost it moral standing with the Global South. Supporters answer that interest-based balance protects the diaspora and energy security. Another factor is Pakistan: Saudi Arabia reportedly signed a mutual defence pact with Pakistan in 2025, while Turkey and Azerbaijan backed Pakistan in the May 2025 conflict.
Evacuations, energy and diaspora

Evacuations have become a tool of diplomacy: Operation Raahat (Yemen, 2015), Vande Bharat (Covid), Operation Sindhu (Iran, 2025). Diaspora: Kerala and other states rely on Gulf remittances, and the Kafala system raises worker-rights questions. Energy: strategic petroleum reserves (Padur, Mangaluru, Visakhapatnam), more suppliers (US, Brazil, Guyana, Russia). Naval presence: Operation Sankalp (Gulf escorts) and anti-piracy patrols in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. The 2026 war shows how a distant war can threaten fuel prices, jobs and remittances in India at once.
How UPSC asks this

"West Asia is the new geopolitical epicentre for India. Discuss." (typical) "India's balancing between Israel and the Arab world has been successful. Critically examine." (typical) "Examine the importance of the Gulf to India's economy and security." (typical) Structure: (1) energy, diaspora, trade; (2) Gulf partners: UAE CEPA, Saudi SPC, Qatar; (3) Iran and Chabahar; (4) Israel-Palestine policy; (5) 2023–26 shocks: Gaza, Red Sea, Iran war and Hormuz; (6) tools: evacuation, energy diversification, minilaterals; (7) way forward.
India–Israel and New Minilaterals
Two stories: one partner and many small clubs

This lesson joins two fast-changing topics. First, India–Israel , now a Special Strategic Partnership. Second, the new minilaterals : small, flexible groups of three or four states, such as the Quad, I2U2 and IMEC. India has moved from the big multilateral forums of the Cold War to a style where it joins several issue-based coalitions at once. The reason is simple: the UN and the WTO are stuck, while a handful of like-minded countries can act faster. Examiners ask what minilaterals add, whether they undermine multilateralism, and how they match strategic autonomy .
India and Israel: a long, quiet road

India recognised Israel in 1950 but kept the relationship at a low level because of Arab ties and domestic politics. After 1992 ties grew fast, especially in defence . During the 1999 Kargil war, Israel sent ammunition, drones and laser-guided bomb kits. Since then India has been among Israel's top arms buyers: drones such as Heron, missiles such as Barak-8 (MRSAM, co-developed with DRDO), Spike anti-tank missiles, radars and the SPICE bomb kit.
The pillars of India–Israel ties

Defence and security: arms, co-development, counter-terrorism and cyber cooperation. The Pegasus spyware controversy (2021) raised domestic questions; the Supreme Court set up a committee. Agriculture and water: Centres of Excellence in many Indian states, drip irrigation and desalination. Technology and innovation: the I4F fund, start-ups, research grants. Trade: about $3.6 billion in 2024-25 (excluding most defence), diamonds a major item. People: Indian caregivers and construction workers in Israel; the Bnei Menashe community. The two states share a worry about terrorism and a sense of being in tough neighbourhoods.
Modi's visit and the FTA

Modi made a two-day state visit to Israel on 25–26 February 2026 . The countries upgraded their ties to a Special Strategic Partnership and signed a series of MoUs (reported as 16). Talks on a free trade agreement had started in New Delhi shortly before. The sides also agreed to explore linking UPI with Israel's payments system and to update defence arrangements for joint projects. Modi spoke of cooperation in the I2U2 and IMEC formats. The visit drew domestic criticism over the Gaza war. Two days after the visit, on 28 February 2026, the US and Israel struck Iran. Delhi had to manage the new Israel tie in the middle of a regional war. India kept calling for restraint and dialogue. India also stays committed to a two-state solution and sends aid to Palestinians.
What are minilaterals?

The term was popularised by Moisés Naím in Foreign Policy (2009): 'minilateralism' means bringing together the smallest number of countries needed to make the largest possible impact on a problem. Bilateral Two states. Minilateral Three to five like-minded states, informal, issue-based, no big treaty or secretariat. Multilateral Many states, formal institutions and rules (UN, WTO). Advantages: speed, flexibility, shared interests. Drawbacks: exclusion of others, weak enforcement, and the risk of replacing universal rules with great-power clubs. India uses them to supplement , not replace, the UN and WTO.
The Indian map of minilaterals

I2U2 (India, Israel, UAE, US): launched at a virtual leaders' summit on 14 July 2022. Aims: food security, energy, water, space, health, transport. Projects included a food park in Gujarat and a hybrid renewable energy project. IMEC (below). Trilaterals: India–France–UAE, India–France–Australia, India–Japan–Australia (supply chains), Japan–India–Italy, and others. Colombo Security Conclave on Indian Ocean security. The big difference from alliances: no joint command, no common enemy named, and each member keeps its own ties.
IMEC: the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor

Announced at the G20 summit in New Delhi on 9 September 2023 through an MoU among India, the US, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, the EU, France, Germany and Italy. Eastern leg: Indian ports (such as Mundra) to the UAE by sea. Northern leg: rail across the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Jordan to Israel's Haifa port, then by sea to Europe. Plus an electricity cable, a hydrogen pipeline and a data cable. It was meant as an alternative to China's Belt and Road. But the Gaza war froze the northern link, and Gulf politics and the 2026 Hormuz disruption cast doubt on Gulf hubs. In 2026 President Trump publicly backed IMEC again, and analysts urged a 'Hormuz-proof' version. No new official timetable existed as of late 2026.
Strength in numbers or fragmentation?

Realists see minilaterals as balancing . Liberals see them as steps towards rules. India's explanation is reformed multilateralism : it still presses for UN reform while building flexible coalitions. Evidence of the limits: I2U2 has met rarely since 2022, the Quad has not held a leaders' summit since September 2024 and IMEC works only on paper. Strategic autonomy means India can join many and be bound by none.
Using these groupings well

Prefer projects with money and deadlines (ports, grids, chips) to long communiqués. Keep a seat at both Western and Eurasian tables: BRICS and SCO, Quad and I2U2. Use groupings to pull in capital and technology for Indian manufacturing. Keep Israel ties on interests, with Palestine and the Arab world managed separately. For the exam, give examples with dates and one clear criticism. A diagram of overlapping groupings around India is worth marks.
How UPSC asks this

"I2U2 and IMEC: assess their significance for India's West Asia policy." (typical) "Minilateralism is reshaping India's foreign policy. Discuss." (typical) "Evaluate the India-Israel strategic partnership." (typical) Structure: (1) concept of minilateralism; (2) examples: Quad, I2U2, IMEC, trilaterals; (3) India–Israel pillars and the 2026 visit; (4) benefits; (5) limits and risks; (6) way forward: deliver projects, keep multilateralism alive.
Indo-Pacific and the Quad
From 'Asia-Pacific' to 'Indo-Pacific'

For decades the strategic map showed an Asia-Pacific region that stopped at the Malacca Strait. India was at the edge. The new term Indo-Pacific joins the Indian and Pacific Oceans into one theatre and puts India at the centre. Why this matters to India: over 90% of its trade by volume moves by sea, much of its energy passes through the Indian Ocean, and China's naval presence is growing there. Exam questions ask four things: what the concept means, India's version of it, the Quad , and the limits of both. Keep ASEAN centrality and strategic autonomy as your two anchor words.
The idea and the grouping

The term 'Indo-Pacific' was used in a 2007 article by Indian naval analyst Gurpreet Khurana . Japan's Shinzo Abe gave it political life the same year. The US adopted it formally in its 2017 National Security Strategy and renamed Pacific Command as Indo-Pacific Command in 2018. The first Quad dialogue was in 2007 but China protested and Australia's Rudd government withdrew in 2008. The 2017 revival came after Chinese actions in the South China Sea and at Doklam.
India's vision of the Indo-Pacific

At the Shangri-La Dialogue (June 2018) Modi set out India's view: the Indo-Pacific is a natural region, free, open and inclusive , with ASEAN centrality , a rules-based order, and no domination by a single power. He said India does not see it as a club of limited members or as directed against any country. In November 2019 India launched the Indo-Pacific Oceans Initiative (IPOI) with seven pillars: maritime security, ecology, resources, capacity building, disaster risk reduction, science and technology, and trade and connectivity. Earlier, SAGAR (2015) set India's Indian Ocean policy. In 2025 it was widened to MAHASAGAR . India also backs the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific (AOIP, 2019). Notice the difference: the US stresses 'free and open' and competition with China; India stresses 'inclusive'.
How the Quad works

The Quadrilateral Security Dialogue links India, the US, Japan and Australia. It has no charter, no treaty and no secretariat. It meets at several levels. Leaders' summits: virtual in March 2021 and March 2022; in person in Washington (September 2021), Tokyo (May 2022), Hiroshima (May 2023) and Wilmington, Delaware (September 2024). Working areas: health and vaccines (2021 pledge), climate, critical and emerging technology, infrastructure, space, cyber, and maritime security. Programmes: the Quad Fellowship (2023), the Indo-Pacific Partnership for Maritime Domain Awareness (IPMDA) announced in May 2022, Quad-at-Sea Ship Observer mission and a cancer moonshot. Malabar: a naval exercise in which all four have taken part since 2020.
The Quad in a harder year

India was due to host the next leaders' summit in 2025. It was delayed amid friction in India–US ties over tariffs and Trump's ceasefire claims. As of November 2026, no Quad leaders' summit has been held since September 2024 . Foreign ministers met in Washington in July 2025, and in New Delhi on 26 May 2026, announcing work on maritime surveillance, energy security and critical minerals. Reports in 2026 said annual summits were unlikely, with the chair possibly passing to Australia. A possible leaders' meeting at ASEAN-linked events in Manila in November 2026 was reported but unconfirmed. The Trump administration said it still values the Quad, but its focus is on trade and bilateral deals. Check news before the exam: the status of the summit is the key current-affairs fact.
The South China Sea and the Malacca dilemma

About one-third of global trade passes through the South China Sea. China claims most of it under its 'nine-dash line'. In July 2016 an arbitral tribunal under UNCLOS, in a case brought by the Philippines, ruled that the claim has no legal basis. China rejected the ruling. India supports freedom of navigation, peaceful settlement and the 2016 ruling , though it takes no side on sovereignty claims. It has exploration interests (ONGC Videsh in Vietnamese blocks) and sells defence goods to Vietnam and the Philippines. The Malacca dilemma is China's worry that a hostile navy could choke its trade at the Strait. India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands sit near the western mouth of the strait. This gives India a card, and explains China's push for ports in the Indian Ocean. India's own seas: it is building a larger navy, with INS Vikrant (2022) as its first indigenous aircraft carrier.
The wider architecture

AUKUS (2021) US–UK–Australia pact to supply nuclear-powered submarines. India is not a member. It shows the US pays more for formal alliances. IPEF (2022) The Indo-Pacific Economic Framework. India joined three pillars (supply chains, clean economy, fair economy) but not the trade pillar. RCEP (2022 in force) India left in 2019. China, Japan, ASEAN and others are in. China's view Beijing calls the Quad an 'Asian NATO' aimed at containment. It prefers the term 'Asia-Pacific'. India differs from the US by avoiding a military alliance and by stressing ASEAN.
A bulwark or a talking shop?

Realists (Walt, Mearsheimer) see the Quad as a balance against China's rise. Liberals see public goods like vaccines and infrastructure. Constructivists note that the Quad frames a shared identity of 'democracies'. India, however, avoids that label and stresses inclusiveness. A common critique, by Brahma Chellaney and others: the Quad lacks substance. Defenders such as C. Raja Mohan say its value is in habits of cooperation and the signals it sends.
India's choices

Keep strategic autonomy : Quad, plus BRICS and SCO. Build India's own maritime capacity: the Andaman and Nicobar Command, naval bases in Agalega (Mauritius) and Assumption (Seychelles, stalled), the Information Fusion Centre (IFC-IOR) at Gurugram. Use the Quad for capabilities : undersea domain awareness, secure chips and critical minerals. Court Southeast Asia: Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia. The test: can the Quad deliver for India while US policy swings?
How UPSC asks this

"The Quad is an alliance in the making. Critically examine from India's viewpoint." (typical) "Discuss India's Indo-Pacific vision and compare it with that of the US." (typical) "India's maritime strategy in the Indian Ocean Region." (typical) Structure: (1) concept: Indo-Pacific versus Asia-Pacific; (2) India's vision (Shangri-La 2018, IPOI, SAGAR/MAHASAGAR); (3) Quad: origins, 2017 revival, activities; (4) other groupings: AUKUS, IPEF; (5) 2025–26 stall; (6) assessment and way forward.
India's Vision of a New World Order
A rising power writes its own script

India's leaders say the world order built in 1945 no longer reflects today's power. They want a multipolar world, a reformed UN and a bigger role for the Global South . They also say India should be a 'Vishwa Bandhu' (friend of the world) and a 'leading power', not a mere balancer. This lesson covers what India says it wants, the tools it uses (G20 2023, the Voice of the Global South summits, BRICS 2026, solar and disaster alliances, digital public goods) and the criticism that rhetoric runs ahead of capacity. It is also a good place to apply IR theory: Zakaria's 'rise of the rest', Acharya's 'multiplex world', and the idea of a 'swing state'.
From Nehru's 'one world' to Modi's 'Vishwa Bandhu'

The ambition is not new. Nehru spoke of 'one world' and tried to shape global norms on disarmament and decolonisation. Indira Gandhi led the demand for a New International Economic Order. After 1991 the stress shifted to economic strength and strategic partnerships. What is new is the language: 'leading power', 'Vishwa Bandhu' and 'Viksit Bharat'. And what is new in method: India now offers solutions (solar, digital, vaccines) and joins many groupings at once, instead of speaking only for the poor in the abstract.
The building blocks of India's vision

Multipolarity: a world with several centres, in Asia as well as globally. A multipolar Asia matters because India does not want China to dominate it. Strategic autonomy / multi-alignment: India takes decisions on its interests, with no formal allies. S. Jaishankar's The India Way (2020) lays it out. Reformed multilateralism: UNSC, IMF quotas, WTO dispute settlement and the global financial architecture must change. Rules, not might: respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity and international law, and 'dialogue and diplomacy' over war. Modi told Putin at Samarkand in 2022 that today's era is not an era of war. Civilisational values: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (the world is one family), the G20 theme of 2023: 'One Earth, One Family, One Future'.
Three ways to read the new order

Fareed Zakaria, The Post-American World (2008) The 'rise of the rest': China, India and others grow while US dominance relatively declines. Not a decline of America, but the rise of others. Amitav Acharya, The End of the American World Order (2014) The old Western-led order is ending. What follows is a multiplex world , like a cinema with many screens: no single power and many actors, including regional bodies and non-state groups. Kishore Mahbubani, The New Asian Hemisphere (2008) Power is shifting from West to Asia. The West must share power in global institutions. India's own voice stresses that it is a swing state (a term from Kliman and Fontaine, 2012): a democracy that cannot be taken for granted by any camp.
G20 2023 and the Voice of the Global South

Voice of Global South Summit: first held virtually on 12–13 January 2023 with over 100 countries. Further editions followed in November 2023 and August 2024. G20 presidency (December 2022–November 2023): the New Delhi Leaders' Declaration was adopted by consensus on 9 September 2023, despite splits over Ukraine. The African Union was admitted as a permanent member. Global South priorities: debt relief, climate finance, digital public infrastructure, reform of multilateral development banks, food and energy security. India offers itself as a bridge : able to speak with the US and Russia, the West and the South. In 2026 India chaired BRICS (summit in New Delhi, 12–13 September 2026, with a consensus declaration despite sharp Iran–UAE differences) and hosted the AI Impact Summit (February 2026), which ended with a New Delhi Declaration backed by around 88 countries and organisations.
Public goods: solar, disasters, digital

International Solar Alliance (ISA): launched with France at COP21, Paris, in November 2015. Headquarters at Gurugram. Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI): launched in 2019. Global Biofuels Alliance: launched at the 2023 G20. Mission LiFE (Lifestyle for Environment), launched in 2022. Digital public infrastructure: UPI, Aadhaar-style identity and the 'India Stack' offered to other states. Vaccine Maitri (2021) and development aid through ITEC (1964). At COP26 (Glasgow, 2021) Modi announced a net-zero target for 2070 and the 'Panchamrit' goals. India stresses climate justice and common but differentiated responsibilities.
Reforming the system

UN Security Council: India wants permanent membership and has said veto power should not stay with the current five if the Council expands. It supports text-based negotiations (IGN) and works with the G4. See the later lesson. Bretton Woods: more votes for developing countries at the IMF and World Bank (the 15th review of quotas). WTO: a permanent solution for public stockholding for food security, and restoring the Appellate Body. Terrorism: India has pushed since 1996 for a Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism . New domains: rules for AI, cyberspace and space. India argues that a legitimate order needs a legitimate voice for 1.4 billion people.
Leader or free rider?

Supporters point to the G20 consensus and the African Union seat. Critics say India's 'Global South' leadership is thin on money (aid is a fraction of China's), that it avoided firm stands on Ukraine and Gaza, and that the Global South is too diverse to speak with one voice. China is a rival claimant to the Global South mantle. In BRICS and SCO the two sit together but compete for leadership. There is also the question whether India wants to change the order or to join it at the top table . Many scholars say India is a revisionist within the system : it wants more power in the rules, not new rules.
2025–26: a stress test

The year 2025–26 tested every pillar. US tariffs, the Iran war and the Sindoor crisis showed the limits of autonomy. India answered by diversifying trade (UK, EFTA, EU deals), pressing BRICS to keep a balanced line and hosting summits in New Delhi in 2026. Viksit Bharat 2047 , the goal of a developed India by its 100th year of independence, ties the foreign policy vision to economic growth. Without growth, the voice will not carry. A good conclusion line: India's new-order claim rests on three legs: economic weight, public goods and balanced diplomacy . Each leg needs further strength.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine India's role in shaping a multipolar world order." (typical) "India is emerging as the voice of the Global South. Critically evaluate." (typical) "Discuss India's approach to reforming global institutions." (typical) Structure: (1) context: shifting power; (2) India's principles: autonomy, multipolarity, reform; (3) tools: G20, VOGSS, BRICS, ISA, DPI; (4) reforms asked: UNSC, IMF, WTO; (5) critique: capacity gap, selective voice; (6) way forward. Quote one thinker (Zakaria or Acharya) and one 2023–26 event to earn marks.
Central Asia
The 'extended neighbourhood'

Central Asia (Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan) has energy, uranium, minerals and a position between Russia, China, Iran and Afghanistan. India has deep history here but no land access , because Pakistan and Afghanistan lie in between. UPSC asks about connectivity, SCO and rivalry with China.
Why it matters to India
Policy milestones

1991-92: ties with the five new republics after the USSR's breakup. 2012: Connect Central Asia policy (a four-C framework: commerce, connectivity, consular, community). July 2015: Modi visited all five in one tour. 2017: India became a full member of the SCO . 2019: first India-Central Asia Dialogue (Samarkand). January 2022: first India-Central Asia Summit (virtual); a summit mechanism was institutionalised.
Connectivity: INSTC and Chabahar

The International North-South Transport Corridor (2000; India, Iran, Russia) links Mumbai to Bandar Abbas and Russia via the Caspian. Chabahar (Iran) gives a sea route bypassing Pakistan: a 2016 trilateral agreement with Iran and Afghanistan, and a 10-year operating contract (2024). India also joined the Ashgabat Agreement (2018). Chabahar's future depends on US sanctions waivers and Iran's politics; its status in 2026 has been uncertain, so check.
Energy and TAPI

The TAPI pipeline (Turkmenistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan-India, about 1,800 km) has been stuck for years because of security and politics. India buys uranium from Kazakhstan (Kazatomprom contracts) for its nuclear plants. India has stakes in Kazakhstan's oil field Satpayev (ONGC Videsh) and seeks rare earths and critical minerals.
Security cooperation

Joint military exercises: Khanjar (Kyrgyzstan), Dustlik (Uzbekistan), Prabal and Kazind. Tajikistan's Ayni airbase (with India's help) and the Farkhor hospital base show strategic interest. India uses the SCO-RATS (Tashkent) for counter-terrorism. After the Taliban takeover of Kabul in 2021, Central Asian states and India share worry over extremism, and India's Delhi Regional Security Dialogue on Afghanistan (2018, 2021) included them.
Constraints

No direct access : Pakistan blocks transit; Afghanistan is unstable. China's footprint : Belt and Road, pipelines, investment, and the China-Central Asia mechanism. Russia remains the security patron (CSTO). Trade is small, below 2 billion US dollars a year; India's market is far. India declined to join BRI and the SCO's BRI statements.
Soft power and development

Bollywood, Hindi films, yoga and medicine are popular. India's tools: ITEC training, e-networks, an IT centre in each republic, lines of credit, and the proposed India-Central Asia Development Group and a Rare Earth Forum. The people-to-people links also include education: many Central Asian students study in India.
Mapping India's strategy

Policy summary: a multi-alignment approach, using the SCO, INSTC and Chabahar, plus bilateral energy and defence ties. It is part of India's 'Extended Neighbourhood' idea and balances against China without confrontation. Compare with the Look East / Act East policy, which is the east-facing equivalent. The India-Central Asia summit was meant to be held regularly.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine the importance of Central Asia in India's foreign policy." "What are the constraints on India's Connect Central Asia policy?" "How can INSTC and Chabahar help India reach Eurasia?" Structure: strategic importance, policy phases, connectivity, energy, security, constraints, way forward. The first India-Central Asia Summit was held in New Delhi in January 2012, the year India announced its Connect Central Asia policy.
Indian Ocean Islands
Small islands, large stakes

The Indian Ocean carries most of the world's oil trade. Islands such as the Maldives, Mauritius, Seychelles, Sri Lanka, Madagascar and the Comoros sit on its sea lanes. India's aim of being the 'first responder' and net security provider depends on them, and China is competing for the same ports.
India's frameworks
SAGAR was announced in Mauritius in March 2015; MAHASAGAR was announced during Modi's visit there in March 2025 (verify details).
Maldives

The Maldives lies on key sea lanes. India helped in Operation Cactus (1988) against a coup. Politics swing: 'India Out' campaign and the election of President Mohamed Muizzu (November 2023), who asked Indian military personnel to leave and tilted to China, then repaired ties with Indian aid, a currency swap and credit lines. Modi was guest at Maldivian Independence Day in July 2025. Note the pattern: elections change tone.
Mauritius and the Chagos question

Mauritius has a large Indian-origin population (about 70 per cent). India built an airstrip and jetty on Agalega island (inaugurated 2024). The CECPA (2021) was India's first trade pact with an African country. On Chagos , India backs Mauritius's sovereignty claim; a UK-Mauritius treaty (May 2025) transfers sovereignty while the US-UK base on Diego Garcia stays under a long lease.
Seychelles, Sri Lanka, Madagascar, Comoros

Seychelles : Assumption Island military facility plan stalled (2018); coast guard ships and radar help. Sri Lanka : 2022 crisis aid of about 4 billion US dollars; China's Hambantota port on a 99-year lease (2017). Madagascar and Comoros : listening posts, medical aid, and training. Joint: the Colombo Security Conclave (India, Sri Lanka, Maldives, Mauritius; others joined later).
Tools of engagement

Indian tools: the Navy's presence (Mission-based deployments), the Information Fusion Centre-IOR (Gurugram, 2018), coastal radar chains, HADR (relief after the 2004 tsunami, Operation Sagar Bandhu), lines of credit, Vaccine Maitri (2021), and support for the Indian Ocean Rim Association (IORA, 1997). India's Navy is the 'first responder' brand.
China's challenge

China has a base at Djibouti (2017), ports at Gwadar, Hambantota, Kyaukphyu, and research vessels visiting Sri Lanka and the Maldives. The 'string of pearls' theory sees a chain of Chinese-linked ports around India, though critics call it overstated, as many are commercial. Small states practise hedging : they play India, China and the US against each other for aid.
Strategic logic

The islands give surveillance, basing, and chokepoint access . Theory link: Mahan's sea power, Alfred Thayer; K.M. Panikkar's India and the Indian Ocean (1945) argued India's security depends on the ocean. Indian Ocean as 'Indian lake' is a Panikkar-era dream: the Navy now builds a blue-water capacity (INS Vikrant, 2022).
Way forward

Priorities: predictable economic assistance, avoid being seen as big brother, respect domestic politics, maintain HADR roles, deepen the Quad and French/Australian partnerships (Réunion, La Reunion), and help build capacity. UPSC angle: link to Neighbourhood First , SAGAR and the Indo-Pacific. In May 2019 the UN General Assembly backed a resolution asking the UK to end its administration of the Chagos Archipelago, and India voted in favour.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine the strategic importance of Indian Ocean island states for India." "How does Chagos dispute affect India's interests?" "Assess India's SAGAR doctrine." Structure: geography, frameworks, country cases, tools, China, constraints, way forward. The ICJ's advisory opinion of February 2019 held that the UK's separation of Chagos from Mauritius was unlawful and that the UK must end its administration as soon as possible.
Energy and Maritime Security
Fuel and the sea lanes

India imports about 85 per cent of its crude oil and roughly half its gas. Over 90 per cent of its trade by volume moves by sea. Disruption at a chokepoint would hit prices, growth and security alike, which makes energy and maritime security a central Paper II topic.
The energy picture
As of the 2020s, Russia became India's top crude supplier after 2022, which triggered US pressure and tariffs in 2025. India says its energy purchases serve consumer interest and its autonomy.
Energy security strategy

Diversify suppliers and routes. Strategic Petroleum Reserves (Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru, Padur; about 5.3 million tonnes). Overseas assets : ONGC Videsh in Russia (Sakhalin-1), Mozambique, Brazil. Cross-border pipelines (TAPI, IPI both stalled). Transition : solar (International Solar Alliance, 2015), green hydrogen mission (2023), nuclear targets, ethanol blending.
Chokepoints

India's oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz (about a fifth of world oil), Bab-el-Mandeb (Red Sea, Houthi attacks since late 2023) and Malacca . The Indian Navy's Operation Sankalp (2019 on) protects shipping in the Gulf of Oman and the Gulf of Aden, and it deployed ships in the Red Sea in 2023-24 after attacks. The Navy is also fighting piracy; the Maritime Anti-Piracy Act (2022) gave it legal powers.
Maritime doctrine and capability

The Indian Maritime Security Strategy (2015, 'Ensuring Secure Seas') and SAGAR set out the Navy's roles: deterrence, coastal security, HADR, and diplomacy. Assets: INS Vikrant (commissioned September 2022), INS Arihant SSBN, Project 75 submarines, Rafale-M. After 26/11 coastal security was reformed (Coastal Security Scheme, 2005; National Committee). India ratified UNCLOS in 1995.
Partnerships

The Quad (Malabar exercise), IPOI (2019), IMEC corridor (announced at the G20 in 2023), the Information Fusion Centre, 2+2 dialogues, logistics agreements (LEMOA 2016) and Colombo Security Conclave . India stresses a rule-based order and freedom of navigation, supporting the 2016 arbitral award on the South China Sea.
Tensions

Energy autonomy versus sanctions and tariffs from Western partners. Clean-energy targets versus coal dependence. A strong Navy needs funding (the Army and Air Force receive more). China's Indian Ocean presence and research ships. Blue economy and Sagarmala projects can harm coastal communities and the environment.
Blue economy

Maritime security includes fisheries, deep-sea mining (India's Deep Ocean Mission, 2021), ports (Sagarmala, 2015) and shipping. The Blue Economy policy aims to turn the ocean into a development resource, using ideas of sustainable use. This links energy, trade and security as one system. India's Strategic Petroleum Reserves are underground rock caverns at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur, which hold crude oil for emergencies.
Way forward

Priorities: expand reserves, speed up renewables and storage, build domestic shipbuilding, keep multi-vector supplies, and invest in maritime domain awareness. In answers, link energy to strategic autonomy and link the sea to the Indo-Pacific vision. Also tie to GS III energy and infrastructure. The Malabar naval exercise began as a bilateral US-India drill in 1992 and has since grown to include Japan, Australia and others.
How UPSC asks this

"Discuss the challenges to India's energy security and the measures taken." "Examine the role of the Indian Navy in securing the Indian Ocean region." "How do chokepoints affect India's maritime strategy?" Structure: dependence, strategy, chokepoints, doctrine, partnerships, tensions, blue economy, way forward. The Strait of Hormuz carries about a fifth of world oil trade, and the Strait of Malacca is one of the busiest shipping lanes linking India to East Asia.
G20, BRICS and SCO
India in the new clubs

As the old order loosens, India sits in many overlapping groupings. G20 (broad), BRICS (Global South and emerging economies) and the SCO (Eurasian security). They are frequent PYQ topics and they show India's multi-alignment . India hosted the G20 in 2023 under the theme 'One Earth, One Family, One Future', and its leaders' declaration was adopted by consensus. Both BRICS and the SCO include China and Russia, so India's membership balances Western and Eurasian partners.
The three at a glance
G20: roughly 80 per cent of world GDP and the bulk of trade.
G20 and India's 2023 presidency

The G20 started in 1999 after the Asian financial crisis; leaders' summits began in 2008 (Washington). India held the presidency from December 2022, with the theme 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam: One Earth, One Family, One Future' . At New Delhi (9-10 September 2023) the African Union became a permanent member, and a consensus declaration was reached despite Ukraine divisions. Other outcomes: IMEC, Global Biofuels Alliance, a push on digital public infrastructure. Later hosts: Brazil (2024), South Africa (Johannesburg, November 2025, the first in Africa; adopted a declaration despite a US boycott), and the US in 2026.
BRICS

BRIC was a Goldman Sachs term (2001); the first summit was in 2009 (Yekaterinburg); South Africa joined in 2010. The New Development Bank (2015, Shanghai) and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement support members. Expansion : Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE joined in January 2024; Indonesia in January 2025; a 'partner country' tier was added (for example Belarus, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Thailand, Uzbekistan). India holds the 2026 chair and hosted the 18th summit in New Delhi in September 2026 (check its outcomes). India stresses reform of global institutions, not an anti-West bloc, and opposes de-dollarisation as a goal.
SCO

The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation began in 2001, evolving from the 1996 Shanghai Five. India and Pakistan became full members in 2017 (Astana), Iran in 2023 and Belarus in 2024, making ten members. The Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS) sits in Tashkent. India presided in 2022-23. India declines to endorse the Belt and Road . At Tianjin (31 August to 1 September 2025) Modi attended and the declaration condemned the Pahalgam attack.
India's interests
Criticism and tensions

China-Russia pull : BRICS and SCO seen as counterweights to the West. India-China rivalry within both; India-Pakistan in the SCO. BRICS divisions on UNSC reform: Brazil and India want seats; China and others hold back. Is the G20 effective? Consensus is harder with Ukraine and Gaza. 'Global South' voice: the Voice of Global South Summits (2023-) and the AU seat show India's attempt at leadership.
Related minilaterals

Contrast with Quad , I2U2 (India, Israel, UAE, US), IBSA (India, Brazil, South Africa, 2003) and BIMSTEC . India's pattern: join many, lead where possible, avoid exclusive blocs. This supports strategic autonomy as in Jaishankar's phrase of 'multi-alignment'. I2U2 was launched in 2021 as a forum for India, Israel, the UAE and the US, with a focus on water, energy, transport, food security and space.
What to write

Frame in three lines: reformed multilateralism , Global South and strategic autonomy . Cite G20 2023 (AU entry), BRICS expansion, SCO's RATS and Tianjin. Add the caution that being in both Western and Eurasian groupings has costs. Bring recent updates, as these events change quickly.
How UPSC asks this

"Evaluate India's role in BRICS and the SCO." "What were the outcomes of India's G20 presidency?" "Does membership of China-led groups weaken India's strategic autonomy?" Structure: overview, G20 2023, BRICS expansion, SCO, India's interests, tensions, balance. BRICS added Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the UAE in January 2024, and this expansion is a useful example for judging India's strategic autonomy. India's G20 year (2023) also showed how a chair can set agendas on digital public goods and Global South concerns.
Diaspora and Soft Power
People and culture as foreign policy

India has the world's largest diaspora, over 30 million people, and a rich cultural brand. Both feed foreign policy: remittances, political influence, goodwill and knowledge. UPSC asks about diaspora policy and about soft power, often with examples. Pravasi Bharatiya Divas is held on 9 January each year, the day Gandhi returned to India from South Africa in 1915. Fiji and Mauritius have large Indian-origin populations from the indenture era, which shapes their politics and links to India.
Who is the diaspora?
Categories: NRI (Indian citizen abroad), PIO (person of Indian origin), OCI (overseas citizen of India; PIO merged into OCI in 2015).
Policy milestones

1983: Emigration Act (protection of workers). 2000-01: L.M. Singhvi High Level Committee . 2003: Pravasi Bharatiya Divas (9 January, in memory of Gandhi's return in 1915). 2004: Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs, merged into the MEA in 2016. 2005: OCI card. 2014+: Madad, e-Migrate, MADAD portal, PBD held every two years from 2015.
Economic and political weight

India is the top recipient of remittances: about 125 billion US dollars in 2023 (World Bank), over a tenth of global flows, largely from the US, UAE, UK, Saudi Arabia and Singapore. The diaspora drives investment and technology links. The Indian-American community helped win support for the India-US nuclear deal (2008) and holds high office (such as the vice-presidents in some states). In the UK, Singapore and Mauritius, Indian-origin leaders have headed governments.
Protecting citizens abroad

India's evacuations: Operation Raahat (Yemen, 2015), Vande Bharat Mission (2020, Covid), Operation Ganga (Ukraine, 2022), Operation Kaveri (Sudan, 2023), Operation Ajay (Israel, 2023). Issues: Gulf kafala labour system, wage theft, deaths, and trafficking. Remittance dependence makes Kerala, Punjab and Gulf links politically sensitive. Operation Raahat in 2015 evacuated thousands of Indian and foreign nationals from Yemen, and Qatar removed its exit permit rule for most workers in 2020.
Soft power

Joseph Nye (1990) defined soft power as getting what you want by attraction, not coercion, through culture, values and policies. India's assets: yoga (International Day of Yoga on 21 June, UNGA 2014, first marked 2015), Buddhism and Buddhist circuits, Ayurveda, Bollywood and cuisine, democracy and diversity, ICCR (1950), ITEC and development aid, millets (UN International Year of Millets, 2023), and the Gandhian brand.
Limits and risks

Soft power must be matched by policy credibility and human rights records. Diaspora activism can strain ties: Khalistan-linked groups, the 2023 Canada row after the Nijjar killing. Domestic social tensions and press freedom concerns affect India's image. Gulf workers are vulnerable; skilled migration causes 'brain drain' (or 'brain gain' by remittances and returns). Some diaspora groups carry domestic politics abroad.
Compare with others

China uses Confucius Institutes and the Belt and Road; the US uses universities, Hollywood and the dollar; Japan its 'Cool Japan'; Israel and Ireland engage diasporas intensively. India's special advantage: a large, educated, English-speaking diaspora and a plural cultural heritage. 'Diaspora diplomacy' is a Modi-era phrase.
Way forward

Priorities: safer migration and labour agreements, skill and language training, student protection, link the diaspora with investment (Start-up India), preserve culture in new generations, and promote culture through the Indian Council for Cultural Relations and 'Study in India'. For essays, argue that soft and hard power reinforce each other.
How UPSC asks this

"Examine the role of the Indian diaspora in India's foreign policy." "What is soft power? Assess the soft-power assets of India." "What challenges do Indian workers in the Gulf face and how has India responded?" Structure: definition, categories, policy, economic weight, protection, soft power, limits, way forward.
